hexagrams.image: 天行健，君子以自強不息。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 潛龍勿用。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 見龍在田，利見大人。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 君子終日乾乾，夕惕若，厲，无咎。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 或躍在淵，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 飛龍在天，利見大人。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 亢龍，有悔。

lines.label: 用九
lines.text: 見群龍无首，吉。

hexagrams.heading: 乾
hexagrams.name: 乾

wilhelm.name: Das Schöpferische
wilhelm.judgment: Das Schöpferische wirkt erhabenes Gelingen, fördernd durch Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Des Himmels Bewegung ist kraftvoll. So macht der Edle sich stark und unermüdlich.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Verdeckter Drache, handle nicht!
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Erscheinender Drache auf dem Feld. Fördernd ist es, den großen Mann zu sehen.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der Edle ist den ganzen Tag schöpferisch tätig. Des Abends noch ist er voll innerer Sorge. Gefahr. Kein Makel.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Schwankender Aufschwung über die Tiefe. Kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Fliegender Drache am Himmel. Fördernd ist es, den großen Mann zu sehen.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Hochmütiger Drache wird zu bereuen haben.
Wenn lauter Neunen erscheinen, bedeutet das: Es erscheint eine Schar von Drachen ohne Haupt. Heil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Khien
legge.judgment: Khien (represents) what is great and originating, penetrating, advantageous, correct and firm.
legge.image: Heaven, in its motion, (gives the idea of) strength. The superior man, in accordance with this, nerves himself to ceaseless activity.
lines: In the first (or lowest) line, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon lying hid (in the deep). It is not the time for active doing.
In the second line, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon appearing in the field. It will be advantageous to meet with the great man.

In the third line, undivided, (we see its subject as) the superior man active and vigilant all the day, and in the evening still careful and apprehensive. (The position is) dangerous, but there will be no mistake.
In the fourth line, undivided, (we see its subject as the dragon looking) as if he were leaping up, but still in the deep. There will be no mistake.
In the fifth line, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon on the wing in the sky. It will be advantageous to meet with the great man.
In the sixth (or topmost) line, undivided, (we see its subject as) the dragon exceeding the proper limits. There will be occasion for repentance.

(The lines of this hexagram are all strong and undivided, as appears from) the use of the number nine. If the host of dragons (thus) appearing were to divest themselves of their heads, there would be good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 57-58 (Image: Appendix II, p. 267)

en.name: The Creative
en.nameNote: 乾 is not the word for heaven (天) but for what heaven does: strong and untiring (說卦: 乾、健也). 孔穎達: the hexagram is called Qian, not Heaven, so that one takes after heaven's working, not its body. The name follows Wilhelm's "Das Schöpferische".
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: The words record a rite and its outcome. Neither bones nor bronzes write 亨; they write 享, presenting to an ancestor, and the bronzes are cast "用享" (集成 00018). In the Shang bones 貞 puts the question to the oracle (合集 00014), and 利 and 不利 are its answers (合集 36536). The day of the ancestral offering was itself chosen with the stalks (儀禮, 少牢饋食禮).
en.tradition: Great success. Favourable for holding firm to what is right.
en.image: Heaven moves on, strong. So the noble one makes himself strong and does not rest.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text, and moral in its own words. Both trigrams are heaven; 朱熹 reads the doubling as the sky going round today and again tomorrow, which only the utmost strength could do. In the inscriptions 君子 is a title of lords.

lines.text: A dragon under the water. Not to be used.
lines.note: In the Shang bones 勿用 is the negative of using a victim in sacrifice: "勿用羌", do not use Qiang captives (合集 00456). In the songs fish go under in the deep (鶴鳴, Mao 184). No Shang or Western Zhou source has a dragon under water; the first are the 左傳 (513 BC) and the 說文.

lines.text: The dragon shows itself in the field. Favourable to see the great man.
lines.note: A Shang bone makes a dragon at a field for rain: "其作龍于凡田，有雨" (合集 29990). 田 is also the king's hunt. 見 is used of the Dragon's stars appearing (國語, 周語中). In the songs the 大人 is the reader of dreams (斯干, Mao 189). The first 見 is xiàn, to show itself (陸德明).

lines.text: The nobleman strives the whole day through, and at evening is still on his guard. Danger. No blame.
lines.note: Morning and night is what a lord is charged with at his appointment (韓奕, Mao 261; 集成 02816). The Shang divined about the coming night (合集 12163). 咎 is harm sent by a spirit in the bones, and what Chu charges ask to be spared (包山 197). The line names a person: the third place is man's.

lines.text: Perhaps it leaps, there in the deep. No blame.
lines.note: The songs set this line's words for fish beside the next line's for birds: "鳶飛戾天，魚躍于淵" (旱麓, Mao 239). There 或 gives the other of two places. Nothing on the shelf has a dragon leap. 或 marks doubt (朱熹); the leap is made from the deep, the dragon's home (程頤), so there is no blame either way.

lines.text: A dragon flying in the sky. Favourable to see the great man.
lines.note: In the songs it is birds that fly up to the sky: "鴥彼飛隼，其飛戾天" (采芑, Mao 178). The fifth place is the ruler's. The 文言 glosses it: clouds follow the dragon, wind follows the tiger; the sage arises and all things look to him.

lines.text: A dragon gone too high. There is regret.
lines.note: 悔 is already a verdict in the Shang bones, mostly on hunts and journeys: "王其田弗悔" (合集 28563). In Zhou prose 亢 is to stand against, to hold up (左傳, 594 BC). The commentators read it as past the top and unable to come down (朱熹). 悔 is the mildest bad verdict (孔穎達). Height, not Wilhelm's arrogance.

lines.text: A host of dragons shows itself, none at the head. Auspicious.
lines.note: The 左傳 (513 BC) quotes it, naming it by the hexagram all six lines turn into: "其坤曰：見群龍無首，吉". One who casts Qian with all six lines changing reads this (朱熹). Every commentator reads it as strength that does not put itself first (王弼). Legge's "without heads" is what the characters can say, but no Chinese reader takes it so.

essays.title: The dragon
essays.text: Not the hoarding, fire-breathing beast of Europe, and not evil. The 說文 (c. AD 100) makes it chief of the scaled creatures, mounting the sky at the spring equinox and sinking into the deep at the autumn one: the words of the lines. In the 左傳 (513 BC) 蔡墨 says families once reared dragons for the kings, "龍，水物也", and quotes these lines, the oldest quotation of the hexagram we have. The commentators made it a figure for rising yang (馬融), mapped it onto the months (干寶) and onto the rise of Zhou. One thing does not fit: in the 說卦 the dragon belongs to thunder, 震, and Qian's animal is the horse.

essays.title: The six places
essays.text: A hexagram is read from the bottom, and by the time of the commentaries its six lines stood for earth, man and heaven, two lines each (孔穎達). This is why the dragon is in the deep and the field in lines one and two, why lines three and four speak of a person and of hesitation and name no dragon, and why it flies in line five. 干寶 gives the reason for the person: lest the dragons be thought to have nothing to do with human affairs.

readings.title: Four virtues or two statements?
readings.text: The 文言, 子夏傳, 孔穎達 and 程頤 read 元亨利貞 as four qualities: origin, success, benefit, constancy. 朱熹 reads a verdict in two parts. We print two parts: the same words run straight on into instructions elsewhere (屯), and 利 stands before what it favours throughout the book.

readings.title: An offering and a divination?
readings.text: Every commentator on our shelf reads success and steadfastness. We print the offering and the divination: the 說文 glosses 貞 as to ask by divination; the book writes the offering both 享 and 亨; and 貞 stands with every verdict, 貞吉, 貞凶, 貞厲, which as steadfastness needs explaining away. The Shang bones show 貞 putting the question.

readings.title: Who is the great man?
readings.text: 鄭玄: the second line profits by seeing the great man of the fifth. 王弼 and 孔穎達: the second line is itself the great man, and the world profits by seeing him. 朱熹: it depends on who asks. Our translation leaves it as open as the Chinese.

readings.title: Is the dragon the stars?
readings.text: 聞一多 proposed that the dragon is the Azure Dragon, the eastern mansions. We ran the sky of 1000 BC at dusk: hidden at the winter solstice, rising in the east at the spring equinox, across the sky in the fourth month, gone by the autumn equinox. The sequence fits, but that does not show the lines were written about stars.

readings.title: Danger, or as though in danger?
readings.text: 九三 can be cut 夕惕若，厲 (朱熹, the 文言, Wilhelm, Legge) or 夕惕若厲 (王弼). We print the first: the 文言, the oldest reading, takes 厲 as real danger, and 厲 and 无咎 stand as verdicts on their own throughout the book.

pinyinTones.name: Qián
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng, lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: tiān xíng jiàn, jūn zǐ yǐ zì qiáng bù xī.
lines: qián lóng wù yòng.
xiàn lóng zài tián, lì jiàn dà rén.
jūn zǐ zhōng rì qián qián, xī tì ruò, lì, wú jiù.
huò yuè zài yuān, wú jiù.
fēi lóng zài tiān, lì jiàn dà rén.
kàng lóng, yǒu huǐ.
xiàn qún lóng wú shǒu, jí.

pinyinNotes: 見: xiàn (shows itself) in 九二 and 用九, as 陸德明 ("見龍：賢遍反，示也", and the same for the 見龍 below); jiàn (to see) in 利見大人 ("利見：如字")

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨。利牝馬之貞。君子有攸往，先迷，後得主，利。西南得朋，東北喪朋。安貞吉。
hexagrams.image: 地勢坤。君子以厚德載物。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 履霜，堅冰至。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 直、方、大，不習无不利。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 含章，可貞。或從王事，无成有終。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 括囊，无咎无譽。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 黃裳，元吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 龍戰于野，其血玄黃。

lines.label: 用六
lines.text: 利永貞。

hexagrams.heading: 坤
hexagrams.name: 坤

wilhelm.name: Das Empfangende
wilhelm.judgment: Das Empfangende wirkt erhabenes Gelingen, fördernd durch die Beharrlichkeit einer Stute. Hat der Edle etwas zu unternehmen und will voraus, so geht er irre; doch folgt er nach, so findet er Leitung. Fördernd ist es, im Westen und Süden Freunde zu finden, im Osten und Norden der Freunde zu entraten. Ruhige Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
wilhelm.image: Der Zustand der Erde ist die empfangende Hingebung. So trägt der Edle weiträumigen Wesens die Außenwelt.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Tritt man auf Reif, so naht das feste Eis.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Gerade, rechtwinklig, groß. Ohne Absicht bleibt doch nichts ungefördert.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Verborgene Linien; man vermag beharrlich zu bleiben. Folgst du etwa eines Königs Diensten, so suche nicht Werke, aber vollende!
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Zugebundener Sack. Kein Makel; kein Lob.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Gelbes Untergewand bringt erhabenes Heil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Drachen kämpfen auf dem Anger. Ihr Blut ist schwarz und gelb.
Wenn lauter Sechsen erscheinen, bedeutet das: Fördernd ist dauernde Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Khwăn
legge.judgment: Khwăn (represents) what is great and originating, penetrating, advantageous, correct and having the firmness of a mare. When the superior man (here intended) has to make any movement, if he take the initiative, he will go astray; if he follow, he will find his (proper) lord. The advantageousness will be seen in his getting friends in the south-west, and losing friends in the north-east. If he rest in correctness and firmness, there will be good fortune.
legge.image: The (capacity and sustaining) power of the earth is what is denoted by Khwăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, with his large virtue supports (men and) things.
lines: In the first line, divided, (we see its subject) treading on hoarfrost. The strong ice will come (by and by).
The second line, divided, (shows the attribute of) being straight, square, and great. (Its operation), without repeated efforts, will be in every respect advantageous.

The third line, divided, (shows its subject) keeping his excellence under restraint, but firmly maintaining it. If he should have occasion to engage in the king’s service, though he will not claim the success (for himself), he will bring affairs to a good issue.
The fourth line, divided, (shows the symbol of) a sack tied up. There will be no ground for blame or for praise.
The fifth line, divided, (shows) the yellow lower garment. There will be great good fortune.
The sixth line, divided, (shows) dragons fighting in the wild. Their blood is purple and yellow.
(The lines of this hexagram are all weak and divided, as appears from) the use of the number six. If those (who are thus represented) be perpetually correct and firm, advantage will arise.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 59-61 (Image: Appendix II, p. 268)

en.name: The Receptive
en.nameNote: The word says what earth does: yielding, going along (說卦: 坤、順也), the earth from which all things get their nourishment. The graph is late, from a Warring States seal, and was also written 巛, the trigram's broken lines stood on end (陸德明). The name follows Wilhelm's "Das Empfangende".
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination for a mare. The nobleman has somewhere to go: at first he loses the way, later he finds a host. Favourable. To the southwest, friends are gained; to the northeast, friends are lost. The divination about safety: auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: In the Shang bones the sex of a victim is put to the oracle, "貞勿有牝，惟牡" (合集 06653), and so are horses brought in (合集 09177). Mares were a lord's wealth (定之方中, Mao 50). 主 is a traveller's host (左傳, 630 BC). The rest reads as the answer to a traveller's question; no early sentence pairs southwest and northeast.
en.tradition: Great success; favourable for the constancy of a mare; going first he goes astray, following he gains, and it is chiefly favourable; friends gained in the southwest, lost in the northeast; rest in being firm and right: auspicious.
en.image: The lie of the land: yielding. So the noble one, with ample virtue, bears up all things.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 王弼: the shape of the land is not level, but its lie goes along. As the earth carries everything on it, so the person who takes after it carries others. 朱熹: utterly yielding, utterly thick, there is nothing it does not bear.

lines.text: Treading on frost: hard ice is coming.
lines.note: Frost and ice belong to the farming year: "九月肅霜", in the ninth month the sharp frost (七月, Mao 154). Frost falls when a star of the Dragon appears (國語, 周語中). Frost underfoot is a sign read early. The 文言 makes it a law: a son who kills his father did not do it in a morning.

lines.text: Straight, square, great. Unpractised, yet nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: In divination 習 is to repeat it: "乃卜三龜，一習吉", three shells, all alike auspicious (尚書, 金縢); in the Chu records "習之" is a second diviner asking again (包山 223). Shaughnessy reads 直方 as a Shang phrase for inspecting the land. The earth was thought square. 王弼: left to itself the thing grows, untended the work is done.

lines.text: Holding its pattern within. It may be divined. If it follows the king's service: nothing accomplished, but an end reached.
lines.note: 王事 is the king's service, the levies and campaigns: "王事靡盬，不能蓺稷黍", the king's service has no end, we cannot plant the millet (鴇羽, Mao 121). The Shang asked the oracle whether a man would take it up (合集 00505). 章 is an emblem or woven figure. 程頤: the minister keeps his gifts dark and sees the matter through.

lines.text: A sack tied shut. No blame, no praise.
lines.note: Sacks are what provisions are tied in for a journey: "于橐于囊", in bags, in sacks (公劉, Mao 250). 譽 is praise at a lord's court (振鷺, Mao 278). A sack tied shut lets nothing out. 干寶: when heaven and earth close, the worthy hide; no blame, for nothing is risked; no praise, for nothing is done.

lines.text: A yellow skirt: greatly auspicious.
lines.note: The bronzes give skirts among the king's gifts (大盂鼎) but no yellow one; the songs do: "綠衣黃裳" (綠衣, Mao 27). The oldest reading is 南蒯's divination (左傳, 530 BC): he took it as greatly auspicious, and 子服惠伯 told him yellow, skirt and 元 each required loyalty, deference and goodness. His revolt failed.

lines.text: Dragons fight in the wilds. Their blood is dark and yellow.
lines.note: The 左傳 (513 BC) quotes it as one more sighting of dragons. 野 is beyond the fields, where horses graze and battles are fought (閟宮, Mao 300). 玄黃 is said of horses and dyed cloth (卷耳, Mao 3). The 文言: yin rivals yang and must fight; dark and yellow are heaven and earth mixed. 干寶 reads the battle of Muye.

lines.text: A favourable divination for the long run.
lines.note: A divination about a span of time is old: "恆吉", lastingly auspicious (尚書, 洛誥). The Chu records divine for a whole year and answer "恆貞吉", the divination for the long term: auspicious (包山 197), the same construction with 恆 for 永. It is read when all six lines change and 坤 becomes 乾.

essays.title: Earth, yielding
essays.text: The second hexagram is the first turned over: six broken lines for six whole. The judgment repeats the first one's opening words and then turns them to the mare. 干寶: nothing goes through the sky like the dragon, nothing goes over the earth like the horse. 王弼: the horse goes below, and a mare at that: the utmost of going along.

essays.title: The lines in their seasons
essays.text: 干寶 runs the six lines through the six months in which the nights lengthen, the fifth month to the tenth. The first line, frost underfoot, falls at the summer solstice, when the yin breath first stirs; the last falls at the beginning of winter, where the dragons fight.

readings.title: Where to cut 先迷後得主利?
readings.text: 先迷，後得主，利: astray, then finds a host; favourable. This is the 彖, the received 文言, Wilhelm and Legge. 程頤 and 朱熹 cut 先迷後得，主利, chiefly favourable, and 程頤 has to say a 利 dropped out of the 文言. We print the first: it is the wings' cut and needs no emendation.

readings.title: The mare's constancy, or a divination for a mare?
readings.text: Every commentator reads a quality of the mare. We print a divination made for a mare, by the rule for 貞. The construction 利 + whom + 之貞 recurs: 利幽人之貞, 利武人之貞.

readings.title: 朋: friends, or strings of cowries?
readings.text: In the Shang bones every 朋 is a count of cowries, and so are most in the Western Zhou bronzes, where friends are written 倗友. Yet every reader on the shelf gives friends, and the book has 朋 where companions are likelier. Ruled by context: here friends, with the cowrie reading recorded.

readings.title: Does 大 belong in 直方大?
readings.text: The small image and the 文言 gloss only 直 and 方, and some have taken 大 for an addition. Both transcriptions, 陸德明 and every commentator on the shelf have it. We keep it.

pinyinTones.name: Kūn
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng. lì pìn mǎ zhī zhēn. jūn zǐ yǒu yōu wǎng, xiān mí, hòu dé zhǔ, lì. xī nán dé péng, dōng běi sàng péng. ān zhēn jí.
pinyinTones.image: dì shì kūn. jūn zǐ yǐ hòu dé zài wù.
lines: lǚ shuāng, jiān bīng zhì.
zhí, fāng, dà, bù xí wú bù lì.
hán zhāng, kě zhēn. huò cóng wáng shì, wú chéng yǒu zhōng.
kuò náng, wú jiù wú yù.
huáng cháng, yuán jí.
lóng zhàn yú yě, qí xuè xuán huáng.
lì yǒng zhēn.

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨，利貞。勿用有攸往。利建侯。
hexagrams.image: 雲雷，屯。君子以經綸。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 磐桓。利居貞。利建侯。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 屯如邅如，乘馬班如。匪寇，婚媾。女子貞不字，十年乃字。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 即鹿無虞，惟入于林中，君子幾不如舍，往吝。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 乘馬班如，求婚媾。往吉，无不利。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 屯其膏，小貞吉，大貞凶。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 乘馬班如，泣血漣如。

hexagrams.heading: 屯
hexagrams.name: 屯

wilhelm.name: Die Anfangsschwierigkeit
wilhelm.judgment: Die Anfangsschwierigkeit wirkt erhabenes Gelingen. Fördernd durch Beharrlichkeit. Man soll nichts unternehmen. Fördernd ist es, Gehilfen einzusetzen.
wilhelm.image: Wolken und Donner: das Bild der Anfangsschwierigkeit. So wirkt der Edle entwirrend und ordnend.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Zögern und Hemmung. Fördernd ist es, beharrlich zu bleiben. Fördernd ist es, Gehilfen einzusetzen.

Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Schwierigkeiten türmen sich. Pferd und Wagen trennen sich. Nicht Räuber er ist, will freien zur Frist. Das Mädchen ist keusch, verspricht sich nicht. Zehn Jahre, dann verspricht sie sich.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Wer den Hirsch jagt ohne Förster, der verirrt sich nur im Wald. Der Edle versteht die Zeichen der Zeit und steht lieber ab. Weitermachen bringt Beschämung.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Pferd und Wagen trennen sich. Suche nach Vereinigung. Hingehen bringt Heil. Alles wirkt fördernd.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Schwierigkeiten im Segnen. Kleine Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil, große Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Pferd und Wagen trennen sich. Blutige Tränen ergießen sich.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kun
legge.judgment: Kun (indicates that in the case which it presupposes) there will be great progress and success, and the advantage will come from being correct and firm. (But) any movement in advance should not be (lightly) undertaken. There will be advantage in appointing feudal princes.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) clouds and (that representing) thunder form Kun. The superior man, in accordance with this, (adjusts his measures of government) as in sorting the threads of the warp and woof.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows the difficulty (its subject has) in advancing. It will be advantageous for him to abide correct and firm; advantageous (also) to be made a feudal ruler.

The second line, divided, shows (its subject) distressed and obliged to return; (even) the horses of her chariot (also) seem to be retreating. (But) not by a spoiler (is she assailed), but by one who seeks her to be his wife. The young lady maintains her firm correctness, and declines a union. After ten years she will be united, and have children.

The third line, divided, shows one following the deer without (the guidance of) the forester, and only finding himself in the midst of the forest. The superior man, acquainted with the secret risks, thinks it better to give up the chase. If he went forward, he would regret it.

The fourth line, divided, shows (its subject as a lady), the horses of whose chariot appear in retreat. She seeks, however, (the help of) him who seeks her to be his wife. Advance will be fortunate; all will turn out advantageously.

The fifth line, undivided, shows the difficulties in the way of (its subject’s) dispensing the rich favours that might be expected from him. With firmness and correctness there will be good fortune in small things; (even) with them in great things there will be evil.
The topmost line, divided, shows (its subject) with the horses of his chariot obliged to retreat, and weeping tears of blood in streams.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 62-63 (Image: Appendix II, p. 270)

en.name: Difficulty at the Beginning
en.nameNote: 屯 is read zhūn: difficulty, and fullness (陸德明). The graph is a picture: a sprout 屮 piercing the ground 一, its tail bent, coming up with difficulty (說文). 朱熹: out through the ground but not yet straightened. The held inscriptions use 屯 for a pair and for abundance, not difficulty.
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination. Not to be used for going anywhere. Favourable for setting up a lord.
en.judgmentNote: Setting up a lord was the Zhou king's act, with gifts of land and men, once after a divination: "王卜于宜 ... 遷侯于宜" (集成 04320). The songs use this verb: "建爾元子，俾侯于魯" (閟宮, Mao 300). Three Spring and Autumn divinations got 屯, each about gaining a state or a post (左傳, 661 and 535 BC; 國語, 晉語四).
en.tradition: Great success, favourable to be correct; only one should not hurry to go anywhere; whoever divines about setting up a ruler and gets this, it is auspicious.
en.image: Cloud and thunder: Difficulty at the Beginning. So the noble one sets up the warp and sorts the threads.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 經 is the warp on the loom, 綸 silk cord: before cloth is woven the warp is set and the threads ordered; before a state is ruled, the same. In Zhou texts 經 is laying out a site, often after a divination (尚書, 召誥).

lines.text: Circling, holding back. A favourable divination about staying. Favourable for setting up a lord.
lines.note: Both 左傳 divinations that got a changing line got this one. In 535 BC 史朝 read 利居 of an elder son who could not walk: the weak-footed one stays. The Chu records divine about where to stay: "居郢，尚毋有咎" (葛陵 乙四85). 磐桓 is circling, not going on (馬融). 王弼: the people look for a master in a time of trouble.

lines.text: Stuck, turning back; the team of horses pulls apart. Not raiders: a marriage. The divination for the girl: she does not conceive. In ten years, she conceives.
lines.note: A team of four was a king's gift (虢季子白盤). The groom fetches the bride with chariots and torches (儀禮, 士昏禮; 鵲巢, Mao 12), so riders who are not raiders come for a marriage. 字 is to rear or bear a child (說文; 左傳, 531 BC); 朱熹 reads betrothal. 班如 is pulling against each other, not going forward (子夏傳).

lines.text: Going after deer with no forester, one only goes into the middle of the forest. The nobleman is close; better to let it go. Going on: trouble.
lines.note: Deer hunts were put to the oracle with the 悔 verdict (合集 28350). The forester, 虞, was a Western Zhou office (逑盤), and in the 左傳 he comes to the hunt at his own sign (522 BC). Without him the hunter only gets lost among the trees. 幾 is read close; 鄭玄 read a crossbow trigger.

lines.text: The team of horses pulls apart. Seeking a marriage: going on, auspicious. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: A marriage came after a divination: "爾卜爾筮，體無咎言。以爾車來", you cracked the shell and cast the stalks; the form spoke no 咎; come with your chariot (氓, Mao 58). 婚媾 is the bond of houses joined by marriage (左傳, 712 BC). The same halted team, but now going is auspicious. 王弼: seek a union, and you will be received.

lines.text: Holding back its fat. The divination on a small matter: auspicious; on a great one: disaster.
lines.note: 膏 in the songs is what rain gives the crops: "陰雨膏之", the soaking rain fattens them (黍苗, Mao 227). The 周禮's great divination of a state is on setting up a ruler, the matter of this judgment. The ruler's line is sunk in danger and cannot give, so a small matter goes well, a great one badly.

lines.text: The team of horses pulls apart. Weeping blood, streaming.
lines.note: Both words are in the songs: "泣涕漣漣", tears running down and down, sung by a woman waiting for the man who would come with his chariot (氓, Mao 58); "鼠思泣血", grieving, weeping blood (雨無正, Mao 194). The halted horses a third time, and no way on. 王弼: nowhere to rest, nowhere to go.

essays.title: Thunder under water
essays.text: The lower trigram is 震, thunder and movement; the upper is 坎, water, the pit, danger, and as weather cloud and rain. 朱熹: moving in the midst of danger. The commentators put it in the twelfth month, when the thunder lies hidden in the ground and cannot yet come out (九家易), or when things sprout under the ground and have the ice to get through (崔憬).

essays.title: Horses, a bride, a hunt
essays.text: The lines are not abstract. Three have a team of horses that will not go forward; the second has riders taken for raiders who turn out to be a marriage, and a girl who does not bear a child for ten years; the third a hunter after deer without a guide; the fifth something held back; the top line weeping. 干寶 reads the whole hexagram as the turn from Shang to Zhou.

readings.title: 字: to conceive, or to be betrothed?
readings.text: The 說文 and 虞翻 read childbearing; 朱熹 reads betrothal, after the Rites, and Wilhelm follows him. We print childbearing: it is the oldest gloss on the shelf, and 朱熹's needs a ritual sense the line does not otherwise call for.

readings.title: A deer, or the foot of the mountain?
readings.text: 王肅 writes 即麓, the foot of the mountain, and 虞翻 takes 鹿 in that sense; then there is no deer. We print the deer, with the base text, 王弼, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge; the small image, chasing game, supports a hunt.

readings.title: Marriage by capture?
readings.text: Some modern readers see in riders who are "not raiders: a marriage" the memory of a bride taken by horsemen. No reader on our shelf says so. Recorded; the translation says only what the words say.

readings.title: 貞 as steadfastness?
readings.text: The commentators read 小貞吉，大貞凶 and 女子貞不字 as steadfastness, small and great, and the girl's chastity. We print the divination: the topic first, then the verdict.

pinyinTones.name: Zhūn
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng, lì zhēn. wù yòng yǒu yōu wǎng. lì jiàn hóu.
pinyinTones.image: yún léi, zhūn. jūn zǐ yǐ jīng lún.
lines: pán huán. lì jū zhēn. lì jiàn hóu.
zhūn rú zhān rú, shèng mǎ bān rú. fěi kòu, hūn gòu. nǚ zǐ zhēn bù zì, shí nián nǎi zì.
jí lù wú yú, wéi rù yú lín zhōng, jūn zǐ jī bù rú shě, wǎng lìn.
shèng mǎ bān rú, qiú hūn gòu. wǎng jí, wú bù lì.
zhūn qí gāo, xiǎo zhēn jí, dà zhēn xiōng.
shèng mǎ bān rú, qì xuè lián rú.

pinyinNotes: 屯: zhūn (difficulty), not tún, as 陸德明 ("張倫反，難也")
乘: shèng (a team of four), not chéng, as 陸德明 ("乘馬：繩證反，四馬曰乘"); the book reads 乘馬 as a team of four
幾: jī (close), as 陸德明's 又音機，近也, the book's choice; 徐邈 read qí, a particle
舍: shě (let go), as 徐邈 in 陸德明 ("徐音捨"); 陸德明's own 式夜反 (shè, to stop) is the other reading

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。匪我求童蒙，童蒙來求我。初筮告，再三瀆，瀆則不告。利貞。
hexagrams.image: 山下出泉，蒙。君子以果行育德。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 發蒙，利用刑人，用說桎梏，以往吝。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 苞蒙，吉。納婦吉。子克家。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 勿用取女，見金夫，不有躬。无攸利。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 困蒙，吝。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 童蒙，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 擊蒙，不利為寇，利禦寇。

hexagrams.heading: 蒙
hexagrams.name: 蒙

wilhelm.name: Die Jugendtorheit
wilhelm.judgment: Jugendtorheit hat Gelingen. Nicht ich suche den jungen Toren, der junge Tor sucht mich. Beim ersten Orakel gebe ich Auskunft. Fragt er zwei-, dreimal, so ist das Belästigung. Wenn er belästigt, so gebe ich keine Auskunft. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Unten am Berg kommt ein Quell hervor: das Bild der Jugend. So nährt der Edle durch gründliches Handeln seinen Charakter.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Um den Toren zu entwickeln, ist es fördernd, den Menschen in Zucht zu nehmen. Man soll die Fesseln abnehmen. So weitermachen bringt Beschämung.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Toren ertragen in Milde, bringt Heil. Die Frauen zu nehmen wissen, bringt Heil. Der Sohn ist dem Hauswesen gewachsen.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Nicht sollst Du ein Mädchen nehmen, das einen ehernen Mann sieht und sich nicht im Besitz behält. Nichts ist fördernd.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Beschränkte Jugendtorheit bringt Beschämung.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Kindliche Torheit bringt Heil.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Beim Bestrafen der Torheit ist es nicht fördernd, Übergriffe zu begehen. Fördernd ist nur, Übergriffe abzuwehren.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Măng
legge.judgment: Măng (indicates that in the case which it presupposes) there will be progress and success. I do not (go and) seek the youthful and inexperienced, but he comes and seeks me. When he shows (the sincerity that marks) the first recourse to divination, I instruct him. If he apply a second and third time, that is troublesome; and I do not instruct the troublesome. There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain, and beneath it that for a spring issuing forth form Măng. The superior man, in accordance with this, strives to be resolute in his conduct and nourishes his virtue.
lines: The first line, divided, (has respect to) the dispelling of ignorance. It will be advantageous to use punishment (for that purpose), and to remove the shackles (from the mind). But going on in that way (of punishment) will give occasion for regret.

The second line, undivided, (shows its subject) exercising forbearance with the ignorant, in which there will be good fortune; and admitting (even the goodness of women, which will also be fortunate. (He may be described also as) a son able to (sustain the burden of) his family.

The third line, divided, (seems to say) that one should not marry a woman whose emblem it might be, for that, when she sees a man of wealth, she will not keep her person from him, and in no wise will advantage come from her.
The fourth line, divided, (shows its subject as if) bound in chains of ignorance. There will be occasion for regret.
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject as a simple lad without experience. There will be good fortune.
In the topmost line, undivided, we see one smiting the ignorant (youth). But no advantage will come from doing him an injury. Advantage would come from warding off injury from him.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 64-66 (Image: Appendix II, p. 271)

en.name: Youthful Folly
en.nameNote: 蒙 is to cover (爾雅, 方言), and from that the covered state of a young thing or a mind: when a thing is born it is covered (序卦). 童蒙 is the young and unknowing. The Chu manuscript (c. 300 BC) writes 尨, a shaggy dog, a graph of like sound.
en.judgment: An offering. It is not I who seek the ignorant youth; the ignorant youth comes to seek me. The first casting is answered. A second and third profane it; profaned, it is not answered. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: Someone says "I": an oracle answering the young who come to ask. 筮 is the stalks, already in a Western Zhou bronze (集成 09714). How often one may ask was a live matter: Lu asked four times about the suburban sacrifice and was refused, "非禮也" (左傳, 629 BC). 瀆 is the word for profaning spirits and covenants (國語, 楚語下; 左傳, 516 BC).
en.tradition: From 亨 on these are the words of the reading. Who gets this hexagram has the way through. If the one who casts is clear-sighted, others should come to him and the way through is theirs; if he is in the dark, he should seek others and the way through is his; whoever answers should judge whether to answer, and whoever asks should ask with a single mind, and both the clear-sighted who nourish the ignorant and the ignorant who nourish themselves are favoured by being correct.
en.image: Below the mountain a spring comes out: Youthful Folly. So the noble one is resolute in what he does and rears his virtue.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 王弼: a spring come out under a mountain does not yet know where to go: the image of Meng. 果 is resolve (左傳, 607 BC); 育 is rearing young, which keeps the hexagram's play on the young.

lines.text: Uncovering the ignorant. Favourable to use in punishing people, to use in taking off fetters and manacles. Going on so: trouble.
lines.note: 刑人 in an early Zhou document is to punish people (尚書, 康誥). 桎梏 are fetters on the feet and manacles on the hands (陸德明); taking them off was a spring act in the 禮記, 月令. 發 with 矇 is lifting blindness. 王弼: the covering lifted, punishing and releasing are both apt, but punishing cannot be kept up.

lines.text: Wrapping the ignorant: auspicious. Taking in a wife: auspicious. A son able for the house.
lines.note: 納 is the word of the marriage rite's steps: bringing in the choice, the auspicious result, the pledge (儀禮, 士昏禮). The songs set 克 and 家 beside marriage: "匪斧不克 ... 匪媒不得" (伐柯, Mao 158). 苞 is to wrap (野有死麇, Mao 23). 王弼: the strong middle line wraps the youths in and does not refuse them.

lines.text: Not to be used for taking a wife: seeing a man of bronze, she does not keep her person. Nothing is favourable.
lines.note: In the Western Zhou 金 is bronze, a king's gift (利簋). 躬 is one's own person (谷風, Mao 35). The Chu slip has the same words. The man is strong (王弼), rich (程頤), or tempts with gold (朱熹); the English does not choose. 王弼: she sees a strong man and goes after him.

lines.text: Hemming in the ignorant: trouble.
lines.note: In the 左傳 困 is to be cornered: "困獸猶鬭", a cornered beast still fights (597 BC). The Chu slip has the same words. We read 困 as the verb, as 發, 苞 and 擊 are in the other lines; every commentator reads it as hemmed in by ignorance. 王弼: alone, far from the yang lines, in a darkness nobody lifts.

lines.text: The ignorant youth: auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip writes "僮尨，吉". In the songs 童 is a youth, or a beast not yet horned (抑, Mao 256). 王弼: a yin line in the ruler's place that hands the matter to the second line; without tiring its wits, the work is done. 荀爽: like King Cheng relying on the Dukes of Zhou and Shao.

lines.text: Striking the ignorant. Not favourable for being raiders; favourable for warding off raiders.
lines.note: In a Western Zhou bronze a raid on a man's grain brought a suit (集成 02838). In a 左傳 divination (563 BC) Lady Ding read the crack: "征者喪雄，禦寇之利也", the one who campaigns loses his hero; favourable to ward off raiders. The attack is not favourable, the defence is. 馬融 and 鄭玄 read 繫, to tie.

essays.title: Water under the mountain
essays.text: The lower trigram is 坎, water, the pit, danger; the upper 艮, the mountain, stopping. The 彖: danger under the mountain; danger, and a stop. 王弼: go back and one is caught in the danger, go forward and the mountain blocks: not knowing where to go is what Meng means. The Image sees the same figure as a spring under a mountain.

essays.title: An oracle that speaks
essays.text: The judgment is in the first person. Someone says "I", and says what happens when the young and unknowing come to ask: the first casting of the stalks is answered, a second and third are not. Legge sees it: an oracular response received by the party divining. The commentators turn the "I" into a teacher and the youth into his pupil, and the lines with it; 干寶 reads the young King Cheng under the Duke of Zhou.

readings.title: The ignorant, or a shaggy dog?
readings.text: The Chu manuscript writes 尨, a shaggy dog. Most take it as a graph of like sound; 大野裕司 argues the lines were about a dog, bound, struck, wrapped, a puppy. The youth who comes to ask the stalks cannot be a dog, and every reader has 蒙: we print the ignorant, and record the oldest witness.

readings.title: Punishing people, or a punished man?
readings.text: 刑人 is punishing people in 康誥 and in every commentator, a mutilated man in the 禮記. Shaughnessy: favourable to use a punished person. We print the first: the book's 利用 is followed by an act (利用享祀, 利用侵伐, 利用禦寇).

readings.title: Hemming in, or hemmed in?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 困蒙 as the subject stuck in ignorance. We print the verb, on the pattern of the hexagram's other lines, 發蒙, 苞蒙, 擊蒙. The English does not say who hems in whom.

readings.title: A son able for the house, or a son can marry?
readings.text: The commentators: a son equal to the household's affairs. Shaughnessy: a son can marry, beside the Fuyang slip's 利嫁. We print the house, with the commentators and the plain sense of 家.

readings.title: Comes to seek me?
readings.text: The base has 童蒙來求我; every commentator lacks 來, but 陸德明 knew a copy with it. We print the base's 來. It changes "seeks me" to "comes to seek me" and nothing else.

pinyinTones.name: Méng
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. fěi wǒ qiú tóng méng, tóng méng lái qiú wǒ. chū shì gào, zài sān dú, dú zé bù gào. lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: shān xià chū quán, méng. jūn zǐ yǐ guǒ xìng yù dé.
lines: fā méng, lì yòng xíng rén, yòng tuō zhì gù, yǐ wǎng lìn.
bāo méng, jí. nà fù jí. zǐ kè jiā.
wù yòng qǔ nǚ, jiàn jīn fū, bù yǒu gōng. wú yōu lì.
kùn méng, lìn.
tóng méng, jí.
jī méng, bù lì wéi kòu, lì yù kòu.

pinyinNotes: 行: xìng (conduct) in 果行, as 陸德明 ("果行：下孟反"); standard Mandarin now says xíng
說: tuō (to take off, 脫), not shuō, as 陸德明 ("用說：吐活反")

hexagrams.judgment: 有孚，光亨。貞吉。利涉大川。
hexagrams.image: 雲上於天，需。君子以飲食宴樂。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 需于郊，利用恆，无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 需于沙，小有言，終吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 需于泥，致寇至。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 需于血，出自穴。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 需于酒食，貞吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 入于穴，有不速之客三人來，敬之，終吉。

hexagrams.heading: 需
hexagrams.name: 需

wilhelm.name: Das Warten, (die Ernährung)
wilhelm.judgment: Das Warten. Wenn du wahrhaftig bist, so hast du Licht und Gelingen. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren.
wilhelm.image: Wolken steigen am Himmel auf: das Bild des Wartens. So isst und trinkt der Edle und ist heiter und guter Dinge.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Warten auf dem Anger. Fördernd ist es, im Dauernden zu bleiben. Kein Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Warten auf dem Sand. Es gibt ein wenig Gerede. Das Ende bringt Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Warten im Schlamm bewirkt das Kommen des Feindes.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Warten im Blut. Heraus aus dem Loch.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Warten bei Wein und Speise. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Man gerät in das Loch. Da kommen ungebetener Gäste drei. Ehre sie, so kommt am Ende Heil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hsü
legge.judgment: Hsü intimates that, with the sincerity which is declared in it, there will be brilliant success. With firmness there will be good fortune; and it will be advantageous to cross the great stream.
legge.image: (The trigram for) clouds ascending over that for the sky forms Hsü. The superior man, in accordance with this, eats and drinks, feasts and enjoys himself (as if there were nothing else to employ him).
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject waiting in the distant border. It will be well for him constantly to maintain (the purpose thus shown), in which case there will be no error.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject waiting on the sand (of the mountain stream). He will (suffer) the small (injury of) being spoken (against), but in the end there will be good fortune.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject in the mud (close by the stream). He thereby invites the approach of injury.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject waiting in (the place of) blood. But he will get out of the cavern.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject waiting amidst the appliances of a feast. Through his firmness and correctness there will be good fortune.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject entered into the cavern. (But) there are three guests coming, without being urged, (to his help). If he receive them respectfully, there will be good fortune in the end.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 67-68 (Image: Appendix II, pp. 272-273)

en.name: Waiting (Nourishment)
en.nameNote: 需 is to wait, to halt: the 說文 explains it as meeting rain and not going on, rain over 而. The 彖: "需，須也", to wait. The 序卦 gives another sense, the way of drinking and eating, nourishment, which is Wilhelm's bracket. The 歸藏 writes 溽, damp.
en.judgment: There is confirmation. A bright offering. The divination: auspicious. Favourable to ford the great river.
en.judgmentNote: In Shang divination 孚 is the result borne out: "茲孚。獲狐十又三", this was borne out: thirteen foxes caught (合集 37473, at second hand). An early Zhou document says it of turtle and stalks: "罔不是孚" (尚書, 君奭). Fording a river came after divination: "筮之，吉：涉河" (左傳, 645 BC). In the bronzes 光 is honour.
en.tradition: Xu is waiting: the strong meets danger and does not rush in: that is waiting. 孚 is good faith within. So one who divines, having something to wait for and good faith, will have bright success; if he is also correct, auspicious, and favourable to cross the great river.
en.image: Cloud rises up to heaven: Waiting. So the noble one drinks and eats, feasts and is glad.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. Cloud rising shows heaven about to rain, waiting its time to fall (孔穎達). 宴樂 is the court's word for feasting lords (左傳, 623 BC). 朱熹: in a matter one must wait for, only eat, drink, feast, and wait for it to come of itself.

lines.text: Waiting in the outskirts. Favourable to use for the long term. No blame.
lines.note: 郊 is the ground just outside the walls; beyond it pasture, wilds, forest (爾雅, 釋地). In the Chu records 恆 is the span asked about, "恆貞吉", the divination for the long term: auspicious. The Chu slip has the same words. Furthest from the danger, the line can hold back and wait (王弼). The commentators read 恆 as constancy.

lines.text: Waiting on the sand. There is a little talk. In the end, auspicious.
lines.note: Sand by water is a song's place: "鳧鷖在沙" (鳧鷖, Mao 248). 鄭玄 read 沚, an islet; the Chu slip has 沙. 王弼: closer to the danger, so the sand; not close enough to bring raiders, so only a little talk. 有言 is reproach (孔穎達), the least of injuries (程頤). Both phrases recur in the book.

lines.text: Waiting in the mud. It brings raiders on.
lines.note: Mud in the songs is where an exiled lord is left: "胡為乎泥中", why would we be here in the mud? (式微, Mao 36). 鄭玄 and 王肅 read 戎, war; the Chu slip has 寇. 王弼: strong and pressing on the danger, it calls up raiders; they come because I call them, and careful, one is not beaten.

lines.text: Waiting in blood. Coming out of the pit.
lines.note: 穴 is a pit: the Zhou ancestor's dug dwelling (緜, Mao 237) and the grave, "死則同穴" (大車, Mao 73). 血 can write 恤, anxiety, in a bronze (集成 04629), but the line's places ask for blood. 孔穎達: of fighting, the line is blood; of dwelling, the pit. 朱熹: though in a place of wounds, he gets out in the end.

lines.text: Waiting with wine and food. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: Wine and food are what the offering is made with and what the living eat after: "以為酒食，以享以祀", we make wine and food, to offer, to sacrifice (楚茨, Mao 209). The Chu slip has lost this line. 王弼: already in heaven's place, nothing more to wait for: so only wine and food. 于 here is with, not in.

lines.text: Going into the pit. There are guests not invited, three men, coming. Treat them with respect: in the end, auspicious.
lines.note: 速 is to invite: "以速諸父", to invite my father's kin (伐木, Mao 165). 王弼: when the danger ends the three yang lines come uncalled, and the one yin line, their host, must treat them with respect. 荀爽 reads rain going back into the earth. Legge declines a historical identity for the three: "I dare not be so confident".

essays.title: Heaven under water
essays.text: The lower trigram is 乾, strength; the upper 坎, water, the pit, danger. The 彖: the danger is in front; strong, and not falling in. 程頤: the strong must go forward, but it stands under the danger, which blocks it, so it waits and then goes. The Image takes 坎 as cloud, rain not yet fallen.

essays.title: Where one waits
essays.text: The lines name a place each, moving closer to the water: the outskirts, the sand, the mud, blood, wine and food, the pit. 王弼 reads the order as nearness to the danger. A court song has the same shape: 鳧鷖 (Mao 248), five stanzas, each opening with the ducks at a new place, on the Jing, on the sand, on the islet, and each going on to the wine and food of the offering. We note the likeness and build nothing on it.

readings.title: 孚: confirmation, good faith, or booty?
readings.text: The commentators, Wilhelm and Legge read good faith. The bronzes mostly use 孚 for 俘, booty or captives. 張玉金 and 王寧 read the diviner's word for an outcome borne out. Here "confirmation", on 君奭's "罔不是孚"; ruled by context book-wide: confirmation, trust, or captives and booty.

readings.title: Where to cut 光亨貞吉?
readings.text: The teachers in 陸德明 end at 光 and read 亨貞吉; 馬融 and 鄭玄 make one phrase. We keep the base's 有孚，光亨。貞吉: 亨 takes a word before it (元亨, 小亨), and 貞吉 is the book's most frequent verdict.

readings.title: 血: blood, or anxiety?
readings.text: 血 writes 恤 in a bronze, and the book pairs 血 with 惕 elsewhere. No reader on the shelf reads anxiety here, and the line's 穴 and the hexagram's places ask for a place. We print blood.

readings.title: Waiting, or nourishing?
readings.text: The 彖 and 雜卦 read waiting; the 序卦 nourishing; 鄭玄 read 秀; Shaughnessy calls the Chu graph "Suckling". The lines are all "waiting in ...", and the name is translated so.

pinyinTones.name: Xū
pinyinTones.judgment: yǒu fú, guāng hēng. zhēn jí. lì shè dà chuān.
pinyinTones.image: yún shàng yú tiān, xū. jūn zǐ yǐ yǐn shí yàn lè.
lines: xū yú jiāo, lì yòng héng, wú jiù.
xū yú shā, xiǎo yǒu yán, zhōng jí.
xū yú ní, zhì kòu zhì.
xū yú xuè, chū zì xué.
xū yú jiǔ shí, zhēn jí.
rù yú xué, yǒu bù sù zhī kè sān rén lái, jìng zhī, zhōng jí.

hexagrams.judgment: 有孚窒，惕，中吉，終凶。利見大人。不利涉大川。
hexagrams.image: 天與水違行，訟。君子以作事謀始。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 不永所事，小有言，終吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 不克訟，歸而逋，其邑人三百戶无眚。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 食舊德，貞厲，終吉。或從王事，无成。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 不克訟，復即命，渝。安貞吉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 訟，元吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 或錫之鞶帶，終朝三褫之。

hexagrams.heading: 訟
hexagrams.name: 訟

wilhelm.name: Der Streit
wilhelm.judgment: Der Streit: Du bist wahrhaftig und wirst gehemmt. Sorgliches Innehalten auf halbem Weg bringt Heil. Zu Ende führen bringt Unheil. Fördernd ist es, den großen Mann zu sehen. Nicht fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren.
wilhelm.image: Himmel und Wasser gehen einander entgegengesetzt: das Bild des Streites. So überlegt der Edle bei allen Geschäften, die er tut, den Anfang.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Wenn man die Sache nicht verewigt, so gibt es ein kleines Gerede. Am Ende kommt Heil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Man kann nicht streiten, kehrt heim und weicht aus. Die Menschen seiner Stadt, dreihundert Häuser, bleiben frei von Schuld.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Von alter Tugend sich nähren gibt Beharrlichkeit. Gefahr, am Ende kommt Heil. Folgst du etwa eines Königs Diensten, so suche nicht Werke.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Man kann nicht streiten, kehrt um und fügt sich dem Geschick, ändert sich und findet Frieden in Beharrlichkeit. Heil!
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Streiten vor ihm bringt erhabenes Heil.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Wenn einem etwa auch ein Ledergürtel verliehen wird, am Ende eines Morgens wird er ihm dreimal entrissen.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Sung
legge.judgment: Sung intimates how, though there is sincerity in one’s contention, he will yet meet with opposition and obstruction; but if he cherish an apprehensive caution, there will be good fortune, while, if he must prosecute the contention to the (bitter) end, there will be evil. It will be advantageous to see the great man; it will not be advantageous to cross the great stream.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) heaven and (that representing) water, moving away from each other, form Sung. The superior man, in accordance with this, in the transaction of affairs takes good counsel about his first steps.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject not perpetuating the matter about which (the contention is). He will suffer the small (injury) of being spoken against, but the end will be fortunate.

The second line, undivided, shows its subject unequal to the contention. If he retire and keep concealed (where) the inhabitants of his city are (only) three hundred families, he will fall into no mistake.

The third line, divided, shows its subject keeping in the old place assigned for his support, and firmly correct. Perilous as the position is, there will be good fortune in the end. Should he perchance engage in the king’s business, he will not (claim the merit of) achievement.

The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject unequal to the contention. He returns to (the study of Heaven’s) ordinances, changes (his wish to contend), and rests in being firm and correct. There will be good fortune.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject contending;—and with great good fortune.
The topmost line, undivided, shows how its subject may have the leathern belt conferred on him (by the sovereign), and thrice it shall be taken from him in a morning.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 69-70 (Image: Appendix II, p. 274)

en.name: Dispute
en.nameNote: 訟 is to contend before a judge, a lawsuit: "爭也，言之於公也", contending, saying it before the lord (陸德明); 鄭玄: disputing over goods. In the lines it is a suit won or lost, as in the Western Zhou bronzes. Wilhelm's "Streit" is the wider word, taken for the name.
en.judgment: There is confirmation, blocked; alarm. Midway, auspicious; in the end, disaster. Favourable to see the great man. Not favourable to ford the great river.
en.judgmentNote: In the Western Zhou bronzes 訟 is the lawsuit and hearing suits an office: the king charges Yu "敏諫罰訟" (大盂鼎). 尚書, 呂刑: "獄成而孚", the case decided and confirmed. In the 左傳 (563 BC) Wang Shu lost his suit at the king's court and fled. The great man here is naturally the one who hears suits.
en.tradition: A suit is contending and arguing: the figure has good faith that is blocked, fear, and the middle kept; the top line has the suit pushed to its end; the fifth has the great man; so one who divines will have a dispute, and auspicious or disastrous goes by where he stands in it.
en.image: Heaven and water go opposite ways: Dispute. So the noble one, in starting an undertaking, plans its beginning.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. Heaven turns from the west, water flows from the east (荀爽). 王弼: what is needed is that there be no suits, and that lies in planning at the start: unclear contracts are where suits come from.

lines.text: Not prolonging the matter. There is a little talk. In the end, auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has a different line: "不出御事", not going out to the 御事, the officers who manage affairs (尚書, 大誥). 永 is the span of time, as in 永貞. 王弼: at the start of a suit, which must not be carried to the end: so not prolonging the matter, and then auspicious. 有言 is the least of harms (程頤).

lines.text: Not winning the suit. Going back, and running away. His townspeople, three hundred households: no blight.
lines.note: Losing a suit and fleeing is in the 左傳 (563 BC). 逋 is to run away from one's lord (尚書, 大誥, 費誓). Towns and households were given and counted (集成 04320). 眚 is a film on the eye (說文), an ill omen (子夏傳). The Chu slip may read three or four households. 王弼: suing his superior, he does not win.

lines.text: Feeding on old favour. The divination: danger. In the end, auspicious. If following the king's service: nothing accomplished.
lines.note: 舊德 in the 左傳 is an old favour done (578 BC); a noble lived on what his forebears had been granted, and appointments renew a man in his forefathers' office (集成 02838). The Chu slip has the same words. 朱熹: 食 as in eating a town's revenue; one who divines should keep to what is usual and not go out.

lines.text: Not winning the suit. Going back to receive the command; a change. The divination about safety: auspicious.
lines.note: 即命 is the act of receiving a command at the Zhou court: "即令，王受作冊尹書", came forward to receive the command; the king handed over the written charge (集成 04240). 渝 is to change, above all to go back on a covenant (左傳, 711 BC). The commentators read 命 as right principle, or the former order changed.

lines.text: The suit: greatly auspicious.
lines.note: The judge's office: "訊訟罰", hearing suits and punishing (集成 04215). The Chu slip has the same words. 王弼: in the honoured place, master of the suit, deciding crooked and straight. 朱熹: one who gets this line with right on his side will have it upheld. The line does not say whether it is the judge's or the litigant's.

lines.text: Perhaps he is granted a leather belt: before the morning is out, it is stripped from him three times.
lines.note: Garments of office were the king's gift at an appointment (集成 02813). 鞶 is a man's leather belt (說文), and a lord's insignia show his rank by their number (左傳, 710 BC). 褫 is to take away clothing. 終朝 is dawn to the morning meal (馬融). 王弼: a gift won by a suit: how can the honour be kept?

essays.title: Heaven and water going apart
essays.text: The lower trigram is 坎, water, danger; the upper 乾, heaven, strength. The 彖: strong above, danger below; dangerous and strong: a suit. The Image: heaven and water go opposite ways. 荀爽: heaven turns from the west, water flows from the east. 程頤 adds a third reading, danger within and strength without, a person given to suits.

essays.title: A suit, from bringing to judgment
essays.text: The lines go through a suit: dropping the matter; losing and fleeing; keeping one's old portion; losing and going back to receive the command; the suit itself; a gift of investiture won and stripped away. 程頤 reads the judgment as the whole course of one: a suit is contending with another and waiting for someone to decide.

readings.title: Where does 其邑 go?
readings.text: The base and 王弼: he goes back and hides in his town; the people, three hundred households. 虞翻, 程頤, 朱熹 and the Chu slip: going back and running away; his townspeople, three hundred households. We print the second: 邑人 is a unit elsewhere in the book.

readings.title: 窒: blocked, or a feeling?
readings.text: The commentators read 窒塞, blocked. 鄭玄 read 咥, looking regretful, and the Chu manuscript writes 懥, with the heart. We print blocked, with the received graph; the others leave open two feelings, resentment and fear.

readings.title: A different first line?
readings.text: The Chu text has "不出御事", not going out to the managers of affairs, for 不永所事. It is older than any witness we print from. We print the received text and record the Chu reading.

readings.title: Receiving the command, or right principle?
readings.text: The commentators make 命 heaven's order or right principle (程頤, 朱熹), or the former command changed (王弼). The Western Zhou bronzes have 即命 as the court act of receiving an appointment. We print the court act; it fits the suit, and the top line's belt.

pinyinTones.name: Sòng
pinyinTones.judgment: yǒu fú zhì, tì, zhōng jí, zhōng xiōng. lì jiàn dà rén. bù lì shè dà chuān.
pinyinTones.image: tiān yǔ shuǐ wéi xíng, sòng. jūn zǐ yǐ zuò shì móu shǐ.
lines: bù yǒng suǒ shì, xiǎo yǒu yán, zhōng jí.
bù kè sòng, guī ér bū, qí yì rén sān bǎi hù wú shěng.
shí jiù dé, zhēn lì, zhōng jí. huò cóng wáng shì, wú chéng.
bù kè sòng, fù jí mìng, yú. ān zhēn jí.
sòng, yuán jí.
huò xī zhī pán dài, zhōng zhāo sān chǐ zhī.

pinyinNotes: 朝: zhāo (morning) in 終朝, as 馬融 in 陸德明 ("旦至食時為終朝")

hexagrams.image: 地中有水，師。君子以容民畜眾。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 師出以律，否臧，凶。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 在師中，吉，无咎。王三錫命。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 師或輿尸，凶。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 師左次，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 田有禽。利執言，无咎。長子帥師，弟子輿尸，貞凶。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 大君有命，開國承家，小人勿用。

hexagrams.heading: 師
hexagrams.name: 師

wilhelm.name: Das Heer
wilhelm.judgment: Das Heer braucht Beharrlichkeit und einen starken Mann. Heil ohne Makel.
wilhelm.image: Inmitten der Erde ist Wasser: das Bild des Heeres. So mehrt der Edle durch Weitherzigkeit gegen das Volk seine Massen.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Ein Heer muss ausziehen nach der Ordnung. Ist die nicht gut, droht Unheil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Inmitten des Heeres! Heil! Kein Makel! Der König verleiht dreifache Auszeichnung.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Das Heer führt etwa im Wagen Leichen. Unheil!
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Das Heer zieht sich zurück. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Im Feld ist ein Wild. Es ist fördernd, es zu fangen. Ohne Makel. Der Älteste führe das Heer. Der Jüngere fährt Leichen, da bringt Beharrlichkeit Unheil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Der große Fürst erlässt Befehle, gründet Staaten, belehnt Familien. Gemeine Menschen soll man nicht benützen.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Sze
legge.judgment: Sze indicates how, in the case which it supposes, with firmness and correctness, and (a leader of) age and experience, there will be good fortune and no error.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth and in the midst of it that representing water, form Sze. The superior man, in accordance with this, nourishes and educates the people, and collects (from among them) the multitudes (of the hosts).
lines: The first line, divided, shows the host going forth according to the rules (for such a movement). If these be not good, there will be evil.
The second line, undivided, shows (the leader) in the midst of the host. There will be good fortune and no error. The king has thrice conveyed to him the orders (of his favour).
The third line, divided, shows how the host may, possibly, have many inefficient leaders. There will be evil.
The fourth line, divided, shows the host in retreat. There is no error.

The fifth line, divided, shows birds in the fields, which it will be advantageous to seize (and destroy). In that case there will be no error. If the oldest son leads the host, and younger men (idly occupy offices assigned to them), however firm and correct he may be, there will be evil.

The topmost line, divided, shows the great ruler delivering his charges, (appointing some) to be rulers of states, and others to undertake the headship of clans; but small men should not be employed (in such positions).
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 71-72 (Image: Appendix II, p. 275)

en.name: The Army
en.nameNote: 師 is the army, the host in the field; the wings gloss it "眾也", the multitude. In the Western Zhou bronzes it is the standing army and its camp: "西六師、殷八師", the six armies of the west and the eight of Yin (集成 02834).
en.judgment: The divination: for the elder, auspicious. No blame.
en.judgmentNote: Armies were put to the oracle (左傳, 645 BC), and the songs keep the rites of war at home and in the field (皇矣, Mao 241). A late Western Zhou bronze tells how the king's armies were afraid and could not defeat E, until a man sent at their head took its lord (集成 02834). 丈人 is in no held Zhou text; the Chu slip has it.
en.tradition: Shi is the troops; the strong second line acts below, the yielding fifth trusts it from above: a ruler sending out a general. 丈人 is a name for an elder. In using an army it is favourable to be correct and to trust a seasoned man; then auspicious and without blame. He warns one who divines to do the same.
en.image: Within the earth there is water: The Army. So the noble one makes room for the people and gathers the multitude.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. The army was the farmers under arms: the seasonal hunts are war practice in the slack of farming (左傳, 718 BC). 朱熹: water is not outside the earth, troops are not outside the people; nourish the people, and one gets the multitude.

lines.text: The army goes out by the rules. Not good: disaster.
lines.note: The oldest reading is a council of war (左傳, 597 BC): "此師殆哉！", this army is in danger, quoting the line as a saying; carried through in order is 臧, against it 否. Jin was defeated. The Chu slip writes 不臧, not good. 王弼 reads: bad or good, both disaster, for success against orders is not pardoned.

lines.text: In the midst of the army: auspicious, no blame. The king three times grants a command.
lines.note: The king's command to a commander is the act of the bronzes: "王親令晉侯穌：率乃師", the king in person commanded Su: lead your army (晉侯穌編鐘). In the 左傳 命 is counted, and the third is the highest a minister holds (627 BC). 王弼: winning the states over, no gift is weightier, and the line receives the full command.

lines.text: The army perhaps carts corpses: disaster.
lines.note: 尸 in Zhou texts is the ancestor's Corpse at the offering, to preside, and the dead body (說文: laid out). 輿 in this book is a cart (小畜, 大畜, 剝). The Chu graph for 尸 has the element of death. 虞翻: corpses on the cart. 程頤 reads many in command, and Legge follows him.

lines.text: The army camps on the left: no blame.
lines.note: 次 is a camp of more than two nights: "過信為次" (左傳, 691 BC). The king's orders in the bronzes place armies left and right (班簋). The Chu slip has the same words. 王弼: in its place but unanswered, it cannot march but can stay. 程頤 and 朱熹 read retreat; the Chinese says the left.

lines.text: In the field there is game. Favourable to seize and question: no blame. The eldest son leads the army; the younger son carts corpses. The divination: disaster.
lines.note: 執訊, seizing men for questioning, is the formula of the Western Zhou war bronzes: "折首五百，執訊五十", five hundred heads cut off, fifty taken for questioning (虢季子白盤); and the songs, "執訊獲醜" (出車, Mao 168). Hunting and war were one practice. 禽 is game. The commentators read holding to one's words, or proclaiming the charge.

lines.text: The great lord has a command: opening states, receiving houses. Small men: not to be used.
lines.note: The Chu text reads 啟邦承家; 開國 is a Han substitution for the emperors' names (Shaughnessy). Land and people were granted after a war (大盂鼎). 大君 addresses the Zhou king (左傳, 552 BC). In the early Zhou 小人 is the common man, against the 君子 (尚書, 無逸). 程頤: small men with merit get gold and silk, never a state.

essays.title: Four hexagrams on a Western Zhou paddle
essays.text: A pottery paddle from a late Western Zhou kiln site near Chang'an has four groups of six numerals cut round its handle. Read odd as whole lines and even as broken, they are 師, 比, 小畜 and 履, the seventh to the tenth of the received order. 李學勤 argues that four real castings could not fall in exactly this order, so the paddle copies the sequence. Shaughnessy draws the limit: the sequence was there by the end of the Western Zhou, not necessarily the full text. The reports are not held.

essays.title: A campaign, from going out to the rewards
essays.text: The lines run through a campaign: the army goes out; the commander in its midst, and the king's commands; corpses carted; a camp; game in the fields, men taken, the elder son and the younger; the great lord's command after victory. 干寶 reads the Zhou conquest, with King Wu sharing the field with his men. 程頤 reads the duties of a ruler who sends a general out. The 雜卦: Bi is joy, Shi is grief.

readings.title: 丈人 or 大人?
readings.text: The 子夏傳 read 大人, and 李鼎祚 corrects the text to it: a king must be a great man. Every other witness has 丈人, and so does the Chu slip of c. 300 BC. We print 丈人, the elder.

readings.title: Rules, or pitch-pipes?
readings.text: The 左傳 and every commentator read 律 as the army's order. The 周禮 has the Music-Master listen to the army with the pipes and announce the verdict. The 周禮 is late and idealised, and the 左傳's reading is the oldest; we print the rules.

readings.title: Carting corpses, or many in command?
readings.text: 王弼, 虞翻, 朱熹: corpses on carts. 程頤 and Legge: many in command, and 尸 does mean to preside in the songs, the 左傳 and 大盂鼎. But 輿 is a cart in every other line of the book, and the Chu graph has the element of death. We print carts corpses.

readings.title: 利執言
readings.text: Hold to one's words (王弼); carry out his words (荀爽); proclaim the charge (程頤); seize them, 言 a particle (朱熹); grasp prisoners (Shaughnessy). We print seize and question, on the bronzes' 執訊 and the songs, with 毛傳 and 鄭玄.

pinyinTones.name: Shī
pinyinTones.judgment: zhēn zhàng rén jí, wú jiù.
pinyinTones.image: dì zhōng yǒu shuǐ, shī. jūn zǐ yǐ róng mín chù zhòng.
lines: shī chū yǐ lǜ, fǒu zāng, xiōng.
zài shī zhōng, jí, wú jiù. wáng sān xī mìng.
shī huò yú shī, xiōng.
shī zuǒ cì, wú jiù.
tián yǒu qín. lì zhí yán, wú jiù. zhǎng zǐ shuài shī, dì zǐ yú shī, zhēn xiōng.
dà jūn yǒu mìng, kāi guó chéng jiā, xiǎo rén wù yòng.

pinyinNotes: 畜: chù (to gather), as 陸德明 ("敕六反，聚也"); 王肅 read xù, to rear
否: fǒu (= 不, not), as 馬融, 鄭玄 and 王肅 in 陸德明 ("方有反") and the book's choice; 陸德明 himself reads bǐ ("音鄙，惡也")
長: zhǎng (eldest), as 陸德明 ("長子：丁丈反")

hexagrams.judgment: 吉。原筮元，永貞无咎。不寧方來，後夫凶。
hexagrams.image: 地上有水，比。先王以建萬國，親諸侯。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 有孚比之，无咎。有孚盈缶，終來，有它吉。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 比之自內，貞吉。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 比之匪人。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 外比之，貞吉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 顯比，王用三驅，失前禽，邑人不誡，吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 比之无首，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 比
hexagrams.name: 比

wilhelm.name: Das Zusammenhalten
wilhelm.judgment: Das Zusammenhalten bringt Heil. Ergründe das Orakel nochmals, ob du Erhabenheit, Dauer und Beharrlichkeit hast; dann ist kein Makel da. Die Unsicheren kommen allmählich herbei. Wer zu spät kommt, hat Unheil.
wilhelm.image: Auf der Erde ist Wasser: das Bild des Zusammenhaltens. So haben die Könige der Vorzeit die einzelnen Staaten als Lehen vergeben und mit den Lehnsfürsten freundlichen Verkehr gepflegt.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Halte wahr und treu zu ihm: das ist kein Makel. Wahrheit wie eine volle Tonschüssel: so kommt schließlich von außen her das Heil.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Halte zu ihm im Innern. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Du hältst zusammen mit Menschen, die nicht die rechten sind.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Auch äußerlich halte zu ihm. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.

Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Offenbarung des Zusammenhaltens. Der König lässt bei der Jagd nur von drei Seiten treiben und verzichtet auf das Wild, das vorne abbiegt. Die Bürger bedürfen nicht der Warnung. Heil!
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Er findet zum Zusammenhalten kein Haupt. Unheil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Pî
legge.judgment: Pî indicates that (under the conditions which it supposes) there is good fortune. But let (the principal party intended in it) re-examine himself, (as if) by divination, whether his virtue be great, unintermitting, and firm. If it be so, there will be no error. Those who have not rest will then come to him; and with those who are (too) late in coming it will be ill.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth, and over it (that representing) water, form Pî. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, established the various states and maintained an affectionate relation to their princes.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject seeking by his sincerity to win the attachment of his object. There will be no error. Let (the breast) be full of sincerity as an earthenware vessel is of its contents, and it will in the end bring other advantages.
In the second line, divided, we see the movement towards union and attachment proceeding from the inward (mind). With firm correctness there will be good fortune.
In the third line, divided, we see its subject seeking for union with such as ought not to be associated with.
In the fourth line, divided, we see its subject seeking for union with the one beyond himself. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.

The fifth line, undivided, affords the most illustrious instance of seeking union and attachment. (We seem to see in it) the king urging his pursuit of the game (only) in three directions, and allowing the escape of all the animals before him, while the people of his towns do not warn one another (to prevent it). There will be good fortune.
In the topmost line, divided, we see one seeking union and attachment without having taken the first step (to such an end). There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 73-75 (Image: Appendix II, p. 277)

en.name: Holding Together
en.nameNote: 比 is to stand side by side, to join, to ally with; the graph is two persons side by side. The 彖: "比，輔也", to support. In a Western Zhou bronze it is to march beside an ally: "以乃師左比毛父", with your army keep beside Mao Fu on the left (班簋).
en.judgment: Auspicious. The original casting: great. The divination for the long run: no blame. States not at peace come. The man who comes late: disaster.
en.judgmentNote: 原 is the source (說文); 干寶 takes it for one of the 周禮's three kinds of turtle crack. In the Western Zhou the king's task is to bring in the states that do not come to court: "率懷不庭方" (毛公鼎; 韓奕, Mao 261). Coming late was punished: Yu killed the chief of Fangfeng, who came late to Mount Kuaiji (國語, 魯語下).
en.tradition: Bi is joining and supporting: the fifth line, strong and correct at the top centre, with the five yin lines joining it: one man caring for ten thousand states, the four seas looking up to one man. Whoever gets this hexagram will be joined and supported by others; but he must cast again to examine himself, whether he has the virtues of the great, the lasting and the correct, before he can take on their coming without blame. Those not yet joined and uneasy will all come; whoever is slow and comes late, the bond is already made, he comes too late, and it is disaster.
en.image: On the earth there is water: Holding Together. So the former kings set up the ten thousand states and held the lords close.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. For the setting up of lords in the Western Zhou see 屯: "遷侯于宜" (集成 04320). The bronzes say 萬邦 where the Image says 萬國 (史牆盤). 朱熹: the 彖 means others come to join me; the Image, my going to join others.

lines.text: There is trust: joining them, no blame. There is booty, filling the jar. In the end it comes; there is something else: auspicious.
lines.note: 缶 is a clay pot for wine, beaten to keep time in song (說文; 宛丘, Mao 136). In the bronzes 孚 is most often booty, and bronze is taken as booty (集成 02734). 它 is the snake: people once greeted each other "no snake?" (說文). The Chu slip has 海 for 盈. 王弼 reads good faith in a plain vessel.

lines.text: Joining them from within. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "比之自內，吉", without 貞. Inner and outer are the two trigrams for the commentators; the shelf gives nothing older for them in a joining. 王弼: central and in its place, tied to its partner the fifth. 程頤: answering the call from above in the central way; rushing to join is losing oneself.

lines.text: Joining them: not one's own people.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the same words; 王肅's text added 凶. 匪 is not, as in 屯's 匪寇, and the same 匪人 opens 否. 王弼: near, it does not get on; far, it has no partner; all it joins are not its own. The small image: is it not hurtful? 朱熹: great disaster, which need not be said.

lines.text: Joining them from outside. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "外比之，亡不利", nothing is unfavourable, in place of 貞吉. An ally keeping beside another's army (班簋) is joining from outside. 王弼: it joins the fifth outside it and stands in its proper place; joining, it does not miss the worthy. The small image: joining the worthy outside, to follow the one above.

lines.text: An illustrious joining. The king uses three drives and loses the game in front. The townspeople are not warned: auspicious.
lines.note: The royal hunt had limits: the Son of Heaven does not close the ring (禮記, 王制, later). Game was driven from left and right to the king (吉日, Mao 180). 顯 is the bronzes' word of praise. 王弼: game coming towards one is let go, game running away is shot; the townspeople have nothing to fear.

lines.text: Joining them, none at the head: disaster.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "比亡首，凶". 无首 is the phrase of 乾 用九, where it is auspicious; here it is disaster. 王弼: at the end of the hexagram it is the man who comes late; the bond is made, there is no one to end with. 程頤 reads 首 as the beginning: there is no end without a beginning.

essays.title: Water on the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is 坤, earth; the upper 坎, water. 子夏傳: earth gets water and is soft, water gets earth and flows: the image of Bi. 程頤: of things close and without a gap, none is like water on the earth. The figure is the reverse of 師: one strong line, there in the second place, the general, here in the fifth, the ruler.

essays.title: Joining, and coming late
essays.text: The lines go through ways of joining: with trust, from within, with those who are not one's own, from outside, the king's illustrious joining, and joining with none at the head. The judgment adds those who come, and the one who comes late. 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤 and 朱熹 read the whole as subjects joining a ruler; 干寶 reads the Zhou founding the state at Luo by divination.

readings.title: 原筮: original, probed, repeated, or the turtle?
readings.text: 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤: 原 is to trace to the source. 朱熹: a second casting. 干寶: the turtle, the 周禮's 原兆. Shaughnessy: the first step of a two-step divination. We print "the original casting", on the 說文's sense and the book's 初筮.

readings.title: Where to cut 原筮元永貞?
readings.text: 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹 and the Chu slip as punctuated read 元永貞 together, great, lasting, correct. The base cuts after 元, here and in 萃 九五, and we keep its cut: a casting, and its result.

readings.title: 孚 in 有孚盈缶: good faith, or booty?
readings.text: The commentators read good faith filling a plain jar, a figure. The bronzes' 孚 is mostly booty, and bronze was taken as booty. Ruled by context: here "trust" in the first clause, "booty" in the second.

readings.title: 有它: something else, or harm?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 它 as other, what is outside. The 說文 makes it the snake, and "無它" the old greeting; then 有它吉 would be "there is harm: yet auspicious". We print something else, and record the other.

readings.title: Different verdicts in the Chu slip
readings.text: The Chu slip has "nothing is unfavourable" for 六四's 貞吉, and a 吉 in the judgment after 元永貞. Both are recorded; we print the received text.

pinyinTones.name: Bì
pinyinTones.judgment: jí. yuán shì yuán, yǒng zhēn wú jiù. bù níng fāng lái, hòu fū xiōng.
pinyinTones.image: dì shàng yǒu shuǐ, bì. xiān wáng yǐ jiàn wàn guó, qīn zhū hóu.
lines: yǒu fú bì zhī, wú jiù. yǒu fú yíng fǒu, zhōng lái, yǒu tā jí.
bì zhī zì nèi, zhēn jí.
bì zhī fěi rén.
wài bì zhī, zhēn jí.
xiǎn bì, wáng yòng sān qū, shī qián qín, yì rén bù jiè, jí.
bì zhī wú shǒu, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 比: bì (to join, hold together), as 陸德明 ("毗志反，卦內並同"), in the name and every line; 徐邈 read bǐ, today's common reading

hexagrams.image: 風行天上，小畜。君子以懿文德。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 復自道，何其咎，吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 牽復，吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 輿說輻。夫妻反目。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 有孚，血去惕出，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 有孚攣如，富以其鄰。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 既雨既處，尚德載。婦貞厲。月幾望，君子征凶。

hexagrams.heading: 小畜
hexagrams.name: 小畜

wilhelm.name: Des Kleinen Zähmungskraft
wilhelm.judgment: Des Kleinen Zähmungskraft hat Gelingen. Dichte Wolken, kein Regen von unserm westlichen Gebiet.
wilhelm.image: Der Wind fährt über den Himmel hin: das Bild der Zähmungskraft des Kleinen. So verfeinert der Edle die äußere Form seines Wesens.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Wiederkehr auf den Weg. Wie wäre das ein Makel! Heil!
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Lässt sich mitziehen zur Wiederkehr. Heil!
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Dem Wagen springen die Speichen ab. Mann und Frau verdrehen die Augen.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Bist du wahrhaftig, so schwindet Blut und weicht Angst. Kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Bist du wahrhaftig und treu verbunden, so bist du reich in deinem Nächsten.
