Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Es kommt zum Regen, es kommt zur Ruhe. Das ist der dauernden Wirkung des Charakters zu verdanken. Die Frau kommt durch Beharrlichkeit in Gefahr. Der Mond ist fast voll. Macht der Edle fort, so kommt Unheil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hsiâo Khû
legge.judgment: Hsiâo Khû indicates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and success. (We see) dense clouds, but no rain coming from our borders in the west.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the sky, and that representing wind moving above it, form Hsiâo Khû. The superior man, in accordance with this, adorns the outward manifestation of his virtue.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject returning and pursuing his own course. What mistake should he fall into? There will be good fortune.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject, by the attraction (of the former line), returning (to the proper course). There will be good fortune.
The third line, undivided, suggests the idea of a carriage, the strap beneath which has been removed, or of a husband and wife looking on each other with averted eyes.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject possessed of sincerity. The danger of bloodshed is thereby averted, and his (ground for) apprehension dismissed. There will be no mistake.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject possessed of sincerity, and drawing others to unite with him. Rich in resources, he employs his neighbours (in the same cause with himself).

The topmost line, undivided, shows how the rain has fallen, and the (onward progress) is stayed;—(so) must we value the full accumulation of the virtue (represented by the upper trigram). But a wife (exercising restraint), however firm and correct she may be, is in a position of peril, (and like) the moon approaching to the full. If the superior man prosecute his measures (in such circumstances), there will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 76-77 (Image: Appendix II, p. 278)

en.name: The Taming Power of the Small
en.nameNote: 畜 is to hold, to keep back, and to rear and store up (陸德明; 鄭玄 reads "to rear"). 程頤: to stop, and what is stopped gathers. 小 is small, set against 大畜, the great holding. The Qin 歸藏 writes 少督. The English renders Wilhelm's "Des Kleinen Zähmungskraft".
en.judgment: An offering. Dense clouds, no rain, from our western outskirts.
en.judgmentNote: Rain was put to the oracle by the Shang, and the songs wait for it: "其雨其雨？杲杲出日", let it rain! and the sun comes out blazing (伯兮, Mao 62). The western land is the Zhou's own name for its home (尚書, 牧誓), and a turtle divination warned of "大艱于西土", great hardship in the western land (大誥).
en.tradition: The yin holds the yang; one yin line, and the five yang above and below all held by it: so a small holding. The reading is getting through; but the holding is not complete and the benefit not yet given: hence dense clouds and no rain from our western outskirts. Dense cloud is a yin thing, the west a yin quarter; "we" is King Wen speaking, who expounded the Yi at Youli and looked towards Qi and Zhou in the west: just the time of small holding. Whoever casts this gets the reading as the image gives it.
en.image: Wind moves above heaven: The Taming Power of the Small. So the noble one makes fine his civil virtue.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 懿德 and 文德 are the songs' words: "矢其文德，洽此四國", he spreads his civil virtue and brings the four states into accord (江漢, Mao 262). 九家易: wind is heaven's command; above heaven, it has not yet come down.

lines.text: Returning from the road: what blame is there? Auspicious.
lines.note: 道 is a road, as in the songs' "周道如砥", the Zhou road smooth as a whetstone (大東, Mao 203). Going and coming back was put to the oracle by the Shang. 何其咎 is the book's own question (隨 九四). 王弼: the yang rises to the yin and returns by its own way; what blame could it incur?

lines.text: Led back: auspicious.
lines.note: 牽 is to lead by a rope: "象引牛之縻也", the ox's halter (說文); in a 左傳 saying a man leads his ox across another's field and loses it (598 BC). 王弼: the fifth does not hold it fast, so it can be led back. 程頤: second and fifth draw each other along. Who leads is not said.

lines.text: The cart sheds its spokes. Husband and wife turn their eyes away.
lines.note: A 左傳 stalk-casting (645 BC) on marrying a Jin princess to Qin had the verse "車說其輹，火焚其旗，不利行師", the cart sheds its axle block, fire burns its banners: not favourable to move the army. Jin was defeated by Qin. 說 is 脫, to come off. 王弼: held by the growing yin, unable to return, like husband and wife turning their eyes away.

lines.text: There is confirmation: the anxiety goes, the alarm departs. No blame.
lines.note: 馬融 reads this 血 as 恤, anxiety, and a bronze writes 恤 with the graph 血 (集成 04629). 血 stands beside 惕, fear, two feelings that go together, as again in 渙 上九. 恤 is the songs' anxiety (谷風, Mao 35). The commentators read blood: 王弼, the yang attacks the yin, but the fourth is not harmed.

lines.text: There is confirmation, bound together: rich with one's neighbours.
lines.note: The songs' neighbours: "洽比其鄰，昏姻孔云", he joins close with his neighbours, and his in-laws are many (正月, Mao 192). The book has 不富以其鄰 twice (泰, 謙). 攣 is joined (馬融). 王弼: full, and not keeping it to itself. 程頤: like a rich man who shares his wealth with his neighbours. 朱熹: able to direct them.

lines.text: It has rained, it has stopped: still favour is loaded. The divination for a wife: danger. The moon is almost full. The nobleman campaigning: disaster.
lines.note: The bronzes date events by the moon's phases: "二月既望", second month, after the full moon (晉侯穌編鐘). 望 is the full moon, 幾望 near it. 征 is a campaign. The songs: the moon in the Net stars brings pouring rain, and soldiers march east (漸漸之石, Mao 232). 王弼: a wife ruling her husband; full and going on, there will be war.

essays.title: Wind above heaven
essays.text: The lower trigram is 乾, heaven, strength; the upper 巽, wind, yielding. One yin line, the fourth, among five yang. The 彖: the soft has its place and those above and below answer it. 程頤: one yin holding five yang can tie them but not hold them fast; so the holding is small.

essays.title: Cloud without rain
essays.text: The judgment's cloud that does not rain runs through the lines: a return, a cart that will not go, and at the end it has rained and stopped. 王弼: the 彖 speaks of the whole figure, hence cloud without rain; the lines each of their own, hence, at the top, the rain. The same words open 小過 六五.

readings.title: Holding back, or rearing?
readings.text: 畜 as restraining (程頤, 王弼; Wilhelm; Legge "small restraint"), storing up (陸德明), or rearing (鄭玄; Shaughnessy "Lesser Livestock"). The lines speak of holding back, the cart and the rain, and the name is Wilhelm's.

readings.title: Spokes, or axle block?
readings.text: The base, 王弼, 程頤 and 朱熹 have 輻, spokes. Another copy, 馬融 and 鄭玄 have 輹, the axle block, as do the 左傳's verse and 大畜 九二; spokes do not come off as an axle block does. We print the base's 輻; the stronger case is 輹.

readings.title: Blood, or anxiety?
readings.text: We read 血 as 恤, anxiety, with 馬融, on the bronze loan and the pairing with 惕. 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge read blood: the blood goes, the alarm departs.

readings.title: Whose western outskirts?
readings.text: 荀爽 and 朱熹 make "our" King Wen's, and Legge the house of Zhou's. The text says only "our". 大誥 shows the Zhou calling their home the western land; whether the line was written of it is not shown.

readings.title: 尚德載
readings.text: The commentators: it honours virtue, piled up to a load. Wikisource's 得: still it can be loaded. We print 德 with the sense of 訟's 舊德, a favour held: still favour is loaded. The line is obscure, and the English is literal.

pinyinTones.name: Xiǎo Chù
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. mì yún bù yǔ, zì wǒ xī jiāo.
pinyinTones.image: fēng xíng tiān shàng, xiǎo chù. jūn zǐ yǐ yì wén dé.
lines: fù zì dào, hé qí jiù, jí.
qiān fù, jí.
yú tuō fú. fū qī fǎn mù.
yǒu fú, xuè qù tì chū, wú jiù.
yǒu fú luán rú, fù yǐ qí lín.
jì yǔ jì chǔ, shàng dé zài. fù zhēn lì. yuè jī wàng, jūn zǐ zhēng xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 畜: chù (to hold, gather), as 陸德明 ("敕六反，積也，聚也"), so the name is Xiǎo Chù; 鄭玄 read xù ("許六反，養也"), to rear
說: tuō (to come off, 脫), not shuō, as 陸德明 ("車說：吐活反")
幾: jī (near) in 月幾望, as 陸德明's 又音機 and 子夏傳's 近; 徐邈 read qí
處: chǔ (to rest, stop)

hexagrams.image: 上天下澤，履。君子以辯上下，定民志。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 素履往，无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 履道坦坦，幽人貞吉。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 眇能視，跛能履，履虎尾，咥人，凶。武人為于大君。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 履虎尾，愬愬，終吉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 夬履，貞厲。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 視履考祥，其旋，元吉。

hexagrams.heading: 履
hexagrams.name: 履

wilhelm.name: Das Auftreten
wilhelm.judgment: Auftreten auf des Tigers Schwanz. Er beißt den Menschen nicht. Gelingen.
wilhelm.image: Oben der Himmel, unten der See: das Bild des Auftretens. So unterscheidet der Edle hoch und niedrig und festigt dadurch den Sinn des Volkes.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Einfaches Auftreten. Fortschreiten ohne Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Auftreten auf schlichter, ebener Bahn. Eines dunklen Mannes Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.

Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Ein Einäugiger kann sehen, ein Lahmer kann auftreten. Er tritt auf des Tigers Schwanz. Der beißt den Menschen. Unheil! Ein Krieger handelt so für seinen großen Fürsten.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er tritt auf des Tigers Schwanz. Vorsicht und Behutsamkeit führt endlich zum Heil.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Entschlossenes Auftreten. Beharrlichkeit bei Bewusstsein der Gefahr.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Blicke auf dein Auftreten und prüfe die günstigen Zeichen. Ist alles vollkommen, so kommt erhabenes Heil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Lî
legge.judgment: (Lî suggests the idea of) one treading on the tail of a tiger, which does not bite him. There will be progress and success.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the sky above, and below it (that representing the waters of) a marsh, form Lî. The superior man, in accordance with this, discriminates between high and low, and gives settlement to the aims of the people.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject treading his accustomed path. If he go forward, there will be no error.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject treading the path that is level and easy;—a quiet and solitary man, to whom, if he be firm and correct, there will be good fortune.

The third line, divided, shows a one-eyed man (who thinks he) can see; a lame man (who thinks he) can walk well; one who treads on the tail of a tiger and is bitten. (All this indicates) ill fortune. We have a (mere) bravo acting the part of a great ruler.
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject treading on the tail of a tiger. He becomes full of apprehensive caution, and in the end there will be good fortune.
The fifth line, undivided, shows the resolute tread of its subject. Though he be firm and correct, there will be peril.
The sixth line, undivided, tells us to look at (the whole course) that is trodden, and examine the presage which that gives. If it be complete and without failure, there will be great good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 78-80 (Image: Appendix II, p. 280)

en.name: Treading
en.nameNote: 履 is to tread, and the shoe one treads in: "足所依也", what the foot rests on (說文). In the 左傳 it is the ground a lord was given to walk (656 BC). The 序卦 makes it the rites; the Mawangdui manuscript writes 禮. In the lines it is treading.
en.judgment: Treading on the tiger's tail: it does not bite the man. An offering.
en.judgmentNote: The songs make tackling a tiger the type of rash courage: "不敢暴虎，不敢馮河", none dare take a tiger barehanded, none dare wade the River, and then "如履薄冰", as if treading thin ice (小旻, Mao 195). The bronzes have the king's tiger guards. The saying in 尚書, 君牙 is a fourth-century AD forgery.
en.tradition: 履 is stepping on something as one goes forward; the lake meets heaven, gladly treading behind the hard and strong: the image of treading on a tiger's tail and not being hurt; so the hexagram is Treading, and the reading is so. Whoever can be like this will be in danger and not be hurt.
en.image: Heaven above, the lake below: Treading. So the noble one tells apart above and below and settles the people's minds.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. A song sets nobleman and small men on one road: "君子所履，小人所視", the nobleman treads it, the small men look on (大東, Mao 203). 程頤: when the ranks of above and below are clear, the people's minds are settled.

lines.text: Plain treading, going on: no blame.
lines.note: 素 is undyed silk, white, plain: "素絲五紽" (羔羊, Mao 18), and the white cap of mourning (素冠, Mao 147). 王弼: the way of treading hates show, so plain is without blame. 荀爽: the commoner not yet in office, practising the rites alone. The English keeps the verb, so the word means one thing through the six lines.

lines.text: The road trodden is level, level. The divination for the hidden man: auspicious.
lines.note: The road: "周道如砥，其直如矢。君子所履" (大東, Mao 203). 坦坦 is level, at ease. 幽 is dark, deep, hidden: a bird comes out of the dark valley (伐木, Mao 165). 虞翻 makes the hidden man a prisoner; the commentators a recluse: 王弼, in the dark and correct, it is fitting that it be auspicious.

lines.text: The one-eyed can see, the lame can tread: treading on the tiger's tail, it bites the man: disaster. A warrior acts for the great lord.
lines.note: 眇 is a small or blind eye, 跛 a lame foot (陸德明). 武人 in the songs is the soldier on campaign: "武人東征" (漸漸之石, Mao 232). 王弼: seeing so is one-eyed seeing, walking so lame walking, treading danger so, being bitten. 朱熹: a martial man running wild, like the First Emperor or Xiang Yu: how could it last?

lines.text: Treading on the tiger's tail, in terror. In the end, auspicious.
lines.note: 愬愬 is "恐懼貌", the look of terror (子夏傳); 馬融's text had 虩虩, the book's word for the thunder's terror in 震. 王弼: pressing close to the highest, in a place of many fears; but yang in a yin place, humility its root, it gets its wish in the end. 程頤: if one can fear, it will end well.

lines.text: Resolute treading. The divination: danger.
lines.note: 夬 is the name of hexagram 43, glossed "決也", to cut through, to decide (雜卦; 干寶). The shelf has nothing older for 夬履. 王弼: honoured and deciding by strength; the way of treading hates fullness, and the fifth is full: so danger. 程頤: trusting one's own strength and going on regardless is a way of danger.

lines.text: Watch the treading, examine the omens. Its turning back: greatly auspicious.
lines.note: 祥 is an omen, good or bad: when six fish-hawks flew backwards over Song, the duke asked "是何祥也？吉凶焉在", what omen is this? (左傳, 644 BC). The line names an act of divination: looking at the treading and reading the signs in it. 王弼: the omens of fortune come from what one treads. 程頤 reads 旋 as coming full circle.

essays.title: Heaven above the lake
essays.text: The lower trigram is 兌, the lake, gladness; the upper 乾, heaven, strength. One yin line, the third. The 彖: the soft treads on the hard; glad, and answering the strong. 朱熹: the lake meets heaven, gladly treading behind the hard and strong. 虞翻 rejects the scholars who take 兌 for the tiger.

essays.title: The tiger's tail
essays.text: The tiger's tail is trodden on three times: in the judgment it does not bite; in 六三 it bites; in 九四 the one who treads is terrified, and it ends well. The other lines tread the road: plain, level, resolute, and at the top watched and read for omens.

readings.title: To bite, or to laugh?
readings.text: Every reader on the shelf reads 咥 as to bite. The songs use the graph for laughing ("咥其笑矣", 氓). A tiger that does not laugh at the man would be a strange sentence; we print bite, and record the other sense.

readings.title: The hidden man: hermit, prisoner, or somber man?
readings.text: The commentators make 幽人 a recluse; 虞翻 a man in prison; Shaughnessy a somber person. We print "the hidden man", and the line does not say which.

readings.title: Acts for, or becomes, the great lord?
readings.text: Wilhelm: a warrior acts for his great lord. 程頤 and Legge: a bravo acting the part of a great ruler, reading 為 as to be. We print "acts for".

readings.title: Omens, or in detail?
readings.text: The base, 王弼, 虞翻, 程頤 and 朱熹 have 考祥, examine the omens; a copy known to 陸德明 and Wikisource have 考詳, examine in detail. We print the omens.

pinyinTones.name: Lǚ
pinyinTones.judgment: lǚ hǔ wěi, bù dié rén. hēng.
pinyinTones.image: shàng tiān xià zé, lǚ. jūn zǐ yǐ biàn shàng xià, dìng mín zhì.
lines: sù lǚ wǎng, wú jiù.
lǚ dào tǎn tǎn, yōu rén zhēn jí.
miǎo néng shì, bǒ néng lǚ, lǚ hǔ wěi, dié rén, xiōng. wǔ rén wéi yú dà jūn.
lǚ hǔ wěi, sè sè, zhōng jí.
guài lǚ, zhēn lì.
shì lǚ kǎo xiáng, qí xuán, yuán jí.

pinyinNotes: 咥: dié (to bite), not xì, as 陸德明 ("直結反，齧也")
愬: sè (fearful), not sù, as 陸德明 ("山革反", 子夏傳: 恐懼貌)

hexagrams.image: 天地交，泰。后以財成天地之道，輔相天地之宜，以左右民。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 拔茅茹以其彙。征吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 苞荒，用馮河，不遐遺。朋亡，得尚于中行。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 无平不陂，无往不復。艱貞，无咎。勿恤其孚，于食有福。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 翩翩，不富以其鄰，不戒以孚。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 帝乙歸妹，以祉，元吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 城復于隍，勿用師，自邑告命，貞吝。

hexagrams.heading: 泰
hexagrams.name: 泰

wilhelm.name: Der Friede
wilhelm.judgment: Der Friede. Das Kleine geht hin, das Große kommt her. Heil! Gelingen!
wilhelm.image: Himmel und Erde vereinigen sich: das Bild des Friedens. So teilt und vollendet der Herrscher den Lauf von Himmel und Erde, verwaltet und ordnet die Gaben von Himmel und Erde und steht so dem Volke bei.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Zieht man Bandgras aus, so geht der Rasen mit. Jeder nach seiner Art. Unternehmungen bringen Heil.

Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Ungebildeten in Milde tragen, entschlossen den Fluss durchschreiten, das Ferne nicht vernachlässigen, die Genossen nicht berücksichtigen: so mag man es fertigbringen, in der Mitte zu wandeln.

Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Keine Ebene, auf die nicht ein Abhang folgt, kein Hingang, auf den nicht die Wiederkehr folgt. Ohne Makel ist, wer beharrlich bleibt in Gefahr. Beklage dich nicht über diese Wahrheit, genieße das Glück, das du noch hast.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er flattert hernieder, nicht pochend auf Reichtum, zusammen mit seinem Nächsten, arglos und wahrhaftig.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der Herrscher I gibt seine Tochter in die Ehe. Das bringt Segen und erhabenes Heil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Der Wall fällt wieder in den Graben. Jetzt brauche keine Heere. In der eigenen Stadt verkünde deine Befehle. Beharrlichkeit bringt Beschämung.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Thâi
legge.judgment: In Thâi (we see) the little gone and the great come. (It indicates that) there will be good fortune, with progress and success.
legge.image: (The trigrams for) heaven and earth in communication together form Thâi. The (sage) sovereign, in harmony with this, fashions and completes (his regulations) after the courses of heaven and earth, and assists the application of the adaptations furnished by them,—in order to benefit the people.
lines: The first line, undivided, suggests the idea of grass pulled up, and bringing with it other stalks with whose roots it is connected. Advance (on the part of its subject) will be fortunate.

The second line, undivided, shows one who can bear with the uncultivated, will cross the Ho without a boat, does not forget the distant, and has no (selfish) friendships. Thus does he prove himself acting in accordance with the course of the due Mean.

The third line, undivided, shows that, while there is no state of peace that is not liable to be disturbed, and no departure (of evil men) so that they shall not return, yet when one is firm and correct, as he realises the distresses that may arise, he will commit no error. There is no occasion for sadness at the certainty (of such recurring changes); and in this mood the happiness (of the present) may be (long) enjoyed.

The fourth line, divided, shows its subject fluttering (down);—not relying on his own rich resources, but calling in his neighbours. (They all come) not as having received warning, but in the sincerity (of their hearts).
The fifth line, divided, reminds us of (king) Tî-yî’s (rule about the) marriage of his younger sister. By such a course there is happiness and there will be great good fortune.

The sixth line, divided, shows us the city wall returned into the moat. It is not the time to use the army. (The subject of the line) may, indeed, announce his orders to the people of his own city; but however correct and firm he may be, he will have cause for regret.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 81-82 (Image: Appendix II, p. 281)

en.name: Peace
en.nameNote: 泰 is to get through, to be at ease, and great: a great getting-through (陸德明); 鄭玄, getting through; 馬融, great. The 序卦: nothing can get through for ever, so Pi follows. Wilhelm's "Friede", peace, is the commentators' sense of a time when all gets through. The Qin 歸藏 writes 柰.
en.judgment: The small goes, the great comes. Auspicious. An offering.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment is in a Spring and Autumn divination (國語, 晉語四, 636 BC): the exile Chong'er stands at the River, and 董因 casts the stalks, gets Tai, and says: heaven and earth matched in the offering, the small goes, the great comes; how should you not cross? 韋昭: the small is the ruler then in Jin, the great the returning heir.
en.tradition: Tai is getting through: heaven and earth join and their two breaths get through; it is the hexagram of the first month. The small is yin and the great yang: Kun has gone to stay outside, Qian has come to stay within; or, coming from Guimei, the six has gone to the fourth place and the nine come to the third. One who divines and has the strength of yang will have it auspicious and getting through.
en.image: Heaven and earth join: Peace. So the sovereign measures out and completes the way of heaven and earth, assists what befits heaven and earth, and so supports the people.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 后 in the songs is a ruler (文王有聲, Mao 244). 王弼: when above and below are all through, things lose their measure; so the sovereign cuts to measure and assists. 孔穎達: the way of heaven and earth is the four seasons, kept in order.

lines.text: Pulling up the rushes, roots tangled, by their kind. Campaigning: auspicious.
lines.note: 茅, the white rush, served the offering: Qi charged Chu that its tribute of rushes had not come in, "無以縮酒", nothing to strain the wine (左傳, 656 BC). The 說文: rushes laid on the libation tablet, the likeness of the spirit drinking. 彙 is a hedgehog (說文) or kind (陸德明). 王弼: pull one root and the others follow.

lines.text: Wrapping the hollow, using it to wade the River; the far is not left behind. Friends gone: it gets a match in the middle file.
lines.note: 馮河 is wading a river on foot (小旻, Mao 195; 毛傳). Gourds were tied on for crossing: "苦匏不材於人，共濟而已" (國語, 魯語下). 荒 is hollow, empty to 鄭玄 and 翟玄, weeds and waste to 王弼. 中行 is the middle column of an army in the 左傳 (632 BC). 王弼: wide-hearted, it casts nothing far away.

lines.text: No level without a slope, no going without a return. The divination about hardship: no blame. Do not be anxious over its confirmation: in the eating there is blessing.
lines.note: 福 was something eaten: the meat of the offering sent home. Li Ji was told to "歸福", and poisoned the wine and the meat (國語, 晉語二). 陂 is a slope (說文). 王弼: where heaven and earth meet each returns to its place, so nothing goes that does not return. 程頤: peace long kept turns to Pi.

lines.text: Fluttering, fluttering: not rich with one's neighbours. Not warned, with captives.
lines.note: 翩翩 is birds coming down: "翩翩者鵻，載飛載下", fluttering, the doves, now flying, now coming down (四牡, Mao 162). 不富以其鄰 is 小畜's formula with a negative, also in the Chu slip of 謙. 戒 is to be on guard in war (采薇, Mao 167). 王弼: all share its wish, so it needs no warning.

lines.text: Di Yi marries off the younger sister: with bounty. Greatly auspicious.
lines.note: Di Yi is the Shang king before the last (尚書, 酒誥). In a 左傳 divination (486 BC) 陽虎 met this line and said Song, descended from Di Yi, was in good fortune: "祉、祿也", 祉 is bounty; Jin held back. The songs tell of King Wen's divined marriage (大明, Mao 236). 朱熹: Di Yi himself cast this line.

lines.text: The wall goes back into the moat. Not to be used for the army. From the town, the command is announced. The divination: trouble.
lines.note: The 說文: "隍，城池也 ... 無水曰隍", a dry moat, quoting this line. A wall is rammed from the earth of its ditch (文王有聲, 緜). Shaughnessy sets the line out as a rhymed oracle. 程頤: earth dug from the moat makes the wall, as good government heaped up makes peace; at its end the earth slumps back.

essays.title: Heaven below, earth above
essays.text: The lower trigram is 乾, heaven; the upper 坤, earth. The Image: heaven and earth join. 荀爽: the breath of earth rises, the breath of heaven sinks; now they meet, and all gets through. The figure is 否 turned over, and the 雜卦 pairs them. 朱熹 makes it the hexagram of the first month.

essays.title: The small going, the great coming
essays.text: The judgment's 小往大來 is set against 否's 大往小來. 虞翻: yin bent outward is the small going; yang stretching within is the great coming. The 彖 turns it to men: the nobleman within and the small man without. The lines go from pulling up rushes to a wall fallen back into its moat; 程頤 reads the turn in the third line: peace that lasts must turn to Pi.

readings.title: 苞荒: hollow, waste, wide water, or a gourd?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤 and 朱熹 read weeds and waste: bearing with the uncultivated. 鄭玄 and 翟玄: empty, hollow. The 說文: wide water. A modern reading: a gourd for floating across, with support from 陸德明's sound and 國語. We print "wrapping the hollow", on the line's own Han glosses.

readings.title: Matched, or rising?
readings.text: 尚 as 配, to be matched (王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤), or as 上, to rise (虞翻, 荀爽). 中行 is the fifth line (王弼), the mean (朱熹), or the 左傳's middle column. We print "gets a match in the middle file".

readings.title: Sister or daughter?
readings.text: 妹 is a younger sister (大明; Legge). Wilhelm and Shaughnessy make her a daughter. 陽虎 applies the line to Di Yi's son marrying off a sister; 程頤 makes Di Yi a lawgiver on royal marriages. We print "the younger sister" and leave whose.

readings.title: 孚 in 九三 and 六四
readings.text: The commentators read good faith; Shaughnessy "trust" in 九三 and "not warned by captives" in 六四. Ruled by context: 九三 prints "confirmation", beside the offering-meat; 六四 "captives", beside the guard of war.

pinyinTones.name: Tài
pinyinTones.judgment: xiǎo wǎng dà lái, jí, hēng.
pinyinTones.image: tiān dì jiāo, tài. hòu yǐ cái chéng tiān dì zhī dào, fǔ xiàng tiān dì zhī yí, yǐ zuǒ yòu mín.
lines: bá máo rú yǐ qí huì. zhēng jí.
bāo huāng, yòng píng hé, bù xiá yí. péng wáng, dé shàng yú zhōng háng.
wú píng bù pō, wú wǎng bù fù. jiān zhēn, wú jiù. wù xù qí fú, yú shí yǒu fú.
piān piān, bù fù yǐ qí lín, bù jiè yǐ fú.
Dì Yǐ guī mèi, yǐ zhǐ, yuán jí.
chéng fù yú huáng, wù yòng shī, zì yì gào mìng, zhēn lìn.

pinyinNotes: 相: xiàng (to assist), as 陸德明 ("輔相：息亮反")
馮: píng (to wade), not féng, as 陸德明 ("音憑")
陂: pō (to slope, tilt), not bēi, as 陸德明's 又破河反; his first reading is 彼僞反 (bì), the same sense

帝乙: Dì Yǐ, a king's name, capitalised

hexagrams.judgment: 否之匪人。不利君子貞。大往小來。
hexagrams.image: 天地不交，否。君子以儉德辟難，不可榮以祿。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 拔茅茹，以其彙。貞吉亨。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 苞承，小人吉，大人否。亨。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 苞羞。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 有命，无咎，疇離祉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 休否，大人吉。其亡其亡，繫于苞桑。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 傾否，先否後喜。

hexagrams.heading: 否
hexagrams.name: 否

wilhelm.name: Die Stockung
wilhelm.judgment: Die Stockung. Schlechte Menschen sind nicht fördernd für die Beharrlichkeit des Edlen. Das Große geht hin, das Kleine kommt herbei.
wilhelm.image: Himmel und Erde vereinigen sich nicht: das Bild der Stockung. So zieht sich der Edle auf seinen inneren Wert zurück, um den Schwierigkeiten zu entgehen. Er lässt sich nicht durch Einkünfte ehren.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Zieht man Bandgras aus, so geht der Rasen mit. Jeder nach seiner Art. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil und Gelingen.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Sie tragen und dulden, das bedeutet für die Gemeinen Heil. Dem großen Mann dient die Stockung zum Gelingen.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Sie tragen Scham.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Wer auf Befehl des Höchsten wirkt, bleibt ohne Makel. Die Gleichgesinnten genießen des Segens.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Die Stockung lässt nach. Dem großen Manne Heil! Wenn es misslänge, wenn es misslänge Daher bindet er es an ein Bündel von Maulbeerstauden.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Die Stockung hört auf. Erst Stockung, dann Heil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Phî
legge.judgment: In Phî there is the want of good understanding between the (different classes of) men, and its indication is unfavourable to the firm and correct course of the superior man. We see in it the great gone and the little come.
legge.image: (The trigrams of) heaven and earth, not in intercommunication, form Phî. The superior man, in accordance with this, restrains (the manifestation) of) his virtue, and avoids the calamities (that threaten him). There is no opportunity of conferring on him the glory of emolument.
lines: The first line, divided, suggests the idea of grass pulled up, and bringing with it other stalks with whose roots it is connected. With firm correctness (on the part of its subject), there will be good fortune and progress.

The second line, divided, shows its subject patient and obedient. To the small man (comporting himself so) there will be good fortune. If the great man (comport himself) as the distress and obstruction require, he will have success.
The third line, divided, shows its subject ashamed of the purpose folded (in his breast).
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject acting in accordance with the ordination (of Heaven), and committing no error. His companions will come and share in his happiness.

In the fifth line, undivided, we see him who brings the distress and obstruction to a close,—the great man and fortunate. (But let him say), ‘We may perish! We may perish!’ (so shall the state of things become firm, as if) bound to a clump of bushy mulberry trees.
The sixth line, undivided, shows the overthrow (and removal of) the condition of distress and obstruction. Before this there was that condition. Hereafter there will be joy.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 83-85 (Image: Appendix II, p. 282)

en.name: Stagnation
en.nameNote: 否 is to be closed, blocked, read pǐ throughout the hexagram (陸德明); in another sound, "not", as in the songs: "人涉卬否", others cross, not I (匏有苦葉, Mao 34). Wilhelm's "Stockung", a stoppage, is the closed sense. The Mawangdui manuscript writes 婦, the Tsinghua 別卦 啚.
en.judgment: Blocking them: not one's own people. A divination not favourable for the nobleman. The great goes, the small comes.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment opens with the name, as in 履, and its words 之匪人 are 比 六三's; 朱熹 suspected they came in from there. 否 answers and completes a pair in the songs, and the book has the same pair in 六二: "小人吉，大人否". 大往小來 is 泰's judgment reversed. The 彖 makes the nobleman and small man the yang and yin lines.
en.tradition: Pi is closed and blocked, the hexagram of the seventh month; the exact reverse of Tai, so "not of men", not the way of man; the reading is unfavourable to the nobleman's right way; Qian has gone outside, Kun come inside; or, from Jian, the nine has gone to the fourth and the six come to the third.
en.image: Heaven and earth do not join: Stagnation. So the noble one keeps his virtue frugal and avoids troubles; he cannot be honoured with emolument.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. "儉、德之共也", frugality is the common ground of virtue (左傳, 670 BC). 孔穎達: in a time of blocking he makes frugality his virtue and must not hold salaried office. 朱熹: he hides his virtue, and others cannot honour him with rank.

lines.text: Pulling up the rushes, roots tangled, by their kind. The divination: auspicious; an offering.
lines.note: The words of 泰 初九, with 貞吉亨 for 征吉. The rushes of the offering: 泰 初九. 程頤: Tai and Pi both use the rushes, for three like lines together below, pulling on one another: in Tai it is auspicious to campaign together, in Pi to keep correct together. 朱熹: warned to be correct, the small man becomes a nobleman.

lines.text: Wrapping and holding up. For the small man, auspicious; for the great man, blocked. An offering.
lines.note: 承 is to hold up in the hands, to present: "女承筐无實", a woman holds up an empty basket (歸妹 上六). 苞 is to wrap. The pair of verdicts returns in 遯 九四. 王弼: the small man's way is open; the great man blocks it, and his way gets through. 程頤: the great man will not bend to comply.

lines.text: Wrapping the delicacies.
lines.note: 羞 is food presented: "進獻也" (說文); plants of the streams "可羞於王公", may be served to kings and dukes (左傳, 720 BC). Chu owed wrapped rushes for the king's sacrifice (左傳, 656 BC). Every commentator reads shame: 王弼, using the small way to serve those above, it wraps up shame. The line has no verdict.

lines.text: There is a command: no blame. Companions meet with bounty.
lines.note: 命 is the king's command of appointment (訟 九四; 師 九二). 疇 is "who" in the 爾雅, whose note quotes this line; the commentators read companions. 離 is to meet with, to be caught: a goose caught in a fish net (新臺, Mao 43). 祉 is bounty. 朱熹: the command is heaven's, and the three yang lines share the blessing.

lines.text: The blocking comes to rest: for the great man, auspicious. "It may be lost, it may be lost": tied to the bushy mulberry.
lines.note: 苞桑 in the songs is a bushy mulberry where birds settle: "集于苞桑。王事靡盬" (鴇羽, Mao 121). 休 is grace in the bronzes, rest in the songs (民勞, Mao 253). The 繫辭 quotes the line: the noble one, safe, does not forget danger. 孔穎達: mulberry for the rhyme. 鄭玄: King Wen in prison at Youli, freed at last.

lines.text: The blocking overturned: first blocked, afterwards joy.
lines.note: 喜 is a verdict of the Chu divination records: "將有大喜，邦知之", there will be great joy, and the state will know it (包山 211). 先 ... 後 ... as in 同人 九五. 侯果: when the blocking runs out it is overturned; the overturning is still blocked, so first blocked; when it is done there is passage, so joy.

essays.title: Earth below, heaven above
essays.text: The figure is 泰 turned over. The Image: heaven and earth do not join. 宋衷: the breath of heaven rises and does not come down, the breath of earth sinks and does not come up; the two are cut apart. 朱熹 makes it the hexagram of the seventh month.

essays.title: The name at the head
essays.text: The judgment begins with the name, which is also the first word of the sentence, as in 履 and 艮. The words 之匪人 are 比 六三's, "比之匪人", and 朱熹 suspected they came in from there by mistake.

readings.title: 否之匪人
readings.text: Ours: "blocking them: not one's own people", on the pattern of 比之匪人. 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹: the blocking is not the way of man. 虞翻: not human, a minister killing his lord. Wilhelm: bad men. 朱熹 also doubted the words, as an intrusion from 比.

readings.title: 羞: delicacies, or shame?
readings.text: Every commentator, Wilhelm and Legge read shame. The 說文 and the 左傳 give food presented; the verbs of 六二 call for an object; Shaughnessy reads sacrificial meats. Ruled by context: here "the delicacies", with shame recorded.

readings.title: 休: rest, or fine?
readings.text: 陸德明 gives both. Rest: 程頤 and the songs. Fine: 孔穎達, and the Western Zhou 休 of grace and of a fine divination. We print "comes to rest", which the overturning of 上九 carries on.

readings.title: 疇: companions, or who?
readings.text: Companions (王弼, 九家易, 程頤, 朱熹); "who" (爾雅, with 郭璞's note quoting this line). We print companions.

pinyinTones.name: Pǐ
pinyinTones.judgment: pǐ zhī fěi rén. bù lì jūn zǐ zhēn. dà wǎng xiǎo lái.
pinyinTones.image: tiān dì bù jiāo, pǐ. jūn zǐ yǐ jiǎn dé bì nàn, bù kě róng yǐ lù.
lines: bá máo rú, yǐ qí huì. zhēn jí hēng.
bāo chéng, xiǎo rén jí, dà rén pǐ. hēng.
bāo xiū.
yǒu mìng, wú jiù, chóu lí zhǐ.
xiū pǐ, dà rén jí. qí wáng qí wáng, xì yú bāo sāng.
qīng pǐ, xiān pǐ hòu xǐ.

pinyinNotes: 否: pǐ (blocked), not fǒu, as 陸德明 ("備鄙反，卦內同，閉也，塞也"), in the name and every line, 大人否 included
辟: bì (to avoid, 避), as 陸德明 ("辟難：上音避")
難: nàn (trouble), as 陸德明 ("下乃旦反")

hexagrams.judgment: 同人于野，亨。利涉大川。利君子貞。
hexagrams.image: 天與火、同人。君子以類族辨物。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 同人于門，无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 同人于宗，吝。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 伏戎于莽，升其高陵，三歲不興。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 乘其墉，弗克攻，吉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 同人先號咷而後笑，大師克，相遇。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 同人于郊，无悔。

hexagrams.heading: 同人
hexagrams.name: 同人

wilhelm.name: Gemeinschaft mit Menschen
wilhelm.judgment: Gemeinschaft mit Menschen im Freien: Gelingen. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren. Fördernd ist des Edlen Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Der Himmel zusammen mit Feuer: das Bild der Gemeinschaft mit Menschen. So gliedert der Edle die Stämme und unterscheidet die Dinge.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Gemeinschaft mit Menschen im Tore. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Gemeinschaft mit Menschen im Klan: Beschämung.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Versteckt Waffen im Dickicht, steigt auf den hohen Hügel davor. Drei Jahre lang erhebt er sich nicht.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er steigt auf seine Mauer, er kann nicht angreifen. Heil!
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Die gemeinsamen Menschen weinen erst und klagen, aber nachher lachen sie. Nach großen Kämpfen gelingt es ihnen, sich zu treffen.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Gemeinschaft mit Menschen auf dem Anger: keine Reue.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Thung Zăn
legge.judgment: Thung Zăn (or ‘Union of men’) appears here (as we find it) in the (remote districts of the) country, indicating progress and success. It will be advantageous to cross the great stream. It will be advantageous to maintain the firm correctness of the superior man.
legge.image: (The trigrams for) heaven and fire form Thung Zăn. The superior man, in accordance with this), distinguishes things according to their kinds and classes.
lines: The first line, undivided, (shows the representative of) the union of men just issuing from his gate. There will be no error.
The second line, divided, (shows the representative of) the union of men in relation with his kindred. There will be occasion for regret.
The third line, undivided, (shows its subject) with his arms hidden in the thick grass, and at the top of a high mound. (But) for three years he makes no demonstration.
The fourth line, undivided, (shows its subject) mounted on the city wall; but he does not proceed to make the attack (he contemplates). There will be good fortune.
In the fifth line, undivided, (the representative of) the union of men first wails and cries out, and then laughs. His great host conquers, and he (and the subject of the second line) meet together.
The topmost line, undivided, (shows the representative of) the union of men in the suburbs. There will be no occasion for repentance.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 86-87 (Image: Appendix II, p. 284)

en.name: Fellowship with People
en.nameNote: 同 is to be together, to gather, to be the same; 人, people. In the songs 同 is the gathering of men and game: "射夫既同", the archers are gathered (車攻, Mao 179); before an attack, "同爾兄弟", gather your brothers (皇矣, Mao 241). The 左傳 (513 BC) uses the name.
en.judgment: Together with people in the wilds: an offering. Favourable to ford the great river. A favourable divination for the nobleman.
en.judgmentNote: The zones outside a town run outskirts, pasture, wilds, forest (爾雅, 釋地): the 野 here is farther out than the 郊 of 上九. The songs' 同 of men is a gathering before an attack, or of archers on a hunt (皇矣, 車攻). The Qin 歸藏 tells a war of the Yellow and Flame Thearchs under this name.
en.tradition: Tongren is being together with people: fire meeting heaven rises to join it; the second has its place and centre and answers the fifth; and the one yin is joined by all five yang. In the wilds is far and without favour, and it gets through; going with strength, it can ford the river. One who divines and is like this gets through and can cross danger; but it is favourable only if what he joins in accords with the nobleman's way.
en.image: Heaven with fire: Fellowship with People. So the noble one groups the clans and tells things apart.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. Clan and lineage as degrees of kinship: at a lord's death each laments in its own temple (左傳, 561 BC). 程頤: heaven with fire, for fire flames up and is the same as heaven. 朱熹: examining difference to bring about sameness.

lines.text: Together with people at the gate: no blame.
lines.note: The gate is the inner limit of the series that runs to the wilds. In the 左傳 the gate is where men gather and where an ambush waits: armoured men hidden behind a curtain outside the gate (522 BC). 王弼: its heart tied to nothing, going out of the gate it is one with all: who would blame it?

lines.text: Together with people at the ancestral temple: trouble.
lines.note: 宗 is the ancestral temple and the lineage it gathers: "同宗於祖廟" (左傳, 561 BC); "宗子維城", the lineage's heir is the city wall (板, Mao 254). A place, like the gate and the outskirts. The commentators read faction or kin: 王弼, joining only its lord, a narrow heart, the way of meanness.

lines.text: Troops hidden in the thicket; climbing its high hill; for three years, no rising.
lines.note: Ambush is in the 左傳: wine given with armoured men hidden (607 BC). 莽 is a thicket (鄭玄), 陵 a great mound (爾雅). 興 is to rise up. Shaughnessy sets the line out as a rhymed oracle. 王弼: its enemy too strong to face, it hides its troops, climbs the hill to look, and for three years cannot rise.

lines.text: Mounting its wall, unable to attack: auspicious.
lines.note: 墉 is a city wall: "以伐崇墉 ... 崇墉言言", to attack the walls of Chong, high, high (皇矣, Mao 241). 攻 is to strike (說文). 王弼: it has the strength to mount the wall, but it quarrels out of its place and no one sides with it; not winning, it turns back, and turning back it is auspicious.

lines.text: Together with people: first wailing, and afterwards laughing. The great army prevails; they meet.
lines.note: 號咷 is loud weeping: in Chu a child that will not stop crying (說文). 旅 上九 has the reverse order. 大師 is the great army (板, Mao 254). The 繫辭 quotes the line: two people of one heart, their sharpness cuts metal. 王弼: cut off by the two strong lines it wails; central and honoured, it wins, and laughs.

lines.text: Together with people in the outskirts: no regret.
lines.note: 郊 is the zone just outside the town (爾雅), within a hundred li of the capital (說文). 悔 is a Shang verdict on the outcome; 无悔 its negative. 王弼: at the edge, it has no one of its mind and is far from the quarrels within: so no regret, but its aim is not met. 朱熹: desolate.

essays.title: Fire below, heaven above
essays.text: The lower trigram is 離, fire; the upper 乾, heaven. 鄭玄: heaven is above, and fire flames upward to follow it: by nature it is the same as heaven. The one yin line is the second, and the 彖 builds the hexagram on it: the soft has its place and the centre and answers Qian. The figure is 師 with every line changed.

essays.title: From the gate to the outskirts
essays.text: Four of the lines and the judgment place the gathering: at the gate, at the ancestral temple, in the outskirts, in the wilds. The three middle lines are a fight: troops in hiding, a wall mounted, a great army and a meeting. 王弼 reads the whole as the narrow gathering that ends in war: whoever gathers with others without all getting through will end by using the army.

readings.title: Together, joined in heart, or a muster?
readings.text: The commentators: being one with others, at large (王弼) or in private (程頤). The songs' 同 of men is often a gathering for war or the hunt, and the three middle lines are a fight. We print "together with people", which leaves the kind of gathering open.

readings.title: 宗: temple, faction, or crowd?
readings.text: The temple and lineage is the Zhou sense, and a place like the other lines'. 程頤 and 朱熹 read faction, 荀爽 the crowd, 侯果 the fifth line. We print "the ancestral temple".

readings.title: Unable to attack, or not winning?
readings.text: 王弼 and the small image read 克 as winning: by right it does not win. 程頤 makes it a choice not to attack. We print "unable to attack", keeping the line's order: the wall mounted, then no attack.

readings.title: Who meets?
readings.text: The two partners, second and fifth (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹), or the armies, which the words allow. Left open.

pinyinTones.name: Tóng Rén
pinyinTones.judgment: tóng rén yú yě, hēng. lì shè dà chuān. lì jūn zǐ zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: tiān yǔ huǒ, tóng rén. jūn zǐ yǐ lèi zú biàn wù.
lines: tóng rén yú mén, wú jiù.
tóng rén yú zōng, lìn.
fú róng yú mǎng, shēng qí gāo líng, sān suì bù xīng.
chéng qí yōng, fú kè gōng, jí.
tóng rén xiān háo táo ér hòu xiào, dà shī kè, xiāng yù.
tóng rén yú jiāo, wú huǐ.

pinyinNotes: 號: háo (to wail) in 號咷, as 陸德明 ("戶羔反")
興: xīng (to rise up), not xìng

hexagrams.image: 火在天上，大有。君子以遏惡揚善，順天休命。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 无交害，匪咎，艱則无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 大車以載，有攸往，无咎。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 公用亨于天子，小人弗克。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 匪其彭，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 厥孚交如，威如，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 自天祐之，吉无不利。

hexagrams.heading: 大有
hexagrams.name: 大有

wilhelm.name: Der Besitz von Großem
wilhelm.judgment: Der Besitz von Großem: Erhabenes Gelingen!
wilhelm.image: Das Feuer am Himmel oben: das Bild des Besitzes von Großem. So hemmt der Edle das Böse und fördert das Gute und gehorcht so des Himmels gutem Willen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Keine Beziehung zu Schädlichem, das ist nicht ein Makel. Bleibt man der Schwierigkeit bewusst, so bleibt man ohne Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Ein großer Wagen zum Beladen. Man mag etwas unternehmen. Kein Makel.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Ein Fürst bringt ihn dem Sohn des Himmels dar. Ein kleiner Mensch kann das nicht.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er macht einen Unterschied zwischen sich und seinem Nächsten. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Wessen Wahrheit umgänglich ist und doch würdig, der hat Heil.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Vom Himmel her wird er gesegnet, Heil! Nichts, das nicht fördernd ist.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Tâ Yû
legge.judgment: Tâ Yû indicates that, (under the circumstances which it implies), there will be great progress and success.
legge.image: (The trigram for) heaven and (that of) fire above it form Tâ Yû. The superior man, in accordance with this, represses what is evil and gives distinction to what is good, in sympathy with the excellent Heaven-conferred (nature).
lines: In the first line, undivided, there is no approach to what is injurious, and there is no error. Let there be a realisation of the difficulty (and danger of the position), and there will be no error (to the end).
In the second line, undivided, we have a large waggon with its load. In whatever direction advance is made, there will be no error.
The third line, undivided, shows us a feudal prince presenting his offerings to the Son of Heaven. A small man would be unequal (to such a duty).
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject keeping his great resources under restraint. There will be no error.
The fifth line, divided, shows the sincerity of its subject reciprocated by that of all the others (represented in the hexagram). Let him display a proper majesty, and there will be good fortune.
The topmost line, undivided, shows its subject with help accorded to him from Heaven. There will be good fortune, advantage in every respect.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), p. 88 (Image: Appendix II, p. 285)

en.name: Possession of Great Things
en.nameNote: 大有 is "great having". 有 is also the year's harvest: the 春秋 records "冬，大有年", in winter, a great harvest year (593 BC). The 雜卦: "《大有》、眾也", many. 辛亞民 argues the name was taken from 上九's 祐: the Qin 歸藏 calls the hexagram 右.
en.judgment: A great offering.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment is two words. The book's own 亨 of presenting is in this hexagram's 九三, which the 左傳 writes 享. Harvest and offering stand together in the songs: "以假以享 ... 豐年穰穰", we come, we make offering ... abundant years heaped high (烈祖, Mao 302).
en.tradition: Dayou is the greatness of what is had: fire above heaven, shining on everything; the one yin in the honoured centre with five yang answering it. Strength and brightness, honoured and answering heaven: the way of getting through. One who divines and has these virtues will have great good and get through.
en.image: Fire is above heaven: Possession of Great Things. So the noble one stops the bad and raises up the good, and follows heaven's fine command.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 休命 is a phrase of the bronzes: "天降休命于朕邦", heaven sent down a fine command on our state (中山王器). 朱熹: when what one has is great and nothing governs it, trouble sprouts within; stopping the bad and raising the good is following heaven.

lines.text: No crossing with harm: not blame. Hardship, and then no blame.
lines.note: 交 is a crossing: "交脛也", legs crossed (說文). 咎 in the Shang and Chu records is harm sent or feared, in the songs a fault; this line has both 害, harm, and 咎. 程頤: wealth seldom comes without harm; having is not itself blame; one who has and knows it is hard to keep will have no blame.

lines.text: A great cart for loading. Has somewhere to go: no blame.
lines.note: 大車 is the heavy cart: "無將大車，祇自塵兮", do not push the great cart: you only raise dust on yourself (無將大車, Mao 206). A loaded cart loses its load in 正月 (Mao 192). 王弼: strong and central, trusted by the fifth, it carries weight without danger and goes far without sticking.

lines.text: The duke uses it in an offering to the Son of Heaven. The small man is not able.
lines.note: The line in a 左傳 divination (635 BC): Jin cast the stalks on restoring the fled king and met this line: "戰克而王饗，吉孰大焉？", victory in battle and a feast from the king. Jin restored him and was feasted and given lands. The 左傳 writes 享. 王弼 reads getting through; 朱熹 presenting at court.

lines.text: Not its throng: no blame.
lines.note: 彭彭 in the songs is a press of men or horses: "行人彭彭", the travellers are many (載驅, Mao 105); "駟騵彭彭", the teams of bays pounding at Muye (大明, Mao 236). The Chu slip keeps only the verdict. 王弼 reads 旁, the neighbouring third line; 朱熹: the sense of 彭 is not known.

lines.text: Its captives, crossing; awesome: auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the same words, 交 written 洨. 威 in the bronzes is the dignity of bearing (集成 00241). Shaughnessy reads captives. 王弼 reads good faith: fair and trusted, what needs guarding? Teaching goes without words: how could it not be awesome? 程頤: softness alone breeds contempt.

lines.text: From heaven, help for it: auspicious; nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: Heaven's help in the songs: "保右命之，自天申之", protects him, helps him, commands him; from heaven it is extended to him (假樂, Mao 249), written 右, as the Chu slip has it. 右 at court is the one who leads a man in to be appointed. The 繫辭 quotes the line: 祐 is to help; heaven helps the compliant.

essays.title: Fire above heaven
essays.text: The lower trigram is 乾, heaven; the upper 離, fire. The Image: fire is above heaven. 荀爽: the summer fire rules in the sky and all things grow together. The one yin line is the fifth, the ruler's place, and the 彖 builds the hexagram on it: the soft has the honoured place, and above and below answer it. The figure is 比 with every line changed.

readings.title: 亨 in 九三: getting through, or an offering?
readings.text: 陸德明 reads hēng, but all the other readers read xiǎng, to present; the 左傳 writes 享, and 朱熹 follows it; 王弼 reads getting through. We print the offering.

readings.title: 彭: throng, neighbour, pride, or lame?
readings.text: Throng (程頤, the songs' 彭彭); the neighbour, 旁 (子夏傳, 王弼, 孔穎達); swollen pride (干寶); lame (虞翻). 朱熹 says the sense is not known. We print throng, from the songs, the only Zhou usage on the shelf.

readings.title: 孚 in 六五
readings.text: Every commentator reads good faith; Shaughnessy reads captives. Ruled by context: here "captives", a thing owned in great possession, as the bronzes' 孚 taken in war, shown with awe.

readings.title: Where does the name come from?
readings.text: 辛亞民: from 上九's 祐, since the Qin 歸藏 has 右 and the Tsinghua 別卦 少又. The commentators: the greatness of what is had. We translate Wilhelm's name and record the argument.

pinyinTones.name: Dà Yǒu
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng.
pinyinTones.image: huǒ zài tiān shàng, dà yǒu. jūn zǐ yǐ è è yáng shàn, shùn tiān xiū mìng.
lines: wú jiāo hài, fěi jiù, jiān zé wú jiù.
dà chē yǐ zài, yǒu yōu wǎng, wú jiù.
gōng yòng xiǎng yú tiān zǐ, xiǎo rén fú kè.
fěi qí péng, wú jiù.
jué fú jiāo rú, wēi rú, jí.
zì tiān yòu zhī, jí wú bù lì.

pinyinNotes: 亨: xiǎng (to present, 享) in 九三, as 京房, 干寶 and 姚信 in 陸德明 ("衆家並香兩反") and the 左傳, the book's choice; 陸德明 himself reads hēng ("許庚反，通也")

hexagrams.image: 地中有山，謙。君子以裒多益寡，稱物平施。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 謙謙君子，用涉大川，吉。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 鳴謙，貞吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 勞謙，君子有終，吉。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 无不利，撝謙。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 不富以其鄰，利用侵伐，无不利。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 鳴謙，利用行師，征邑國。

hexagrams.heading: 謙
hexagrams.name: 謙

wilhelm.name: Die Bescheidenheit
wilhelm.judgment: Bescheidenheit schafft Gelingen. Der Edle bringt zu Ende.
wilhelm.image: Inmitten der Erde ist ein Berg: das Bild der Bescheidenheit. So verringert der Edle, was zu viel ist, und vermehrt, was zu wenig ist. Er wägt die Dinge und macht sie gleich.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Ein bescheiden-bescheidener Edler mag das große Wasser durchqueren. Heil!
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Sich äußernde Bescheidenheit. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Ein verdienstvoll-bescheidener Edler bringt zu Ende. Heil!
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Nichts, das nicht fördernd wäre für Bescheidenheit in der Bewegung.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Nicht pochen auf Reichtum seinem Nächsten gegenüber. Fördernd ist es, mit Gewalt anzugreifen. Nichts, das nicht fördernd wäre.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Sich äußernde Bescheidenheit. Fördernd ist es, Heere marschieren zu lassen, um die eigene Stadt und das eigene Land zu züchtigen.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Khien
legge.judgment: Khien indicates progress and success. The superior man, (being humble as it implies), will have a (good) issue (to his undertakings).
legge.image: (The trigram for) the earth and (that of) a mountain in the midst of it form Khien. The superior man, in accordance with this, diminishes what is excessive (in himself), and increases where there is any defect, bringing about an equality, according to the nature of the case, in his treatment (of himself and others).
lines: The first line, divided, shows us the superior man who adds humility to humility. (Even) the great stream may be crossed with this, and there will be good fortune.
The second line, divided, shows us humility that has made itself recognised. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.
The third line, undivided, shows the superior man of (acknowledged) merit. He will maintain his success to the end, and have good fortune.
The fourth line, divided, shows one, whose action would be in every way advantageous, stirring up (the more) his humility.
The fifth line, divided, shows one who, without being rich, is able to employ his neighbours. He may advantageously use the force of arms. All his movements will be advantageous.
The sixth line, divided, shows us humility that has made itself recognised. The subject of it will with advantage put his hosts in motion; but (he will only) punish his own towns and state.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 89-90 (Image: Appendix II, p. 286)

en.name: Modesty
en.nameNote: 謙 is to lower oneself, to hold back: "屈己下物也", bending oneself below others (陸德明); the 說文: respectful. The 子夏傳 and the Mawangdui manuscript write 嗛, which 韋昭 glosses "small, small". The word is in none of the songs and no early chapter of the 尚書.
en.judgment: An offering. The nobleman reaches an end.
en.judgmentNote: 有終 is in the songs: "靡不有初，鮮克有終", none is without a beginning; few can reach an end (蕩, Mao 255). The only 謙 in the 左傳 is a casting at a birth (昭公五年), read as a lack: "謙不足，飛不翔", Qian is not enough: flying, but not soaring; the child would fall "少不終", somewhat short of the end.
en.tradition: Modesty is having and not dwelling in it: stopping within and yielding without; the mountain, highest, bent down and stopping under the earth, lowest. One who divines and is like this will get through and reach an end; "reaching an end" is first bending, afterwards straightening.
en.image: In the middle of the earth there is a mountain: Modesty. So the noble one takes from the many and adds to the few; he weighs things and makes the giving even.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. 裒 is "to take" in 鄭玄's and 荀爽's texts (捊), set against 益, to add; the 爾雅 has "to gather". 程頤: the height held within the low. 朱熹: lessening the high and adding to the low to bring them level.

lines.text: Modest, modest, the nobleman. Using it to ford the great river: auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has one 謙: "謙君子，用涉大川，吉". 涉 is to cross on foot. The shelf gives nothing for 謙謙. 王弼: at the bottom of modesty, the modest of the modest; used to cross great difficulty, nothing harms it. 荀爽: lowest, it is modest, and the two yin lines holding up the yang are modest too.

lines.text: Calling modesty. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: 鳴 is a bird's call (說文), a call that carries: "鶴鳴于九皋，聲聞于野", the crane calls in the nine marshes; its voice is heard in the wilds (鶴鳴, Mao 184). A pheasant crowing was an omen in 尚書, 高宗肜日. 王弼: calling is the name and fame being heard. 程頤: modesty filling the heart shows in voice and face.

lines.text: Toiling modesty. The nobleman reaches an end: auspicious.
lines.note: 勞 is toil: the graph is fire burning a house and the one who strives at it (說文); "生我劬勞", who bore me with toil (蓼莪, Mao 202). The 繫辭 quotes the line: toiling and not boasting, having merit and not making it a virtue. 王弼: it toils in modesty without slackening. 程頤: the Duke of Zhou.

lines.text: Nothing is unfavourable: waving modesty.
lines.note: 撝 is 麾, to wave a signal: "右秉白旄以麾", the king, the white yak tail in his right hand, waved the army on (尚書, 牧誓). The Chu slip writes 貨. 王弼: serving above and lowering itself below, so nothing is unfavourable; every pointing and waving is modest. 朱熹: it must put its modesty forth the more.

lines.text: Not rich with one's neighbours. Favourable to use in incursion and attack. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: 不富以其鄰 is the phrase of 泰 六四, also in the Chu slip. A bronze warns "毋富而驕 ... 鄰邦難親", do not be rich and arrogant: neighbouring states are hard to hold close (中山王器). With bells and drums an army attacks (伐); without, it is an incursion (侵) (左傳, 665 BC). 程頤: modesty must be joined with martial awe.

lines.text: Calling modesty. Favourable to use in marching the army, campaigning against towns and states.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "可用行師，征邦": it can be used, against the state. 征 + 邦 is the Warring States wording (中山王器), and the bronzes write 邦 where received texts write 國. 王弼: outermost, with no part in government, it has a name only; it can campaign against towns and states, no more. 程頤 and 朱熹 make them one's own.

essays.title: A mountain in the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is 艮, the mountain; the upper 坤, earth. 鄭玄: the mountain's body is high and now it is under the earth: in human terms, the high able to put itself below the low. The one strong line is the third, at the top of the lower trigram, which the commentators make the master of the hexagram. The figure is 豫 turned upside down, and 謙 六二's 鳴謙 answers 豫 初六's 鳴豫.

essays.title: No bad verdict
essays.text: Every verdict in the hexagram is good: an offering; auspicious three times; nothing is unfavourable twice; favourable twice. 王弼: although its six lines are out of place, without partners, riding on the strong, none has disaster, blame, regret or trouble: modesty rules it. Wilhelm: there are few hexagrams in the book whose lines are all favourable.

readings.title: Modesty, or a falling short?
readings.text: Every gloss we hold reads modesty. But the word is absent from the songs and the early 尚書; the one 左傳 casting reads it as a lack; and the 子夏傳's 嗛 is glossed "small, small". 謙 may first have meant short, slight. We print modesty.

readings.title: Where to cut 九三?
readings.text: The small image, 王弼, 孔穎達 and 朱熹: "the toiling, modest nobleman: an end reached, auspicious". The base and the 繫辭's quotation: the judgment's sentence repeated, 君子有終. Same words, same verdict; we keep the base's cut.

readings.title: 征邑國, 征國 or 征邦?
readings.text: The base and every commentator have 征邑國; 陸德明's text 征國, calling 邑 wrong; the Chu slip 征邦. Shaughnessy takes 邑 as a vestige of the graph 邦. We print the base, and record that the older witnesses lack 邑.

readings.title: 撝: wave, lift, part, or spread?
readings.text: 陸德明: to wave, as 麾 in 牧誓. 荀爽: to lift. 馬融: to part. 鄭玄 and 程頤: to spread. 朱熹: to put forth. We print "waving", the sense with a Zhou text behind it.

pinyinTones.name: Qiān
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. jūn zǐ yǒu zhōng.
pinyinTones.image: dì zhōng yǒu shān, qiān. jūn zǐ yǐ póu duō yì guǎ, chēng wù píng shì.
lines: qiān qiān jūn zǐ, yòng shè dà chuān, jí.
míng qiān, zhēn jí.
láo qiān, jūn zǐ yǒu zhōng, jí.
wú bù lì, huī qiān.
bù fù yǐ qí lín, lì yòng qīn fá, wú bù lì.
míng qiān, lì yòng xíng shī, zhēng yì guó.

pinyinNotes: 施: shì (to bestow), as 陸德明 ("平施：始豉反")

hexagrams.image: 雷出地奮，豫。先王以作樂崇德，殷薦之上帝以配祖考。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 鳴豫，凶。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 介于石，不終日，貞吉。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 盱豫，悔，遲有悔。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 由豫，大有得，勿疑。朋盍簪。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 貞疾，恆不死。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 冥豫成，有渝，无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 豫
hexagrams.name: 豫

wilhelm.name: Die Begeisterung
wilhelm.judgment: Die Begeisterung. Fördernd ist es, Gehilfen einzusetzen und Heere marschieren zu lassen.
wilhelm.image: Der Donner kommt aus der Erde hervorgetönt: das Bild der Begeisterung. So machten die alten Könige Musik, um die Verdienste zu ehren, und brachten sie herrlich dem höchsten Gott dar, indem sie ihre Ahnen dazu einluden.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Begeisterung, die sich äußert, bringt Unheil.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Fest wie ein Stein. Kein ganzer Tag. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Nach oben blickende Begeisterung schafft Reue. Zögern bringt Reue.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Ursprung der Begeisterung. Er erreicht Großes. Zweifle nicht! Die Freunde scharen sich um dich wie um eine Haarspange.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlich krank und stirbt doch immer nicht.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Verblendete Begeisterung. Aber wenn man nach der Vollendung zur Änderung kommt, so ist das kein Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Yü
legge.judgment: Yü indicates that, (in the state which it implies), feudal princes may be set up, and the hosts put in motion, with advantage.
legge.image: (The trigrams for) the earth and thunder issuing from it with its crashing noise form Yü. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, composed their music and did honour to virtue, presenting it especially and most grandly to God, when they associated with Him (at the service) their highest ancestor and their father.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject proclaiming his pleasure and satisfaction. There will be evil.
The second line, divided, shows one who is firm as a rock. (He sees a thing) without waiting till it has come to pass; with his firm correctness there will be good fortune.

The third line, divided, shows one looking up (for favours), while he indulges the feeling of pleasure and satisfaction. If he would understand!—If he be late in doing so, there will indeed be occasion for repentance.

The fourth line, undivided, shows him from whom the harmony and satisfaction come. Great is the success which he obtains. Let him not allow suspicions to enter his mind, and thus friends will gather around him.
The fifth line, divided, shows one with a chronic complaint, but who lives on without dying.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject with darkened mind devoted to the pleasure and satisfaction (of the time); but if he change his course even when (it may be considered as) completed, there will be no error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 91-92 (Image: Appendix II, pp. 287-288)

en.name: Enthusiasm
en.nameNote: 豫 is ease and contentment, and also forethought: gladness, being prepared (陸德明); 馬融: joy. The Western Zhou texts use it for ease and being well: "王有疾，弗豫", the king was ill and not well (金縢). The Chu and Mawangdui manuscripts write 余; the Qin 歸藏 calls the figure 介.
en.judgment: Favourable for setting up a lord and marching the army.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment in a Spring and Autumn casting (國語, 晉語四, 637 BC): the exiled Chong'er asked "尚有晉國", may I have the state of Jin, and got Zhun and Yu. The scribes said not auspicious; 司空季子 said both say favourable for setting up a lord: at home at ease, abroad in awe; hexagrams for getting a state.
en.tradition: Yu is harmony and joy: the hearts of the people glad, answering those above; the one yang line of the fourth answered above and below, its aim carried out; earth meeting thunder, compliance moving: so the hexagram is Yu, and the reading is favourable for setting up a ruler and using the army.
en.image: Thunder comes out of the earth, rousing: Enthusiasm. So the former kings made music and exalted virtue, and offered it in abundance to the High God, pairing it with their ancestors and fathers.
en.imageNote: A wing, later than the text. An early Western Zhou bronze has the king offering to his father King Wen and serving the High God (天亡簋); the songs pair Hou Ji with heaven (思文, Mao 275). 鄭玄: the king, his work done, makes music, and the ancestors share heaven's feast.

lines.text: Calling ease: disaster.
lines.note: 豫 as ease and leisure in the Western Zhou: "無康好逸豫", do not love ease and idle leisure (尚書, 康誥); "無敢戲豫", do not dare to play and idle (板, Mao 254). 鳴 is a bird's call. The Chu slip has the same words. 王弼: joy past measure is excess; how can ease be called out?

lines.text: Lodged against a stone. Not the whole day. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: In the 左傳 介於 is a small state set hard against great ones: "介於大國" (542 BC). The book's 困于石 is quoted as an oracle in a 左傳 casting (548 BC). The 繫辭 quotes this line: the nobleman sees the first sign and acts, not waiting the whole day, reading 介 as firm as stone. 王弼: firm as stone.

lines.text: Staring ease: regret. Late: there is regret.
lines.note: 盱 is to open the eyes wide (說文); in the songs it is distress (何人斯, Mao 199, with 鄭玄). The Chu slip has 可. 王弼: if it gapes up to be at ease, regret comes; if slow to follow, ease dislikes it. 向秀: the fawning look of a small man. 朱熹: repent quickly; if slowly, there will be regret.

lines.text: From it, ease: a great gain. Do not doubt. Friends gather quickly.
lines.note: The Chu slip has 猷, the same word as 猶; 馬融 read 猶豫, hesitating. In the 儀禮 簪 is to pin together; no Zhou text on the shelf uses it for a hairpin. 王弼: the only yang line, followed by all the yin; if it does not doubt, friends gather fast. 程頤 reads the hairpin.

lines.text: A divination about illness: in the long term, not dying.
lines.note: The Chu divination records put this very question: "以其有瘇病 ... 尚毋死。義占之：恆貞，不死", because he has a swelling illness, may he not die; the divination for the long term: not dying (包山 249). The king's illness in 金縢 was divined with three turtles. The commentators: a ruler always ill, never dying, under a strong minister.

lines.text: Dark ease, completed. There is a change: no blame.
lines.note: 冥 is dark (說文). 渝 is a change: "敬天之渝", revere heaven's changes, in the same stanza as "無敢戲豫" (板, Mao 254). 鄭玄 read 冥 as 鳴, calling. 王弼: at the height of ease, joy exhausted; ease past measure cannot last, so it must change; then no blame. 程頤: to urge a turn to the good.

essays.title: Thunder out of the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is 坤, earth; the upper 震, thunder. The Image: thunder comes out of the earth, rousing. The one strong line is the fourth, the minister's place below the ruler, and all five yin lines answer it. 程頤: the yang, shut in the earth, moves, comes out and sounds forth, open and at ease. The figure is 謙 turned upside down, and four lines here are two-word figures ending in 豫, as the lines of 謙 end in 謙.

readings.title: 豫: ease, joy, forethought, or excess?
readings.text: The commentators: gladness, joy. The 繫辭 and the 左傳 also use it for being prepared. The Chu and Mawangdui 余 is read 餘, excess, by 廖名春. We print "ease": the Western Zhou texts use the word for ease, leisure and being well.

readings.title: Lodged against, or firm as, a stone?
readings.text: The 繫辭, 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹: firm as stone. 虞翻: slight. 鄭玄: grinding. 馬融: the sound of striking small stones. We print "lodged against a stone", from the 左傳's 介於 + place and the book's own 困于石.

readings.title: 由豫 or 猶豫?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹: ease comes through the fourth. 馬融's text and the Chu slip have 猶, hesitating; then the line would begin "Hesitating: a great gain. Do not doubt". We print the base's 由.

readings.title: 朋盍簪: quickly, or a hairpin?
readings.text: The 子夏傳, 鄭玄 and 王弼: fast. 侯果, 程頤 and Wilhelm: a hairpin gathering hair. 虞翻's text: clumped together. We print "gather quickly", the oldest gloss we hold.

readings.title: Who is ill?
readings.text: The commentators: the ruler under a strong minister, like the last lords of Han and Wei (程頤). Read with the Chu records, the words are an answer to a question about illness. We print the words.

pinyinTones.name: Yù
pinyinTones.judgment: lì jiàn hóu xíng shī.
pinyinTones.image: léi chū dì fèn, yù. xiān wáng yǐ zuò yuè chóng dé, yīn jiàn zhī shàng dì yǐ pèi zǔ kǎo.
lines: míng yù, xiōng.
jiè yú shí, bù zhōng rì, zhēn jí.
xū yù, huǐ, chí yǒu huǐ.
yóu yù, dà yǒu dé, wù yí. péng hé zān.
zhēn jí, héng bù sǐ.
míng yù chéng, yǒu yú, wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 樂: yuè (music) in 作樂

hexagrams.image: 澤中有雷，隨。君子以嚮晦入宴息。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 官有渝，貞吉，出門交有功。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 係小子，失丈夫。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 係丈夫，失小子，隨有求，得。利居貞。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 隨有獲，貞凶。有孚在道，以明，何咎？

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 孚于嘉，吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 拘係之，乃從維之，王用亨于西山。

hexagrams.heading: 隨
hexagrams.name: 隨

wilhelm.name: Die Nachfolge
wilhelm.judgment: Die Nachfolge hat erhabenes Gelingen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.image: Inmitten des Sees ist der Donner: das Bild der Nachfolge. So kehrt der Edle zur Zeit des Abenddunkels zu Erholung und Ruhe ein.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Das Maßgebende ändert sich. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Zur Tür hinausgehen im Verkehr schafft Werke.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Hängt man sich an den kleinen Knaben, so verliert man den starken Mann.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Hängt man dem starken Mann an, so verliert man den kleinen Knaben. Durch Nachfolge findet man, was man sucht. Fördernd ist es, beharrlich zu bleiben.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Die Nachfolge schafft Erfolg. Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil. Mit Wahrhaftigkeit auf dem Weg zu wandeln, bringt Klarheit. Wie könnte das ein Makel sein?
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Wahrhaft im Guten. Heil!
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Er findet feste Anhänglichkeit und wird noch dazu gebunden. Der König stellt ihn dem Westberg vor.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Sui
legge.judgment: Sui indicates that (under its conditions) there will be great progress and success. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. There will (then) be no error.
legge.image: (The trigram for the waters of) a marsh and (that for) thunder (hidden) in the midst of it form Sui. The superior man in accordance with this, when it is getting towards dark, enters (his house) and rests.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows us one changing the object of his pursuit; but if he be firm and correct, there will be good fortune. Going beyond (his own) gate to find associates, he will achieve merit.
The second line, divided, shows us one who cleaves to the little boy, and lets go the man of age and experience.

The third line, divided, shows us one who cleaves to the man of age and experience, and lets go the little boy. Such following will get what it seeks; but it will be advantageous to adhere to what is firm and correct.

The fourth line, undivided, shows us one followed and obtaining (adherents). Though he be firm and correct, there will be evil. If he be sincere (however) in his course, and make that evident, into what error will he fall?
The fifth line, undivided, shows us (the ruler) sincere in (fostering all) that is excellent. There will be good fortune.
The topmost line, divided, shows us (that sincerity) firmly held and clung to, yea, and bound fast. (We see) the king with it presenting his offerings on the western mountain.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 93-94 (Image: Appendix II, p. 289)

en.name: Following
en.nameNote: 隨 is to follow, to go along after: "從也" (陸德明). The 繫辭 says yoking the ox and riding the horse, drawing heavy loads far, was taken from Sui. In a Western Zhou song it is a bad following: "無縱詭隨", do not indulge the crooked followers (民勞).
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination. No blame.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment in a casting (左傳, 564 BC): 穆姜, confined after plotting, met Sui. The scribe read the name: Sui is going out, you will soon go out. She read the four words as virtues a person must have, said she had none, and would die there. So in 564 BC the four-virtue reading was one reading among others.
en.tradition: Sui is following: one follows things, things come to follow one; following each other, the way through is easy: so the reading is great success; but it must favour the correct to be without blame; if what is followed is not correct, even great success does not escape blame.
en.image: In the middle of the lake there is thunder: Following. So the noble one, towards dusk, goes in to rest and repose.
en.imageNote: A later layer. Thunder, the yang breath, works in spring and summer; in the lake it is autumn and winter, and the noble one takes after it: at sunrise he sees to affairs, at dusk he withdraws to rest (翟玄).

lines.text: The office: there is a change. The divination: auspicious. Going out of the gate, crossing: there is achievement.
lines.note: 官 is an office and its proper charge: Jin is praised because "官不易方", its offices do not change their rules (左傳, 564 BC). 渝 is a change. 功 is achievement, merit; the Chu slip writes 工. 蜀才's text had 館, a lodging-house (陸德明).

lines.text: Tied to the young one, losing the grown man.
lines.note: 係 is to tie, to bind round (說文). 小子 are the young, the juniors: young men in war (晉侯穌編鐘), and the king's word for himself, "余小子" (毛公鼎). 丈夫 is a grown man, a male, against 女子 (國語). The line has no verdict. 朱熹: the young one is the near first line, the grown man the distant fifth.

lines.text: Tied to the grown man, losing the young one. Following, there is seeking: it is got. A favourable divination about staying.
lines.note: The first half mirrors the line below word for word. The Chu slip has "隨求有得", following, seeking: there is gain. 利居貞 is the phrase of 3 初九, which a Spring and Autumn diviner read as the lame son staying at home (左傳, 昭公七年).

lines.text: Following, there is a catch. The divination: disaster. There are captives on the road, and so it is clear: what blame?
lines.note: 獲 is game taken in the hunt and men taken in war: "獵所獲也" (說文); "休獲厥君馭方" (禹鼎). Beside it, 孚 on the road reads as captives brought home: a raid coming home. The Chu slip has 貞工(功), achievement, for 貞凶. 王弼 reads a minister winning the people for himself.

lines.text: Confirmation in the fine: auspicious.
lines.note: 孚于 with a noun is a Western Zhou phrase: "永孚于寧" (NA1607). 嘉 is fine, good: the fine guests of a feast (鹿鳴, Mao 161) and a marriage, "文王嘉止" (大明, Mao 236). The commentators read the same words as trust in the good.

lines.text: Seizing and tying them; then, following, tethering them. The king uses it in an offering at the western mountain.
lines.note: 拘 is to arrest (尚書, 酒誥). 維 is to tether, as a guest's colt is tethered (白駒, Mao 186). The Zhou's mountain in the west is 岐, where the Old Duke settled and "began to cut down Shang" (閟宮, Mao 300). 用亨于 is the offering; the Chu slip writes 享 (Shaughnessy).

essays.title: Thunder in the lake
essays.text: The lower trigram is thunder, the upper the lake. 九家易: in the eighth month thunder hides in the lake, the world following the season. 程頤 adds the youngest daughter (the lake) following the eldest son (thunder), and the strong line come down below the soft.

essays.title: Tied and lost
essays.text: The three yin lines are each tied: the second to the young one, losing the grown man; the third to the grown man, losing the young one; the top seized, tied and tethered. The commentators read the pairs as the lines next to each line: the young one below, the grown man above (王弼).

readings.title: 孚 in the fourth and fifth lines: confirmation, good faith, or captives?
readings.text: The fourth line sets 獲, a catch, beside 孚 on the road: read as captives, it is a plain account of a raid coming home, among the strongest cases for the bronzes' sense. The commentators read good faith. 孚 is rendered by context: the fourth prints "captives", the fifth "confirmation".

readings.title: The judgment: four virtues or a verdict?
readings.text: 穆姜 (左傳, 564 BC) and 鄭玄 read the four virtues one must have; the scribe in the same story reads the name only; 朱熹 says the four virtues are not the original sense. We print the verdict, as in 1 and 3.

readings.title: 官: office, the mind's charge, or a lodging?
readings.text: 孔穎達 reads what the mind holds; 程頤 what one holds to; 九家易 the place of earth; 蜀才's text has 館, a lodging. We print "the office".

readings.title: Seized and tied, then following?
