readings.text: 王弼 and 孔穎達 cut 拘係之乃從，維之: seized and tied, it then follows; it is tethered. The small image, the Chu slip (從乃維之), 虞翻 and 程頤 read 乃從維之 together. We print the second, against the base text.

readings.title: An offering at the western mountain, or getting through?
readings.text: 王弼 and 孔穎達 read 亨 as getting through, to the western mountain by force. 陸績, 程頤 and 朱熹 read the offering, 享, and the Chu slip by Shaughnessy's report writes 享. We print the offering.

pinyinTones.name: Suí
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng, lì zhēn, wú jiù.
pinyinTones.image: zé zhōng yǒu léi, suí. jūn zǐ yǐ xiàng huì rù yàn xī.
lines: guān yǒu yú, zhēn jí, chū mén jiāo yǒu gōng.
xì xiǎo zǐ, shī zhàng fū.
xì zhàng fū, shī xiǎo zǐ, suí yǒu qiú, dé. lì jū zhēn.
suí yǒu huò, zhēn xiōng. yǒu fú zài dào, yǐ míng, hé jiù?
fú yú jiā, jí.
jū xì zhī, nǎi cóng wéi zhī, wáng yòng xiǎng yú xī shān.

pinyinNotes: 亨 (上六): xiǎng (offering, read 享), as 陸績 "許兩反，云祭也" in 陸德明 and the book's "an offering"; 陸德明's first 許庚反 (hēng) is 王弼's "getting through"

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨。利涉大川，先甲三日，後甲三日。
hexagrams.image: 山下有風，蠱。君子以振民育德。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 幹父之蠱，有子，考无咎，厲，終吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 幹母之蠱，不可貞。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 幹父之蠱，小有悔，无大咎。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 裕父之蠱，往見吝。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 幹父之蠱，用譽。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 不事王侯，高尚其事。

hexagrams.heading: 蠱
hexagrams.name: 蠱

wilhelm.name: Die Arbeit am Verdorbenen
wilhelm.judgment: Die Arbeit am Verdorbenen hat erhabenes Gelingen. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren. Vor dem Anfangspunkt drei Tage, nach dem Anfangspunkt drei Tage.
wilhelm.image: Unten am Berg weht der Wind: das Bild des Verderbens. So rüttelt der Edle die Leute auf und stärkt ihren Geist.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Zurechtbringen des vom Vater Verdorbenen. Wenn ein Sohn da ist, bleibt auf dem heimgegangenen Vater kein Makel. Gefahr. Schließlich Heil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Zurechtbringen des von der Mutter Verdorbenen. Man darf nicht zu beharrlich sein.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Zurechtbringen des vom Vater Verdorbenen. Ein wenig wird es Reue geben. Kein großer Makel.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Dulden des vom Vater Verdorbenen. Beim Fortmachen sieht man Beschämung.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Zurechtbringen des vom Vater Verdorbenen. Man findet Lob.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Dient nicht Königen und Fürsten. Steckt sich höhere Ziele.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kû
legge.judgment: Kû indicates great progress and success (to him who deals properly with the condition represented by it). There will be advantage in (efforts like that of) crossing the great stream. (He should weigh well, however, the events of) three days before the turning point, and those (to be done) three days after it.
legge.image: (The trigram for) a mountain, and below it that for wind, form Kû. The superior man, in accordance with this, (addresses himself to) help the people and nourish his own virtue.
lines: The first line, divided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his father. If he be an (able) son, the father will escape the blame of having erred. The position is perilous, but there will be good fortune in the end.
The second line, undivided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his mother. He should not (carry) his firm correctness (to the utmost).
The third line, undivided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his father. There may be some small occasion for repentance, but there will not be any great error.
The fourth line, divided, shows (a son) viewing indulgently the troubles caused by his father. If he go forward, he will find cause to regret it.
The fifth line, divided, shows (a son) dealing with the troubles caused by his father. He obtains the praise of using (the fit instrument for his work).
The sixth line, undivided, shows us one who does not serve either king or feudal lord, but in a lofty spirit prefers (to attend to) his own affairs.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 95-96 (Image: Appendix II, p. 290)

en.name: Work on What Has Been Spoiled
en.nameNote: 蠱 is worms in a vessel, and the sickness and poison they stand for: "皿蟲為蠱" (左傳; 說文), and the Chu slip writes worm over vessel. The 序卦 gives the wing's sense, "蠱者，事也", affairs to see to. 程頤 keeps both: where there is ruin there are affairs.
en.judgment: A great offering. Favourable to ford the great river. Three days before jia, three days after jia.
en.judgmentNote: 蠱 was an illness: a physician says one lord's comes "not from ghosts, not from food" but from women (左傳, 541 BC). 甲 is the first day of the Shang ten-day week, divined on every 癸 day (合集 00137正.1); three days before are 辛, 壬, 癸, three after 乙, 丙, 丁 (子夏傳).
en.tradition: Gu is ruin at its height, with affairs to see to; at the height of ruin, disorder must turn to order: so the reading is a great success and favourable to cross the great river. When the former affair is about to fail, renew it (辛, 新) and make it the start of the next; when the next is just begun, give it repeated care (丁, 丁寧).
en.image: Below the mountain there is wind: Work on What Has Been Spoiled. So the noble one relieves the people and nurtures virtue.
en.imageNote: A later layer. The wind stirs, spreads and moistens: relieving the people is the wind below; nurturing virtue is the mountain above (孔穎達). 振 is "濟也", to relieve (陸德明); Wilhelm takes it as to stir up.

lines.text: Managing the father's affliction. There is a son: the dead father, no blame. Danger; in the end, auspicious.
lines.note: 考 in the Western Zhou bronzes is the dead father to whom offering is made: "朕皇考". A son who does not see to his father's affairs "wounds his father's heart" (尚書, 康誥). 幹 is the trunk, and to hold firm (韓奕, Mao 261). 朱熹: as a trunk holds the branches, the son holds up what was left ruined.

lines.text: Managing the mother's affliction. It may not be divined.
lines.note: 不可貞: a matter not fit to be put to the oracle; its pair 可貞 is in 2 六三. The shelf gives nothing for a mother's affliction. Every commentator reads "one may not be rigidly correct": a son should guide his mother gently (程頤).

lines.text: Managing the father's affliction. There is a little regret; no great blame.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "幹父之蠱，少(小)有" and breaks off. 小有 with a verdict is the shape of 5 九二 "小有言"; 无大咎 sets a measure on 无咎. 朱熹: too firm and not central, so a little regret; correct, so no great blame.

lines.text: Being lenient with the father's affliction. Going on: trouble is seen.
lines.note: 裕 in the early Zhou documents is to be generous, to give ease: "乃裕民" (尚書, 康誥); "寬也", lenient (馬融). 虞翻: 裕 is not remonstrating with the father. 朱熹: lenient with the affliction, it will deepen day by day.

lines.text: Managing the father's affliction. Using it: praise.
lines.note: 譽 is praise and good name: "以永終譽", to keep their praise to the end (振鷺, Mao 278). 2 六四 has 无譽. What is used the line leaves unsaid. 程頤: a weak heir who employs strong ministers wins a good name, as Taijia and King Cheng did.

lines.text: Not serving king or lords; holding high one's own affairs.
lines.note: 事 in the Western Zhou is service to a lord or a spirit: "事喜上帝" (天亡簋). Here it is first a verb, to serve, then the noun, affairs. 荀爽: old, his work done, out of place, he serves no king. 程頤: the worthy man out of step with his time.

essays.title: Wind below the mountain
essays.text: The lower trigram is wind, the upper the mountain. 何妥: the mountain high and still, the wind spreading and quick, like a lord at rest above and a minister carrying out orders below. 程頤: wind under the mountain meets it and turns back, and things are thrown into disorder. The 左傳 reads the trigrams as the eldest daughter beguiling the youngest son, wind bringing down the mountain. In a casting of 645 BC the trigrams are read as wind blowing on a mountain in autumn: "we bring down their fruit and take their timber".

essays.title: Father and mother
essays.text: Five lines name a parent: four the father, one the mother, and the first the dead father. The commentators read them as a son seeing to what his parents left undone or spoiled. The top line alone names no parent and serves no king.

readings.title: 蠱: affliction, affairs, or ruin?
readings.text: The old evidence is worms in a vessel and an illness from ghosts or food; the wings read affairs; the commentators ruin and disorder. We print "affliction", keeping the worm, the sickness and the curse. Whether the father suffered it, caused it, or sends it as a dead ancestor, the line leaves open.

readings.title: There is a son: the dead father, no blame?
readings.text: The base, 王弼, 孔穎達 and the Chu punctuation cut after 子: there is a son; the dead father has no blame. 馬融, 王肅, 周弘正 and 虞翻 cut after 考. We print the base.

readings.title: It may not be divined, or one may not be correct?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 不可貞 in the second line as "one may not hold rigidly to the right". By the edition's rule for 貞 we print "it may not be divined".

readings.title: Three days before jia: which days, and why?
readings.text: 子夏傳: 辛壬癸 and 乙丙丁. 鄭玄 and 朱熹: the days 辛 and 丁, for renewal and repeated warning. 馬融 and 王弼: a decree given three days before and after. 程頤: causes before, consequences after. We print the words.

readings.title: 振民: relieve or stir up?
readings.text: 陸德明's old reading, 王弼 and 程頤: relieve the people. Wilhelm: stir them up. We print "relieves".

pinyinTones.name: Gǔ
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng. lì shè dà chuān, xiàn jiǎ sān rì, hòu jiǎ sān rì.
pinyinTones.image: shān xià yǒu fēng, gǔ. jūn zǐ yǐ zhèn mín yù dé.
lines: gàn fù zhī gǔ, yǒu zǐ, kǎo wú jiù, lì, zhōng jí.
gàn mǔ zhī gǔ, bù kě zhēn.
gàn fù zhī gǔ, xiǎo yǒu huǐ, wú dà jiù.
yù fù zhī gǔ, wǎng jiàn lìn.
gàn fù zhī gǔ, yòng yù.
bù shì wáng hóu, gāo shàng qí shì.

pinyinNotes: 先: xiàn in 先甲 (before), as 陸德明 息薦反 ("彖并注同"); so 先庚 in 57

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨，利貞。至于八月有凶。
hexagrams.image: 澤上有地，臨。君子以教思无窮，容保民无疆。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 咸臨，貞吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 咸臨，吉，无不利。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 甘臨，无攸利；既憂之，无咎。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 至臨，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 知臨，大君之宜，吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 敦臨，吉，无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 臨
hexagrams.name: 臨

wilhelm.name: Die Annäherung
wilhelm.judgment: Die Annäherung hat erhabenes Gelingen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Kommt der achte Monat, so gibt’s Unheil.
wilhelm.image: Oberhalb des Sees ist die Erde: das Bild der Annäherung. So ist der Edle in seiner Absicht zu lehren unerschöpflich und im Ertragen und Schützen des Volkes ohne Grenzen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Gemeinsame Annäherung. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Gemeinsame Annäherung. Heil! Alles ist fördernd.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Behagliche Annäherung. Nichts, das fördernd wäre. Erreicht man Trauer darüber, so wird man ohne Makel.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Vollkommene Annäherung. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Weise Annäherung. Das ist recht für einen großen Fürsten. Heil!
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Großherzige Annäherung. Heil. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Lin
legge.judgment: Lin (indicates that under the conditions supposed in it) there will be great progress and success, while it will be advantageous to be firmly correct. In the eighth month there will be evil.
legge.image: (The trigram for) the waters of a marsh and that for the earth above it form Lin. The superior man, in accordance with this, has his purposes of instruction that are inexhaustible, and nourishes and supports the people without limit.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject advancing in company (with the subject of the second line). Through his firm correctness there will be good fortune.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject advancing in company (with the subject of the first line). There will be good fortune; (advancing) will be in every way advantageous.
The third line, divided, shows one well pleased (indeed) to advance, (but whose action) will be in no way advantageous. If he become anxious about it (however), there will be no error.
The fourth line, divided, shows one advancing in the highest mode. There will be no error.
The fifth line, divided, shows the advance of wisdom, such as befits the great ruler. There will be good fortune.
The sixth line, divided, shows the advance of honesty and generosity. There will be good fortune, and no error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 97-98 (Image: Appendix II, p. 291)

en.name: Approach
en.nameNote: 臨 is to look down on, to oversee: "視也" (爾雅). In the Western Zhou it is what heaven does to the king: "臨保我有周", watched over and kept our Zhou (毛公鼎); "上帝臨女", the High God looks down on you (大明, Mao 236). The 序卦 reads it as great.
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination. Coming to the eighth month: there is disaster.
en.judgmentNote: Records name a month as the term of what they foretell: "未盡八月，疾必瘥", before the eighth month is out the illness will abate (葛陵, 4th century BC). A Western Zhou bronze dates a stalk-casting "隹八月" (集成 09714). In the songs the eighth month is the reaping (七月, Mao 154). Which calendar is meant, the text does not say.
en.tradition: Lin is advancing and pressing on things: two yang lines growing and pressing on the yin. Below, the lake is glad; above, earth complies: so one who divines will have great success, and it is favourable to be correct. But at the eighth month there will be disaster, when the yin grows and the yang retreats. A warning attached to the reading.
en.image: Above the lake there is earth: Approach. So the noble one teaches and cares without end, and holds and protects the people without bound.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 无疆, without bound, is the bronzes' wish: "萬年無疆". 朱熹: earth over the lake is the high over the low; teaching without end is the lake, holding without bound is earth.

lines.text: Joint overseeing. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: 咸 is all, together: "皆也" (爾雅). A conquest song has the hexagram's words together: "上帝臨女。敦商之旅，克咸厥功" (閟宮, Mao 300), where 鄭玄 glosses 咸 "同也". In the bronzes 咸 closes an act: done. 王弼 reads 感, to move, from a later wing; 朱熹 reads all.

lines.text: Joint overseeing: auspicious; nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: The figure repeats the first line's. The small image says "未順命也", not yet obeying the command; 孔穎達: the minister weighs the matter, following in some things and not in others. 朱熹 calls the small image unclear.

lines.text: Sweet overseeing: nothing is favourable. Already anxious over it: no blame.
lines.note: 甘 is sweetness (說文). In the songs and the 左傳 it is the sweet words of one who deceives: "盜言孔甘" (巧言, Mao 198); "幣重而言甘，誘我也" (左傳, 650 BC). It is also the good rain, "甘雨". 既 is already, as in the bronzes' dates. 王弼: flattery that grieves and mends loses its blame.

lines.text: Arriving overseeing: no blame.
lines.note: 至 is to arrive, the verb of the judgment's 至于: "至于艽野" (小明, Mao 207). The commentators read the utmost (王弼, 程頤: utmost because closest) or coming down to its answer below (虞翻).

lines.text: Knowing overseeing, what befits the great lord: auspicious.
lines.note: 宜 in the songs is fitting: "宜其室家" (桃夭, Mao 6). It is also the offering at the altar of the soil before a campaign (爾雅; 周禮), in texts later than this one. 陸德明 reads 知 first as 智, wise. 王弼: a lord who leaves each to his ability, done without doing.

lines.text: Thick overseeing: auspicious; no blame.
lines.note: In the bronzes and songs 敦 presses an attack: "王敦伐其至" (宗周鐘); "敦商之旅" (閟宮). It is also a heap: "丘一成為敦丘" (爾雅). Every commentator reads 厚, thick, generous: honoured, it answers the low (程頤). The same word is in 24 六五 and 52 上九.

essays.title: Earth above the lake
essays.text: The lower trigram is the lake, the upper earth. 程頤: the earth above the lake is the shore, close over the water. Two yang lines stand at the bottom under four yin, and the 彖 says the strong soaks upward and grows. In the commentators' twelve-month scheme this is the twelfth month's hexagram, behind every reading of the eighth month. Turned upside down it is 觀 (20); Shaughnessy names the pair "Looking Down" and "Looking Up".

essays.title: The oldest reading of the name
essays.text: In a council of war of 597 BC (左傳), a Jin commander crosses the river against orders, and 知莊子 quotes 7 初六 at Shi changing to Lin: the multitude scattered is weakness, a river blocked becomes a lake; "not moving is called Lin: to have a commander and not follow him, what could be more Lin than that?"

readings.title: 臨: approach, great, overseeing, or standing still?
readings.text: Wilhelm: approach. The 序卦: great. The 爾雅, the bronzes and the songs: looking down, as heaven on the king. The 左傳: not moving. We print "overseeing" in the lines: looking down on, with the charge of what is seen.

readings.title: Which eighth month?
readings.text: Counted from 復 to 遯 (程頤, 朱熹); from 臨 to 否 (李鼎祚, 孔穎達); the Xia eighth month, whose hexagram is 觀 (褚氏, 朱熹's "some say"); the Zhou eighth month of 遯 (虞翻); a warning to Yin (鄭玄). We print "the eighth month" and leave the reckoning open.

readings.title: 咸: moved, all, together, or done?
readings.text: 王弼, 虞翻 and 程頤 read 感, moved, from the 彖 of 31. 朱熹: all. 鄭玄 in the songs: together. The bronzes: done. We print "joint".

readings.title: What befits, or the great lord's offering?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 宜 as fitting. The 爾雅, 周禮 and 王制 name 宜 as the offering before a campaign, which would make the line the great lord's yi offering; but those texts are later, and the songs use 宜 for fitting. We print "what befits".

readings.title: 敦: thick, or pressing?
readings.text: Every commentator reads thick, generous. The bronzes and songs use the word for pressing an attack. We print "thick".

pinyinTones.name: Lín
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng, lì zhēn. zhì yú bā yuè yǒu xiōng.
pinyinTones.image: zé shàng yǒu dì, lín. jūn zǐ yǐ jiào sì wú qióng, róng bǎo mín wú jiāng.
lines: xián lín, zhēn jí.
xián lín, jí, wú bù lì.
gān lín, wú yōu lì; jì yōu zhī, wú jiù.
zhì lín, wú jiù.
zhī lín, dà jūn zhī yí, jí.
dūn lín, jí, wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 思 (Image): sì (thought, care, the noun), as 陸德明 "息吏反" and the book

hexagrams.image: 風行地上，觀。先王以省方觀民設教。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 童觀，小人无咎，君子吝。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 闚觀，利女貞。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 觀我生進退。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 觀國之光，利用賓于王。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 觀我生，君子无咎。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 觀其生，君子无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 觀
hexagrams.name: 觀

wilhelm.name: Die Betrachtung, (der Anblick)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Betrachtung. Die Waschung ist geschehen, aber noch nicht die Darbringung. Vertrauensvoll blicken sie zu ihm auf.
wilhelm.image: Der Wind geht über die Erde hin: das Bild der Betrachtung. So besuchten die alten Könige die Weltgegenden, betrachteten das Volk und spendeten Belehrung.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Knabenhaftes Betrachten. Für einen geringen Menschen kein Makel. Für einen Edlen beschämend.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Betrachtung durch die Türspalte. Fördernd ist die Beharrlichkeit einer Frau.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Betrachtung meines Lebens entscheidet über Fortschritt oder Rückzug.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Betrachtung des Lichtes des Reiches. Fördernd ist es, als Gast eines Königs zu wirken.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Betrachtung meines Lebens. Der Edle ist ohne Makel.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Betrachtung seines Lebens. Der Edle ist ohne Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kwân
legge.judgment: Kwân shows (how he whom it represents should be like) the worshipper who has washed his hands, but not (yet) presented his offerings;—with sincerity and an appearance of dignity (commanding reverent regard).
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth, and that for wind moving above it, form Kwan. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, examined the (different) regions (of the kingdom), to see the (ways of the) people, and set forth their instructions.
lines: The first line, divided, shows the looking of a lad;—not blamable in men of inferior rank, but matter for regret in superior men.
The second line, divided, shows one peeping out from a door. It would be advantageous if it were (merely) the firm correctness of a female.
The third line, divided, shows one looking at (the course of) his own-life, to advance or recede (accordingly).
The fourth line, divided, shows one contemplating the glory of the kingdom. It will be advantageous for him, being such as he is, (to seek) to be a guest of the king.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject contemplating his own life(-course). A superior man, he will (thus) fall into no error.
The sixth line, undivided, shows its subject contemplating his character to see if it be indeed that of a superior man. He will not fall into error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 99-100 (Image: Appendix II, p. 292)

en.name: Contemplation (The View)
en.nameNote: 觀 is to look with attention; 陸德明 reads the name as showing, "示也". In the Spring and Autumn a 觀 was also a tower: the duke went up "觀臺" to record the cloud-signs (左傳, 655 BC). In the songs one looks over a site, then asks the turtle (Mao 50).
en.judgment: Washing, and not presenting. There is confirmation, solemn.
en.judgmentNote: 盥 is washing the hands before an offering: "澡手也" (說文). In the 儀禮 the washing comes before each presenting of dishes, 薦, and the rite opens with a casting of the stalks. 顒 is great-headed, grave in bearing: "其大有顒" (六月, Mao 177). Who washes, and whether "not" is "not yet", the text does not say.
en.tradition: Guan is having something to show others and being looked up to by them: the fifth line above, four yin looking up at it. The washing is cleansing the hands before the offering; the presenting is offering wine and food. Being pure and not acting lightly, one's good faith is within and one can be looked up to with awe: a warning to whoever divines to be so.
en.image: The wind goes over the earth: Contemplation. So the former kings inspected the regions, watched the people and set up teaching.
en.imageNote: A later layer. The wind is the command going over the earth, as the former kings' teaching is over the people (孔穎達). 程頤: where the people are lavish, restrain them with thrift; where thrifty, show them the rites.

lines.text: Watching as a child: for the small man, no blame; for the nobleman, trouble.
lines.note: 童 is a child, and in Zhou usage also a young servant: "童子佩觿" (芄蘭, Mao 60). 鄭玄: young; 馬融: alone. The same act has a verdict for each. 程頤: the common people see dimly, and that is no fault; a nobleman so would be shameful.

lines.text: Watching by peeping: a favourable divination for a woman.
lines.note: 闚 is to glance, with the gate in the graph (說文): a look through a door. The verdict stands again in 37. 虞翻: for a woman it is favourable not to look wantonly. The line gives a verdict for a woman and says nothing of a man.

lines.text: Watching my people advance and withdraw.
lines.note: In the Western Zhou bronzes the clans are 百生, written with 生: "我諸侯、百生" (集成 10174). The small image reads it so: "觀我生，觀民也". 王弼, 程頤 and 朱熹 read one's own conduct; Wilhelm and Legge my life. Whether the people advance or the watcher decides by them is left open.

lines.text: Watching the light of the state: favourable to use in being a guest to the king.
lines.note: In a casting for the boy 陳完 (左傳, told under 672 BC) a Zhou scribe met this line: he or his descendants will have a state elsewhere, guest to the king; the house later rose in Qi. Guests of the states were led into the Zhou temple (集成 02839). 光 is the founders' glory (毛公鼎).

lines.text: Watching my people: for the nobleman, no blame.
lines.note: As the third line: the bronzes' 百生, and this line's small image, "觀民也". 王弼: the high changes the low as the wind bends the grass, so it watches the people's customs to examine its own way.

lines.text: Watching their people: for the nobleman, no blame.
lines.note: 其, their, for the fifth line's 我, my. 王弼 reads the other way: the watcher watched by all under heaven. 朱熹: the same warning as the fifth, a small difference of host and guest.

essays.title: Wind over the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is earth, the upper wind. Two yang lines stand at the top over four yin: the figure is 臨 (19) turned upside down, and Shaughnessy names it "Looking Up". In the twelve-month scheme it is the eighth month's hexagram (朱熹), the month 19's judgment warns of. Every line has 觀, and the commentators divide them by who looks at whom: the hexagram means showing, the lines looking up at the fifth (朱熹).

essays.title: Watching before divining
essays.text: In the songs 觀 is surveying land, and once it is followed by the turtle. On the founding of a new capital: "he came down and looked over the mulberries; the turtle said auspicious, and in the end it was truly good" (定之方中, Mao 50). So 公劉 looks over the springs and streams choosing a site, and heaven "監觀四方" (皇矣, Mao 241).

readings.title: Washing the hands, or the poured libation?
readings.text: The 說文, 虞翻 and 朱熹 read washing the hands. 馬融: offering the cup and pouring it on the ground to bring down the spirit; 程頤 joins both. The Qin 歸藏's name 灌 is the libation's word. We print "washing", by the 說文 and the 儀禮's order.

readings.title: My people, my conduct, or my life?
readings.text: The small image of the fifth line and 虞翻 read the people; the bronzes write the clans 百生. 王弼 and 孔穎達: what goes out from me; 程頤 and 朱熹: my acts. Wilhelm and Legge: my life. We print "my people".

readings.title: Not presenting, or not yet?
readings.text: 王弼: one looks at the washing and not at the presenting. Wilhelm and Legge: not yet. 王肅's text has "washing, and watching the presenting". We print "not presenting", without "yet".

readings.title: The name: looking or showing?
readings.text: 陸德明 and the 彖 read the name as showing (guàn), the lines as looking (guān). We print "watching" in the lines, and Wilhelm's name.

pinyinTones.name: Guān
pinyinTones.judgment: guàn ér bù jiàn. yǒu fú yóng ruò.
pinyinTones.image: fēng xíng dì shàng, guān. xiān wáng yǐ xǐng fāng guān mín shè jiào.
lines: tóng guān, xiǎo rén wú jiù, jūn zǐ lìn.
kuī guān, lì nǚ zhēn.
guān wǒ shēng jìn tuì.
guān guó zhī guāng, lì yòng bīn yú wáng.
guān wǒ shēng, jūn zǐ wú jiù.
guān qí shēng, jūn zǐ wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 觀: guān (to look) throughout, as 陸德明 "餘不出者並音官" for the lines; he reads the name guàn ("官喚反，示也", to show), which the book records but does not print
省 (Image): xǐng (to inspect), as 陸德明 "悉井反"

hexagrams.image: 雷電噬嗑。先王以明罰勑法。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 屨校滅趾，无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 噬膚滅鼻，无咎。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 噬腊肉遇毒，小吝，无咎。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 噬乾胏，得金矢。利艱貞，吉。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 噬乾肉，得黃金。貞厲，无咎。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 何校滅耳，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 噬嗑
hexagrams.name: 噬嗑

wilhelm.name: Das Durchbeißen
wilhelm.judgment: Das Durchbeißen hat Gelingen. Fördernd ist es, Gericht walten zu lassen.
wilhelm.image: Donner und Blitz: das Bild des Durchbeißens. So festigten die früheren Könige die Gesetze durch klar bestimmte Strafen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Steckt mit den Füßen im Block, dass die Zehen verschwinden. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Beißt durch weiches Fleisch, dass die Nase verschwindet. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Beißt auf altes Dörrfleisch und trifft auf Giftiges. Kleine Beschämung. Kein Makel.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Beißt auf getrocknetes Knorpelfleisch. Erhält Metallpfeile. Fördernd ist es, der Schwierigkeiten eingedenk und beharrlich zu sein. Heil!
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Beißt auf getrocknetes Muskelfleisch. Erhält gelbes Gold. Beharrlich der Gefahr bewusst sein. Kein Makel.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Steckt mit dem Hals im hölzernen Kragen, dass die Ohren verschwinden. Unheil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Shih Ho
legge.judgment: Shih Ho indicates successful progress (in the condition of things which it supposes). It will be advantageous to use legal constraints.
legge.image: (The trigrams representing) thunder and lightning form Shih Ho. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, framed their penalties with intelligence, and promulgated their laws.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows one with his feet in the stocks and deprived of his toes. There will be no error.
The second line, divided, shows one biting through the soft flesh, and (going on to) bite off the nose. There will be no error.
The third line, divided, shows one gnawing dried flesh, and meeting with what is disagreeable. There will be occasion for some small regret, but no (great) error.

The fourth line, undivided, shows one gnawing the flesh dried on the bone, and getting the pledges of money and arrows. It will be advantageous to him to realise the difficulty of his task and be firm,—in which case there will be good fortune.
The fifth line, divided, shows one gnawing at dried flesh, and finding the yellow gold. Let him be firm and correct, realising the peril (of his position). There will be no error.
The sixth line, undivided, shows one wearing the cangue, and deprived of his ears. There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 101-102 (Image: Appendix II, p. 293)

en.name: Biting Through
en.nameNote: 噬嗑 is biting and closing the jaws: "噬，齧也。嗑，合也" (王弼). The 雜卦 says eating. The figure is the open jaws of 27 with the fourth line lodged between them. 噬 stands in four lines, 嗑 nowhere; the Qin 歸藏 names it 筮.
en.judgment: An offering. Favourable to use in trials.
en.judgmentNote: 獄 is a case at law. The 周禮 keeps it apart from 訟, the suit: a bundle of arrows is paid in before a suit, a jun of bronze before a case. A Western Zhou official is charged "訊訟罰", to hear suits and fine (集成 04215). A lord who lost a lawsuit saw his advocate killed (左傳, 632 BC).
en.tradition: To bite and close: where something is between, bite it and close. Yang above and below and empty within, the figure of the jaws; the one yang of the fourth line must be bitten before they close. What is between blocks; bitten and closed, there is passage. In conducting trials awe and clarity, held to the mean, are what count.
en.image: Thunder and lightning: Biting Through. So the former kings made the penalties clear and put the laws in order.
en.imageNote: A later layer, in the words of an early Zhou chapter: King Wen "克明德慎罰", made his virtue bright and was careful in punishing (尚書, 康誥). 程頤 and 朱熹 think 雷電 should be 電雷, as every other Image puts the upper trigram second.

lines.text: The stocks on the feet, the toes lost: no blame.
lines.note: The 周禮 grades fetters by offence. Cutting the feet was a Zhou punishment: "劓刖人" (康誥); "刖強鉏" (左傳, 678 BC). 校 is the wooden fetter (王弼). The Fuyang slips add "tying a prisoner in fetters and manacles: auspicious". The 繫辭: a small punishment and a great warning, the small man's good fortune.

lines.text: Biting the skin-meat, the nose lost: no blame.
lines.note: 膚 is an offering meat: "倫膚九，實于一鼎", nine pieces of skin-meat in one cauldron (儀禮, 少牢); 38 六五 has "厥宗噬膚" at the ancestral temple. Cutting the nose was a Zhou punishment (康誥). 程頤: 滅 is to sink, the nose buried in the meat.

lines.text: Biting dried meat, meeting poison: a little trouble; no blame.
lines.note: 腊 is dried game in the offerings: "腊用麋", the dried meat is elk (儀禮). 毒 is "害人之艸", a plant that harms men (說文). 王弼: the dried meat is those who do not submit, the poison the resentment that grows. 虞翻: the poison of arrows.

lines.text: Biting dried meat on the bone, getting a bronze arrow. A favourable divination about hardship: auspicious.
lines.note: 胏 is meat with the bone in (馬融). The dried meat is game, and game was shot: Kunst lists the arrowhead in the meat among the book's omens (via Shaughnessy). 朱熹 cites the 周禮's bronze and arrows paid in before a case. 金 in the Western Zhou is bronze (集成 02838).

lines.text: Biting dried meat, getting yellow bronze. The divination: danger. No blame.
lines.note: Bronze is the metal of payment and fines: the 周禮's jun of bronze before a case; "金作贖刑", metal for redeeming punishment (舜典, later). 黃金 is not in the held bronzes, which have 赤金 and 吉金. 朱熹: dried meat is harder than skin-meat and easier than meat on the bone.

lines.text: The cangue carried on the neck, the ears lost: disaster.
lines.note: 何 is 荷, to carry (王肅). The bronzes count the left ears cut from the enemy dead (集成 02839), a practice of war, not of law. The 繫辭: the bad piles up until it cannot be hidden. 王弼: the punishment reaches the head; no disaster is worse.

essays.title: Thunder and lightning
essays.text: The lower trigram is thunder, the upper fire and lightning. The 彖: moving and bright, thunder and lightning joined and manifest. 宋衷: thunder moves with awe, lightning with light; the way of punishment needs awe and clarity together.

essays.title: Two strands
essays.text: Four lines bite meats, each harder than the last (skin-meat, dried meat, meat on the bone, dried meat), and two find metal in them; the bottom and top lines are fetters and the body. The commentators make all six one figure of punishment: the outer lines, without place, are the punished; the middle four the punishers (朱熹). Read as a diviner's text, the meats are the offering meats of the cauldrons, and the fetters are what the judgment's trials end in.

readings.title: Punishment, or eating?
readings.text: Every commentator reads all six lines as punishment, inflicted or suffered. The 雜卦 says eating; the middle lines name the offering meats; the Zhou texts give nothing of biting as punishment. We translate the words and leave the two strands as the text has them.

readings.title: 滅: hidden, or cut off?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤, 虞翻 and Wilhelm: covered, sunk. Legge and Shaughnessy: cut off. The Zhou punishments of cutting the feet and nose favour the second for those lines; the Fuyang formula speaks only of fetters. We print "lost", which holds both.

readings.title: A bronze arrow, or bronze and arrows?
readings.text: 王弼, 陸績 and 程頤: metal and arrow as hardness and straightness. 朱熹 and Legge: the bronze and bundle of arrows paid in before a case. Kunst: an arrowhead found in the meat, an omen. We print "a bronze arrow", one thing found in the meat.

readings.title: 黃金: gold or bronze?
readings.text: Wilhelm and Legge: gold. We print "yellow bronze": the metal of the Western Zhou is bronze, and 朱熹 takes this 金 for the 周禮's jun of bronze.

pinyinTones.name: Shì Hé
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. lì yòng yù.
pinyinTones.image: léi diàn shì hé. xiān wáng yǐ míng fá chì fǎ.
lines: jù jiào miè zhǐ, wú jiù.
shì fū miè bí, wú jiù.
shì xī ròu yù dú, xiǎo lìn, wú jiù.
shì gān zǐ, dé jīn shǐ. lì jiān zhēn, jí.
shì gān ròu, dé huáng jīn. zhēn lì, wú jiù.
hè jiào miè ěr, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 嗑: hé (to close), as 陸德明 "胡臘反，合也"; not kè
校 (初九, 上九): jiào (the wooden cangue), as 馬融 "音教" in 陸德明; not xiào
腊 (六三): xī (dried meat), as 陸德明 "音昔"; not là (臘)
乾 (九四, 六五): gān (dried), as 陸德明 "音干"
何 (上九): hè (to carry, 荷), as 陸德明 "何可反" and 王肅 "荷擔"

hexagrams.image: 山下有火，賁。君子以明庶政，无敢折獄。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 賁其趾，舍車而徒。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 賁其須。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 賁如濡如，永貞吉。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 賁如皤如，白馬翰如，匪寇，婚媾。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 賁于丘園，束帛戔戔，吝，終吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 白賁，无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 賁
hexagrams.name: 賁

wilhelm.name: Die Anmut
wilhelm.judgment: Anmut hat Gelingen. Im Kleinen ist es fördernd, etwas zu unternehmen.
wilhelm.image: Unten am Berg ist das Feuer: das Bild der Anmut. So verfährt der Edle bei der Klarstellung der laufenden Angelegenheiten, aber er wagt es nicht, danach große Streitfragen zu entscheiden.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Macht seine Zehen anmutig, verlässt den Wagen und geht.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Macht seinen Kinnbart anmutig.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Anmutig und feucht. Dauernde Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Anmut oder Einfachheit? Ein weißes Pferd kommt wie geflogen: Nicht Räuber er ist, will freien zur Frist.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Anmut in Hügeln und Gärten. Das Seidenbündel ist ärmlich und klein. Beschämung, doch schließlich Heil.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Schlichte Anmut. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Pî
legge.judgment: Pî indicates that there should be free course (in what it denotes). There will be little advantage (however) if it be allowed to advance (and take the lead).
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain and that for fire under it form Pî. The superior man, in accordance with this, throws a brilliancy around his various processes of government, but does not dare (in a similar way) to decide cases of criminal litigation.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows one adorning (the way of) his feet. He can discard a carriage and walk on foot.
The second line, divided, shows one adorning his beard.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject with the appearance of being adorned and bedewed (with rich favours). But let him ever maintain his firm correctness, and there will be good fortune.

The fourth line, divided, shows one looking as if adorned, but only in white. As if (mounted on) a white horse, and furnished with wings, (he seeks union with the subject of the first line), while (the intervening third pursues), not as a robber, but intent on a matrimonial alliance.

The fifth line, divided, shows its subject adorned by (the occupants of) the heights and gardens. He bears his roll of silk, small and slight. He may appear stingy; but there will be good fortune in the end.
The sixth line, undivided, shows one with white as his (only) ornament. There will be no error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 103-104 (Image: Appendix II, p. 294)

en.name: Grace
en.nameNote: 賁 is ornament, pattern: "飾也", with the cowrie in the graph (說文). In a song the bright white colt comes "賁然", in splendour (白駒, Mao 186). Written 蕡 it is the fullness of fruit (桃夭, Mao 6). The 雜卦: Bi is without colour.
en.judgment: An offering. Favourable in small things to have somewhere to go.
en.judgmentNote: 亨 is the offering, as in hexagram 1. 小利 with a matter is the shape of 小利貞, a divination favourable in small things. The shelf gives nothing more for the judgment.
en.tradition: Bi is ornament: the soft coming to pattern the strong, the strong going up to pattern the soft; brightness within and stopping without, each in its share. Since the yang is helped by the yin and brightness is within, success; since the strong goes up to adorn the soft and stopping is without, favourable in small things to have somewhere to go.
en.image: Under the mountain there is fire: Grace. So the noble one makes the many affairs of government clear, and does not dare to decide trials.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 獄 is the graver case at law of 21. 程頤: trials need the plain facts, and ornament hides them. 朱熹: fire under a mountain does not light far; the many affairs are small matters, trials great ones.

lines.text: Adorning his toes: leaving the cart and going on foot.
lines.note: 車 and 徒, chariot and foot, are the two parts of a Zhou host and a hunt: "徒御不驚" (車攻, Mao 179). 鄭玄's text had 輿, the cart box. 趾 comes only in bottom lines (Shaughnessy). 程頤: if riding is not right, the nobleman will rather walk.

lines.text: Adorning his beard.
lines.note: 須 is the beard: "面毛也" (說文). The line has no verdict. 侯果: the lines above form the jaw, and the second is under it. 程頤: the beard moves with the jaw; good and bad lie in the substance, not the ornament.

lines.text: Adorned, glossy. The divination for the long run: auspicious.
lines.note: 濡如 in the songs is the gloss of fine things: "六轡如濡", the six reins glossy (皇皇者華, Mao 163; 毛傳: fresh and lustrous); "羔裘如濡" (Mao 80). 朱熹: it must not drown in its ease, hence the warning of the long run.

lines.text: Adorned, white. A white horse, as if flying. Not raiders: a marriage.
lines.note: 皤 is the white of an old man's hair (說文, quoting this line). 翰 in the songs is a bird's high flight: "翰飛戾天" (小宛, Mao 196); 鄭玄 reads it white, and the 檀弓 says the Yin drove white 翰 horses to war. "Not raiders: a marriage" are the words of 3 六二, a marriage party.

lines.text: Adorning at the hill garden. The bundle of silk, scant: trouble; in the end, auspicious.
lines.note: 束帛 is the betrothal gift: "玄纁束帛、儷皮", black and red silk and a pair of deerskins (儀禮, 士昏禮), sent after an auspicious crack at the temple. A Western Zhou lady gives "帛束" in return (集成 04195). 朱熹: 戔戔 is shallow and small; in ceremonies thrift is better than extravagance.

lines.text: White adorning: no blame.
lines.note: The 雜卦's "Bi is without colour" is this line. 王弼: at the end of ornament, ornament returns to plainness. 程頤: not no ornament, but not letting the flower bury the fruit.

essays.title: Fire under the mountain
essays.text: The lower trigram is fire, the upper the mountain. 王廙: the mountain, with its tiers and peaks, is already like carving; add the fire's light and the pattern shows the more. The figure is 21 turned upside down.

essays.title: From the toes to a bride
essays.text: The lines run from the toes to the beard and then to a bride and her gifts: the white horse and "not raiders: a marriage", the words of 3 六二, and the bundle of silk, which in the 儀禮 is the betrothal gift.

readings.title: The line sequence: a bride?
readings.text: The white horse, "not raiders: a marriage" and the bundle of silk are the words of a marriage party and its gifts. The commentators read degrees of ornament and the ruler's thrift; 荀爽 and "the scholars" in 孔穎達 a recluse summoned. We translate the words; the reading is not built into them.

readings.title: 翰如: flying, or white?
readings.text: 程頤, 朱熹 and 馬融 read flying high, as the songs' 翰飛. 鄭玄: white, as the 檀弓's 翰. 董遇: the horse's head held high. We print "as if flying".

readings.title: 戔戔: scant, or heaped?
readings.text: 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge: scant. 馬融, 薛虞, 虞翻 and 孔穎達: heaped, abundant. 程頤: cut up. We print "scant", which agrees with the verdict "trouble".

readings.title: 賁: adorning, patterned, or many?
readings.text: The 說文, 毛傳 and every commentator: to adorn. 傅氏: 斑, patterned; 王肅: yellow and white. Mawangdui writes 蘩. We print "adorning", and keep Wilhelm's name.

pinyinTones.name: Bì
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. xiǎo lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
pinyinTones.image: shān xià yǒu huǒ, bì. jūn zǐ yǐ míng shù zhèng, wú gǎn zhé yù.
lines: bì qí zhǐ, shě chē ér tú.
bì qí xū.
bì rú rú rú, yǒng zhēn jí.
bì rú pó rú, bái mǎ hàn rú, fěi kòu, hūn gòu.
bì yú qiū yuán, shù bó jiān jiān, lìn, zhōng jí.
bái bì, wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 賁: bì (adorned), as 陸德明 "彼僞反"; not bēn
舍 (初九): shě (to leave), as 陸德明 "音捨"

hexagrams.image: 山附於地，剝。上以厚下安宅。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 剝床以足，蔑貞凶。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 剝床以辨，蔑貞凶。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 剝之无咎。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 剝床以膚，凶。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 貫魚，以宮人寵，无不利。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 碩果不食，君子得輿，小人剝廬。

hexagrams.heading: 剝
hexagrams.name: 剝

wilhelm.name: Die Zersplitterung
wilhelm.judgment: Die Zersplitterung. Nicht fördernd ist es, wohin zu gehen.
wilhelm.image: Der Berg ruht auf der Erde: das Bild der Zersplitterung. So können die Oberen nur durch reiches Spenden an die Unteren ihre Stellung sichern.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Das Bett wird zersplittert am Bein. Die Beharrlichen werden vernichtet. Unheil.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Das Bett wird zersplittert am Rand. Die Beharrlichen werden vernichtet. Unheil.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Er zersplittert sich mit Ihnen. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Das Bett wird zersplittert bis zur Haut. Unheil.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Ein Zug Fische. Durch die Palastdamen kommt Gunst. Alles ist förderlich.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Eine große Frucht ist noch ungegessen da. Der Edle erhält einen Wagen. Dem Gemeinen zersplittert sein Haus.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Po
legge.judgment: Po indicates that (in the state which it symbolises) it will not be advantageous to make a movement in any direction whatever.
legge.image: (The trigrams representing) the earth, and (above it) that for a mountain, which adheres to the earth, form Po. Superiors, in accordance with this, seek to strengthen those below them, to secure the peace and stability of their own position.
lines: The first line, divided, shows one overturning the couch by injuring its legs. (The injury will go on to) the destruction of (all) firm correctness, and there will be evil.
The second line, divided, shows one overthrowing the couch by injuring its frame. (The injury will go on to) the destruction of (all) firm correctness, and there will be evil.
The third line, divided, shows its subject among the overthrowers; but there will be no error.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject having overthrown the couch, and (going to injure) the skin (of him who lies on it). There will be evil.

The fifth line, divided, shows (its subject leading on the others like) a string of fishes, and (obtaining for them) the favour that lights on the inmates of the palace. There will be advantage in every way.

The topmost line, undivided, shows its subject (as) a great fruit which has not been eaten. The superior man finds (the people again) as a chariot carrying him. The small men (by their course) overthrow their own dwellings.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 105-106 (Image: Appendix II, p. 296)

en.name: Splintering
en.nameNote: 剝 is to strip, flay, split off: "裂也" (說文); "落也", to fall away (馬融). In the Zhou texts it is flaying at an offering, "或剝或亨" (楚茨, Mao 209), paring melons for the ancestor (信南山, Mao 210), and knocking down dates, "八月剝棗" (七月, Mao 154).
en.judgment: Not favourable to have somewhere to go.
en.judgmentNote: In the Shang bones 利 and 不利 answer the question (合集 36536): the judgment is the bare negative verdict on going. The line names no one. A 歸藏 entry under this name: "良人得其玉，小人得其粟", the good man gets his jade, the small man gets his grain.
en.tradition: Bo is falling away: five yin below and growing, one yang above and about to end: the hexagram of the ninth month. The yin strong and the yang weak, the small men thrive and the nobleman suffers; earth within and the mountain without give the figure of going along with the time and stopping: so whoever gets it in a casting may not go anywhere.
en.image: The mountain clings to the earth: Splintering. So those above give generously to those below, and make the dwellings safe.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 宅, a dwelling and a settlement, is divined in an early Zhou document: "卜宅", the Grand Protector divined about the settlement at Luo (尚書, 召誥). 程頤: stripping of those above always begins below.

lines.text: Stripping the bed at the legs. No divination: disaster.
lines.note: The bed in the songs is where one sleeps and a newborn son is laid (斯干, Mao 189); in the 儀禮 the dying are laid on one. 蔑 is "none" in the Zhou texts: "喪亂蔑資" (板, Mao 254; 毛傳 "無"). 鄭玄 reads slighting, 王弼 paring, 朱熹 destroying.

lines.text: Stripping the bed at the joint. No divination: disaster.
lines.note: The shelf gives nothing for 辨 as a part of a bed or body in Zhou texts. 鄭玄: below the knee, where the leg bends; "辯，分也". 孔穎達: where the legs and the body of the bed part. 程頤 and 朱熹: the frame.

lines.text: Stripping them: no blame.
lines.note: 陸德明's text read 剝无咎, without 之. 王弼: the yin lines all strip the yang; this one alone answers the top line and sides with it. 程頤: siding with the right, it is alone and weak: only no blame.

lines.text: Stripping the bed at the skin: disaster.
lines.note: Flaying at an offering: "或剝或亨" (楚茨). 膚 is the skin-meat of the offering cauldron in 21; 京房's text has 簠, an offering vessel. 王弼: the bed stripped through, it reaches the person. 崔憬: the bed's skin is its mat. 程頤: no longer "no divination", only disaster.

lines.text: Stringing fish: with the palace people, favour. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: Fish are an omen of plenty: "眾維魚矣，實維豐年" (無羊, Mao 190), and fourteen fish go into the marriage cauldron (士昏禮). 貫 is to pierce and string. 宮人 are the palace people (左傳, 524 BC). 程頤: the yin lines in order like strung fish win the favour of the yang above.

lines.text: A big fruit, not eaten. The nobleman gets a cart; the small man strips the hut.
lines.note: 碩 is big: "碩鼠" (Mao 113). 廬 is a hut lived in for a season (說文): the field huts of 信南山, beside the pared melons. The 歸藏's good man and small man are set against each other as here. 程頤: the last yang left, a fruit that will grow again.

essays.title: A mountain on the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is earth, the upper the mountain. Five yin lines run up under one yang: the commentators' figure of the yin stripping the yang from below, the small men the nobleman. 鄭玄: the yin breath encroaches up to the fifth line, and all things fall and scatter. 朱熹: the ninth month's hexagram. The figure is 24 turned upside down; Shaughnessy suggests the picture itself, one solid line left at the top, could have suggested the name.

essays.title: The bed
essays.text: The lines climb a bed: its legs, its joint, then the skin. The fifth and top lines change the figure: strung fish and palace people, then a fruit, a cart and a hut. Read as a diviner's text, the lines give a bed stripped from the legs up and two verdicts of "no divination"; the commentators read small men wearing away the nobleman.

readings.title: 蔑貞: none, slighting, paring, or destroying?
readings.text: 馬融 and 程頤: none. 鄭玄: slighting. 王弼 and 孔穎達: paring. 荀爽's text 滅; 朱熹: destroying. We print "No divination": the Zhou sense of 蔑 is "none", set before a noun as here. The 國語's verb and 鄭玄's own gloss make "slighting the divination" the strongest alternative.

readings.title: 辨: the joint, the frame, the slats, or the leg?
readings.text: 馬融, 鄭玄 and 王弼: above the foot. 黃穎: the slats. 崔憬: the crosspiece. 程頤 and 朱熹: the frame. 虞翻: between the fingers. We print "the joint".

readings.title: 得輿 or 德車?
readings.text: The base and the main line of commentators have 得輿, the nobleman gets a cart. 京房 has 德輿, 董遇 德車, and 虞翻 reads virtue taken for a cart. We print 得輿.

readings.title: Who gives favour to whom?
readings.text: 王弼: the ruler favours the small men no more than palace people. 何妥: the consorts in their order. 程頤 and 朱熹: the yin lines, led in a string, receive favour from the yang above. The line names none of them.

pinyinTones.name: Bō
pinyinTones.judgment: bù lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
pinyinTones.image: shān fù yú dì, bō. shàng yǐ hòu xià ān zhái.
lines: bō chuáng yǐ zú, miè zhēn xiōng.
bō chuáng yǐ biàn, miè zhēn xiōng.
bō zhī wú jiù.
bō chuáng yǐ fū, xiōng.
guàn yú, yǐ gōng rén chǒng, wú bù lì.
shuò guǒ bù shí, jūn zǐ dé yú, xiǎo rén bō lú.

pinyinNotes: 剝: bō, the reading of the written language, as 陸德明 "邦角反"; not the colloquial bāo

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。出入无疾。朋來无咎。反復其道，七日來復。利有攸往。
hexagrams.image: 雷在地中，復。先王以至日閉關，商旅不行，后不省方。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 不遠復，无祗悔，元吉。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 休復，吉。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 頻復，厲，无咎。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 中行獨復。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 敦復，无悔。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 迷復，凶，有災眚。用行師，終有大敗，以其國君凶，至于十年不克征。

hexagrams.heading: 復
hexagrams.name: 復

wilhelm.name: Die Wiederkehr, (die Wendezeit)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Wiederkehr. Gelingen. Ausgang und Eingang ohne Fehl. Freunde kommen ohne Makel. Hin und her geht der Weg. Am siebten Tage kommt die Wiederkehr. Fördernd ist es, zu haben, wohin man geht.
wilhelm.image: Der Donner inmitten der Erde: das Bild der Wendezeit. So schlossen die alten Könige zur Sonnwendzeit die Pässe. Händler und Fremdlinge wanderten nicht, und der Herrscher bereiste nicht die Gegenden.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Wiederkehr aus geringer Entfernung. Es bedarf keiner Reue. Großes Heil!
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Ruhige Wiederkehr. Heil!
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Mehrfache Wiederkehr. Gefahr. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: In der Mitte der andern wandelnd, kehrt man allein wieder.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Großzügige Wiederkehr. Keine Reue.

Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Verfehlung der Wiederkehr. Unheil. Unglück von außen und innen. Wenn man so Heere marschieren lässt, wird man schließlich eine große Niederlage erleiden, so dass es für den Landesherrn unheilvoll ist. Zehn Jahre lang ist man nicht mehr imstande anzugreifen.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Fû
legge.judgment: Fû indicates that there will be free course and progress (in what it denotes). (The subject of it) finds no one to distress him in his exits and entrances; friends come to him, and no error is committed. He will return and repeat his (proper) course. In seven days comes his return. There will be advantage in whatever direction movement is made.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth and that for thunder in the midst of it form Fû. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, on the day of the (winter) solstice, shut the gates of the passes (from one state to another), so that the travelling merchants could not (then) pursue their journeys, nor the princes go on with the inspection of their states.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject returning (from an error) of no great extent, which would not proceed to anything requiring repentance. There will be great good fortune.
The second line, divided, shows the admirable return (of its subject). There will be good fortune.
The third line, divided, shows one who has made repeated returns. The position is perilous, but there will be no error.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject moving right in the centre (among those represented by the other divided lines), and yet returning alone (to his proper path).
The fifth line, divided, shows the noble return of its subject. There will be no ground for repentance.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject all astray on the subject of returning. There will be evil. There will be calamities and errors. If with his views he put the hosts in motion, the end will be a great defeat, whose issues will extend to the ruler of the state. Even in ten years he will not be able to repair the disaster.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 107-108 (Image: Appendix II, p. 297)

en.name: The Return (The Turning Point)
en.nameNote: 復 is to go back, to come back: "往來也" (說文); "反也，還也" (陸德明). The 序卦: exhausted at the top, it turns back below, so Fu follows 剝. The 繫辭 calls it the root of virtue. The word is the book's own: 9 初九 "復自道".
en.judgment: An offering. Going out and coming in: no illness. Friends come: no blame. Turning back and returning on its road: in seven days it comes back. Favourable to have somewhere to go.
en.judgmentNote: The Shang asked about the king's illness (合集 00456正). "Going out and coming in" is the span of the Chu yearly divinations for service to the king (包山 197). The Shang verification counts days: "七日丁亥既執", in seven days they had been seized (合集 00643丙正). A casting of 575 BC met Fu before Yanling (左傳).
en.tradition: Fu is the yang coming back to life below; gone and come back, so it gets through. The reading is that one's own going out and coming in are without illness, and friends who come are without blame; seven lines from the first yin of 姤 the yang returns, the course of heaven; and the strong growing, favourable to have somewhere to go. Seven days is the term the reading gives for the return.
en.image: Thunder in the middle of the earth: The Return. So the former kings, on the solstice day, shut the passes; merchants and travellers did not go; the sovereign did not inspect the regions.
en.imageNote: A later layer. The solstice was recorded: "日南至", the duke went up the watchtower to look (左傳, 655 BC). The 月令 (later) has gates plastered up at midwinter. 程頤: the yang just born is very weak and grows only in quiet.

lines.text: Returning from not far: no coming to regret. Greatly auspicious.
lines.note: 祇 in the songs is "just, come to": "祇自疧兮", you will only make yourself sick (Mao 206; "適也"). 程頤 and 朱熹: "抵也", reaching. The 繫辭 applies the line to Master Yan's son, who never did a wrong twice. 韓康伯: great; 鄭玄: illness; 王肅: ease.

lines.text: Fine returning: auspicious.
lines.note: 休 in the Western Zhou is the fine thing given and the fine outcome of a divination: "卜休" (洛誥). The Fuyang slips add after this line "出妻皆復", wives who have left all come back. 王弼: it lowers itself to the humane first line.

lines.text: Returning again and again: danger; no blame.
lines.note: 頻 in a Zhou song: "國步斯頻" (桑柔, Mao 257), where 鄭箋 reads "比也", one after another, and 毛傳 "急也", pressing. In 召旻 毛傳 glosses it the edge. 王弼 and 虞翻: a frown. 程頤: returning often, often losing it.

lines.text: In the middle file, returning alone.
lines.note: 中行 is a column of an army: "荀林父將中行" (左傳, 632 BC). The line has no verdict. 王弼: the fourth, between two yin above and two below, alone answers the first line. 虞翻: the middle is the first line, and the common reading is wrong.

lines.text: Thick returning: no regret.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the line in the received words. 敦 in the bronzes is pressing an attack (宗周鐘); every commentator reads 厚, thick. 王弼: not up to the fine returning, but returning in thickness, regret can be escaped.

lines.text: Returning, losing the way: disaster. There is calamity and blight. Using it to march the army: in the end, a great defeat; with the lord of its state, disaster. Coming to ten years, not able to campaign.
lines.note: Quoted in 545 BC (左傳): the king of Chu "wants to get back his wish and throws away the root; returning, he has nowhere to go back to", and for close on ten years Chu will not care for the lords. He died that year. 子夏傳: harm done is 災, an ominous sign 眚.

essays.title: Thunder in the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is thunder, the upper earth. One yang line at the bottom under five yin: the figure is 23 turned upside down, and the commentators read the two as the yang stripped away at the top and coming back at the bottom. 荀爽: the hexagram of the winter solstice; 朱熹: the eleventh month. Every line but the fourth names a kind of returning in two words, the manner first and 復 second.

essays.title: The heart of heaven and earth
essays.text: On the 彖's "天地之心", 王弼: returning is going back to the root; heaven and earth take the root as their heart, and stillness and utter nothing are the root. 程頤 answers him: the earlier scholars all took stillness for heaven and earth's heart; they did not know that the first stir of movement is.

readings.title: 七日: days or months?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤 (seven changes), 朱熹 (seven lines from 姤) and the 易緯 reckoning: days. 侯果, 褚氏 and 莊氏: months, the ancients calling months days; Legge agrees. We print "seven days": the book counts days in 51 and 63, and the Shang verifications count days.

readings.title: 祗: come to, great, illness, ease, or a particle?
readings.text: 程頤 and 朱熹: reaching, the songs' "適也". 韓康伯, 侯果 and 孔穎達: "no great regret". 鄭玄: illness. 王肅's text 禔, ease. 馬融 and 陸德明: a particle. We print "no coming to regret".

readings.title: 頻: again and again, pressing, frowning, or the brink?
readings.text: 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge: again and again, with 鄭箋's "比也" in a Zhou song. 毛傳: pressing. 王弼, 虞翻 and 侯果: frowning. 毛傳 on 召旻: the edge, "returning at the brink". We print "again and again".

readings.title: 中行: where is the middle?
readings.text: 王弼: the fourth line in the middle of the yin lines. 虞翻: the first line, calling the other reading common and wrong. We print "the middle file" and leave where it is.

readings.title: 以其國君凶: using, or reaching to?
readings.text: 孔穎達: 以 is using it in the state. 朱熹: reaching to the lord. 荀爽: the lord is the first line. We print "with".

pinyinTones.name: Fù
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. chū rù wú jí. péng lái wú jiù. fǎn fù qí dào, qī rì lái fù. lì yǒu yōu wǎng.

lines: bù yuǎn fù, wú zhī huǐ, yuán jí.
xiū fù, jí.
pín fù, lì, wú jiù.
zhōng xíng dú fù.
dūn fù, wú huǐ.

pinyinNotes: 省 (Image): xǐng (to inspect), as 陸德明 "悉井反" in 20
祗 (初九): zhī, as 陸德明 "音支"

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨，利貞。其匪正有眚，不利有攸往。
hexagrams.image: 天下雷行，物與无妄。先王以茂對時育萬物。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 无妄，往吉。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 不耕穫，不菑畬，則利有攸往。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 无妄之災，或繫之牛，行人之得，邑人之災。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 可貞，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 无妄之疾，勿藥有喜。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 无妄，行有眚，无攸利。

hexagrams.heading: 无妄
hexagrams.name: 无妄

wilhelm.name: Die Unschuld, (das Unerwartete)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Unschuld. Erhabenes Gelingen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Wenn jemand nicht recht ist, so hat er Unglück, und nicht fördernd ist es, irgend etwas zu unternehmen.
wilhelm.image: Unter dem Himmel geht der Donner: alle Dinge erlangen den Naturzustand der Unschuld. So pflegten und nährten die alten Könige, reich an Tugend und entsprechend der Zeit, alle Wesen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Unschuldiger Wandel bringt Heil!
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Wenn man beim Pflügen nicht ans Ernten denkt und beim Roden nicht an das Benützen des Feldes: dann ist es fördernd, etwas zu unternehmen.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Unverschuldetes Unglück: Die Kuh, die von jemand angebunden war, ist des Wanderers Gewinn, des Bürgers Verlust.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Wer vermag beharrlich zu sein, bleibt ohne Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Bei unverschuldeter Krankheit gebrauche keine Arznei. Es wird schon von selber gut werden.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Unschuldiges Handeln bringt Unglück. Nichts ist fördernd.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Wû Wang
legge.judgment: Wû Wang indicates great progress and success, while there will be advantage in being firm and correct. If (its subject and his action) be not correct, he will fall into errors, and it will not be advantageous for him to move in any direction.
legge.image: The thunder rolls all under the sky, and to (every)thing there is given (its nature), free from all insincerity. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, (made their regulations) in complete accordance with the seasons, thereby nourishing all things.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject free from all insincerity. His advance will be accompanied with good fortune.

The second line, divided, shows one who reaps without having ploughed (that he might reap), and gathers the produce of his third year’s fields without having cultivated them the first year for that end. To such a one there will be advantage in whatever direction he may move.

The third line, divided, shows calamity happening to one who is free from insincerity;—as in the case of an ox that has been tied up. A passer by finds it (and carries it off), while the people in the neighbourhood have the calamity (of being accused and apprehended).
The fourth line, undivided, shows (a case) in which, if its subject can remain firm and correct, there will be no error.
The fifth line, undivided, shows one who is free from insincerity, and yet has fallen ill. Let him not use medicine, and he will have occasion for joy (in his recovery).
The topmost line, undivided, shows its subject free from insincerity, yet sure to fall into error, if he take action. (His action) will not be advantageous in any way.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 109-111 (Image: Appendix II, p. 299)

en.name: Innocence (The Unexpected)
en.nameNote: 妄 is disorder, falseness: "亂也" (說文). For 馬融, 鄭玄 and 王肅 it is 望, expectation: nothing hoped for. The manuscripts write 亡忘, 毋亡, 无亡, 无孟: the word was heard more surely than it was written. The 雜卦: it is calamity.
en.judgment: A great offering. A favourable divination. If it is not correct, there is blight: not favourable to have somewhere to go.
en.judgmentNote: The Zhouyuan oracle bones (Western Zhou) end their charges with wishes: "囟又正", may there be correctness, and "囟亡眚", may there be no blight (H11:1, H11:20; via Shaughnessy). The judgment's 正 and 眚 are those words. The Fuyang slips add divinations about rain, serving the lord, hunting and fishing.
en.tradition: No recklessness is the natural working of the true pattern; the 史記's "nothing looked for" is another sense that works. Thunder moving and heaven strong, the fifth line central and answering the second: so the reading is a great getting through, favourable for holding to what is right; if not right, there is blight and no going anywhere is favourable.
en.image: Under heaven thunder goes; all things share in it: Innocence. So the former kings, in abundance, matched the seasons and nurtured the myriad things.
en.imageNote: A later layer. In the 月令 (later) the spring thunder sounds forth and the creatures in the ground stir and come out. 九家易: the yang breath reaches everywhere and no thing is left out; things receive it and live.

lines.text: Unlooked-for: going on, auspicious.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "亡忘，吉", without 往; the Fuyang slips add a divination about hunting and fishing: something got. 程頤 reconciles the line with the judgment: go by the way of no recklessness.

lines.text: Not ploughing, yet reaping; not breaking new ground, yet a third-year field: then favourable to have somewhere to go.
lines.note: Fields by their years: "歲曰菑，二歲曰新田，三歲曰畬" (爾雅); "如何新畬" (臣工, Mao 276). The words are the Zhou farm calendar's. The Chu slip has "不耕而穫". 王弼: finishing what another has made, the minister's way. 朱熹: doing nothing before, hoping for nothing after.

lines.text: An unlooked-for calamity: someone ties up an ox; the traveller's gain, the townspeople's calamity.
lines.note: An early document forbids chasing strayed oxen and stealing horses and oxen (尚書, 費誓). 行人 in the songs is a man on the road (載驅, Mao 105), in the 左傳 an envoy. 朱熹: a traveller leads off an ox, and those who live there are questioned for it.

lines.text: It may be divined. No blame.
lines.note: The Chu slip: "可貞，亡咎". 可貞 is a matter fit to be put to the oracle. 程頤: 可貞 is not 利貞; its place can be held firmly. 朱熹: a reading against undertaking anything.

lines.text: An unlooked-for illness: do not dose it; there is joy.
lines.note: An illness beyond medicine: the Qin doctor finds the lord of Jin's "above the diaphragm and below the heart", where "藥不至焉", and he died as the shaman foretold (左傳, 581 BC). 喜 is a verdict of the Chu records; the Chu slip has 菜. The small image: the medicine is not to be tried.

lines.text: Unlooked-for: going, there is blight. Nothing is favourable.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the received words. 眚 is the Zhouyuan charges' "囟亡眚". 行, going, is set against the first line's 往吉. 王弼: at the extreme, keep still and guard oneself.

essays.title: Thunder under heaven
essays.text: The lower trigram is thunder, the upper heaven. The 彖: the strong comes from outside and becomes master within, moving and strong. 无妄 heads three lines and is joined to two misfortunes, a calamity and an illness. Shaughnessy is tempted to relate the manuscripts' names to forest demons, which would make 无妄 a malady to be propitiated, and then prefers a literal translation.

readings.title: No recklessness, or nothing looked for?
readings.text: 陸德明, the 說文, the 序卦, 王弼 and 程頤: no recklessness; Wilhelm's "Unschuld". 馬融, 鄭玄, 王肅, 京房 and the 史記: nothing looked for. We print "unlooked-for" in the lines, the oldest gloss we hold, which reads the calamity and the illness as they stand. The name stays Wilhelm's.

readings.title: 其匪正: the conduct, or the divination?
readings.text: The commentators: if one is not right in conduct. The Zhouyuan charges use 正 and 眚 of the divination itself. We print "if it is not correct" and leave which.

readings.title: Without ploughing, yet reaping; or neither?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤, 孔穎達 and the Chu slip (不耕而穫): reaping without having ploughed. 朱熹 and Wilhelm: no work begun, no harvest looked for. We print "not ploughing, yet reaping".

readings.title: Who takes the ox?
readings.text: 王弼 and 孔穎達: an officer seizes it from one who presumed to plough. 程頤: a supposition, gain against loss. 朱熹 and Legge: a traveller leads it off and the townspeople are blamed. We print the words.

pinyinTones.name: Wú Wàng
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng, lì zhēn. qí fěi zhèng yǒu shěng, bù lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
pinyinTones.image: tiān xià léi xíng, wù yǔ wú wàng. xiān wáng yǐ mào duì shí yù wàn wù.
lines: wú wàng, wǎng jí.
bù gēng huò, bù zī yú, zé lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
wú wàng zhī zāi, huò xì zhī niú, xíng rén zhī dé, yì rén zhī zāi.
kě zhēn, wú jiù.
wú wàng zhī jí, wù yào yǒu xǐ.
wú wàng, xíng yǒu shěng, wú yōu lì.

pinyinNotes: 菑 (六二): zī (first-year field), as 陸德明 "側其反"; not zāi
畬 (六二): yú (third-year field), as 陸德明 "音餘"; not shē

hexagrams.judgment: 利貞。不家食，吉。利涉大川。
hexagrams.image: 天在山中，大畜。君子以多識前言往行以畜其德。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 有厲，利己。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 輿說輹。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 良馬逐，利艱貞，曰閑輿衛，利有攸往。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 童牛之牿，元吉。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 豶豕之牙，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 何天之衢，亨。

hexagrams.heading: 大畜
hexagrams.name: 大畜

wilhelm.name: Des Großen Zähmungskraft
wilhelm.judgment: Des Großen Zähmungskraft. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Nicht zu Hause essen bringt Heil. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren.
wilhelm.image: Der Himmel inmitten des Berges: das Bild von des Großen Zähmungskraft. So lernt der Edle viele Worte der Vorzeit und Taten der Vergangenheit kennen, um dadurch seinen Charakter zu festigen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Es ist Gefahr da. Fördernd ist es, abzustehen.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Dem Wagen werden die Achsenlager abgenommen.

Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Ein gutes Pferd, das andern folgt. Fördernd ist Bewusstsein der Gefahr und Beharrlichkeit. Täglich übe dich im Wagenfahren und Waffenschutz. Fördernd ist es, zu haben, wohin man geht.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Das Schutzbrett eines jungen Stieres. Großes Heil!
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Eines verschnittenen Ebers Zahn. Heil!
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Man erlangt den Himmelsweg. Gelingen.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Tâ Khû
legge.judgment: Under the conditions of Tâ Khû it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. (If its subject do not seek to) enjoy his revenues in his own family (without taking service at court), there will be good fortune. It will be advantageous for him to cross the great stream.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain, and in the midst of it that (representing) heaven, form Tâ Khû. The superior man, in accordance with this, stores largely in his memory the words and deeds of former men, to subserve the accumulation of his virtue.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject in a position of peril. It will be advantageous for him to stop his advance.
The second line, undivided, shows a carriage with the strap under it removed.

The third line, undivided, shows its subject urging his way with good horses. It will be advantageous for him to realise the difficulty (of his course), and to be firm and correct, exercising himself daily in his charioteering and methods of defence; then there will be advantage in whatever direction he may advance.
The fourth line, divided, shows the young bull, (and yet) having the piece of wood over his horns. There will be great good fortune.
The fifth line, divided, shows the teeth of a castrated hog. There will be good fortune.
The sixth line, undivided, shows its subject (as) in command of the firmament of heaven. There will be progress.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 112-113 (Image: Appendix II, p. 300)

en.name: The Taming Power of the Great
en.nameNote: 畜 is to keep, to store, to rear; its other sense is livestock (Shaughnessy: "Greater Livestock"). The word is in none of the lines, but three lines have a horse, an ox and a pig. 向秀: the mountain stopping the great vessel of heaven.
en.judgment: A favourable divination. Not eating at home: auspicious. Favourable to ford the great river.
en.judgmentNote: To eat is to live from a source: "公食貢，大夫食邑，士食田，庶人食力", the duke eats from tribute, the officers from their towns, the knights from their fields, the commoners from their labour (國語, 晉語四). The Chu slip writes "不家而食，吉". Where one eats instead, the words do not say.
en.tradition: Great is the yang; the mountain taming heaven is taming the great; heaven strong within, the mountain solid and shining without, renewing its virtue daily. So the reading is favourable for holding to what is right, and not eating at home is auspicious; the fifth answers heaven below, so favourable to ford the great river. Not eating at home is drawing a salary at court.
en.image: Heaven within the mountain: The Taming Power of the Great. So the noble one learns many words of former times and deeds of the past, to store up his virtue.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 朱熹: there need be no such thing as heaven within a mountain; it is said only of the figure. 程頤: in a person, learning and virtue stored within are the great store.

lines.text: There is danger: favourable to stop.
lines.note: The Chu slip has "有厲利巳", the oldest use of 厲 for danger on the shelf. The base's 己 is read as 已, to stop, with 陸德明's first reading and every commentator; 姚信 read "oneself". 王弼: the fourth line is taming it and may not be challenged.

lines.text: The cart sheds its axle-block.
lines.note: The same omen is in 9 九三 and in a casting of 645 BC: "車說其輹，火焚其旗", the carriage sheds its axle-block, fire burns its banner (左傳). 輹 is the block that holds the box on the axle, the "crouching hare" (釋名). Kunst counts it among the book's omens. Mishap or a halt, the line does not say.

lines.text: Good horses chasing. A favourable divination about hardship. It says: drill the carts and the guard. Favourable to have somewhere to go.
lines.note: "良馬四之", four good horses (干旄, Mao 53). 鄭玄 read "日習車徒", daily drill chariots and footmen; the songs make chariots ready for a royal hunt (車攻, Mao 179). The Chu slip has "曰：班車衛", with 曰 and no 吉.

lines.text: The horn-board of a young bull: greatly auspicious.
lines.note: Offering bulls were reared in summer with boards across their horns, "lest they gore people" (閟宮, Mao 300, with 鄭箋); the 周禮's 封人 fits them at every offering. The 說文's 告 is a board across a goring ox's horns, to warn people. In 費誓 the graph names penned beasts.

lines.text: The tusk of a gelded boar: auspicious.
lines.note: 豶 is a castrated pig (說文; 劉表). Pigs are offering beasts: "特豚" in the marriage cauldrons (士昏禮). 鄭玄 read 牙 as 互, a rack. The phrase is two nouns, as in the line below: what is done to the tusk is not said. 程頤: geld the boar and the fury stops.

lines.text: Bearing heaven's crossroads: an offering.
lines.note: 何天之 is a phrase of the songs: "何天之休", he bore heaven's grace (長發, Mao 304; 鄭箋: carrying on his shoulders). 衢 is "四達謂之衢" (爾雅). The Chu slip has 何, against 胡瑗's view that it was added from the small image. 王弼 reads a question, 朱熹 an exclamation.

essays.title: Heaven within the mountain
essays.text: The lower trigram is heaven, the upper the mountain. The commentators divide the lines in two: the three strong lines below are held back, the soft lines above hold them (程頤). The cart, the horses, the bull and the boar are the things held. Wilhelm finds three senses in the name: holding together, holding back, and nourishing.

readings.title: Stop, or oneself?
readings.text: 陸德明's first reading, 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge: 已, to stop. 姚信: 己, oneself. Shaughnessy: "beneficial to change". We print the base's 己 and read it "stop".

readings.title: 曰, or 日 and 吉?
readings.text: The base, 王弼, 孔穎達, 陸德明's lemma and the Chu slip have 曰. 鄭玄, 虞翻, 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge read 日, "daily"; 虞翻's text adds 吉. We print 曰, "it says", and no 吉.

readings.title: 牿: a horn-board, or a pen?
readings.text: The 九家 text and the 說文, 虞翻, 侯果, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge: the board across the horns. 劉表: the horn itself. 費誓 uses 牿 for penned beasts. We print "the horn-board".

readings.title: 何天之衢: bearing, what, or how?
readings.text: 虞翻 and 梁武帝: bearing. 王弼, 孔穎達 and the small image: a question, "what taming? heaven's crossroads". 朱熹: an exclamation. 胡瑗: an intrusion, which the Chu slip disproves. We print "bearing", on the song's 何天之休.

readings.title: Not eating at home: at court, or abroad?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹 and Legge: eating at court, in office. The words say only "not at home", and the Chu slip the same. We print the words.

pinyinTones.name: Dà Chù
pinyinTones.judgment: lì zhēn. bù jiā shí, jí. lì shè dà chuān.
pinyinTones.image: tiān zài shān zhōng, dà chù. jūn zǐ yǐ duō shí qián yán wǎng xìng yǐ chù qí dé.
lines: yǒu lì, lì yǐ.
yú tuō fù.
liáng mǎ zhú, lì jiān zhēn, yuē xián yú wèi, lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
tóng niú zhī gù, yuán jí.
fén shǐ zhī yá, jí.
hè tiān zhī qú, hēng.

pinyinNotes: 畜: chù (to store), as 陸德明 ("勑六反", "義與小畜同"), so the name is Dà Chù, as 9 is Xiǎo Chù; today commonly read xù
行 (Image, 往行): xìng (deeds), as 陸德明 "下孟反"
己 (初九): yǐ, read 已 (to stop), as 陸德明 "夷止反" and the book; not jǐ
說 (九二): tuō (to shed), as 陸德明 "吐活反"
何 (上九): hè (to bear, 荷), 梁武帝's "音賀" in 陸德明, as the book; 陸德明's first is 音河

hexagrams.image: 山下有雷，頤。君子以慎言語、節飲食。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 舍爾靈龜，觀我朵頤，凶。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 顛頤，拂經，于丘頤，征凶。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 拂頤，貞凶，十年勿用，无攸利。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 顛頤，吉。虎視眈眈，其欲逐逐，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 拂經，居貞吉，不可涉大川。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 由頤，厲，吉。利涉大川。

hexagrams.heading: 頤
hexagrams.name: 頤

wilhelm.name: Die Mundwinkel, (die Ernährung)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Mundwinkel. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Sieh auf die Ernährung und womit einer selbst sucht seinen Mund zu füllen.
wilhelm.image: Unten am Berg ist der Donner: das Bild der Ernährung. So hat der Edle acht auf seine Worte und ist mäßig im Essen und Trinken.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Du lässt deine Zauberschildkröte fahren und blickst nach mir mit herabhängenden Mundwinkeln. Unheil!
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Nach dem Gipfel sich wenden um Ernährung. Vom Wege abweichen, um von dem Hügel Ernährung zu suchen: wenn man so fortmacht, bringt es Unheil.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Abweichen von der Ernährung. Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil. Zehn Jahre handle nicht danach. Nichts ist fördernd.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Nach dem Gipfel sich wenden um Ernährung bringt Heil. Mit scharfen Augen wie ein Tiger umherspähen in unersättlichem Begehren. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Abweichen vom Weg. Bleiben in Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Man soll nicht das große Wasser durchqueren.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Die Quelle der Ernährung. Bewusstsein der Gefahr bringt Heil. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren.
