wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Î
legge.judgment: Î indicates that with firm correctness there will be good fortune (in what is denoted by it). We must look at what we are seeking to nourish, and by the exercise of our thoughts seek for the proper aliment.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain and under it that for thunder form Î. The superior man, in accordance with this, (enjoins) watchfulness over our words, and the temperate regulation of our eating and drinking.
lines: The first line, undivided, (seems to be thus addressed), ‘You leave your efficacious tortoise, and look at me till your lower jaw hangs down.’ There will be evil.
The second line, divided, shows one looking downwards for nourishment, which is contrary to what is proper; or seeking it from the height (above), advance towards which will lead to evil.

The third line, divided, shows one acting contrary to the method of nourishing. However firm he may be, there will be evil. For ten years let him not take any action, (for) it will not be in any way advantageous.

The fourth line, divided, shows one looking downwards for (the power to) nourish. There will be good fortune. Looking with a tiger’s downward unwavering glare, and with his desire that impels him to spring after spring, he will fall into no error.
The fifth line, divided, shows one acting contrary to what is regular and proper; but if he abide in firmness, there will be good fortune. He should not, (however, try to) cross the great stream.
The sixth line, undivided, shows him from whom comes the nourishing. His position is perilous, but there will be good fortune. It will be advantageous to cross the great stream.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 114-115 (Image: Appendix II, p. 301)

en.name: The Corners of the Mouth (Nourishment)
en.nameNote: 頤 is the jaws, the part of the face that works in eating: "口車輔之名也", the jaw and cheek (鄭玄). The 爾雅 and the 序卦 give the other sense, to nourish. The text writes 頤 five times, always the noun, and never 養.
en.judgment: The divination: auspicious. Watching the jaws: seeking for oneself what fills the mouth.
en.judgmentNote: 口實 is what fills the mouth: at the laying-out of the dead the mourner fills the mouth with rice and cowries (儀禮, 士喪禮). In 548 BC it is a man's livelihood: "臣君者，豈為其口實？社稷是養", is it for his own mouth's filling that he serves? (左傳). Whose jaws are watched, the text does not say.
en.tradition: The jaws are the sides of the mouth; the mouth eats to nourish itself, so the word means nourishing. "The divination: auspicious": if the one who divines is right, good fortune. Watching the jaws is watching the way of what one nourishes; seeking the mouth's filling is watching how one feeds oneself; in both, rightness brings good fortune.
en.image: Under the mountain there is thunder: The Corners of the Mouth. So the noble one is careful in words and speech and measured in drink and food.
en.imageNote: A later layer, with old counsels: "慎爾出話", be careful of the words you put out (抑, Mao 256); drink only at offerings, and do not get drunk (尚書, 酒誥). 孔穎達: misfortune goes out by the mouth, harm comes in by it.

lines.text: Setting aside your numinous turtle, watching my moving jaws: disaster.
lines.note: The great turtle was the king's oracle and a treasure of state: "寧王遺我大寶龜" (尚書, 大誥); a family's treasure turtle was stolen to divine with (左傳, 517 BC). 靈龜 is a kind of divination turtle (爾雅; 周禮). 程頤 and 朱熹: a turtle that does not eat. 朵 is moving (陸德明).

lines.text: Jaws overturned. Going against the rule. At the hill, jaws. Campaigning: disaster.
lines.note: 顛 is falling headlong, upside down: "顛倒衣裳" (東方未明, Mao 100). 經 is the constant, the rule (毛傳 on 小旻). 丘 is a height of earth not made by men (說文). "At the hill, jaws" has no verb; the commentators supply seeking nourishment. 王弼 cuts after 丘.

lines.text: Going against the jaws. The divination: disaster. For ten years, not to be used. Nothing is favourable.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the line in these words, with 弗 for 拂. 勿用 is the Shang term for victims not to be used. 程頤: ten is the end of the numbers, never to be used. 朱熹: having gone against the jaws, even if correct, disaster.

lines.text: Jaws overturned: auspicious. A tiger looks, glaring, glaring; its desire, chasing, chasing. No blame.
lines.note: The 說文 quotes the line for 眈. A tiger's eyes meant greed: "是虎目而豕喙 ... 是不可饜也", this one can never be sated (國語, 晉語八). 逐 is to chase, as strayed cattle (費誓). The Chu slip and the 子夏傳 have 攸攸, a word of length or distance.

lines.text: Going against the rule. The divination about staying: auspicious. The great river may not be forded.
lines.note: 居貞 is 3 初九's divination about staying, which 史朝 read as the lame son staying at home (左傳, 昭公七年). The Chu slip has no 居 in our copy. 程頤: a ruler who depends on others for nourishment goes against the constant, and cannot meet times of upheaval.

lines.text: From it, the jaws: danger; auspicious. Favourable to ford the great river.
lines.note: 由 as in 16 九四 由豫. 王弼: yin cannot be master alone, so none but gets its nourishment from the top line. 馬融 and 王肅 read 厲 as danger; 王弼 stern. 程頤: a minister in the tutor's office must keep the sense of danger, as Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou.

essays.title: The mouth
essays.text: The lower trigram is thunder, moving; the upper the mountain, still. The two yang lines at the bottom and top are the jaws, the four yin lines between the open mouth (程頤). 鄭玄: the lower jaw moves up and chews against the upper. The commentators divide the lines into those who nourish and those who seek it: the lower three nourish mouth and body, the upper three virtue and right (程頤). In the Chu slips the graph is written with the head over a mouth with teeth.

readings.title: 頤: the jaws, or nourishing?
readings.text: The 爾雅, the 序卦 and every commentator read nourishing; Wilhelm keeps both in his name. The 說文, 鄭玄 and the judgment's 口實 give the body part, and the text never writes 養. We print "the jaws", and leave the nourishing to the wings.

readings.title: The turtle of divination, or a turtle that does not eat?
readings.text: 王弼 and 孔穎達: the turtle's omens, as a likeness for virtue. 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge: a creature that needs no food. The Zhou texts know the great turtle as the instrument of divination. Read so, the line sets the turtle's answer against another's chewing.

readings.title: Where to cut the second line?
readings.text: 王弼 and the base: 拂經于丘，頤，征凶. 程頤, 朱熹, the Chu punctuation, Wilhelm and Legge: 拂經，于丘頤，征凶. We print the second: 拂經 stands alone in the fifth line, and the small image quotes 征凶 without 頤.

readings.title: 逐逐: chasing, steady, quick, or far?
readings.text: 王弼: solid; 薛虞: quick; 程頤 and 朱熹: one after another; the 子夏傳 and 荀爽 攸攸, 悠悠, which the Chu slip confirms as the old text. We print the received graph, "chasing", and record that the oldest witness has a word of distance.

readings.title: 厲: danger, or stern?
readings.text: 馬融 and 王肅: danger. 王弼, 孔穎達 and 陸德明: stern, not to be slighted. We print "danger".

pinyinTones.name: Yí
pinyinTones.judgment: zhēn jí. guān yí, zì qiú kǒu shí.
pinyinTones.image: shān xià yǒu léi, yí. jūn zǐ yǐ shèn yán yǔ, jié yǐn shí.
lines: shě ěr líng guī, guān wǒ duǒ yí, xiōng.
diān yí, fú jīng, yú qiū yí, zhēng xiōng.
fú yí, zhēn xiōng, shí nián wù yòng, wú yōu lì.
diān yí, jí. hǔ shì dān dān, qí yù zhú zhú, wú jiù.
fú jīng, jū zhēn jí, bù kě shè dà chuān.
yóu yí, lì, jí. lì shè dà chuān.

pinyinNotes: 舍 (初九): shě (to leave), as 陸德明 "音捨"
拂 (六二, 六三, 六五): fú (to go against), as 陸德明 "符弗反，違也"

hexagrams.image: 澤滅木，大過。君子以獨立不懼，遯世无悶。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 藉用白茅，无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 枯楊生稊，老夫得其女妻，无不利。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 棟橈，凶。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 棟隆，吉。有它，吝。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 枯楊生華，老婦得其士夫，无咎无譽。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 過涉滅頂，凶。无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 大過
hexagrams.name: 大過

wilhelm.name: Des Großen Übergewicht
wilhelm.judgment: Des Großen Übergewicht. Der Firstbalken biegt sich durch. Fördernd ist es, zu haben, wohin man gehe. Gelingen.
wilhelm.image: Der See geht über die Bäume weg: das Bild des Übergewichts im Großen. So ist der Edle, wenn er allein steht, unbesorgt, und wenn er auf die Welt verzichten muss, unverzagt.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Unterlegen mit weißem Schilfgras. Kein Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Ein trockener Pappelbaum treibt einen Wurzelspross. Ein älterer Mann bekommt eine junge Frau. Alles ist fördernd.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der Firstbalken biegt sich durch. Unheil.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Firstbalken wird gestützt. Heil. Sind Hintergedanken da, ist es beschämend.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Eine dürre Pappel treibt Blüten. Ein älteres Weib bekommt einen Mann. Kein Makel. Kein Lob.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Man muss durchs Wasser. Es geht über den Scheitel. Unheil. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Tâ Kwo
legge.judgment: Tâ Kwo suggests to us a beam that is weak. There will be advantage in moving (under its conditions) in any direction whatever; there will be success.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) trees hidden beneath that for the waters of a marsh forms Tâ Kwo. The superior man, in accordance with this, stands up alone and has no fear, and keeps retired from the world without regret.
lines: The first line, divided, shows one placing mats of the white mâo grass under things set on the ground. There will be no error.
The second line, undivided, shows a decayed willow producing shoots, or an old husband in possession of his young wife. There will be advantage in every way.
The third line, undivided, shows a beam that is weak. There will be evil.
The fourth line, undivided, shows a beam curving upwards. There will be good fortune. If (the subject of it) looks for other (help but that of line one), there will be cause for regret.
The fifth line, undivided, shows a decayed willow producing flowers, or an old wife in possession of her young husband. There will be occasion neither for blame nor for praise.
The topmost line, divided, shows its subject with extraordinary (boldness) wading through a stream, till the water hides the crown of his head. There will be evil, but no ground for blame.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 116-117 (Image: Appendix II, p. 302)

en.name: Preponderance of the Great
en.nameNote: 大過 is the great passing beyond: "罪過也，超過也", fault and going beyond (陸德明). The 彖: the great goes beyond, the four yang lines in the middle. The 雜卦: it is toppling. 過 stands in the text only in the top line; 辛亞民 takes the name from there.
en.judgment: The ridge-beam sags. Favourable to have somewhere to go. An offering.
en.judgmentNote: The ridge-beam is the man who holds up the state: "子於鄭國，棟也。棟折、榱崩，僑將厭焉", if the beam breaks and the rafters fall, I shall be crushed (左傳, 542 BC). In 548 BC 崔杼 met this hexagram casting about marrying a widow; the scribes said auspicious, 陳文子 said no; he married her, and killed his lord that year.
en.tradition: The great is yang; four yang in the middle, in excess: so Daguo. The two yin above and below cannot bear the weight: so the figure of the sagging beam. Yet though the four yang are in excess, the second and fifth are central, compliant within and glad without: there is a way that can be walked, so it is favourable to go somewhere, and there is getting through.
en.image: The lake submerges the trees: Preponderance of the Great. So the noble one stands alone and does not fear, withdraws from the world and is not troubled.
en.imageNote: A later layer; "遯世无悶" is also the 文言's, on 1 初九. 孔穎達: a lake does not drown trees; to say it does is the lake in its extreme. 程頤: the whole world condemns him and he pays no heed.

lines.text: Using white rushes for a mat: no blame.
lines.note: A mat of rushes is what an offering is laid on: after a burial millet is offered on the rush bundle three times (儀禮, 士虞禮; 鄭玄 "苴猶藉也"). "藉，祭藉也" (說文). Rushes strained the king's wine (左傳, 656 BC) and wrapped a gift in courting (野有死麕, Mao 23). What is set on the mat is not said.

lines.text: A withered willow puts out shoots; an old husband gets his girl wife. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: The willow marks the marriage season: "東門之楊 ... 昏以為期" (Mao 140), whose full leaves say the time has been missed (鄭箋). 鄭玄's text 荑, a shoot, is a girl's gift in 靜女 (Mao 42). The Fuyang slips add: the sick man will not die. Shaughnessy pairs this line and the fifth as omens.

lines.text: The ridge-beam sags: disaster.
lines.note: As the judgment, 子產's ridge-beam of the state. The judgment goes on to "favourable to have somewhere to go"; here the verdict is disaster. The small image: it cannot be propped. 程頤: strong to excess, like the sagging beam, it brings the house down.

lines.text: The ridge-beam stands high: auspicious. There is something else: trouble.
lines.note: 隆 is "豐大也", full and great (說文). 有它 with a verdict as in 8 初六. What the something else is, the line does not say. 王弼: it is answered by the first line, and its heart is narrow. 程頤: having another aim.

lines.text: A withered willow puts out flowers; an old wife gets her young husband. No blame, no praise.
lines.note: Flowers and marrying: "灼灼其華。之子于歸" (桃夭, Mao 6). 士 is the young man to be married in the songs: "求我庶士" (摽有梅, Mao 20). The small image calls it shameful; 王弼 and 程頤 barren; the line says only no blame, no praise.

lines.text: Wading across, the crown of the head lost: disaster. No blame.
lines.note: Wading: "濟有深涉。深則厲", the ford has a deep wading (匏有苦葉, Mao 34). 頂 is the crown of the head (說文). The commentators reconcile the two verdicts: a good aim (王弼; 孔穎達 names Longfeng and Bi Gan), no one else to blame (程頤), the time's fault (九家易).

essays.title: The lake over the wood
essays.text: The lower trigram is wind and wood, the upper the lake. 李鼎祚: of trees that grow near water the willow is one; when the water is too much the trees are drowned: that is the withered willow. The figure is four yang between two yin: the yang in excess in the middle, weak above and below, the sagging ridge-beam (程頤). The 繫辭 says inner and outer coffins were taken from this hexagram.

essays.title: Two images
essays.text: Two images run through the lines, each twice: the ridge-beam (judgment, third and fourth lines) and the withered willow with a marriage (second and fifth), set against each other in pairs: sagging and standing high; shoots and a girl wife against flowers and a young husband. The first and top lines are a mat of rushes and a wading.

readings.title: The great passing beyond, or a fault?
readings.text: 陸德明 gives both senses; the 彖, 孔穎達 and every commentator read the yang going beyond the measure. 辛亞民 takes the name for a word lifted from the top line. We follow Wilhelm for the name and translate 過 there as "across".

readings.title: 稊: shoots, or root?
readings.text: 虞翻 and 陸德明: the new leaf; 鄭玄 荑, the tree sprouting again; 程頤 and 朱熹: the root. We print "shoots", the older glosses; the fifth line's flowers set both above ground.

readings.title: A willow, or a mountain elm?
readings.text: 鄭玄 reads 枯 as 姑, the mountain elm. Every other reader has the withered willow. We print the willow.

readings.title: The fifth line's shame
readings.text: The small image and 孔穎達 make the old woman with a young husband shameful; 王弼 and 程頤 barren. The line says only "no blame, no praise". We print the line.

pinyinTones.name: Dà Guò
pinyinTones.judgment: dòng náo, lì yǒu yōu wǎng, hēng.
pinyinTones.image: zé miè mù, dà guò. jūn zǐ yǐ dú lì bù jù, dùn shì wú mèn.
lines: jiè yòng bái máo, wú jiù.
kū yáng shēng tí, lǎo fū dé qí nǚ qī, wú bù lì.
dòng náo, xiōng.
dòng lóng, jí. yǒu tā, lìn.
kū yáng shēng huā, lǎo fù dé qí shì fū, wú jiù wú yù.
guò shè miè dǐng, xiōng. wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 橈 (judgment, 九三): náo (bent), as 陸德明 "乃教反，曲折也"; not ráo
華 (九五): huā (flowers), as 徐邈 "音花" in 陸德明; not huá
藉 (初六): jiè (to lay beneath), as 陸德明 "在夜反"; not jí

hexagrams.judgment: 習坎，有孚，維心，亨。行有尚。
hexagrams.image: 水洊至，習坎。君子以常德行、習教事。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 習坎，入于坎窞，凶。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 坎有險，求小得。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 來之坎坎，險且枕，入于坎窞，勿用。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 樽酒，簋貳，用缶，納約自牖，終无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 坎不盈，衹既平，无咎。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 係用徽纆，寘于叢棘，三歲不得，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 習坎
hexagrams.name: 坎

wilhelm.name: Das Abgründige, das Wasser
wilhelm.judgment: Das wiederholte Abgründige. Wenn du wahrhaftig bist, so hast du im Herzen Gelingen, und was du tust, hat Erfolg.
wilhelm.image: Das Wasser fließt ununterbrochen und kommt ans Ziel: das Bild des wiederholten Abgründigen. So wandelt der Edle in dauernder Tugend und übt das Geschäft des Lehrens.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Wiederholung des Abgründigen. Man gerät im Abgrund in ein Loch. Unheil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Der Abgrund hat Gefahr. Man soll nur Kleines zu erreichen streben.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Vorwärts und rückwärts, Abgrund über Abgrund. In solcher Gefahr halte zunächst inne, sonst kommst du im Abgrund in ein Loch. Handle nicht so.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Ein Krug Wein, eine Reisschale als Zugabe, Tongeschirr, einfach zum Fenster hineingereicht. Das ist durchaus kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der Abgrund wird nicht überfüllt, wird nur bis an den Rand gefüllt. Kein Makel.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Mit Stricken und Tauen gebunden, eingeschlossen zwischen dornumhegten Kerkermauern; drei Jahre lang findet man sich nicht zurecht. Unheil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Khan
legge.judgment: Khan, here repeated, shows the possession of sincerity, through which the mind is penetrating. Action (in accordance with this) will be of high value.
legge.image: (The representation of) water flowing on continuously forms the repeated Khan. The superior man, in accordance with this, maintains constantly the virtue (of his heart) and (the integrity of) his conduct, and practises the business of instruction.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject in the double defile, and (yet) entering a cavern within it. There will be evil.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject in all the peril of the defile. He will, however, get a little (of the deliverance) that he seeks.

The third line, divided, shows its subject, whether he comes or goes (=descends or ascends), confronted by a defile. All is peril to him and unrest. (His endeavours) will lead him into the cavern of the pit. There should be no action (in such a case).

The fourth line, divided, shows its subject (at a feast), with (simply) a bottle of spirits, and a subsidiary basket of rice, while (the cups and bowls) are (only) of earthenware. He introduces his important lessons (as his ruler’s) intelligence admits. There will in the end be no error.
The fifth line, undivided, shows the water of the defile not yet full, (so that it might flow away); but order will (soon) be brought about. There will be no error.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject bound with cords of three strands or two strands, and placed in the thicket of thorns. But in three years he does not learn the course for him to pursue. There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 118-119 (Image: Appendix II, p. 303)

en.name: The Abysmal, Water
en.nameNote: 坎 is not the word for water (水). It is a pit, a hollow in the ground: "險也，陷也" (陸德明); "《坎》者、陷也" (序卦). The 說卦 gives the trigram water. The text's own word is 坎, nine times; 水 not once. Only this hexagram adds a word, 習, to its name.
en.judgment: The pit doubled. There is confirmation, binding the heart. An offering. Going, there is honour.
en.judgmentNote: In the 左傳 a pit is dug when a covenant is sworn, the victim killed over it and the oath laid on it or buried: "坎，用牲，加書" (529 BC). 習 is the word for a divination repeated: "乃卜三龜，一習吉" (尚書, 金縢). 維 is to tie, as in 17 上六.
en.tradition: 習 is doubling; 坎 is a pit to fall into; its figure is water, the yang fallen within the yin, empty outside and solid within. Both trigrams are Kan: danger doubled. The solid middle is the figure of good faith and a heart that gets through; going so, there will surely be achievement.
en.image: Water comes again and again: the pit doubled. So the noble one keeps his virtue and conduct constant and practises the work of teaching.
en.imageNote: A later layer, playing on 習 as to practise. 陸績: water comes twice and flows the more freely, not stopping day or night. 程頤: from drops to rivers and seas, water comes on again and again and never in a rush; so teaching must be heard until familiar.

lines.text: The pit doubled: going into a hollow in the pit. Disaster.
lines.note: The 說文 quotes this line for 窞: "坎中小坎也", a small pit within a pit. 干寶 reads it of floods: when the rivers overflow the plains and pour into the hollows, water has lost its way. The small image: it loses the way.

lines.text: The pit has peril. Seeking, a little is got.
lines.note: The shelf gives nothing for these words in Zhou use. 求 and 得 stand together as in 17 六三. 險 is a steep and dangerous place, kept apart from the verdict 厲. 王弼: it cannot get out, but can seek and get a little.

lines.text: Coming and going: pit, pit. Peril, and a headrest. Going into a hollow in the pit. Not to be used.
lines.note: 坎坎 in the songs is a thud: "坎坎伐檀兮" (伐檀, Mao 112). 鄭玄's text has 檢 for 險: "木在手曰檢，木在首曰枕", wood on the hands and on the head, two restraints. 王弼: going out to a pit, staying in a pit; 枕 is being propped and not at rest.

lines.text: A vessel of wine, two tureens, using jars. Passing the bond in through the window. In the end, no blame.
lines.note: 尊 and 簋 are the Zhou offering bronzes (利簋); "陳饋八簋" (伐木, Mao 165). Offerings were set "宗室牖下", under the lineage temple's window (采蘋, Mao 15). 約 is to wrap and tie, and a pledge (左傳, 597 BC). 晁說之 and 朱熹 cut "樽酒簋，貳用缶".

lines.text: The pit is not full; it has come to be level. No blame.
lines.note: The 彖: water flows and does not fill. 衹 is read as the 祗 of 24 初九, "come to" (程頤, "抵也"). 王弼: a particle; 虞翻 and 京房 (禔): at ease; 鄭玄 (坻): a small mound, the islet of 蒹葭 (Mao 129).

lines.text: Tied with cords of three strands and two, set in the thorn thicket. For three years, nothing is got. Disaster.
lines.note: "三股為徽，兩股為纆" (劉表). The 周禮 sets wrongdoers within a round wall, freed after three years for the gravest offences, and hears suits under nine thorn trees. 虞翻: a prison with thorns planted outside. That it is a prison the English leaves out. Shaughnessy hears a rhymed oracle.

essays.title: The pit doubled
essays.text: Both trigrams are the pit. The 彖: the pit doubled is danger twice over; water flows and does not fill. 程頤: 習 is doubling, as in study and review; only this hexagram adds 習, to show danger within danger. 王弼 and 孔穎達 give 習 a second sense, to be practised in hardship. The Mawangdui manuscript writes 習贛, the two words together; the Qin 歸藏 writes 勞, toil, the 說卦's word for the trigram.

readings.title: The name: 坎 or 習坎?
readings.text: The base heads the hexagram 習坎, and every commentator reads 習坎 at the head of the judgment; the 序卦, 雜卦 and 說卦 say 坎. We name the hexagram 坎, keep 習坎 as the judgment's first words, and record the heading.

readings.title: Binding the heart; an offering, or the heart gets through?
readings.text: 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤 and 朱熹 read 維心亨 together: the heart, sincere, gets through. We print 亨 apart as the offering, with the base's mark, and 維 as "binding", the verb of 17 上六.

readings.title: Two tureens, or a tureen and jars besides?
readings.text: The base, 陸德明, 王弼, 孔穎達 and 程頤 divide in three: two tureens. The "old reading", 晁說之 and 朱熹 make 貳 a verb, added; 虞翻's spare goes with it, and Wilhelm and Legge follow that side. We print the base.

readings.title: 衹: come to, a particle, at ease, or a mound?
readings.text: 程頤: reaching, as in 24. 王弼: a particle. 虞翻, 京房 and the 說文: at ease. 鄭玄: a small mound, "the mound is levelled". We print "come to".

readings.title: Peril and propped, or two restraints?
readings.text: 王弼, 程頤 and 朱熹: in peril and leaning, without rest. 干寶 and 虞翻: resting easy. 鄭玄 and the old text: wood on the hands and on the head, restraints, joining this line to the top line. We print "peril, and a headrest", the words.

pinyinTones.name: Kǎn
pinyinTones.judgment: xí kǎn, yǒu fú, wéi xīn, hēng. xíng yǒu shàng.
pinyinTones.image: shuǐ jiàn zhì, xí kǎn. jūn zǐ yǐ cháng dé xìng, xí jiào shì.
lines: xí kǎn, rù yú kǎn dàn, xiōng.
kǎn yǒu xiǎn, qiú xiǎo dé.
lái zhī kǎn kǎn, xiǎn qiě zhěn, rù yú kǎn dàn, wù yòng.
zūn jiǔ, guǐ èr, yòng fǒu, nà yuē zì yǒu, zhōng wú jiù.
kǎn bù yíng, zhī jì píng, wú jiù.
xì yòng huī mò, zhì yú cóng jí, sān suì bù dé, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 行 (Image, 德行): xìng (conduct), as 陸德明 "下孟反"
衹 (九五): zhī, as 陸德明 "音支"; not zhǐ

hexagrams.image: 明兩作，離。大人以繼明照于四方。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 履錯然，敬之，无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 黃離，元吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 日昃之離，不鼓缶而歌，則大耋之嗟，凶。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 突如，其來如，焚如，死如，棄如。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 出涕沱若，戚嗟若，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 王用出征，有嘉折首，獲匪其醜，无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 離
hexagrams.name: 離

wilhelm.name: Das Haftende, das Feuer
wilhelm.judgment: Das Haftende. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Sie bringt Gelingen. Pflege der Kuh bringt Heil.
wilhelm.image: Das Helle erhebt sich zweimal: das Bild des Feuers. So erleuchtet der große Mann durch Fortsetzung dieser Helle die vier Weltgegenden.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Die Fußspuren laufen kreuz und quer. Wenn man ernst dabei ist: kein Makel.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Gelber Schein. Erhabenes Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Beim Schein der untergehenden Sonne schlagen die Menschen entweder auf den Topf und singen, oder sie seufzen laut über das nahende Greisenalter. Unheil.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Plötzlich ist sein Kommen; es brennt auf, erstirbt, wird weggeworfen.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Weinend in Strömen, seufzend und klagend. Heil!
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Der König gebraucht ihn, auszuziehen und zu züchtigen. Am besten ist es dann, die Häupter zu töten und die Nachläufer gefangen zu nehmen. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Lî
legge.judgment: Lî indicates that, (in regard to what it denotes), it will be advantageous to be firm and correct, and that thus there will be free course and success. Let (its subject) also nourish (a docility like that of) the cow, and there will be good fortune.
legge.image: (The trigram for) brightness, repeated, forms Lî. The great man, in accordance with this, cultivates more and more his brilliant (virtue), and diffuses its brightness over the four quarters (of the land).
lines: The first line, undivided, shows one ready to move with confused steps. But he treads at the same time reverently, and there will be no mistake.
The second line, divided, shows its subject in his place in yellow. There will be great good fortune.

The third line, undivided, shows its subject in a position like that of the declining sun. Instead of playing on his instrument of earthenware, and singing to it, he utters the groans of an old man of eighty. There will be evil.
The fourth line, undivided, shows the manner of its subject’s coming. How abrupt it is, as with fire, with death, to be rejected (by all)!
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject as one with tears flowing in torrents, and groaning in sorrow. There will be good fortune.

The topmost line, undivided, shows the king employing its subject in his punitive expeditions. Achieving admirable (merit), he breaks (only) the chiefs (of the rebels). Where his prisoners were not their associates, he does not punish. There will be no error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 120-122 (Image: Appendix II, p. 304)

en.name: The Clinging, Fire
en.nameNote: 離 is not the word for fire (火). In the songs it is to be caught in, to lodge at: "雉離于羅", the pheasant is caught in the net (兔爰, Mao 70); "月離于畢", the moon lodges in the Net mansion (Mao 232). Mawangdui writes 羅, a net. The 說卦: bright.
en.judgment: A favourable divination. An offering. Rearing a cow: auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: The Shang put female cattle to the oracle as victims: "甲貞翌侑于牛牝", divined: on the next day offer a female ox (合集 15090). In 537 BC a diviner reads "純《離》為牛", pure Li is the ox (左傳). Whether the cow is for the offering, the text does not say.
en.tradition: Li is clinging: yin clings to yang; its figure is fire, yin in body and yang in use. What a thing clings to should be right. The cow is soft and compliant. So whoever divines, if right, gets through, and rearing a cow is auspicious.
en.image: Brightness rises twice: The Clinging. So the great man continues the brightness and shines on the four quarters.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 作 is "起也", to rise (鄭玄). 程頤: not two lights but light twice, one following the other; the great man, by virtue the sage, by rank the king, hands on bright virtue from generation to generation.

lines.text: Treading crosswise. Being reverent to it: no blame.
lines.note: 錯 as crossing is in the songs: "獻醻交錯", toasts going back and forth at the offering feast (楚茨, Mao 209). The Fuyang slips have "履□然". 王弼: 錯然 is wariness at the start of the light. 程頤: though it has not moved, its tracks already have.

lines.text: Yellow clinging: greatly auspicious.
lines.note: Yellow is the colour of the yellow skirt of 2 六五. The 說文's 離黃 is the oriole, which sings in spring and flies at a girl's marriage (東山, Mao 156); whether 黃離 names the bird is not argued on the shelf. The commentators: yellow, the colour of the middle.

lines.text: The clinging of the declining sun. Not beating the jar and singing, then the sighing of great old age: disaster.
lines.note: "今者不樂，逝者其耋", if we do not make merry now, we shall be old (車鄰, Mao 126; 毛傳: eighty is 耋). The men of Qin beat the jar to keep time to songs (說文). 昃 is the sun leaning west. 鄭玄's text lacks 凶. 程頤: enjoying the ordinary is how to meet life and death.

lines.text: Sudden. Its coming. Burning. Dying. Cast away.
lines.note: Five states, each with 如, and no verdict. The 周禮 burns kin-killers and lays out the bodies of murderers; nothing ties it to this line. 荀爽: the flame dies and the ash is thrown out. 程頤: death and casting away are the worst of disasters, so the line need not say "disaster".

lines.text: Tears coming out, streaming; grieving, sighing: auspicious.
lines.note: Weeping in the songs: "涕泗滂沱", tears and snivel streaming (澤陂, Mao 145); "泣涕如雨" (燕燕, Mao 28). The 子夏傳 writes 嘁 for 戚. 王弼: the many help one so grieved, so after streaming and sighing, good fortune.

lines.text: The king uses it in going out on campaign. There is the fine: heads cut off; the catch, not their host. No blame.
lines.note: 折首 is the bronzes' war formula: "折首五百，執訊五十" (虢季子白盤, late Western Zhou). "執訊獲醜", they seized men to question and took the host (出車, Mao 168; 鄭箋 "醜，衆也"). 程頤: cut off only the chiefs, and do not take their followers. Shaughnessy reads 醜 as chief.

essays.title: Fire doubled
essays.text: Both trigrams are 離: fire, the sun, lightning (說卦). 荀爽 reads the lines as the sun's day: the first line sunrise, the second noon, the third the sun declining; Wilhelm the same. The 彖 reads the figure as the soft attached in the middle of the strong. In the text 離 stands twice, and we print "clinging" there, the sense of the songs and the oldest gloss.

readings.title: 離: clinging, net, light, or a bird?
readings.text: Clinging, lodging, caught in: the songs, the 彖, the 序卦, 陸德明 and Wilhelm's name. Netted: Mawangdui and Tsinghua 羅, and Shaughnessy. Bright: the 說卦, the Image, Wilhelm's lines. The 說文: the oriole. We print "clinging", which also holds the songs' "caught in a net".

readings.title: The third line: with or without 凶?
readings.text: The received text and every commentator have it; 鄭玄's text and the "old text" lack it. We print the base.

readings.title: Whose burning?
readings.text: 王弼: the line itself, rash and cast off. 荀爽: the fire flaring and dying. 程頤: a minister who seizes the succession. The 周禮's burning of kin-killers is recorded only.

readings.title: 醜: the host, the kind, or the chief?
readings.text: 鄭箋: the multitude. 虞翻: the kind. 程頤: followers. Shaughnessy: chief. We print "host".

pinyinTones.name: Lí
pinyinTones.judgment: lì zhēn. hēng. xù pìn niú, jí.
pinyinTones.image: míng liǎng zuò, lí. dà rén yǐ jì míng zhào yú sì fāng.
lines: lǚ cuò rán, jìng zhī, wú jiù.
huáng lí, yuán jí.
rì zè zhī lí, bù gǔ fǒu ér gē, zé dà dié zhī jiē, xiōng.
tū rú, qí lái rú, fén rú, sǐ rú, qì rú.
chū tì tuó ruò, qī jiē ruò, jí.
wáng yòng chū zhēng, yǒu jiā zhé shǒu, huò fěi qí chǒu, wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 畜 (judgment): xù (to rear), as 陸德明 "許六反"; not chù

hexagrams.image: 山上有澤，咸。君子以虛受人。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 咸其拇。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 咸其腓，凶。居吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 咸其股，執其隨，往吝。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 貞吉。悔亡。憧憧往來，朋從爾思。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 咸其脢，无悔。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 咸其輔頰舌。

hexagrams.heading: 咸
hexagrams.name: 咸

wilhelm.name: Die Einwirkung, (die Werbung)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Einwirkung. Gelingen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Ein Mädchen nehmen bringt Heil.
wilhelm.image: Auf dem Berge ist ein See: das Bild der Einwirkung. So lässt der Edle durch Aufnahmebereitschaft die Menschen an sich herankommen. (Wörtlich: So nimmt der Edle durch Leere die Menschen auf.)
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Die Einwirkung äußert sich in der großen Zehe.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Einwirkung äußert sich in den Waden. Unheil! Verweilen bringt Heil!
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Die Einwirkung äußert sich in den Schenkeln. Hält sich an das, was ihm folgt. Weitermachen ist beschämend.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil! Die Reue schwindet. Wenn man aufgeregt hin und her denkt, so folgen nur die Freunde, auf die man bewusste Gedanken richtet.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Die Einwirkung äußert sich im Nacken. Keine Reue.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Die Einwirkung äußert sich in Kinnladen, Wangen und Zunge.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hsien
legge.judgment: Hsien indicates that, (on the fulfilment of the conditions implied in it), there will be free course and success. Its advantageousness will depend on the being firm and correct, (as) in marrying a young lady. There will be good fortune.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain and above it that for (the waters of) a marsh form Hsien. The superior man, in accordance with this, keeps his mind free from pre-occupation, and open to receive (the influences of) others.
lines: The first line, divided, shows one moving his great toes.
The second line, divided, shows one moving the calves of his leg. There will be evil. If he abide (quiet in his place), there will be good fortune.
The third line, undivided, shows one moving his thighs, and keeping close hold of those whom he follows. Going forward (in this way) will cause regret.

The fourth line, undivided, shows that firm correctness which will lead to good fortune, and prevent all occasion for repentance. If its subject be unsettled in his movements, (only) his friends will follow his purpose.
The fifth line, undivided, shows one moving the flesh along the spine above the heart. There will be no occasion for repentance.
The sixth line, divided, shows one moving his jaws and tongue.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 123-124 (Image: Appendix II, p. 305)

en.name: Influence (Wooing)
en.nameNote: 咸 by itself is "all" (爾雅). Here it is a verb before a part of the body, and the 彖 reads it as 感, to stir. The manuscripts write 欽, and in the songs 欽欽 is the stirred, anxious heart: "憂心欽欽" (晨風, Mao 132). The 雜卦: quick.
en.judgment: An offering. A favourable divination. Taking a wife: auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: A marriage was put to the oracle: the groom's side cracks the turtle in the temple, and the envoy reports "占曰吉", the reading said auspicious (儀禮, 士昏禮). The lord of Jin wanted Li Ji as his wife: the turtle said not auspicious, the stalks auspicious; "follow the stalks" (左傳, 656 BC).
en.tradition: 咸 is mutual stirring: the soft above, the hard below, answering each other; stillness makes the stirring single, delight makes the answer full; the youngest son goes below the youngest daughter, the man first: the right order of man and woman, the time of marriage. So the reading is: success, favourable for what is right; taking a wife, auspicious.
en.image: On the mountain there is a lake: Influence. So the noble one receives people by being empty.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 崔憬: the mountain high and coming down, the lake low and going up: mountain and lake share their breath. 程頤: empty within, one can receive; full, nothing gets in; being empty within is having no self.

lines.text: Stirring its big toe.
lines.note: The Shang asked about illness in parts of the body, the eye, the body (合集 00456正). 拇 is "將指也", the leading digit (說文); the big toe for 馬融 and 鄭玄. The Chu slip has the line word for word. No verdict: 朱熹, the stirring is still shallow.

lines.text: Stirring its calf: disaster. Staying: auspicious.
lines.note: 腓 is the calf (說文; 鄭玄). 王廙: when the calf moves, one walks. 居 is staying, as in 3 初九. 王弼: the calf is the restless part; restless, disaster; staying, auspicious.

lines.text: Stirring its thigh, grasping its following. Going on: trouble.
lines.note: 股 is the thigh: "斯螽動股", the locust moves its thighs (七月, Mao 154). 隨 is the word of 17; 52 六二 has it again beside the calf. The Chu slip writes 隓 and has no 往. 王弼: the thigh follows the foot. Shaughnessy: torn flesh.

lines.text: The divination: auspicious. Regret gone. Unsettled, unsettled, going and coming: friends follow your thought.
lines.note: 憧 is "意不定也", the mind unsettled (說文). "往來行言，心焉數之", talk coming and going, the heart weighs it (巧言, Mao 198). The Chu slip has 亡悔 and 志, aim, for 思. 程頤: where the heart would be, the line takes no figure, for stirring is the heart.

lines.text: Stirring the flesh of its back. No regret.
lines.note: The 說文 quotes the line: "背肉也", the flesh of the back; 孔穎達: all the readers put it above the heart. The Chu slip has 拇, the big toe, here. 程頤: the back is turned from the heart and unseen.

lines.text: Stirring its jawbone, cheeks and tongue.
lines.note: 輔 is the jawbone (說文): "輔車相依，脣亡齒寒" (左傳, 655 BC). "莫捫朕舌，言不可逝矣", words once gone cannot be followed (抑, Mao 256). No verdict. The small image and the commentators: the mouth running on in talk.

essays.title: A body from the toe up
essays.text: Five of the six lines name a part of the body, from the bottom of the figure to the top: the big toe, the calf, the thigh, the flesh of the back, the jaw, cheeks and tongue. The fourth line, where the heart would be, has none, and speaks of going and coming and of thought. 52 has the same frame. Shaughnessy sets these lines beside a mid-Western Zhou jade figure of a person, the clearest case of line texts ordered from the bottom up.

essays.title: Husband and wife
essays.text: The lower trigram is the mountain, the youngest son; the upper the lake, the youngest daughter. The 序卦 opens the second half of the book here: there are heaven and earth, then the myriad things, then male and female, then husband and wife. Wilhelm reads the attraction of the sexes, the man taking the first step.

readings.title: 咸: stirring, all, quick, or cutting?
readings.text: The 彖, every commentator, Wilhelm and Legge read 感, to stir; the manuscripts' 欽 is the stirred heart. 程頤 keeps "all" beside it. The 雜卦: quick. Shaughnessy once read 減, to cut. We print "stirring": the oldest gloss, the manuscripts' graph, and a verb before a part of the body.

readings.title: Grasping its following?
readings.text: What the thigh follows, or the people it follows (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹); the line below (崔憬); a part of the body (隨 among the body words here and in 52). The Chu 隓 is not explained on the shelf. We print "grasping its following" and leave which.

readings.title: The back, or the big toe?
readings.text: The received text, the 說文 and every reader have 脢, the back, in the fifth line. The Chu slip has 拇, which would repeat the first line. We print 脢.

readings.title: Whose body?
readings.text: 其 is "its" throughout. Wilhelm reads the wooing of a girl by a young man; the commentators stages of a stirring, from shallow to deep and out again in talk; Shaughnessy a body from the toe up. The lines say only which part is stirred.

pinyinTones.name: Xián
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. lì zhēn. qǔ nǚ jí.
pinyinTones.image: shān shàng yǒu zé, xián. jūn zǐ yǐ xū shòu rén.
lines: xián qí mǔ.
xián qí féi, xiōng. jū jí.
xián qí gǔ, zhí qí suí, wǎng lìn.
zhēn jí. huǐ wáng. chōng chōng wǎng lái, péng cóng ěr sī.
xián qí méi, wú huǐ.
xián qí fǔ jiá shé.

hexagrams.image: 雷風，恆。君子以立不易方。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 浚恆，貞凶，无攸利。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 悔亡。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 不恆其德，或承之羞，貞吝。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 田无禽。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 恆其德，貞，婦人吉，夫子凶。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 振恆，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 恆
hexagrams.name: 恆

wilhelm.name: Die Dauer
wilhelm.judgment: Gelingen. Kein Makel. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Fördernd ist, zu haben, wohin man gehe.
wilhelm.image: Donner und Wind: das Bild der Dauer. So steht der Edle fest und wandelt seine Richtung nicht.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Zu rasch Dauer wollen, bringt beharrlich Unheil. Nichts, was fördernd wäre.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Reue schwindet.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Wer seinem Charakter nicht Dauer gibt, dem bietet man Schande. Beharrliche Beschämung.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Im Feld ist kein Wild.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Seinem Charakter Dauer geben durch Beharrlichkeit, das ist für eine Frau von Heil, für einen Mann von Unheil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Rastlosigkeit als dauernder Zustand bringt Unheil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hăng
legge.judgment: Hăng indicates successful progress and no error (in what it denotes). But the advantage will come from being firm and correct; and movement in any direction whatever will be advantageous.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) thunder and that for wind form Hăng. The superior man, in accordance with this, stands firm, and does not change his method (of operation).
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject deeply (desirous) of long continuance. Even with firm correctness there will be evil; there will be no advantage in any way.
The second line, undivided, shows all occasion for repentance disappearing.
The third line, undivided, shows one who does not continuously maintain his virtue. There are those who will impute this to him as a disgrace. However firm he may be, there will be ground for regret.
The fourth line, undivided, shows a field where there is no game.
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject continuously maintaining the virtue indicated by it. In a wife this will be fortunate; in a husband, evil.
The topmost line, divided, shows its subject exciting himself to long continuance. There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 125-126 (Image: Appendix II, p. 307)

en.name: Duration
en.nameNote: 恆 is constancy, lasting: "久也" (陸德明; 序卦). The 說文 gives an old form with the moon and quotes "如月之恒" (天保, Mao 166), where 毛傳 glosses 恆 as the crescent moon. In the Chu divination records 恆 is the span a divination asks about: "恆貞吉".
en.judgment: An offering. No blame. A favourable divination. Favourable to have somewhere to go.
en.judgmentNote: In the Chu divination records the answer is given for the long term: "占之：恆貞吉", the divination for the long term is auspicious (包山 197). The judgment is four of the book's fixed verdicts in a row. The Chu slip has them in another order and without 利有攸往.
en.tradition: 恆 is constancy: thunder hard above, wind soft below, joined; yielding and moving; every line answered: all four are the constant order of things. The reading: one who can last in his way gets through without blame; but he must hold to what is right, and then he has the constant way, and it is favourable to go somewhere.
en.image: Thunder and wind: Duration. So the noble one stands and does not change his direction.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 宋衷: thunder moves things and wind scatters them; the two always press on each other and serve the myriad things. 方 is a direction, a quarter; 孔穎達: "方猶道也", like a way.

lines.text: Deepening constancy. The divination: disaster. Nothing is favourable.
lines.note: 浚 is to dredge, to deepen: "冬，浚洙", in winter they dredged the Zhu (春秋, 685 BC); "莫浚匪泉" (小弁, Mao 197; 毛傳 "深也"). The Chu slip has the line word for word, and the same words again for the top line. 王弼: seeking the depth at the very start.

lines.text: Regret gone.
lines.note: The line is the verdict alone, and the Chu slip has it so; Shaughnessy lists it among the two-character line texts. 王弼: out of its place, it stays in the middle and can dissolve regret.

lines.text: Not keeping its favour constant: someone holds up the delicacies. The divination: trouble.
lines.note: One song of blessing has 德, 恆 and 或承 beside an offering of food and a divination (天保, Mao 166). 羞 is "進獻也", food presented (說文). The 禮記 (緇衣) quotes the line as shame, after a saying that a man without constancy cannot be made a diviner. Shaughnessy: 德 as 得, the catch.

lines.text: In the field there is no game.
lines.note: The Shang put the king's hunt to the oracle and recorded the catch: "王往田从利擒" (屯南 2299). The negative of 7 六五 田有禽; the Chu slip writes 畋. 朱熹: whoever gets this will catch nothing, and in all things will not get what he seeks.

lines.text: Keeping its favour constant. The divination: for the wife, auspicious; for the husband, disaster.
lines.note: Two verdicts by who asks, as 貞丈人吉 in 7. 夫子 in the 左傳 is a man spoken of with respect, "that gentleman"; against 婦人 the pair is wife and husband. The 緇衣 writes 偵 for 貞. The small image: the wife follows one to the end; the husband decides what is right.

lines.text: Shaking constancy. Disaster.
lines.note: 振 is to shake: "六月莎雞振羽" (七月, Mao 154); "動也" (馬融); "搖落也" (鄭玄). 虞翻's text writes 震. The Chu slip has "浚恆，貞凶" here, the words of the first line. 王弼: at the height of movement, to make this one's constancy gets nothing.

essays.title: Thunder and wind
essays.text: The lower trigram is wind, the upper thunder. The 彖: the hard above and the soft below, thunder and wind joined, yielding and moving, every hard line answered by a soft. The 序卦 follows 31 with it: the way of husband and wife may not but last. Wilhelm reads it as the counterpart of 31: there the wooing, here union as a lasting state. The word 恆 stands in four of the six lines.

readings.title: 羞: delicacies or shame?
readings.text: Every commentator, the 禮記, the 論語, Wilhelm and Legge read shame. For food presented: the 說文, the 左傳, 承 "to hold up" before it, and the 天保 stanza; Shaughnessy reads a meat offering. The moral quotations set the line in talk about diviners. We print "the delicacies"; "shame" is recorded.

readings.title: 德: favour, virtue, or the catch?
readings.text: "Favour" as in 6 and 9; "virtue" with every commentator, Wilhelm and Legge; 得, the catch, with Shaughnessy. We print "favour".

readings.title: 振恆, 震恆, or 浚恆，貞凶?
readings.text: The base, 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹, 馬融 and 鄭玄 have 振; 虞翻 and 張璠 震; the Chu slip repeats the first line. We print 振; 震 would give the same English.

readings.title: 或: someone, there is, or constantly?
readings.text: "Someone" with 朱熹 and 25 六三; "there is" with 陸德明 and 鄭箋 on 天保; "constantly" in 陸德明's other reading; 鄭玄's text has 咸承. We print "someone".

pinyinTones.name: Héng
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. wú jiù. lì zhēn. lì yǒu yōu wǎng.
pinyinTones.image: léi fēng, héng. jūn zǐ yǐ lì bù yì fāng.
lines: jùn héng, zhēn xiōng, wú yōu lì.
huǐ wáng.
bù héng qí dé, huò chéng zhī xiū, zhēn lìn.
tián wú qín.
héng qí dé, zhēn, fù rén jí, fū zǐ xiōng.
zhèn héng, xiōng.

hexagrams.image: 天下有山，遯。君子以遠小人，不惡而嚴。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 遯尾，厲，勿用有攸往。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 執之用黃牛之革，莫之勝說。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 係遯，有疾，厲。畜臣妾，吉。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 好遯，君子吉，小人否。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 嘉遯，貞吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 肥遯，无不利。

hexagrams.heading: 遯
hexagrams.name: 遯

wilhelm.name: Der Rückzug
wilhelm.judgment: Der Rückzug. Gelingen. Im Kleinen ist fördernd Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Unter dem Himmel ist der Berg: das Bild des Rückzugs. So hält der Edle den Gemeinen fern, nicht zornig, sondern gemessen.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Beim Rückzug am Schwanz: das ist gefährlich. Man darf nicht etwas unternehmen wollen.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Er hält ihn fest mit gelbem Ochsenleder. Niemand vermag ihn loszureißen.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Aufgehaltener Rückzug ist peinlich und gefahrvoll. Die Menschen als Knechte und Mägde zu halten, bringt Heil.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Freiwilliger Rückzug bringt dem Edlen Heil, dem Gemeinen Niedergang.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Freundlicher Rückzug. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Heiterer Rückzug. Alles ist fördernd.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Thun
legge.judgment: Thun indicates successful progress (in its circumstances). To a small extent it will (still) be advantageous to be firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the sky and below it that for a mountain form Thun. The superior man, in accordance with this, keeps small men at a distance, not by showing that he hates them, but by his own dignified gravity.
lines: The first line, divided, shows a retiring tail. The position is perilous. No movement in any direction should be made.
The second line, divided, shows its subject holding (his purpose) fast as if by a (thong made from the) hide of a yellow ox, which cannot be broken.
The third line, undivided, shows one retiring but bound,—to his distress and peril. (If he were to deal with his binders as in) nourishing a servant or concubine, it would be fortunate for him.
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject retiring notwithstanding his likings. In a superior man this will lead to good fortune; a small man cannot attain to this.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject retiring in an admirable way. With firm correctness there will be good fortune.
The sixth line, undivided, shows its subject retiring in a noble way. It will be advantageous in every respect.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 127-128 (Image: Appendix II, p. 308)

en.name: Retreat
en.nameNote: 遯 is to withdraw, to run off and hide: "隱退也" (陸德明); "the name for running away" (鄭玄). In the songs a man in drought asks whether the High God would have him flee (雲漢, "寧俾我遯"). The graph holds 豚, the piglet.
en.judgment: An offering. A divination favourable in small things.
en.judgmentNote: Withdrawing from danger is a Zhou theme: in the 尚書 (微子), set at the fall of Shang, a speaker says he does not look to going into hiding. 小利貞 is a divination favourable in small things; the Chu slip writes 少利貞.
en.tradition: If the nobleman can withdraw, his body goes back but his way gets through; for the small man, it is favourable to hold to what is right and not press on the yang because he is growing.
en.image: Under heaven there is a mountain: Retreat. So the noble one keeps small men at a distance, not hating them, but stern.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. Heaven stands for the nobleman, the mountain for the small man pressing on it; heaven keeps its distance (崔憬). Harsh words only earn hatred; gravity keeps small men off (程頤).

lines.text: Withdrawing the tail. Danger. Not to be used for going anywhere.
lines.note: The Chu slip has 遯其尾, withdrawing its tail, the shape of 咸其拇 (31) and 艮其趾 (52): the tail is the object. Every commentator reads it as being at the tail of the withdrawal, where the harm reaches (王弼).

lines.text: Holding it with the hide of a yellow ox: no one can get it loose.
lines.note: In the Shang bones the yellow ox is a victim, split in burnt offerings (合集 14314.4). 革 is the hide, as in the songs (羔羊). 說 is read 脫, to loosen (徐邈); the Chu slip writes 敓. 革 初九 has the same words.

lines.text: Tied withdrawing. There is illness: danger. Rearing bondmen and bondwomen: auspicious.
lines.note: 臣妾, bondmen and bondwomen, are property that runs off and is returned, with straying cattle (尚書, 費誓). 畜 is the verb used of the cow in 30. Tied where it is, it can rear servants, but not do great things (王弼; the small image).

lines.text: Fond withdrawing. For the nobleman, auspicious; for the small man, blocked.
lines.note: The pair 君子 and 小人 as in 12 六二, "小人吉，大人否". 好 is read hào, to be fond of (陸德明). Whether the fondness is for what is left behind or for withdrawing itself is open. 否 is blocked (鄭玄, 王肅).

lines.text: Fine withdrawing. The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: 嘉 is fine, as in 17 九五 and the songs' "嘉賓". The Chu slip has 嘉遯，吉, without 貞.

lines.text: Fat withdrawing. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: 肥 is fat, the word of the fattened beasts for the feast in the songs (伐木). Shaughnessy (2022) reads "fat piglets", with piglets offered on a Western Zhou oracle bone (Zhouyuan H11:1). The 子夏傳 reads 肥 as ample.

essays.title: Mountain under heaven
essays.text: The lower trigram is mountain, the upper heaven. The commentators read the figure as two yin lines rising under four yang: the two yin grow little by little and the yang must withdraw, so this is the hexagram of the sixth month (朱熹). The 彖 says yin "grows by soaking in". 遯 stands in every line but the second.

readings.title: Withdrawing, or a piglet?
readings.text: The wings, 鄭玄, every commentator, Wilhelm and Legge read withdrawing, and the songs have the verb. Shaughnessy names the hexagram "Piglet", on the graph and the manuscripts' names with 彖; tail, binding, rearing and fattening would all fit a beast. We print "withdrawing", and record the piglet.

readings.title: The tail as object, or at the tail?
readings.text: The commentators, Wilhelm and Legge: one is at the tail of the withdrawal. The Chu 遯其尾 and the shape of 咸其拇 make the tail the object. We print "withdrawing the tail", leaving whose.

readings.title: Loosen, explain, or say?
readings.text: 說 in the second line is 脫, to loosen (徐邈, 虞翻, the Chu 敓); 王肅 reads it as to explain; 程頤 as "beyond saying". We print "get it loose".

readings.title: Fat, or ample?
readings.text: The 子夏傳, 程頤 and 朱熹 read 肥 as ample, at ease; Shaughnessy as fat piglets. We print "fat".

pinyinTones.name: Dùn
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. xiǎo lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: tiān xià yǒu shān, dùn. jūn zǐ yǐ yuàn xiǎo rén, bù wù ér yán.
lines: dùn wěi, lì, wù yòng yǒu yōu wǎng.
zhí zhī yòng huáng niú zhī gé, mò zhī shèng tuō.
xì dùn, yǒu jí, lì. xù chén qiè, jí.
hào dùn, jūn zǐ jí, xiǎo rén pǐ.
jiā dùn, zhēn jí.
féi dùn, wú bù lì.

pinyinNotes: 遯: dùn (to withdraw), as 陸德明 徒巽反
遠: yuàn (to keep at a distance, a verb), as 陸德明 袁万反
惡: wù (to hate), as the book
說: tuō (to get loose, read 脫), as 徐邈 吐活反 in 陸德明 and the book
畜: xù (to keep, rear)
好: hào (fond of), as 陸德明 呼報反
否: pǐ (blocked), as 鄭玄 and 王肅 備鄙反 in 陸德明 and the book

hexagrams.image: 雷在天上，大壯。君子以非禮弗履。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 壯于趾，征凶，有孚。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 貞吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 小人用壯，君子用罔，貞厲。羝羊觸藩，羸其角。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 貞吉，悔亡。藩決不羸，壯于大輿之輹。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 喪羊于易，无悔。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 羝羊觸藩，不能退，不能遂，无攸利，艱則吉。

hexagrams.heading: 大壯
hexagrams.name: 大壯

wilhelm.name: Des Großen Macht
wilhelm.judgment: Des Großen Macht. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Der Donner ist am Himmel oben: das Bild der Macht des Großen. So tritt der Edle nicht auf Wege, die nicht der Ordnung entsprechen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Macht in den Zehen. Fortmachen bringt Unheil. Das ist gewisslich wahr.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der Gemeine wirkt durch Macht, der Edle wirkt nicht so. Fortmachen ist gefährlich. Ein Ziegenbock stößt gegen eine Hecke und verwickelt seine Hörner.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Die Reue schwindet. Die Hecke öffnet sich, es gibt keine Verwicklung. Die Macht beruht auf der Achse eines großen Wagens.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Verliert den Bock in Leichtigkeit. Keine Reue.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Ein Bock stößt gegen eine Hecke: Er kann nicht zurück, er kann nicht voran. Nichts ist fördernd. Merkt man die Schwierigkeit, so bringt das Heil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Tâ Kwang
legge.judgment: Tâ Kwang indicates that (under the conditions which it symbolises) it will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) heaven and above it that for thunder form Tâ Kwang. The superior man, in accordance with this, does not take a step which is not according to propriety.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject manifesting his strength in his toes. But advance will lead to evil,—most certainly.
The second line, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune.

The third line, undivided, shows, in the case of a small man, one using all his strength; and in the case of a superior man, one whose rule is not to do so. Even with firm correctness the position would be perilous. (The exercise of strength in it might be compared to the case of) a ram butting against a fence, and getting his horns entangled.

The fourth line, undivided, shows (a case in which) firm correctness leads to good fortune, and occasion for repentance disappears. (We see) the fence opened without the horns being entangled. The strength is like that in the wheel-spokes of a large waggon.
The fifth line, divided, shows one who loses his ram(-like strength) in the ease of his position. (But) there will be no occasion for repentance.

The sixth line, divided, shows (one who may be compared to) the ram butting against the fence, and unable either to retreat, or to advance as he would fain do. There will not be advantage in any respect; but if he realise the difficulty (of his position), there will be good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 129-130 (Image: Appendix II, p. 309)

en.name: The Power of the Great
en.nameNote: 壯 is strong, at full strength: "盛也" (王肅); in Qin and Jin speech, a man's size (方言). But 壯 is also an injury: "傷也" (馬融), and so in Huainan speech (郭璞). Both senses are old.
en.judgment: A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment is the formula alone. The Qin 歸藏's entry under this figure is a divination about cloud and rain. The book has nothing more.
en.tradition: The great is the yang: four yang lines in full growth, the hexagram of the second month. With the yang strong, it goes without saying that the reading is auspicious; the only point is that the profit lies in holding firm to what is right.
en.image: Thunder is above heaven: The Power of the Great. So the noble one does not tread where there is no rite.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. 履, to tread, is 10's word. Strength against the rites is disaster, and disaster loses the strength (王弼); the nobleman's great strength is to master himself and return to the rites (程頤).

lines.text: Strength in the toes. Campaigning: disaster. There is confirmation.
lines.note: 夬 初九 has the same words, "壯于前趾". 有孚 is confirmation, the verdict borne out. The commentators read "it is sure": going forward with strength at the bottom, disaster is certain (王弼, 程頤).

lines.text: The divination: auspicious.
lines.note: The verdict alone, as 32 九二. Central, yang in a yin place, treading modestly and not overreaching (王弼).

lines.text: The small man uses strength, the nobleman uses a net. The divination: danger. A ram butts a fence and tangles its horns.
lines.note: A ram is taken for the road-offering in the songs (生民), and the Shang offered sheep with dogs, pigs and oxen (合集 00378正). 藩 is a hedge (馬融). 羸 is binding, entangling (孔穎達). 罔 is a net (陸德明); 馬融 and 王肅 read "not".

lines.text: The divination: auspicious; regret gone. The fence breaks open, no tangling. Strength in the axle-block of the great cart.
lines.note: In a stalk-casting verse of 645 BC the cart "sheds its axle-block" (左傳); here the axle-block is where the cart's strength is. 大輿 is 14's great cart. 悔亡 follows 吉, as in 31 九四. The fence opens, and it can go on (王弼).

lines.text: Losing the sheep at the border. No regret.
lines.note: 易 is read 埸, the border of the fields (陸績, 朱熹), the word of the songs (信南山). 旅 上九 loses an ox "于易"; a place Yi, where the Shang ancestor Wang Hai lost his oxen, is 顧頡剛's reading. The commentators read "in ease".

lines.text: A ram butts a fence: it cannot go back, it cannot go on. Nothing is favourable. Hardship, and then auspicious.
lines.note: 遂 is to go on: "進也" (虞翻). 艱則吉 has the shape of 14 初九, "hardship, and then no blame". Going forward it hurts its body, going back its horns (程頤).

essays.title: Thunder above heaven
essays.text: The lower trigram is heaven, the upper thunder. Four yang lines have grown from below: the hexagram of the second month, between 泰 and 夬 (朱熹). The 繫辭下 takes the house from it: of old men lived in caves and in the open; the later sages gave them houses, a ridge-beam above and eaves below, against wind and rain, and took it from this hexagram. 壯 stands in three lines, the ram in two, and sheep in one.

readings.title: Strength, or injury?
readings.text: Strength: the 彖, 王肅, 鄭玄, the 方言, every later commentator, Wilhelm, Legge. Injury: 馬融, 郭璞, 虞翻; then the first line is "injury in the toes". We print "strength", and record the injury, which is as old as 馬融.

readings.title: A net, or nothing?
readings.text: A net: 陸德明, 王弼, 孔穎達, 虞翻. Nothing: 馬融, 王肅, 程頤, 朱熹, and Wilhelm and Legge after them. We print "a net": it is the thing used, as strength is, and the ram in the same line is caught as in a net.

readings.title: Ease, the border, or a place called Yi?
readings.text: Ease: 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, Wilhelm, Legge. The border (埸): 陸績, 朱熹's second reading, 王念孫 and others. A place, Yi, with the Wang Hai story: 顧頡剛, 李鏡池, Shaughnessy. We print "at the border": 于 before a place is the book's usage, and it is the place reading the sources can show.

readings.title: Confirmation, or it is sure?
readings.text: In the first line 有孚 is printed "there is confirmation", the verdict borne out, as this edition renders 孚 by its context. The commentators read "it is sure" (王弼, 程頤).

pinyinTones.name: Dà Zhuàng
pinyinTones.judgment: lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: léi zài tiān shàng, dà zhuàng. jūn zǐ yǐ fēi lǐ fú lǚ.
lines: zhuàng yú zhǐ, zhēng xiōng, yǒu fú.
zhēn jí.
xiǎo rén yòng zhuàng, jūn zǐ yòng wǎng, zhēn lì. dī yáng chù fān, léi qí jiǎo.
zhēn jí, huǐ wáng. fān jué bù léi, zhuàng yú dà yú zhī fù.
sàng yáng yú yì, wú huǐ.
dī yáng chù fān, bù néng tuì, bù néng suì, wú yōu lì, jiān zé jí.

pinyinNotes: 壯: zhuàng, as 陸德明 莊亮反
羸: léi (to tangle), as 陸德明 律悲反
輹: fù, as 陸德明 音福
喪: sàng (to lose), as 陸德明 息浪反
易: yì (easy, or the field border), as 陸德明 以豉反

hexagrams.judgment: 康侯用錫馬蕃庶，晝日三接。
hexagrams.image: 明出地上，晉。君子以自昭明德。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 晉如摧如，貞吉。罔孚，裕无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 晉如，愁如，貞吉。受茲介福于其王母。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 眾允，悔亡。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 晉如鼫鼠，貞厲。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 悔亡，失得勿恤。往吉，无不利。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 晉其角，維用伐邑，厲，吉，无咎，貞吝。

hexagrams.heading: 晉
hexagrams.name: 晉

wilhelm.name: Der Fortschritt
wilhelm.judgment: Der Fortschritt: Der starke Fürst wird geehrt durch Pferde in großer Menge. An einem Tag wird er dreimal empfangen.
wilhelm.image: Die Sonne steigt über die Erde empor: das Bild des Fortschritts. So macht der Edle selbst seine klaren Anlagen hell.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Fortschreitend, aber zurückgewiesen. Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Wenn man kein Vertrauen findet, so bleibe man gelassen. Kein Fehler.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Fortschreitend, aber in Trauer: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Man bekommt dann großes Glück von seiner Ahnfrau.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Alle sind einverstanden. Die Reue schwindet.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Fortschritt wie ein Hamster. Beharrlichkeit bringt Gefahr.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Die Reue schwindet. Gewinn und Verlust nimm nicht zu Herzen. Unternehmungen bringen Heil. Alles ist fördernd.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Fortschreiten mit den Hörnern darf man nur, um sein eigenes Gebiet zu strafen. Bewusstsein der Gefahr bringt Heil. Kein Makel. Beharrlichkeit bringt Beschämung.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Ȝin
legge.judgment: In Ȝin we see a prince who secures the tranquillity (of the people) presented on that account with numerous horses (by the king), and three times in a day received at interviews.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth and that for the bright (sun) coming forth above it form Ȝin. The superior man, according to this, gives himself to make more brilliant his bright virtue.
lines: The first line, divided, shows one wishing to advance, and (at the same time) kept back. Let him be firm and correct, and there will be good fortune. If trust be not reposed in him, let him maintain a large and generous mind, and there will be no error.

The second line, divided, shows its subject with the appearance of advancing, and yet of being sorrowful. If he be firm and correct, there will be good fortune. He will receive this great blessing from his grandmother.
The third line, divided, shows its subject trusted by all (around him). All occasion for repentance will disappear.
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject with the appearance of advancing, but like a marmot. However firm and correct he may be, the position is one of peril.

The fifth line, divided, shows how all occasion for repentance disappears (from its subject). (But) let him not concern himself about whether he shall fail or succeed. To advance will be fortunate, and in every way advantageous.

The topmost line, undivided, shows one advancing his horns. But he only uses them to punish the (rebellious people of his own) city. The position is perilous, but there will be good fortune. (Yet) however firm and correct he may be, there will be occasion for regret.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 131-133 (Image: Appendix II, p. 310)

en.name: Progress
en.nameNote: 晉 is to advance: "進也" (彖, 序卦). The 說文 explains the old graph: the sun comes out and the myriad things advance. The 雜卦: "晉、晝也", it is daytime. 孔穎達: the 彖 explains an old word by a current one.
en.judgment: The Lord of Kang uses it in granting horses in abundance. In the daytime, three receptions.
en.judgmentNote: 康侯 is a title on early Western Zhou bronzes, once with a king's attack on the Shang town and land at Wei (集成 04059). Kings gave lords horses at dawn audiences in the great hall (晉侯穌編鐘), and the songs tell of chariots and teams given at court (崧高, 采菽).
en.tradition: 晉 is advancing; 康侯 is a lord who keeps his state at peace. Horses granted in abundance and three receptions in a day: he receives great gifts and is openly shown the rites of closeness. Whoever has the figure's three qualities when he casts it will have such favour too.
en.image: Brightness comes out above the earth: Progress. So the noble one himself makes his bright virtue shine.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. 明德 is a phrase of the early Zhou documents: King Wen "克明德慎罰" (康誥). The earth brings forth all things, but its work is seen only when the sun comes out above it (鄭玄).

lines.text: Advancing, pushed back. The divination: auspicious. No confirmation. Being lenient: no blame.
lines.note: 罔 is the negative of the early Zhou documents, which set it before this very word: "罔不是孚" (君奭). 裕 is to give ease, to be generous (康誥). 摧 is to be pushed back (何氏). Not yet in office, it is not yet trusted (王弼; the small image).

lines.text: Advancing, sorrowful. The divination: auspicious. Receiving this great blessing from his grandmother.
lines.note: 王母 is the father's dead mother (爾雅). In Western Zhou bronzes she receives offerings and is asked for blessing (集成 02777). 介福, great blessing, is the songs' phrase at the offering (楚茨). 朱熹: an auspicious reading for an offering to an ancestress.

lines.text: The multitude assent. Regret gone.
lines.note: In the Shang bones 允 marks the outcome that bore out the forecast: "that day it did indeed rain" (合集 12950.1). So too in the songs: "卜云其吉，終然允臧" (定之方中). 爾雅: "允，信也".

lines.text: Advancing like a big rat. The divination: danger.
lines.note: The big rat of the songs: "碩鼠碩鼠，無食我黍" (碩鼠), greedy and afraid of people, as its preface says. 鄭玄 cites the song here, and the 子夏傳 writes 碩鼠. The 說文's 鼫 is the rat of five skills, none of them complete.

lines.text: Regret gone. Lost or got: do not be anxious. Going on: auspicious. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: 恤 is anxiety beside a divination, as in the songs: turtle and stalks together say the man on campaign is near (杕杜). 王弼: the ruler does not pry; loss and gain need no anxiety, each has its officer.

lines.text: Advancing its horns: using it to attack the town. Danger; auspicious. No blame. The divination: trouble.
lines.note: 伐邑, attacking a town, is the bronzes' act: "王朿伐商邑" (集成 04059). 維 is the songs' particle before a verb (斯干). Horns push and gore, as the ram's in 34. 程頤: attacking one's own town is ruling oneself.

essays.title: The sun over the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is earth; the upper is read by the wings as brightness. The Image: "明出地上". The 彖: compliant and clinging to the great brightness, the soft advances and goes upward, the soft fifth line in the ruler's place. 晉 stands in four lines. The next hexagram is this figure turned over: brightness gone into the earth (序卦: "進必有所傷").

readings.title: The Lord of Kang, or a lord who brings peace?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 康 as praise or peace (王弼, 馬融, 程頤, 朱熹); Wilhelm "der starke Fürst", Legge "a prince who secures the tranquillity". The early Western Zhou bronzes have 康侯 as a title eleven times. We print "the Lord of Kang", as Shaughnessy does.

readings.title: Given horses, or granting them?
readings.text: Every commentator: the lord is given horses by the king. 鄭玄 reads a hunt or a battle. We print the book's construction, "uses it in granting", which makes the lord the subject and leaves the gift's direction open.

readings.title: Assent, or it was so?
readings.text: The commentators read 允 in the third line as trust (虞翻, 朱熹). The Shang bones and the songs use it for an outcome that bore out a forecast, which would make the line a verification. We print "assent", and record the other.

readings.title: Which rat?
readings.text: A big rat (子夏傳, 鄭玄 with the song), the five-skilled rat (說文), the mole cricket (本草), a hamster (Wilhelm), a marmot (Legge). We print "a big rat".

readings.title: Lost, or the arrow?
readings.text: In the fifth line the base has 失, loss. 馬融, 王肅 and 荀爽 read 矢, the arrow, and 虞翻 an oath. We print the base.

pinyinTones.name: Jìn
pinyinTones.judgment: kāng hóu yòng xī mǎ fán shù, zhòu rì sān jiē.
pinyinTones.image: míng chū dì shàng, jìn. jūn zǐ yǐ zì zhāo míng dé.
lines: jìn rú cuī rú, zhēn jí. wǎng fú, yù wú jiù.
jìn rú, chóu rú, zhēn jí. shòu zī jiè fú yú qí wáng mǔ.
zhòng yǔn, huǐ wáng.
jìn rú shí shǔ, zhēn lì.
huǐ wáng, shī dé wù xù. wǎng jí, wú bù lì.
jìn qí jiǎo, wéi yòng fá yì, lì, jí, wú jiù, zhēn lìn.

pinyinNotes: 晉: jìn (to advance)
蕃: fán (many), as 陸德明 音煩
晝: zhòu, as 陸德明 竹又反
介: jiè (great), as 陸德明 音戒
鼫: shí, as 陸德明 音石

hexagrams.image: 明入地中，明夷。君子以莅眾，用晦而明。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 明夷于飛，垂其翼。君子于行，三日不食。有攸往，主人有言。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 明夷，夷于左股，用拯馬壯，吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 明夷于南狩，得其大首，不可疾貞。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 入于左腹，獲明夷之心，于出門庭。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 箕子之明夷，利貞。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 不明，晦。初登于天，後入于地。

hexagrams.heading: 明夷
hexagrams.name: 明夷

wilhelm.name: Die Verfinsterung des Lichts
wilhelm.judgment: Die Verfinsterung des Lichts. Fördernd ist es, in der Not beharrlich zu sein.
wilhelm.image: Das Licht ist in die Erde hineingesunken: das Bild der Verfinsterung des Lichts. So lebt der Edle mit der großen Menge: er verhüllt seinen Schein und bleibt doch hell.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Verfinsterung des Lichts im Fluge. Er senkt seine Flügel. Der Edle auf seiner Wanderschaft isst drei Tage nichts. Aber er hat, wohin er geht. Der Wirt hat über ihn zu reden.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Verfinsterung des Lichts verletzt ihn am linken Schenkel. Er wirkt Hilfe mit der Macht eines Pferdes. Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Die Verfinsterung des Lichts auf der Jagd im Süden. Man bekommt ihr großes Haupt. Man darf nicht zu eilig Beharrlichkeit erwarten.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er dringt in die linke Bauchhöhle ein. Man erhält das Herz der Verfinsterung des Lichts und verlässt Tor und Hof.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Verfinsterung des Lichts wie beim Prinzen Gi. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Nicht Licht, sondern Dunkel. Erst stieg er zum Himmel empor, dann stürzte er in die Tiefen der Erde hinunter.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Ming Î
legge.judgment: Ming Î indicates that (in the circumstances which it denotes) it will be advantageous to realise the difficulty (of the position), and maintain firm correctness.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) the earth and that for the bright (sun) entering within it form Ming Î. The superior man, in accordance with this, conducts his management of men;—he shows his intelligence by keeping it obscured.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Ming Î, flying, but with drooping wings. When the superior man (is revolving) his going away, he may be for three days without eating. Wherever he goes, the people there may speak (derisively of him).
The second line, divided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Ming Î, wounded in the left thigh. He saves himself by the strength of a (swift) horse; and is fortunate.

The third line, undivided, shows its subject, (in the condition indicated by) Ming Î, hunting in the south, and taking the great chief (of the darkness). He should not be eager to make (all) correct (at once).

The fourth line, divided, shows its subject (just) entered into the left side of the belly (of the dark land). (But) he is able to carry out the mind appropriate (in the condition indicated by) Ming Î, quitting the gate and courtyard (of the lord of darkness).
The fifth line, divided, shows how the count of Kî fulfilled the condition indicated by Ming Î. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
The sixth line, divided, shows the case where there is no light, but (only) obscurity. (Its subject) had at first ascended to (the top of) the sky; his future shall be to go into the earth.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 134-135 (Image: Appendix II, p. 311)

en.name: The Darkening of the Light
en.nameNote: 明 is brightness, 夷 a wound: "夷，傷也" (陸德明, 序卦); the 雜卦 calls it a killing. The 彖 reads it as the sun gone into the earth. In the lines 明夷 flies, is wounded, is hunted, and has a heart that can be got.
en.judgment: A favourable divination about hardship.
en.judgmentNote: The formula alone: a divination about hardship, as in 21 九四 and 26 九三. 鄭玄: the sun gone into the earth is a noble man in a disordered age, who should make things hard for himself and keep out of government. 尚賢 (2022) reads 艱 as 隱, hiding.
en.tradition: The sun gone into the earth: the bright, wounded. The top line is the lord of darkness and the fifth is near him: so whoever casts it does well to keep to what is right through hardship and to hide his own brightness.
en.image: Brightness goes into the earth: The Darkening of the Light. So the noble one, presiding over the multitude, uses darkness and is bright.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. Hide the brightness within and one has it; show it without and that is what is shunned (王弼). The ancient sages hung tassels before the cap, not wishing their sight to reach into everything hidden (程頤).

lines.text: The brightness wounded, in flight, droops its wings. The nobleman on the road: for three days he does not eat. There is somewhere to go: the host has talk.
lines.note: In 537 BC a diviner read this line at a birth (左傳): the name as the sun, the flight as a bird, the three days as dawn, the host's talk as slander; the child would die of hunger. Shaughnessy calls the account a retrospective fiction. 君子于行 has the shape of a song (君子于役).

lines.text: The brightness wounded, wounded in the left thigh. Using it to rescue, the horse strong: auspicious.
lines.note: In the royal hunt a kill shot at the left thigh was the lowest grade (毛傳 on 車攻). 拯 is to lift up (說文, which quotes the line). 馬壯 is the horse strong, as 34's 壯.

lines.text: The brightness wounded in the southern hunt: getting its great head. It may not be divined about illness.
lines.note: 狩 is the winter hunt (爾雅), and the Shang put the hunt to the oracle. Zhou war records count heads taken (虢季子白盤). The Shang divined about illness by part of the body; 16 has 貞疾. The commentators read 疾 as haste.

lines.text: Going into the left belly: getting the heart of the brightness wounded, on going out of the gate and courtyard.
lines.note: In the hunt the best kill is shot from the left flank, and the heart is hit (毛傳 and 何休, on 車攻). 朱熹 says the sense of this line is not clear to him: perhaps a hidden place, and finding one's mind in going far away.

lines.text: Jizi's brightness wounded. A favourable divination.
lines.note: 箕子 is a Shang noble in the Zhou texts: King Wu went to ask him (洪範), and he was let out of prison after the conquest (樂記). 馬融: an uncle of Zhou Xin, he let down his hair and feigned madness, making his brightness dark.

lines.text: Not bright: dark. At first it climbs to the sky; afterwards it goes into the earth.
lines.note: 晦 is the dark of the moon, the last day of the month (說文); in 575 BC Chu drew up its ranks on that day, offending a taboo of heaven (左傳). The 歸藏's entry for this figure tells of Qi of the Xia riding dragons up to heaven.

essays.title: Brightness in the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is brightness, the upper earth: the figure is 35 turned over. The 彖 names two men for it. King Wen, bright and patterned within, soft and compliant without, met great hardship; Jizi, with hardship within, kept his aim right. The text itself names only Jizi, in the fifth line.

readings.title: The brightness wounded, or a bird?
