號: háo (to cry out), as 馬融, 鄭玄, 王肅 and 王廙 户羔反 and the book, against 陸德明's own hào
為: wéi (to turn into)
握: wò, as 陸德明 烏學反
禴: yuè, as 陸德明 羊略反
匪: fěi (not, 非)
齎: jī, as 王肅 將啼反 in 陸德明
洟: tì (mucus), as 陸德明 他麗反; modern yí

hexagrams.judgment: 元亨。用見大人，勿恤。南征吉。
hexagrams.image: 地中生木，升。君子以順德，積小以高大。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 允升，大吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 孚乃利用禴，无咎。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 升虛邑。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 王用亨于岐山，吉，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 貞吉，升階。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 冥升，利于不息之貞。

hexagrams.heading: 升
hexagrams.name: 升

wilhelm.name: Das Empordringen
wilhelm.judgment: Das Empordringen hat erhabenes Gelingen. Man muss den großen Mann sehen. Fürchte dich nicht! Aufbruch nach Süden bringt Heil.
wilhelm.image: Inmitten der Erde wächst das Holz: das Bild des Empordringens. So häuft der Edle hingebenden Wesens Kleines, um es zu Hohem und Großem zu bringen.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Empordringen, das Zutrauen findet, bringt großes Heil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Wenn man wahrhaftig ist, so ist es fördernd, ein kleines Opfer zu bringen. Kein Makel.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Man dringt empor in eine leere Stadt.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der König bringt ihn dem Berg Ki dar. Heil. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Man dringt empor auf Stufen.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Empordringen im Dunkeln. Fördernd ist es, unablässig beharrlich zu sein.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Shăng
legge.judgment: Shăng indicates that (under its conditions) there will be great progress and success. Seeking by (the qualities implied in it) to meet with the great man, its subject need have no anxiety. Advance to the south will be fortunate.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) wood and that for the earth with the wood growing in the midst of it form Shăng. The superior man, in accordance with this, pays careful attention to his virtue, and accumulates the small developments of it till it is high and great.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject advancing upwards with the welcome (of those above him). There will be great good fortune.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject with that sincerity which will make even the (small) offerings of the vernal sacrifice acceptable. There will be no error.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject ascending upwards (as into) an empty city.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject employed by the king to present his offerings on mount Khî. There will be good fortune; there will be no mistake.
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject firmly correct, and therefore enjoying good fortune. He ascends the stairs (with all due ceremony).
The sixth line, divided, shows its subject advancing upwards blindly. Advantage will be found in a ceaseless maintenance of firm correctness.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 159-160 (Image: Appendix II, p. 324)

en.name: Pushing Upward
en.nameNote: 升 is to go up, to climb: "what gathers and goes up" (序卦); "高也" (馬融); 鄭玄: wood grows within the earth and rises day by day. The manuscripts write 登, to climb. In the lines 升 is "climbing", as 13 九三.
en.judgment: A great offering. Using it to see the great man: do not be anxious. Campaigning south: auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: Zhou kings campaigned south: King Zhao "南征而不復" (左傳, 656 BC); King Xuan in a song (采芑); a late Western Zhou bronze sends levies to the southern Huai Yi (兮甲盤). 征 is the Western Zhou word for such a march. 用見 stands where the book usually has 利見.
en.tradition: 升 is advancing upward; the figure comes from 解 with the soft line moved up to the fourth; compliant within and without, the strong second line answered by the fifth: so the reading. Going south is going forward.
en.image: Within the earth, wood grows: Pushing Upward. So the noble one follows virtue, piling up the small to make it high and great.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. The songs have "如日之升", like the sun rising (天保). Wood within the earth starts small and grows high and great (孔穎達). 王肅's text has 慎, careful, for 順.

lines.text: Truly climbing. Very auspicious.
lines.note: 允 and 升 stand in one stanza with a divination: the lord of Wei "升彼虛矣", climbed the mound to look out for a new capital; the turtle said auspicious, "終然允臧", and in the end it was truly good (定之方中). 毛傳: "允，信". 大吉 is a Shang verdict.

lines.text: Confirmation: then favourable to use in the yue offering. No blame.
lines.note: The words are 45 六二's: the yue offering of the songs (天保). 干寶 ties the line to King Wen, who made all four seasons' offerings with the plain yue rite, using only a pig; the sources give nothing to check that.

lines.text: Climbing the mound of the town.
lines.note: The same song has the lord climb the mound (虛) of Cao to look out over the land for a new capital, before the turtle was consulted (定之方中; 毛傳 "漕虛"). 馬融: 虛 "丘也". The commentators read an empty town. The line has no verdict.

lines.text: The king uses it in an offering at Mount Qi. Auspicious. No blame.
lines.note: Mount Qi is the old seat of Zhou: Gugong Danfu came to the foot of Qi and notched the turtle before building (緜); the phoenix called there when Zhou rose (國語). A pit at Fengchu, 岐山 county, gave Zhou divination shells (1977). 17 上六 has 王用亨于西山.

lines.text: The divination: auspicious. Climbing the steps.
lines.note: Going up the steps is how the rites enter a hall: the bride goes up by the western steps (儀禮, 士昏禮). In the bronzes the one received comes in at the gate and stands in the court (大克鼎).

lines.text: Dark climbing. A favourable divination about not ceasing.
lines.note: 冥 is dark in the songs: "維塵冥冥", the dust is dark (無將大車); 16 上六 has 冥豫. 息 is to cease, as the Image of 1, 自強不息. 荀爽 reads 息 as the yang's growing.

essays.title: Wood within the earth
essays.text: The lower trigram is wood and wind, the upper earth: "within the earth, wood grows". The lines climb: truly, the mound of the town, the steps, in the dark; and in the fourth the king makes offering at Mount Qi. The figure is 45 turned over, and the two share the yue offering of the second line.

readings.title: Truly climbing?
readings.text: "Truly", 允 as 信 before the verb (毛傳 on the song; 朱熹); "fittingly" (王弼, 孔穎達); "trusting and following" (程頤); "with the welcome of those above" (Legge); Wilhelm "das Zutrauen findet". We print "truly".

readings.title: An empty town, or its mound?
readings.text: Empty: 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 陸德明, Wilhelm, Legge. A mound: 馬融 "丘也", and the song where a lord climbs the mound before divining for a new town. We print the mound.

readings.title: An offering, or prospered?
readings.text: 亨 in the fourth line is an offering, 享 (馬融, 鄭玄, 陸績, 王肅; 朱熹), or "prospered" (陸德明's reading; 程頤: the royal work of Zhou prospered by it). We print the offering.

readings.title: Campaigning south, or going forward?
readings.text: Campaigning south is the word's Zhou sense (虞翻); going forward (程頤, 朱熹); going to the bright quarter (王弼, 孔穎達). We print "campaigning south".

pinyinTones.name: Shēng
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán hēng. yòng jiàn dà rén, wù xù. nán zhēng jí.
pinyinTones.image: dì zhōng shēng mù, shēng. jūn zǐ yǐ shùn dé, jī xiǎo yǐ gāo dà.
lines: yǔn shēng, dà jí.
fú nǎi lì yòng yuè, wú jiù.
shēng xū yì.
wáng yòng xiǎng yú Qí Shān, jí, wú jiù.
zhēn jí, shēng jiē.
míng shēng, lì yú bù xī zhī zhēn.

pinyinNotes: 升: shēng, as 陸德明 式陵反
見: jiàn (to see, meet)
虛: xū (empty), as 陸德明 如字
岐山: Qí Shān, a place, as 陸德明 其宜反
亨: xiǎng in 六四 王用亨于岐山, read as 享 'to offer', as the book takes it and as in 14 九三 and 17 上六; elsewhere 亨 is hēng

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。貞大人吉，无咎。有言不信。
hexagrams.image: 澤无水，困。君子以致命遂志。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 臀困于株木，入于幽谷，三歲不覿。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 困于酒食，朱紱方來。利用享祀。征凶，无咎。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 困于石，據于蒺蔾，入于其宮，不見其妻，凶。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 來徐徐，困于金車，吝，有終。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 劓刖，困于赤紱，乃徐有說，利用祭祀。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 困于葛藟，于臲卼，曰：動悔，有悔，征吉。

hexagrams.heading: 困
hexagrams.name: 困

wilhelm.name: Die Bedrängnis, (die Erschöpfung)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Bedrängnis. Gelingen. Beharrlichkeit. Der große Mann wirkt Heil. Kein Makel. Wenn man etwas zu sagen hat, wird es nicht geglaubt.
wilhelm.image: Im See ist kein Wasser: das Bild der Erschöpfung. So setzt der Edle sein Leben daran, um seinem Willen zu folgen.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Man sitzt bedrängt unter einem kahlen Baum und gerät in ein finsteres Tal. Drei Jahre lang sieht man nichts.

Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Man ist bedrängt bei Wein und Speisen. Der Mann mit den scharlachroten Kniebinden kommt eben. Fördernd ist es, Opfer darzubringen. Aufbrechen ist von Unheil. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Man lässt sich bedrängen durch Stein und stützt sich auf Dornen und Disteln. Man geht in sein Haus und sieht nicht seine Frau. Unheil!
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er kommt ganz sachte, bedrängt in einem goldenen Wagen. Beschämung, aber man kommt zu Ende.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Es werden ihm Nase und Füße abgeschnitten. Man ist bedrängt von dem in purpurnen Kniebinden. Sachte kommt die Freude. Fördernd ist es, Opfer und Spenden zu bringen.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Er ist bedrängt von Ranken. Er bewegt sich unsicher und spricht: Bewegung schafft Reue. Wenn man darüber Reue empfindet und sich aufmacht, so hat man Heil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Khwăn
legge.judgment: In (the condition denoted by) Khwăn there may (yet be) progress and success. For the firm and correct, the (really) great man, there will be good fortune. He will fall into no error. If he make speeches, his words cannot be made good.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a marsh, and (below it that for a defile, which has drained the other dry so that there is) no water in it, form Khwăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, will sacrifice his life in order to carry out his purpose.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject with bare buttocks straitened under the stump of a tree. He enters a dark valley, and for three years has no prospect (of deliverance).

The second line, undivided, shows its subject straitened amidst his wine and viands. There come to him anon the red knee-covers (of the ruler). It will be well for him (to maintain his sincerity as) in sacrificing. Active operations (on his part) will lead to evil, but he will be free from blame.
The third line, divided, shows its subject straitened before a (frowning) rock. He lays hold of thorns. He enters his palace, and does not see his wife. There will be evil.

The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject proceeding very slowly (to help the subject of the first line), who is straitened by the carriage adorned with metal in front of him. There will be occasion for regret, but the end will be good.

The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject with his nose and feet cut off. He is straitened by (his ministers in their) scarlet aprons. He is leisurely in his movements, however, and is satisfied. It will be well for him to be (as sincere) as in sacrificing (to spiritual beings).

The sixth line, divided, shows its subject straitened, as if bound with creepers; or in a high and dangerous position, and saying (to himself), ‘If I move, I shall repent it.’ If he do repent of former errors, there will be good fortune in his going forward.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 161-163 (Image: Appendix II, p. 325)

en.name: Distress (Exhaustion)
en.nameNote: 困 is to be hemmed in, straitened: "窮也", at the end of one's means (陸德明). The 彖: the firm is covered. Legge describes the graph as a tree within an enclosure. In every line a thing does the hemming: a stump, wine and food, stone, a cart, a knee-cover, creepers.
en.judgment: An offering. The divination: for the great man, auspicious. No blame. There is talk, not believed.
en.judgmentNote: The Qin 歸藏 puts a king's question about his state under this figure. The great man in the songs is the reader of dreams, whose reading is believed. In 548 BC a casting under this hexagram was read against a marriage and set aside: "she is a widow: what harm?" (左傳).
en.tradition: The firm lines are covered by the soft; in peril and yet glad, the body is hemmed in but the way gets through. Who but a great man could do it? "Talk not believed" warns him to keep silent and not rely on his mouth, which only brings more straits.
en.image: The lake without water: Distress. So the noble one gives his life to carry through his purpose.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. In the 左傳 and 國語 致命 is to deliver a charge; the commentators read "to give his life". The noble one keeps the way to death, carrying through his purpose without bending (孔穎達).

lines.text: The buttocks hemmed in by a tree stump. Going into a hidden valley: for three years, not seen.
lines.note: 株 is "木根也", the root of a tree (說文). In the songs birds come out of the hidden valley to the tall trees (伐木). The buttocks are what is seated or struck, as 43 九四. Shaughnessy reads an image and a rhymed couplet.

lines.text: Hemmed in by wine and food. The vermilion knee-cover is just coming. Favourable to use in offerings and sacrifices. Campaigning: disaster. No blame.
lines.note: 紱 is the knee-cover given by Zhou kings at an appointment, "易女赤巿 ... 用事" (逑盤); vermilion three times on the bronzes, red sixty-five. A song makes grain "into wine and food, to offer, to sacrifice" (楚茨). Shaughnessy reads 朱紱方 as a people coming.

lines.text: Hemmed in by stone, leaning on caltrops. Going into his palace, he does not see his wife. Disaster.
lines.note: In 548 BC 崔杼 met this line casting about marrying a widow; the scribes said auspicious, but Chen Wenzi read it phrase by phrase against the marriage (左傳). Cui married her, and it ended in a duke's murder. 蒺蔾 is the caltrop (爾雅). 宮 is any dwelling (爾雅).

lines.text: Coming slowly, slowly: hemmed in by a bronze cart. Trouble. An end reached.
lines.note: A bronze cart is a king's gift with the vermilion knee-cover (毛公鼎) and to a man put in charge of horses (集成 04318). 金 is bronze; the lists name its bronze fittings. The sources give no Zhou sentence with 徐徐. 朱熹: the image is not clear to him.

lines.text: Nose cut off, feet cut off: hemmed in by the red knee-cover. Then slowly there is release. Favourable to use in sacrifices.
lines.note: Cutting off noses and feet were Zhou punishments (康誥), and the 左傳 records feet cut off as sentences (678, 632, 574 BC). The red knee-cover is the lords' (說文). 說 is read 脫, release. 陸績: vermilion and red, offering and sacrifice, are only variation of wording.

lines.text: Hemmed in by kudzu and creepers, and by tottering. It says: moving, regret. There is regret. Campaigning: auspicious.
lines.note: In the songs kudzu and creepers bind trees and stand beside blessing (樛木, 旱麓). 臲卼 is tottering: "邦之杌隉，曰由一人" (秦誓); the 說文 glosses "不安也". The Chu slip has the same words.

essays.title: The lake without water
essays.text: The lower trigram is water, the upper the lake: "the lake without water", the water below it (王弼). Two words of rank and offering run through the lines: the knee-cover of the second and fifth, with an offering after each; and the punishments of the body, the buttocks of the first line and the nose and feet of the fifth. The one Spring and Autumn casting the sources show that met this hexagram read its third line.

readings.title: Release or joy?
readings.text: 陸德明 reads every 說 of the hexagram as joy, and so 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm and Legge. Shaughnessy: "slowly having release". We print "release": 說 read 脫 is the book's word for things coming loose, and the line is about being hemmed in.

readings.title: Just coming, or a country?
readings.text: "The vermilion knee-cover is just coming" (程頤, Legge, Wilhelm), or 方 a country, "the Red-Kneepads country comes" (Shaughnessy; 常武's "徐方既來"). We print "just coming" and say no more than the bronzes do: it is a gift of rank.

readings.title: Nose and feet, or tottering?
readings.text: The base has 劓刖, cutting off nose and feet (虞翻, 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹). 荀爽, 王肅 and 陸績 read 臲卼, unsteady, which would repeat the top line's word. We print the base.

readings.title: It says?
readings.text: 曰 is "it says" (as 26 九三); "taking thought" (王弼, 孔穎達); "says to himself" (程頤, Legge, Wilhelm). We print "it says", cut as the Chu slip: 曰：動悔，有悔，征吉.

pinyinTones.name: Kùn
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. zhēn dà rén jí, wú jiù. yǒu yán bù xìn.
pinyinTones.image: zé wú shuǐ, kùn. jūn zǐ yǐ zhì mìng suì zhì.
lines: tún kùn yú zhū mù, rù yú yōu gǔ, sān suì bù dí.
kùn yú jiǔ shí, zhū fú fāng lái. lì yòng xiǎng sì. zhēng xiōng, wú jiù.
kùn yú shí, jù yú jí lí, rù yú qí gōng, bù jiàn qí qī, xiōng.
lái xú xú, kùn yú jīn chē, lìn, yǒu zhōng.
yì yuè, kùn yú chì fú, nǎi xú yǒu tuō, lì yòng jì sì.
kùn yú gé lěi, yú niè wù, yuē: dòng huǐ, yǒu huǐ, zhēng jí.

pinyinNotes: 困: kùn (hemmed in)
臀: tún, as 陸德明 徒敦反
株: zhū, as 陸德明 張愚反
覿: dí, as 陸德明 大歷反
紱: fú, as 陸德明 音弗
享: xiǎng (to offer), as 陸德明 許兩反
蒺蔾: jí lí, as 陸德明 音疾, 音棃
劓刖: yì yuè, as 徐邈 魚器反 and 音月 in 陸德明
說: tuō (release, read 脫), as the book, against 陸德明's 音悅 (yuè) for the hexagram
藟: lěi, as 陸德明 力軌反
臲卼: niè wù, as 陸德明 五結反 and 五骨反
曰: yuē, as 陸德明 音越

hexagrams.judgment: 改邑不改井，无喪无得。往來井井。汔至，亦未繘井，羸其瓶，凶。
hexagrams.image: 木上有水，井。君子以勞民勸相。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 井泥不食。舊井无禽。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 井谷射鮒，甕敝漏。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 井渫不食，為我心惻。可用汲，王明，並受其福。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 井甃，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 井洌寒泉，食。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 井收勿幕，有孚，元吉。

hexagrams.heading: 井
hexagrams.name: 井

wilhelm.name: Der Brunnen
wilhelm.judgment: Der Brunnen. Man mag die Stadt wechseln, aber kann nicht den Brunnen wechseln. Er nimmt nicht ab und nimmt nicht zu. Sie kommen und gehen und schöpfen aus dem Brunnen. Wenn man beinahe das Brunnenwasser erreicht hat, aber noch nicht mit dem Seil drunten ist oder seinen Krug zerbricht, so bringt das Unheil.
wilhelm.image: Über dem Holz ist Wasser: das Bild des Brunnens. So ermuntert der Edle das Volk bei der Arbeit und ermahnt es, einander zu helfen.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Der Schlamm des Brunnens wird nicht getrunken: zu einem alten Brunnen kommen keine Tiere.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Am Brunnenloch schießt man Fische. Der Krug ist zerbrochen und rinnt.

Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der Brunnen ist gereinigt, aber man trinkt nicht daraus. Das ist meines Herzens Leid; denn man könnte daraus schöpfen. Wäre der König klar, so genösse man gemeinsam das Glück.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Brunnen wird ausgemauert, kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Im Brunnen ist ein klarer, kühler Quell, den man trinken kann.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Man schöpft aus dem Brunnen ohne Hinderung. Er ist zuverlässig. Erhabenes Heil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Ȝing
legge.judgment: (Looking at) Ȝing, (we think of) how (the site of) a town may be changed, while (the fashion of) its wells undergoes no change. (The water of a well) never disappears and never receives (any great) increase, and those who come and those who go can draw and enjoy the benefit. If (the drawing) have nearly been accomplished, but, before the rope has quite reached the water, the bucket is broken, this is evil.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) wood and above it that for water form Ȝing. The superior man, in accordance with this, comforts the people, and stimulates them to mutual helpfulness.
lines: The first line, divided, shows a well so muddy that men will not drink of it; or an old well to which neither birds (nor other creatures) resort.

The second line, undivided, shows a well from which by a hole the water escapes and flows away to the shrimps (and such small creatures among the grass), or one the water of which leaks away from a broken basket.

The third line, undivided, shows a well, which has been cleared out, but is not used. Our hearts are sorry for this, for the water might be drawn out and used. If the king were (only) intelligent, both he and we might receive the benefit of it.
The fourth line, divided, shows a well, the lining of which is well laid. There will be no error.
The fifth line, undivided, shows a clear, limpid well, (the waters from) whose cold spring are (freely) drunk.
The topmost line, divided, shows (the water from) the well brought to the top, which is not allowed to be covered. This suggests the idea of sincerity. There will be great good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 164-166 (Image: Appendix II, p. 327)

en.name: The Well
en.nameNote: 井 is the well: "古者穿地取水，以瓶引汲，謂之為井" (孔穎達). The 彖: going into the water and bringing it up, the well nourishes and is not used up. In the bronzes the graph writes a place, a model and a law, never a well. The Chu name is 汬.
en.judgment: Changing the town, not changing the well: nothing lost, nothing got. Going and coming: the well, the well. Almost there, and the well not yet roped: it tangles its pitcher. Disaster.
en.judgmentNote: A well was a fixed point of a town: armies stopped wells up (左傳, 548 BC), and a man hid in a dry well marked with a rush band (597 BC). 繘 is the well-rope (說文, 方言); 瓶 the small drawing jar (蓼莪). 汔 is almost, "汔可小康" (民勞).
en.tradition: The town changes, the well does not, so nothing is lost or gained, and all who go and come well their well. The drawing almost at the top, before the rope is all up, the pitcher breaks: disaster. Things stay as they were; one must still take care not to fail when almost done.
en.image: Above the wood there is water: The Well. So the noble one cheers the people at their toil and urges them to help one another.
en.imageNote: A later layer, and moral in its own words. 勞 is read lào, to cheer those who toil, as in the songs: "郇伯勞之" (下泉). Cheering the people is the lord nourishing them; urging them to help is making them nourish one another (朱熹).

lines.text: The well muddy: not drunk from. An old well: no game.
lines.note: In the book 禽 is what the hunt takes (7 六五, 32 九四). So 王念孫 and 王引之 read 井 here as 阱, a pitfall for game; the Chu name 汬 is the old form of 阱. 崔憬: 禽 is the old graph of 擒, a catch. The commentators read birds.

lines.text: The well's hollow: shooting at small fish. The water-pot worn, leaking.
lines.note: The Chu slip has a pig element in the graph for 鮒 and no water-pot; Shaughnessy reads shooting a wild pig in a trap. 鮒 is a small fish (虞翻) or a frog (子夏傳). 甕 is a drawing jar (說文). 王弼 and 程頤 read 射 as pouring onto.

lines.text: The well cleaned out, not drunk from: it makes my heart ache. It may be used for drawing. The king bright: together they receive its blessing.
lines.note: A clear spring, a sighing heart and a king stand in one song: "洌彼下泉 ... 愾我寤嘆，念彼周京" (下泉); its preface reads longing for a bright king. 渫 is "除去也" (說文). 為 is "to make" (王弼).

lines.text: The well lined. No blame.
lines.note: 甃 is the wall of a well (說文); 馬融: tiles wrapping it from the bottom up. Shaughnessy, after 李發林: excavated wells have earth walls until the end of the Spring and Autumn; lining begins in the fifth century BC.

lines.text: The well clear, a cold spring: drunk.
lines.note: The 說文 quotes this line for 洌, "水清也"; 毛傳: "寒也". A song has a cold spring below a town of Wei: "爰有寒泉，在浚之下" (凱風). 程頤: no verdict, because the water is not yet at the top.

lines.text: The well drawn from: do not cover it. There is confirmation. Greatly auspicious.
lines.note: 收 is to draw (馬融 "汲也"); 陸績 reads the well's frame, 虞翻 the windlass. 幕 is a cover, as over a food stand (說文). The Chu slip has the graph it uses for 渫 in the third line.

essays.title: Water over wood
essays.text: The lower trigram is wood or wind, the upper water. 鄭玄: the wood is the well-sweep, which lowers the pitcher into the spring's mouth and draws water out. The lines go from the bottom of the well to its top: mud, the hollow and the leaking pot, the cleaned well not used, the lining, the clear cold spring, the well drawn from and left uncovered. Two vessels go down into it: the pitcher of the judgment and the water-pot of the second line.

readings.title: A well, or a pitfall?
readings.text: Every commentator: a well. 王念孫 and 王引之 read "an old pitfall has no game"; the Chu name is the old form of 阱, and two Chu graphs have animal elements. Shaughnessy reads some lines as a well and some as a trap. We print "the well", and "no game", which leaves the trap possible.

readings.title: Tangles, or breaks?
readings.text: 羸 is the rope, as 34 and 44 (虞翻 "鉤羅也"), or "breaks" (程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm, Legge). We print "tangles".

readings.title: Shooting, or pouring?
readings.text: 射 is shooting (the word; Wilhelm) or pouring onto (王弼, 程頤, Legge). The Chu slip has no water-pot. We print the received text and "shooting".

readings.title: Going and coming
readings.text: "The well, the well", the doubled word; "all well their well" (朱熹); "not changing" (王弼); Wilhelm and Legge: they draw from the well. We print the doubled word.

pinyinTones.name: Jǐng
pinyinTones.judgment: gǎi yì bù gǎi jǐng, wú sàng wú dé. wǎng lái jǐng jǐng. qì zhì, yì wèi jú jǐng, léi qí píng, xiōng.
pinyinTones.image: mù shàng yǒu shuǐ, jǐng. jūn zǐ yǐ lào mín quàn xiàng.
lines: jǐng nì bù shí. jiù jǐng wú qín.
jǐng gǔ shè fù, wèng bì lòu.
jǐng xiè bù shí, wéi wǒ xīn cè. kě yòng jí, wáng míng, bìng shòu qí fú.
jǐng zhòu, wú jiù.
jǐng liè hán quán, shí.
jǐng shōu wù mù, yǒu fú, yuán jí.

pinyinNotes: 井: jǐng, as 陸德明 精領反
喪: sàng (to lose), as 陸德明 息浪反
汔: qì (nearly), as 陸德明 許訖反
繘: jú (the well rope), as 陸德明 音橘; modern also yù
羸: léi, as 陸德明 律悲反
勞: lào (to encourage), as 陸德明 力報反
相: xiàng (to help), as 陸德明 息亮反
泥: nì (muddy), as 陸德明 乃計反
射: shè (to shoot), as 陸德明 食亦反
為: wéi (to make), as 王弼 使也
甃: zhòu, as 陸德明 側舊反
洌: liè, as 陸德明 音列
幕: mù (to cover), as 陸德明 音莫

hexagrams.judgment: 巳日乃孚。元亨，利貞，悔亡。
hexagrams.image: 澤中有火，革。君子以治厤明時。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 鞏用黃牛之革。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 巳日乃革之，征吉，无咎。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 征凶。貞厲。革言三就，有孚。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 悔亡。有孚，改命，吉。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 大人虎變，未占有孚。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 君子豹變，小人革面，征凶，居貞吉。

hexagrams.heading: 革
hexagrams.name: 革

wilhelm.name: Die Umwälzung, (die Mauserung)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Umwälzung. Am eigenen Tag, da findest du Glauben. Erhabenes Gelingen, fördernd durch Beharrlichkeit. Die Reue schwindet.
wilhelm.image: Im See ist Feuer: das Bild der Umwälzung. So ordnet der Edle die Zeitrechnung und macht die Zeiten klar.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Man wird eingewickelt in das Fell einer gelben Kuh.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Am eigenen Tag, da mag man umwälzen. Aufbruch bringt Heil. Kein Makel.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Aufbruch bringt Unheil. Beharrlichkeit bringt Gefahr. Wenn die Rede von der Umwälzung dreimal ergangen ist, dann mag man sich ihr zuwenden und wird Glauben finden.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Die Reue schwindet. Man findet Glauben. Die Staatsordnung zu wechseln bringt Heil.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der große Mann ändert wie ein Tiger. Noch ehe er das Orakel fragt, findet er Glauben.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Der Edle ändert wie ein Panther. Der Geringe mausert sich im Gesicht. Aufbruch bringt Unheil. In Beharrlichkeit weilen bringt Heil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Ko
legge.judgment: (What takes place as indicated by) Ko is believed in only after it has been accomplished. There will be great progress and success. Advantage will come from being firm and correct. (In that case) occasion for repentance will disappear.
legge.image: (The trigram representing the waters of) a marsh and that for fire in the midst of them form Ko. The superior man, in accordance with this, regulates his (astronomical) calculations, and makes clear the seasons and times.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject (as if he were) bound with the skin of a yellow ox.
The second line, divided, shows its subject making his changes after some time has passed. Action taken will be fortunate. There will be no error.

The third line, undivided, shows that action taken by its subject will be evil. Though he be firm and correct, his position is perilous. If the change (he contemplates) have been three times fully discussed, he will be believed in.
The fourth line, undivided, shows occasion for repentance disappearing (from its subject). Let him be believed in; and though he change (existing) ordinances, there will be good fortune.
The fifth line, undivided, shows the great man (producing his changes) as the tiger (does when he) changes (his stripes). Before he divines (and proceeds to action), faith has been reposed in him.

The sixth line, divided, shows the superior man producing his changes as the leopard (does when he) changes (his spots), while small men change their faces (and show their obedience). To go forward (now) would lead to evil, but there will be good fortune in abiding firm and correct.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 167-168 (Image: Appendix II, p. 328)

en.name: Revolution (Moulting)
en.nameNote: 革 is the hide with the hair taken off, and to alter: "改也" (馬融, 鄭玄, in 陸德明). The 雜卦: "《革》、去故也", putting away the old. In 初九 it is the hide; elsewhere the verb "to alter", kept apart from 改 "to change".
en.judgment: The day done: then confirmation. A great offering. A favourable divination. Regret gone.
en.judgmentNote: Offerings fell on chosen days: the 少牢 offering on 丁 or 己 days, and 鄭玄's note puns 己 on 改, change (儀禮). The Shang checked a divination against what happened, sometimes counting the days (合集 00643). The Chu slip has 巳日孚 without 乃, and 元永貞 for 元亨.
en.tradition: At the start of a change people do not believe it, so only when the day is done is it believed; bright within and gentle without: whatever is changed has a great success and is right, and the regret of changing is gone; if anything is not right, the change is not believed, and there is regret after all.
en.image: Within the lake there is fire: Revolution. So the noble one puts the calendar in order and makes the seasons clear.
en.imageNote: A later layer, in the words of the calendar: the 堯典 has Xi and He reckon sun, moon and stars and "敬授人時", give the people the seasons. 朱熹: "四時之變，革之大者", the change of the seasons is the greatest of changes.

lines.text: Made fast with the hide of a yellow ox.
lines.note: The same words as 33 六二. 鞏 is "固也", firm (爾雅, 陸德明); 程頤 has it bound. 王弼: at the start, the change not yet made; good for keeping, not for doing, and the ox's hide will not change. Who or what is made fast is not said.

lines.text: The day done: then alter it. Campaigning: auspicious. No blame.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the same words. A yin line cannot lead; it follows a change once made (王弼). 朱熹: a warning that one may not yet change in haste.

lines.text: Campaigning: disaster. The divination: danger. Talk of altering, three times completed: there is confirmation.
lines.note: The Chu slip lacks 貞厲. 三就 is otherwise found only in the 舜典, of the five punishments. 程頤: the talk of change weighed three times and found to agree, then it can be trusted. 崔憬 reads three steps of King Wu's changes after the conquest.

lines.text: Regret gone. There is confirmation. Changing the command: auspicious.
lines.note: Later Western Zhou bronzes record the king renewing or adding to a man's command: "今余隹申京乃命" (集成 04296), "今余曾乃令" (集成 04286). The readers' "mandate" comes from the 彖's 湯武革命. The Chu slip breaks off before this line.

lines.text: The great man changes as a tiger does: before the reading, there is confirmation.
lines.note: Beasts change their pelts with the seasons: thin hides in summer, coats renewed in autumn (堯典), and 朱熹 reads the change so. Tiger skins were royal gifts (毛公鼎). 占, the reading, follows the question in the bones; here confirmation comes before it. 王弼: in accord with the mind of the time.

lines.text: The nobleman changes as a leopard does; the small man alters his face. Campaigning: disaster. The divination about staying: auspicious.
lines.note: Leopard skin trims an officer's coat in the songs (羔裘, Mao 80). The shelf has no Zhou sentence with 革面; Shaughnessy reads "leathery face". The commentators: the small man changes his look and follows (孔穎達). 王弼: the change made, staying is right; marching is unrest.

essays.title: The tiger and the leopard
essays.text: The lines run from a hide (初九) to the pelts of the tiger and the leopard (九五, 上六) and a face (上六). The lower trigram is fire, the upper the lake: "within the lake there is fire". 鄭玄: water and fire put each other out and take turns, as a king who receives the command changes the calendar and the colours of dress. 革 and 鼎 (50) are one figure turned over: "革 puts away the old, 鼎 takes up the new" (雜卦).

readings.title: The day done, or the ji day?
readings.text: Every commentator reads 巳 as 已, finished: confirmed only when the day is done. 己, the sixth day-name, has evidence: the book names days by their stems (18, 57), and the 少牢 offering falls on 己 days. Wilhelm reads 己, "one's own day". We print "the day done"; we keep the reading printed.

readings.title: Talk of altering three times
readings.text: The talk completed three times (王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤); the three stages of King Wu's changes (崔憬); "three times fully discussed" (Legge). We print the words.

readings.title: The command, or the mandate?
readings.text: The bronzes renew and add to a man's command, and we print "changing the command". 虞翻 reads the mandate, from the 彖's 湯武革命; Legge "change (existing) ordinances"; Wilhelm the state's order.

readings.title: Altering the face
readings.text: Every commentator: the small man changes his look and follows. Shaughnessy: "with leathery face", 革 as leather. We print "alters his face".

pinyinTones.name: Gé
pinyinTones.judgment: yǐ rì nǎi fú. yuán hēng, lì zhēn, huǐ wáng.
pinyinTones.image: zé zhōng yǒu huǒ, gé. jūn zǐ yǐ zhì lì míng shí.
lines: gǒng yòng huáng niú zhī gé.
yǐ rì nǎi gé zhī, zhēng jí, wú jiù.
zhēng xiōng. zhēn lì. gé yán sān jiù, yǒu fú.
huǐ wáng. yǒu fú, gǎi mìng, jí.
dà rén hǔ biàn, wèi zhān yǒu fú.
jūn zǐ bào biàn, xiǎo rén gé miàn, zhēng xiōng, jū zhēn jí.

pinyinNotes: 巳: yǐ, the base's 巳 read 已, "the day done" (the book's Choice, with every commentator)
占: zhān (divining), not zhàn

hexagrams.image: 木上有火，鼎。君子以正位凝命。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 鼎顛趾，利出否。得妾以其子，无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 鼎有實，我仇有疾，不我能即，吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 鼎耳革，其行塞，雉膏不食，方雨，虧悔，終吉。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 鼎折足，覆公餗，其形渥，凶。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 鼎黃耳金鉉，利貞。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 鼎玉鉉，大吉，无不利。

hexagrams.heading: 鼎
hexagrams.name: 鼎

wilhelm.name: Der Tiegel
wilhelm.judgment: Der Tiegel. Erhabenes Heil. Gelingen.
wilhelm.image: Über dem Holz ist Feuer: das Bild des Tiegels. So festigt der Edle durch Richtigmachung der Stellung das Schicksal.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Ein Tiegel mit umgekippten Beinen. Fördernd zur Entfernung des Stockenden. Man nimmt eine Nebenfrau um ihres Sohns willen. Kein Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Im Tiegel ist Nahrung. Meine Genossen haben Neid, aber sie können mir nichts anhaben. Heil!

Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der Henkel des Tiegels ist verändert. Man ist behindert in seinem Wandel. Das Fett des Fasans wird nicht gegessen. Wenn erst der Regen fällt, dann erschöpft sich die Reue: Endlich kommt Heil.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Tiegel bricht die Beine. Das Mahl des Fürsten wird verschüttet, und die Gestalt wird befleckt. Unheil!
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der Tiegel hat gelbe Henkel, goldne Tragringe. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Der Tiegel hat Nephritringe. Großes Heil! Nichts, das nicht fördernd wäre.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Ting
legge.judgment: Ting gives the intimation of great progress and success.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) wood and above it that for fire form Ting. The superior man, in accordance with this, keeps his every position correct, and maintains secure the appointment (of Heaven).
lines: The first line, divided, shows the caldron overthrown and its feet turned up. (But) there will be advantage in its getting rid of what was bad in it. (Or it shows us) the concubine (whose position is improved) by means of her son. There will be no error.
The second line, undivided, shows the caldron with the things (to be cooked) in it. (If its subject can say), ‘My enemy dislikes me, but he cannot approach me,’ there will be good fortune.

The third line, undivided, shows the caldron with (the places of) its ears changed. The progress (of its subject) is (thus) stopped. The fat flesh of the pheasant (which is in the caldron) will not be eaten. But the (genial) rain will come, and the grounds for repentance will disappear. There will be good fortune in the end.

The fourth line, undivided, shows the caldron with its feet broken; and its contents, designed for the ruler’s use, overturned and spilt. Its subject will be made to blush for shame. There will be evil.
The fifth line, divided, shows the caldron with yellow ears and rings of metal in them. There will be advantage through being firm and correct.
The sixth line, undivided, shows the caldron with rings of jade. There will be great good fortune, and all action taken will be in every way advantageous.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 169-171 (Image: Appendix II, p. 329)

en.name: The Cauldron
en.nameNote: 鼎 is the cauldron, the bronze cooking vessel on legs: "法象也，即鼎器也" (陸德明). The 彖: wood going into fire, cooking; the sage cooks to offer to the High God. The 雜卦: "《鼎》、取新也", taking up the new. Each line names a part of it, from the feet up.
en.judgment: Greatly auspicious. An offering.
en.judgmentNote: In the Shang bones 貞, the divination, is written with the cauldron; in the bronzes 貞 mostly writes 鼎. A dagger-axe of about the eighth century BC carries the words of 初六 and 六五 with this figure in numbers (鼎卦戈). The cauldrons stood for heaven's command: "在德不在鼎" (左傳, 606 BC).
en.tradition: The cooking vessel; its figure is a cauldron, and wood going into fire to cook is its use; gentle within, quick of eye and ear without; the reading is "a great success"; the 吉 is an intrusion.
en.image: Above the wood there is fire: The Cauldron. So the noble one sets his place right and makes the command firm.
en.imageNote: A later layer. Its command beside the cauldron is the 左傳's: King Cheng "set the cauldrons" and divined, "天所命也". 朱熹: the cauldron is a weighty vessel, and the line is what the 左傳 calls joining high and low to receive heaven's grace.

lines.text: The cauldron, its feet overturned: favourable for putting out the bad. Getting a bondwoman, with her son. No blame.
lines.note: The 鼎卦戈 has "鼎趾顛", the cauldron's feet overturned. 否 here is "惡也", the bad (陸德明). 妾 is the bondwoman of 臣妾 (費誓). 王弼: the empty line below is a cauldron upturned, emptying out the filth before the new goes in. 朱熹: success out of failure, rank out of lowliness.

lines.text: The cauldron has its filling. My counterpart has an illness: he cannot approach me. Auspicious.
lines.note: 實 is the filling of a cauldron in the rites (儀禮, 士昏禮). 仇 is both mate and foe in the songs: "公侯好仇" (Mao 7), "與子同仇" (Mao 133). 王弼: full, it can take no more; the partner is held back and cannot come, so it does not overflow.

lines.text: The cauldron's ears altered: its going obstructed. The pheasant fat not eaten. Just as it rains: regret lessened. In the end, auspicious.
lines.note: The pheasant was the gift a 士 brought (儀禮, 士相見禮), and pheasant fat "食之美者" (鄭玄). The ears take the bar that lifts the cauldron. 王弼: the ears should be empty for the bar, but are stopped up; rain is yin and yang joined, and regret wanes.

lines.text: The cauldron's leg broken: the duke's pottage overturned. Its form drenched. Disaster.
lines.note: Dukes made cauldrons (毛公鼎, 集成 02841). 餗 is gruel (馬融), greens (鄭玄). 渥 is to soak, and of faces, "顏如渥丹" (Mao 130). The 繫辭: small favour in high place, "言不勝其任也". Whose form is drenched is left open; 朱熹 follows copies reading 刑剭, heavy punishment.

lines.text: The cauldron: yellow ears, a bronze carrying-bar. A favourable divination.
lines.note: The 鼎卦戈 has "鼎黃耳", the cauldron's yellow ears. 鉉 is "舉鼎也" (說文), the bar passed through the ears to carry it on the shoulders; the 儀禮 calls it 扃 (士昏禮, with 鄭玄). The ears of a bronze cauldron are bronze.

lines.text: The cauldron: a jade carrying-bar. Very auspicious. Nothing is unfavourable.
lines.note: Jade comes among the king's gifts (毛公鼎); the shelf gives no cauldron bar of jade. 干寶: jade is worth more than bronze; the food rises from pot to cauldron to stand to mouth, so the higher the line, the more auspicious. 大吉 is a Shang verdict.

essays.title: The cauldron in the figure
essays.text: The lower trigram is wood, the upper fire: "above the wood there is fire". 朱熹 reads the figure as the vessel itself: the broken line below the feet, the three whole lines the belly, the broken fifth the ears, the whole top line the carrying-bar; 程頤 the same. The lines too go up the cauldron: feet, filling, ears, leg, ears and bar, bar. 革 (49) and 鼎 are one figure turned over: one puts away the old, the other takes up the new (雜卦).

readings.title: Greatly auspicious, or a great offering?
readings.text: Every witness has 元吉，亨. 王弼 and 孔穎達 explain the order: auspicious first, then success. 程頤 and 朱熹 delete 吉 by the 彖's 元亨, and Legge follows them. We print the base.

readings.title: A bondwoman, with her son
readings.text: We print the words. 孔穎達 and 朱熹: a concubine raised by her son to be mistress of the house; Wilhelm: taken for her son's sake; 程頤 reads the son as the master.

readings.title: Its form drenched, or punishment?
readings.text: 渥 is "沾也", soaked (陸德明, 王弼, Wilhelm); 程頤 and Legge read a face red with shame; 鄭玄's text and the copies 朱熹 follows have 刑剭, a heavy punishment. We print the base's words.

readings.title: Counterpart or foe?
readings.text: 仇 is "匹也" (孔穎達) and "怨耦曰仇" (鄭玄). Legge and Shaughnessy have "enemy". "My counterpart" holds both.

pinyinTones.name: Dǐng
pinyinTones.judgment: yuán jí, hēng.
pinyinTones.image: mù shàng yǒu huǒ, dǐng. jūn zǐ yǐ zhèng wèi níng mìng.
lines: dǐng diān zhǐ, lì chū pǐ. dé qiè yǐ qí zǐ, wú jiù.
dǐng yǒu shí, wǒ qiú yǒu jí, bù wǒ néng jí, jí.
dǐng ěr gé, qí xíng sè, zhì gāo bù shí, fāng yǔ, kuī huǐ, zhōng jí.
dǐng zhé zú, fù gōng sù, qí xíng wò, xiōng.
dǐng huáng ěr jīn xuàn, lì zhēn.
dǐng yù xuàn, dà jí, wú bù lì.

pinyinNotes: 否: pǐ (bad), as 陸德明 悲巳反, "惡也"
仇: qiú (counterpart), as 陸德明 音求, "匹也"
行: xíng (going), as the book reads 其行塞; 陸德明 gives 下孟反 (xìng)
塞: sè (obstructed), as 陸德明 悉則反

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。震來虩虩，笑言啞啞，震驚百里，不喪匕鬯。
hexagrams.image: 洊雷，震。君子以恐懼脩省。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 震來虩虩，後笑言啞啞，吉。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 震來厲，億喪貝，躋于九陵，勿逐，七日得。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 震蘇蘇，震行无眚。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 震遂泥。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 震往來厲，意无喪有事。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 震索索，視矍矍，征凶。震不于其躬，于其鄰，无咎。婚媾有言。

hexagrams.heading: 震
hexagrams.name: 震

wilhelm.name: Das Erregende, (das Erschüttern, der Donner)
wilhelm.judgment: Das Erschüttern bringt Gelingen. Das Erschüttern kommt: Hu, Hu! Lachende Worte: Ha, Ha! Das Erschüttern erschreckt hundert Meilen, und er lässt nicht Opferlöffel und Kelch fallen.
wilhelm.image: Fortgesetzter Donner: das Bild des Erschütterns. So macht der Edle unter Furcht und Zittern sein Leben recht und erforscht sich selbst.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Das Erschüttern kommt: Hu, Hu! Darauf folgen lachende Worte: Ha, Ha! Heil!

Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Das Erschüttern kommt mit Gefahr. Hunderttausendfach verlierst du deine Schätze und musst auf die neun Hügel steigen. Jage ihnen nicht nach. Nach sieben Tagen bekommst du sie wieder.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Das Erschüttern kommt und macht fassungslos. Wenn man infolge des Erschütterns handelt, so bleibt man frei von Unglück.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Das Erschüttern gerät in Schlamm.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Das Erschüttern geht hin und her: Gefahr. Aber man verliert durchaus nichts, nur gibt es Geschäfte.

Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Die Erschütterung bringt Verfall und ängstliches Umherblicken. Vorangehen bringt Unheil. Wenn sie noch nicht den eignen Leib erreicht, sondern erst den Nachbar erreicht hat, so ist es kein Makel. Die Genossen haben zu reden.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kăn
legge.judgment: Kăn gives the intimation of ease and development. When (the time of) movement (which it indicates) comes, (the subject of the hexagram) will be found looking out with apprehension, and yet smiling and talking cheerfully. When the movement (like a crash of thunder) terrifies all within a hundred lî, he will be (like the sincere worshipper) who is not (startled into) letting go his ladle and (cup of) sacrificial spirits.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) thunder, being repeated, forms Kăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, is fearful and apprehensive, cultivates (his virtue), and examines (his faults).
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject, when the movement approaches, looking out and around with apprehension, and afterwards smiling and talking cheerfully. There will be good fortune.

The second line, divided, shows its subject, when the movement approaches, in a position of peril. He judges it better to let go the articles (in his possession), and to ascend a very lofty height. There is no occasion for him to pursue after (the things he has let go); in seven days he will find them.
The third line, divided, shows its subject distraught amid the startling movements going on. If those movements excite him to (right) action, there will be no mistake.
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject, amid the startling movements, supinely sinking (deeper) in the mud.

The fifth line, divided, shows its subject going and coming amidst the startling movements (of the time), and always in peril; but perhaps he will not incur loss, and find business (which he can accomplish).

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject, amidst the startling movements (of the time), in breathless dismay and looking round him with trembling apprehension. If he take action, there will be evil. If, while the startling movements have not reached his own person and his neighbourhood, (he were to take precautions), there would be no error, though his relatives might (still) speak against him.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 172-174 (Image: Appendix II, p. 330)

en.name: The Arousing (The Shaking, Thunder)
en.nameNote: 震 is not the common word for thunder (雷) but the clap that shakes: "劈歷振物者" (說文), quoting the 左傳 where thunder strikes a temple. 陸德明: "動也". The 序卦 ties it to the cauldron: the one who keeps the vessel is the eldest son. We print "thunder" throughout.
en.judgment: An offering. Thunder comes: in terror. Laughing and talking: ha, ha. Thunder startles a hundred li: the ladle and the fragrant wine are not lost.
en.judgmentNote: Thunder struck as punishment: "震夷伯之廟，罪之也" (左傳, 645 BC). 震驚 stands together in a song of war (常武, Mao 263). 匕 is the ladle that takes the meat from the cauldron (儀禮, with 鄭玄); 鬯, fragrant wine of black millet, was a royal gift (大盂鼎, 毛公鼎). Thunder heard a hundred li was later tied to a lord's domain (孔穎達).
en.tradition: One yang line born under two yin; its image thunder, its kin the eldest son; it has the way of success. 虩虩 is the look of fear, glancing round; "startles a hundred li" is said of the thunder; "not losing the ladle and the wine" is said of the eldest son. Whoever can fear brings on blessing and does not lose the weighty charge he holds.
en.image: Thunder again and again: The Arousing. So the noble one, in fear and dread, puts himself in order and examines himself.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 洊 is the "again and again" of 29's water. Thunder was read as heaven's warning (左傳). 程頤: the noble one, fearing heaven's might, sets himself right and examines his faults; not only at thunder, but whenever he is startled.

lines.text: Thunder comes: in terror. Afterwards, laughing and talking: ha, ha. Auspicious.
lines.note: The judgment's words, with "afterwards" and a verdict; a rhymed oracle (Shaughnessy). 孔穎達: the judgment speaks of the thunder, the line of the man who meets it and fears. 干寶: the terror is King Wen's danger at Youli, the laughter his later receiving the states.

lines.text: Thunder comes: danger. Ah, losing cowries. Climbing the nine hills. Do not chase them: in seven days, got.
lines.note: Cowries were wealth and royal gift: "易貝卅朋" (何尊). Losing and not chasing is a formula of the book (38 初九; 63 六二, word for word). 億 in Zhou texts is a number, never an exclamation, but only the exclamation fits here and in 六五 (王弼 "辭也"). 程頤 reads "reckoning"; 朱熹: "未詳".

lines.text: Thunder: coming to, coming to. Thunder, going: no blight.
lines.note: 蘇 in the 左傳 is to come to after being struck down: a spy killed at Jiang "六日而蘇" (601 BC), as 虞翻 cites. The commentators read fear and unrest (陸德明 "疑懼貌"); 程頤 and 朱熹 a spirit slack and lost. Who goes is left open.

lines.text: Thunder goes on into the mud.
lines.note: 泥 is the mud of 5 九三. 遂 is going on with no turning back (程頤); 荀爽's text has 隊, falling. 王弼: among four yin it should be brave to steady the many; if it too is shaken, it ends in hardship. The shelf gives nothing more.

lines.text: Thunder going and coming: danger. Ah, no loss: there is an affair.
lines.note: 有事 is the affair of a rite in the 左傳: "有事于大廟" (601 BC); 虞翻 reads the offering here, that one can keep the temple. The base writes 意 and reads it as 六二's 億. 王弼: holding the high place in time of thunder is an opening for affairs; fearing, it would lose them.

lines.text: Thunder: shrinking, shrinking; looking: darting, darting. Campaigning: disaster. Thunder not at his own person, at his neighbour: no blame. A marriage: there is talk.
lines.note: The Chu charges ask for the client's own person: "躬身尚毋有咎" (包山 197). In the 左傳 a marriage oracle has "西鄰責言", the western neighbour reproaches us (645 BC). 鄭玄: 索索 the feet unsteady, 矍矍 the eyes. 王弼: fearing because the neighbour is shaken, and taking warning, is preparedness.

essays.title: Thunder doubled
essays.text: Both trigrams are thunder; the Image: "thunder again and again". Every line but the first begins with 震, and the first repeats the judgment. In the manuscripts the name is written differently: Mawangdui 辰, the Tsinghua slips a form of 來, the collected 歸藏 釐. 辛亞民 argues the name 來 was taken from the lines' 震來 and 震往來, and the commoner 震 won.

readings.title: Thunder, or fear?
readings.text: The 說文, the 左傳, the 春秋 and the Image make 震 the thunderclap. 王弼 reads it in the lines as the fear it causes; Wilhelm and Legge write shaking and movement. We print "thunder", which leaves the fear to 虩虩 and the other words that say it.

readings.title: 億: ah, or a hundred thousand?
readings.text: An exclamation (王弼, 陸德明, 虞翻, 干寶); a hundred thousand (鄭玄, Wilhelm); to reckon (程頤, Legge). Zhou texts use it as a number, never as an exclamation, but only the exclamation fits both lines. We print "ah".

readings.title: 蘇蘇: coming to, or fearful?
readings.text: Coming to, reviving (虞翻, with three uses in the 左傳); fearful (陸德明, 王弼); dazed and slack (程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge). We print "coming to".

readings.title: Shrinking and darting
readings.text: 鄭玄 reads the feet and the eyes; the commentators a state of mind, fear or a dwindling spirit. We print "shrinking" and "darting", which hold the body and leave the cause open.

pinyinTones.name: Zhèn
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. zhèn lái xì xì, xiào yán è è, zhèn jīng bǎi lǐ, bù sàng bǐ chàng.
pinyinTones.image: jiàn léi, zhèn. jūn zǐ yǐ kǒng jù xiū xǐng.
lines: zhèn lái xì xì, hòu xiào yán è è, jí.
zhèn lái lì, yī sàng bèi, jī yú jiǔ líng, wù zhú, qī rì dé.
zhèn sū sū, zhèn xíng wú shěng.
zhèn suì nì.
zhèn wǎng lái lì, yī wú sàng yǒu shì.
zhèn suǒ suǒ, shì jué jué, zhēng xiōng. zhèn bù yú qí gōng, yú qí lín, wú jiù. hūn gòu yǒu yán.

pinyinNotes: 啞啞: è è (laughing), as 陸德明 烏客反
億: yī (ah), as 陸德明 於其反, "辭也", 本又作噫; 鄭玄 於力反 (yì, a hundred thousand) recorded
意: yī, read as 億 "ah" (六五), as the book and 陸德明 ("六五同")
泥: nì (mired), as 陸德明 乃計反; 荀爽 乃低反 (ní)
省: xǐng (examines), not shěng
喪: sàng (lose), as 陸德明 息浪反

hexagrams.judgment: 艮其背，不獲其身，行其庭，不見其人，无咎。
hexagrams.image: 兼山，艮。君子以思不出其位。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 艮其趾，无咎。利永貞。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 艮其腓，不拯其隨，其心不快。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 艮其限，列其夤，厲薰心。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 艮其身，无咎。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 艮其輔，言有序，悔亡。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 敦艮，吉。

hexagrams.heading: 艮
hexagrams.name: 艮

wilhelm.name: Das Stillehalten, der Berg
wilhelm.judgment: Stillehalten seines Rückens, so dass er seinen Leib nicht mehr empfindet. Er geht in seinen Hof und sieht nicht seine Menschen. Kein Makel.
wilhelm.image: Zusammenstehende Berge: das Bild des Stillehaltens. So geht der Edle mit seinen Gedanken nicht über seine Lage hinaus.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Stillehalten seiner Zehen. Kein Makel. Fördernd ist dauernde Beharrlichkeit.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Stillehalten seiner Waden. Er kann den nicht retten, dem er folgt. Sein Herz ist nicht froh.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Stillehalten seiner Hüften. Steifmachen seines Kreuzbeins. Gefährlich. Das Herz erstickt.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Stillehalten seines Rumpfes. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Stillehalten seiner Kinnladen. Die Worte haben Ordnung. Die Reue schwindet.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Großzügiges Stillehalten. Heil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kăn
legge.judgment: When one’s resting is like that of the back, and he loses all consciousness of self; when he walks in his courtyard, and does not see any (of the persons) in it,—there will be no error.
legge.image: (Two trigrams representing) a mountain, one over the other, form Kăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, does not go in his thoughts beyond the (duties of the) position in which he is.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject keeping his toes at rest. There will be no error; but it will be advantageous for him to be persistently firm and correct.
The second line, divided, shows its subject keeping the calves of his legs at rest. He cannot help (the subject of the line above) whom he follows, and is dissatisfied in his mind.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject keeping his loins at rest, and separating the ribs (from the body below). The situation is perilous, and the heart glows with suppressed excitement.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject keeping his trunk at rest. There will be no error.
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject keeping his jawbones at rest, so that his words are (all) orderly. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
The sixth line, undivided, shows its subject devotedly maintaining his restfulness. There will be good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 175-177 (Image: Appendix II, p. 331-332)

en.name: Keeping Still, Mountain
en.nameNote: 艮 is not the word for mountain (山). It is to stop, keep still: "《艮》、止也" (彖, 序卦). The 說文 has "很也", eyes set against each other that do not give way; Mawangdui writes 根, a root. The 說卦: "艮為山". We print "keeping still", which the lines bear out.
en.judgment: Keeping its back still: not catching its body. Going into its courtyard: not seeing its people. No blame.
en.judgmentNote: The Chu slip writes 庭 as 廷, the court where an appointee stood before the king: "入門，立中廷，北鄉" (大克鼎). 獲 is the catch of the hunt and of war. The slip has the name and then 其背, with no second 艮; Shaughnessy suspects the judgment is a line moved to the head, belonging at 六五.
en.tradition: One yang line at rest on two yin, risen from below to the top and stopped; its image the mountain. Only if one can rest at the back and not keep one's body, walk in the courtyard and not see the people, is there no blame: the body moves, only the back is still. Movement and rest each stopped in its place, both ruled by stillness.
en.image: Mountains joined: Keeping Still. So the noble one, in his thoughts, does not go beyond his place.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 位 is the place taken at a rite or court. 王弼: each stops in its own place and does not encroach on another's office. 程頤: going on when one should stop, or lingering when one should hurry, is going beyond one's place.

lines.text: Keeping its toes still. No blame. A favourable divination for the long run.
lines.note: The Chu slip has the line word for word (止 for 趾). The body is named from the bottom, as in 31; 趾 stands only in bottom lines (Shaughnessy). 王弼: at the start of stopping, with nowhere to go, it keeps its toes still; utterly still and settled, so the long run is favourable.

lines.text: Keeping its calf still: not rescuing its following. Its heart is not pleased.
lines.note: 腓 is the calf of 31 六二. The Chu slip has 艮其足 and 其心不悸, a throbbing heart. A rhymed oracle (Shaughnessy). 王弼: the following is the toes; with the calf held they are not lifted, and the restless calf cannot rest. 程頤 and 朱熹: it cannot rescue the line it follows.

lines.text: Keeping its waist still: splitting the flesh along its spine. Danger, scorching the heart.
lines.note: 限 is "要也", the waist (馬融, 鄭玄, 荀爽, 虞翻); 夤 "夾脊肉也", the flesh along the spine (馬融). A song has a heart smoked with care: "憂心如熏" (雲漢, Mao 258). The Chu slip has 痛心, a painful heart. 王弼: held still in the middle, the body splits.

lines.text: Keeping its body still. No blame.
lines.note: The small image has "止諸躬也", and the Chu slip, by Shaughnessy's reading, writes 躬. 王弼: above the middle is the body; in its place, it keeps itself still. 虞翻 reads the belly, pregnancy (大明, "大任有身"). 程頤: one in high place who can only keep himself.

lines.text: Keeping its jawbone still: words have order. Regret gone.
lines.note: 輔 is the jawbone of 31 上六. Words with pattern in a song: "出言有章" (都人士, Mao 225). The Chu slip has 言有序, against Wikisource's 孚. 王弼: kept still at the jaw, the mouth has no words to regret.

lines.text: Thick keeping still. Auspicious.
lines.note: 敦 before a verb is 19's and 24's word: thick, solid. 程頤: stopping is hardest to keep to the end; this line is thick to the end, and alone of the six it is auspicious. Shaughnessy calls the line anomalous and proposes the present 六五 once stood here.

essays.title: A body from the toes up
essays.text: Both trigrams are the mountain; the Image: "mountains joined". The lines name the body from the bottom: toes, calf, waist and the flesh along the spine, body, jawbone, as 31 does (toe, calf, thigh, back, jawbone), and the judgment names the back. Shaughnessy sets the two hexagrams beside a Western Zhou jade figurine of the human body.

readings.title: Keeping still, or glaring?
readings.text: Keeping still, stopping (the 彖, 序卦, 說卦, every commentator; Wilhelm, Legge); glaring, stubborn (說文 很, 鄭玄, the 歸藏's 狠); a root (Mawangdui 根). We print "keeping still", which the lines bear out: the jawbone kept still, words in order.

readings.title: Whose following?
readings.text: The toes, lifted by the calf (王弼, 孔穎達); the one it follows and cannot rescue (程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm, Legge); the marrow, 隨 for 髓 (Shaughnessy). We print "its following", as 31.

readings.title: Scorching, gatekeeper, or pain?
readings.text: Scorching the heart (the base; 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹); the gatekeeper's heart (虞翻's 閽); a painful heart (the Chu slip). We print the base.

readings.title: Waist and spine
readings.text: The waist and the flesh along the spine (馬融, 鄭玄, 虞翻, 朱熹); the dividing line between upper and lower (程頤); Legge's "loins" and "ribs". We print the waist and the spine's flesh.

pinyinTones.name: Gèn
pinyinTones.judgment: gèn qí bèi, bù huò qí shēn, xíng qí tíng, bù jiàn qí rén, wú jiù.
pinyinTones.image: jiān shān, gèn. jūn zǐ yǐ sī bù chū qí wèi.
lines: gèn qí zhǐ, wú jiù. lì yǒng zhēn.
gèn qí féi, bù zhěng qí suí, qí xīn bù kuài.
gèn qí xiàn, liè qí yín, lì xūn xīn.
gèn qí shēn, wú jiù.
gèn qí fǔ, yán yǒu xù, huǐ wáng.
dūn gèn, jí.

背: bèi, as 陸德明 必內反

hexagrams.image: 山上有木，漸。君子以居賢德善俗。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 鴻漸于干。小子厲，有言，无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 鴻漸于磐，飲食衎衎，吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 鴻漸于陸。夫征不復，婦孕不育，凶。利禦寇。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 鴻漸于木，或得其桷，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 鴻漸于陵，婦三歲不孕，終莫之勝，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 鴻漸于陸，其羽可用為儀，吉。

hexagrams.heading: 漸
hexagrams.name: 漸

wilhelm.name: Die Entwicklung, (allmählicher Fortschritt)
wilhelm.judgment: Die Entwicklung. Das Mädchen wird verheiratet. Heil! Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Auf dem Berge ist ein Baum: das Bild der Entwicklung. So weilt der Edle in würdiger Tugend, um die Sitten zu bessern.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich dem Ufer zu. Der junge Sohn ist in Gefahr. Es gibt Gerede. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich dem Felsen zu. Essen und Trinken in Frieden und Eintracht. Heil!

Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich der Hochebene zu. Der Mann zieht aus und kehrt nicht wieder. Die Frau trägt ein Kind, aber bringt es nicht zur Welt. Unheil! Fördernd ist es, Räuber abzuwehren.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich dem Baume zu. Vielleicht bekommt sie einen flachen Ast. Kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich dem Gipfel zu. Die Frau bekommt drei Jahre lang kein Kind. Endlich kann sie nichts verhindern. Heil!
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Die Wildgans zieht allmählich den Wolkenhöhen zu. Ihre Federn können zum heiligen Tanz verwendet werden. Heil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kien
legge.judgment: Kien suggests to us the marriage of a young lady, and the good fortune (attending it). There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain and above it that for a tree form Kien. The superior man, in accordance with this, attains to and maintains his extraordinary virtue, and makes the manners of the people good.
lines: The first line, divided, shows the wild geese gradually approaching the shore. A young officer (in similar circumstances) will be in a position of danger, and be spoken against; but there will be no error.
The second line, divided, shows the geese gradually approaching the large rocks, where they eat and drink joyfully and at ease. There will be good fortune.

The third line, undivided, shows them gradually advanced to the dry plains. (It suggests also the idea of) a husband who goes on an expedition from which he does not return, and of a wife who is pregnant, but will not nourish her child. There will be evil. (The case symbolised) might be advantageous in resisting plunderers.
The fourth line, divided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the trees. They may light on the flat branches. There will be no error.

The fifth line, undivided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the high mound. (It suggests the idea of) a wife who for three years does not become pregnant; but in the end the natural issue cannot be prevented. There will be good fortune.
The sixth line, undivided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the large heights (beyond). Their feathers can be used as ornaments. There will be good fortune.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 178-179 (Image: Appendix II, p. 333)

en.name: Development (Gradual Progress)
en.nameNote: 漸 is to advance by degrees: "《漸》者、進也" (彖, 序卦); "以之前為義，即階漸之道" (陸德明), going forward by steps. The 雜卦: the woman goes in marriage, waiting for the man to act. In the songs 漸 is to soak (氓, Mao 58). In the lines it is "edges towards".
en.judgment: A woman going in marriage: auspicious. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: The wild goose was the gift of the marriage rite: the choosing, the auspicious divination and the asking of the day were each presented with a goose, and the groom carried one in at the wedding (儀禮, 士昏禮, with 鄭玄). 歸 is a woman going to her husband's house. The 歸藏's 漸 has "取女", taking a wife.
en.tradition: Advancing by degrees: still below and yielding above, a figure that does not rush forward, and the sign of a woman going in marriage; the lines from the second to the fifth are all in their proper places; so the reading is "a woman's marrying is auspicious", with the warning that it is favourable to be correct.
en.image: On the mountain there are trees: Development. So the noble one dwells in worthy virtue and makes customs good.
en.imageNote: A later layer; the shelf gives nothing for its words. 孔穎達: trees on the mountain are high because of the mountain, not grown tall all at once. 程頤: changing customs is not done in a morning or an evening, so it goes by degrees.

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the bank. The young one: danger. There is talk. No blame.
lines.note: 鴻 is the big wild goose (毛傳). 干 is the river bank: "寘之河之干兮" (伐檀, Mao 112, 毛傳 "厓也"). The Chu slip has 澗, a ravine stream, and ends "there is talk, not to the end" (不終). 王弼: harassed by small people and slander, it is not harmed in its right.

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the rock. Drinking and eating: merry, merry. Auspicious.
lines.note: 衎 is the joy of a feast: "嘉賓式燕以衎" (南有嘉魚, Mao 171, 毛傳 "樂也"). The Chu slip has 阪, a slope, for 磐. 孔穎達: the goose is a water bird and does not settle on rocks and hills; the places only mark the rising. The small image: not eating for nothing.

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the high plain. The husband campaigns and does not return; the wife is with child and does not give birth. Disaster. Favourable for warding off raiders.
lines.note: A song has the goose on the high plain and a duke who "歸不復" (九罭, Mao 159). A turtle oracle of 563 BC: "有夫出征，而喪其雄", and Ding Jiang reads it as "禦寇之利" (左傳). 王弼 reads a wrong union of the third and fourth lines; 朱熹 a plain omen: "凶莫甚焉".

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the trees. Perhaps it gets its rafter. No blame.
lines.note: 桷 is a square rafter (說文); the carved rafters of Duke Huan's temple were "非禮" (左傳, 670 BC). 程頤: the goose's toes are webbed and cannot grip a branch, so 程頤 and 朱熹 read a level branch. 王弼: getting a rafter is finding a safe perch.

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the hill. The wife for three years is not with child. In the end none wins over it. Auspicious.
lines.note: 陵 stands with a husband's campaign in the turtle oracle of 563 BC. A rhymed oracle (Shaughnessy). 王弼: kept from its partner by the third and fourth lines, the wife is three years without child; but they cannot block the way for long. Who or what none wins over is left open.

lines.text: The wild goose edges towards the high plain. Its feathers can be used for the ceremonies. Auspicious.
lines.note: Feathers were held in the dance: "值其鷺羽" (宛丘, Mao 136); "右手秉翟" (簡兮, Mao 38). 儀 is the forms of a rite: "禮儀有序" (士冠禮). 胡瑗, 程頤 and 朱熹 emend 陸 to 逵, the cloud-road, by sense and rhyme; no witness has it. 朱熹: the feathers trim banners.

essays.title: The wild goose, place by place
essays.text: Every line begins 鴻漸于 and names a place higher than the last: the bank, the rock, the high plain, the trees, the hill, the high plain again. The judgment speaks of a woman going in marriage, and the wild goose was the bird of the marriage rite. Legge: "The goose from the most ancient times played an important part in the marriage ceremonies of the Chinese." Shaughnessy takes 九三 for an oracle of the turtle's kind.

readings.title: Rafter, or level branch?
readings.text: A square rafter (說文; 翟玄, 馬融, 陸績, 虞翻), or a level branch (程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge), since geese do not perch in trees. We print "rafter".

readings.title: The high plain, or the cloud-road?
readings.text: Every text has 陸 in 上九, as in 九三. 胡瑗, 程頤 and 朱熹 emend to 逵, the cloud-road, on the sense and the rhyme with 儀; Wilhelm follows them. We print the base.

readings.title: 九三: one story or two?
readings.text: The husband and wife as the third and fourth lines in a wrong union (王弼, 程頤), or a plain omen of a lost husband and a lost birth (朱熹; the turtle oracle of 563 BC; Shaughnessy). We print the words.

readings.title: Edging, or soaking?
readings.text: Every commentator reads advancing by degrees (Wilhelm, Legge too). The songs' 漸 "to soak" makes no sense with the places. We print "edges towards", kept apart from 晉 (35) and 升 (46).

pinyinTones.name: Jiàn
pinyinTones.judgment: nǚ guī jí. lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: shān shàng yǒu mù, jiàn. jūn zǐ yǐ jū xián dé shàn sú.
lines: hóng jiàn yú gān. xiǎo zǐ lì, yǒu yán, wú jiù.
hóng jiàn yú pán, yǐn shí kàn kàn, jí.
hóng jiàn yú lù. fū zhēng bù fù, fù yùn bù yù, xiōng. lì yù kòu.
hóng jiàn yú mù, huò dé qí jué, wú jiù.
hóng jiàn yú líng, fù sān suì bù yùn, zhōng mò zhī shèng, jí.
hóng jiàn yú lù, qí yǔ kě yòng wéi yí, jí.

hexagrams.image: 澤上有雷，歸妹。君子以永終知敝。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 歸妹以娣。跛能履，征吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 眇能視，利幽人之貞。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 歸妹以須，反歸以娣。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 歸妹愆期，遲歸有時。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 帝乙歸妹，其君之袂不如其娣之袂良。月幾望，吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 女承筐，无實，士刲羊，无血，无攸利。

hexagrams.heading: 歸妹
hexagrams.name: 歸妹

wilhelm.name: Das heiratende Mädchen
wilhelm.judgment: Das heiratende Mädchen. Unternehmungen bringen Unheil. Nichts, das fördernd wäre.
wilhelm.image: Oberhalb des Sees ist der Donner: das Bild des heiratenden Mädchens. So erkennt der Edle durch die Ewigkeit des Endes das Vergängliche.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Das heiratende Mädchen als Nebenfrau. Ein Lahmer, der auftreten kann. Unternehmungen bringen Heil.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Ein Einäugiger, der sehen kann. Fördernd ist die Beharrlichkeit eines einsamen Menschen.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Das heiratende Mädchen als Sklavin. Sie heiratet als Nebenfrau.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Das heiratende Mädchen verzögert die Frist. Eine späte Heirat kommt zu ihrer Zeit.

Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der Herrscher I verheiratet seine Tochter. Da waren die gestickten Kleider der Fürstin nicht so prächtig wie die Kleider der Dienerin. Der Mond, der fast voll ist, bringt Heil.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Die Frau hält den Korb, aber es sind keine Früchte darin. Der Mann sticht das Schaf, aber es fließt kein Blut. Nichts, das fördernd wäre.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kwei Mei
legge.judgment: Kwei Mei indicates that (under the conditions which it denotes) action will be evil, and in no wise advantageous.
legge.image: (The trigram representing the waters of) a marsh and over it that for thunder form Kwei Mei. The superior man, in accordance with this, having regard to the far-distant end, knows the mischief (that may be done at the beginning).
lines: The first line, undivided, shows the younger sister married off in a position ancillary to the real wife. (It suggests the idea of) a person lame on one leg who yet manages to tramp along. Going forward will be fortunate.
The second line, undivided, shows her blind of one eye, and yet able to see. There will be advantage in her maintaining the firm correctness of a solitary widow.
The third line, divided, shows the younger sister who was to be married off in a mean position. She returns and accepts an ancillary position.
The fourth line, undivided, shows the younger sister who is to be married off protracting the time. She may be late in being married, but the time will come.

The fifth line, divided, reminds us of the marrying of the younger sister of (king) Tî-yî, when the sleeves of her the princess were not equal to those of the (still) younger sister who accompanied her in an inferior capacity. (The case suggests the thought of) the moon almost full. There will be good fortune.

The sixth line, divided, shows the young lady bearing the basket, but without anything in it, and the gentleman slaughtering the sheep, but without blood flowing from it. There will be no advantage in any way.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 180-182 (Image: Appendix II, p. 334)

en.name: The Marrying Girl
en.nameNote: 歸妹 is "marries off the younger sister": 歸, a woman going in marriage ("婦人謂嫁曰歸", 陸德明); 妹, a younger sister (說文 "女弟也"). 孔穎達: the lords took nine wives at one marriage, each with a niece and a younger sister following, and this hexagram stands for that.
en.judgment: Campaigning: disaster. Nothing is favourable.
en.judgmentNote: The one casting of the hexagram in the 左傳 is about a marriage: Duke Xian of Jin cast the stalks about marrying Bo Ji to Qin and met Guimei changing to Kui; the scribe Su read it "不吉", with this hexagram's 上六 in his verse (645 BC). In the Qin 歸藏 the hexagram is Heng E's flight to the moon, cast "auspicious".
en.tradition: The youngest daughter following the eldest son, and moved by pleasure: neither is right, so the hexagram is the marrying girl; the lines from the second to the fifth are all out of place, and the third and fifth, soft, ride on the hard; so the reading: campaigning, disaster; nothing favourable.
en.image: Above the lake there is thunder: The Marrying Girl. So the noble one makes the end last long and knows what wears out.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 干寶 ties it to the season: thunder pressing on the lake in the eighth and ninth months, when it is about to go into hiding. 朱熹: seeing a union that is not right, the noble one knows its end will wear out.

lines.text: Marrying off the younger sister as an attendant sister. The lame can tread. Campaigning: auspicious.
lines.note: 娣 is the bride's younger sister who goes with her: "古者嫁女必姪娣從，謂之媵" (鄭玄, on 士昏禮); "諸娣從之，祁祁如雲" (韓奕, Mao 261). 跛能履 is 10 六三's phrase. 程頤: as an attendant, worthy as she is, she can only help her lord, as the lame can tread but not go far.

lines.text: The one-eyed can see. A favourable divination for the hidden man.
lines.note: 眇 is "一目小也" (說文), one eye small; the phrase is 10 六三's, and the hidden man is 10 九二's. 孔穎達: not the proper match, yet the union holds, as a one-eyed man still sees. The commentators' wife true to an unworthy husband is theirs.

lines.text: Marrying off the younger sister as a lower wife. Turning back, married as an attendant sister.
lines.note: 荀爽 and 陸績 write 嬬, "妾也"; the 說文 has 嬬 "一曰下妻也", a lower wife. 須 is also to wait, in a song of geese and marriage: "卬須我友" (匏有苦葉, Mao 34), and 王弼 reads it so: not yet time, she goes back and goes later as an attendant.

lines.text: Marrying off the younger sister: the date passed. Married late: there is a time.
lines.note: A song has the wedding date missed: "匪我愆期，子無良媒 ... 秋以為期" (氓, Mao 58, 毛傳 "愆，過也"), with a divination for the marriage. The wedding date was put to the oracle and announced with a goose (儀禮, 士昏禮). 朱熹: a worthy woman does not follow lightly, and waits.

lines.text: Di Yi marries off the younger sister. Her lord's sleeves are not as fine as her attendant sister's sleeves. The moon is almost full: auspicious.
lines.note: Di Yi giving his sister in marriage is 11 六五's, tied to the marriage of 大明 (Mao 236). 袂 is the sleeve (說文 "袖也"). The 春秋 calls a duke's wife 小君. 程頤: the royal daughter cares for the rite, not for dress; the moon nearly full, not quite, she does not rival her husband.

lines.text: The woman holds up the basket: no filling. The young man stabs the sheep: no blood. Nothing is favourable.
lines.note: The 左傳's oracle of 645 BC has it in another order: "士刲羊，亦無衁也；女承筐，亦無貺也". At the offering "司馬刲羊" (儀禮, 少牢); the blood announces the killing (鄭箋). The basket carried gifts of silk (鹿鳴, Mao 161). 程頤: no filling and no blood, no offering: a marriage without an end.

essays.title: The marriage of a lord
essays.text: The lines name the women of a lord's marriage: the bride's younger sister who goes with her (初九, 六三, 六五), a lower wife (六三), the date passed (九四), Di Yi giving his sister in marriage (六五, as 11 六五), and at the end the basket and the sheep of an offering (上六). The one Spring and Autumn casting of the hexagram is about a marriage, and quotes 上六.

readings.title: As an attendant, or with one?
readings.text: As an attendant sister (王弼, 孔穎達, Wilhelm, Legge), or the younger sister married with the attendant sister going along (the custom of 士昏禮 and 韓奕). We print "as", which the parallel 反歸以娣 bears.

readings.title: 須: a lower wife, or waiting?
readings.text: A lower wife (荀爽, 陸績 嬬; 說文 "下妻"; Wilhelm "Sklavin"); waiting (王弼, 陸德明, 程頤, 朱熹's own); one of ability (鄭玄); an elder sister (嬃). We print "as a lower wife", by the line's parallel with 以娣.

readings.title: Whose sleeves?
readings.text: The bride herself as the lord's lady, her sleeves plainer than her attendant's (王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge), or the groom's (Shaughnessy). We print "her lord's sleeves", which holds both.

readings.title: The line and the scribe's verse
readings.text: 史蘇's verse has 上六's words in another order and with other graphs (衁, 貺), and goes on with words found in 38 and 9. Whether it quotes the line or both draw on one oracle is not settled by the shelf.

pinyinTones.name: Guī Mèi
pinyinTones.judgment: zhēng xiōng, wú yōu lì.
pinyinTones.image: zé shàng yǒu léi, guī mèi. jūn zǐ yǐ yǒng zhōng zhī bì.
lines: guī mèi yǐ dì. bǒ néng lǚ, zhēng jí.
miǎo néng shì, lì yōu rén zhī zhēn.
guī mèi yǐ xū, fǎn guī yǐ dì.
guī mèi qiān qī, chí guī yǒu shí.
Dì Yǐ guī mèi, qí jūn zhī mèi bù rú qí dì zhī mèi liáng. yuè jī wàng, jí.
nǚ chéng kuāng, wú shí, shì kuī yáng, wú xuè, wú yōu lì.
