hexagrams.image: 雷電皆至，豐。君子以折獄致刑。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 遇其配主，雖旬无咎，往有尚。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 豐其蔀，日中見斗。往得疑疾，有孚，發若，吉。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 豐其沛，日中見沬，折其右肱，无咎。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 豐其蔀，日中見斗，遇其夷主，吉。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 來章，有慶譽，吉。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 豐其屋，蔀其家，闚其戶，闃其无人，三歲不覿，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 豐
hexagrams.name: 豐

wilhelm.name: Die Fülle
wilhelm.judgment: Die Fülle hat Gelingen. Der König erreicht sie. Sei nicht traurig; du musst sein wie die Sonne am Mittag.
wilhelm.image: Donner und Blitz kommen beide: das Bild der Fülle. So entscheidet der Edle die Prozesse und führt die Strafen aus.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Wenn man seinem bestimmten Herrn begegnet, so mag man zehn Tage beisammen sein, und es ist kein Fehler. Hingehen findet Anerkennung.

Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Der Vorhang ist von solcher Fülle, dass man am Mittag die Polsterne sieht. Durch Hingehen erreicht man Misstrauen und Hass. Wenn man durch Wahrheit ihn erweckt, kommt Heil.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Das Gestrüpp ist von solcher Fülle, dass man am Mittag die kleinen Sterne sieht. Er bricht seinen rechten Arm. Kein Makel.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Vorhang ist von solcher Fülle, dass man am Mittag die Polsterne sieht. Er begegnet seinem gleichen Herrn. Heil!
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Es kommen Linien, es naht Segen und Ruhm. Heil!
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Sein Haus ist in Fülle. Er verdeckt seine Sippe. Er späht durch das Tor und merkt niemand mehr. Drei Jahre lang sieht er nichts. Unheil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Făng
legge.judgment: Făng intimates progress and development. When a king has reached the point (which the name denotes) there is no occasion to be anxious (through fear of a change). Let him be as the sun at noon.
legge.image: (The trigrams representing) thunder and lightning combine to form Făng. The superior man, in accordance with this, decides cases of litigation, and apportions punishments with exactness.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject meeting with his mate. Though they are both of the same character, there will be no error. Advance will call forth approval.

The second line, divided, shows its subject surrounded by screens so large and thick that at midday he can see from them the constellation of the Bushel. If he go (and try to enlighten his ruler who is thus emblemed), he will make himself to be viewed with suspicion and dislike. Let him cherish his feeling of sincere devotion that he may thereby move (his ruler’s mind), and there will be good fortune.

The third line, undivided, shows its subject with an (additional) screen of a large and thick banner, through which at midday he can see (the small) Mei star. (In the darkness) he breaks his right arm; but there will be no error.

The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject in a tent so large and thick that at midday he can see from it the constellation of the Bushel. But he meets with the subject of the (first) line, undivided like himself. There will be good fortune.
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject bringing around him the men of brilliant ability. There will be occasion for congratulation and praise. There will be good fortune.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject with his house made large, but only serving as a screen to his household. When he looks at his door, it is still, and there is nobody about it. For three years no one is to be seen. There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 183-186 (Image: Appendix II, p. 335)

en.name: Fullness
en.nameNote: 豐 is fullness, greatness: "《豐》者、大也" (彖, 序卦). The 說文: "豆之豐滿者也", an offering stand filled to the brim; under 寷, "大屋也", quoting 上六. The 雜卦: "《豐》、多故也", many causes of trouble. In the lines it is "full".
en.judgment: An offering: the king comes to it. Do not be anxious: fitting at midday.
en.judgmentNote: 假 is 格, to come into, as in the bronzes' "王格大室". 日中 is midday as a time of day: King Wen worked "自朝至于日中昃" without eating (無逸); a burial was done "日中" after rain (左傳, 601 BC). Feng was also King Wen's town (文王有聲, Mao 244); nothing here names a place.
en.tradition: Fullness is greatness: brightness that moves, the force of abundance; so the reading has success in it. But a king at the height must decline, and so there is cause for anxiety; anxiety alone does no good: keep to the constant and do not go past the full; so the warning, "do not be anxious: it befits the midday".
en.image: Thunder and lightning both arrive: Fullness. So the noble one decides trials and carries out punishments.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 21's Image has the same two trigrams the other way up, with laws and punishments. 程頤: deciding a trial needs light on the facts, carrying out punishment needs decision; 噬嗑 is the former kings making the laws, this the noble one applying them.

lines.text: Meeting its matched host: though for ten days, no blame. Going on, there is honour.
lines.note: The Shang divined at the end of every ten days about the next: "旬無 ... 王占曰：不吉" (合集 16794.2), the commonest of all their divinations (Shaughnessy). The small image: "過旬災也", past the ten days, calamity. 王弼 reads 旬 as "equal", both lines yang. 鄭玄's text has 妃 for 配, "嘉耦曰妃".

lines.text: Full is its screen: at midday, seeing the Dipper. Going on: getting doubt and illness. There is confirmation, issuing. Auspicious.
lines.note: The Dipper: "維北有斗，不可以挹酒漿" (大東, Mao 203). The Zhou counted an eclipse an omen of disaster (十月之交, Mao 193; 左傳, 612 BC), but the eclipse here is Wilhelm's reading, not the line's word. 王弼: midday is brightness at full, the Dipper seen is darkness at its worst; 若 is a particle.

lines.text: Full is its curtain: at midday, seeing the small stars. Breaking its right arm. No blame.
lines.note: The Chu slip writes 沛 as 芾, the songs' knee-cover of rank (采芑, Mao 178); 鄭玄 and 干寶 read the knee-cover; other copies 旆, a banner. 沬 is "昧星之小者" (子夏傳). 王弼: a curtain that keeps off strong light; bring light and only a glimmer is seen, act and the right arm breaks.

lines.text: Full is its screen: at midday, seeing the Dipper. Meeting its equal host. Auspicious.
lines.note: 夷 stands with 平 and 均, level, even (爾雅): the pair of 初九's 配主. 程頤 and 朱熹: "等夷", the first line, of one kind with it. 李鼎祚 reads wounding; Shaughnessy "his Yi master", the eastern people. A rhymed oracle (Shaughnessy).

lines.text: The pattern comes: there is reward and praise. Auspicious.
lines.note: 章 and 慶 stand together in a song: "維其有章矣，是以有慶矣" (裳裳者華, Mao 214), with 鄭玄 "章，禮文也". In the offering songs "孝孫有慶" (楚茨, Mao 209), 慶 "賜也". 王弼: a yin line coming to the honoured place, making its virtue plain, gets reward and praise. Who brings the pattern is left open.

lines.text: Full is its roof; screened is its house. Peeping at its door: still, no one there. For three years, not seen. Disaster.
lines.note: In the songs 屋 is the roof, and stands with 家 in one couplet (行露, Mao 17). The 說文 quotes the line under 寷, a great house. 干寶 reads Zhou of Shang's jade chamber and its women: the altars gone, the palace empty, the state lost three years after. 王弼: hiding deep when the time is bright.

essays.title: The sun darkened at midday
essays.text: Three lines see stars at midday: the Dipper twice (六二, 九四), small stars once (九三), each behind something made full, a screen or a curtain. The 彖 draws the lesson: "日中則昃，月盈則食", at midday the sun declines; the moon full is eaten. Wilhelm reads 六二 and 九三 as an eclipse of the sun, the totality at 九三. No commentator on our shelf says so; they read darkness, a screen or clouds. We print what is seen at midday, and behind what.

readings.title: Eclipse, screen, or cloud?
readings.text: The commentators read a screen that shuts out the light, and from it a dim lord (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹), or clouds over the sun (虞翻); 干寶 the fall of Shang. Wilhelm reads an eclipse. We print what is seen and behind what, and leave the cause open.

readings.title: 旬: ten days, or equal?
readings.text: Ten days (the small image's "過旬災也"; the Shang divinations; Wilhelm), or "equal" (王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹; Legge). We print "ten days".

readings.title: 沛: curtain, or knee-cover?
readings.text: A curtain (王弼; 程頤, 朱熹 as 旆); the knee-cover of the rites (the Chu slip's and the 子夏傳's 芾; 鄭玄, 干寶); darkness (九家易); Wilhelm's undergrowth. We print "curtain", the pair of 蔀; the knee-cover has the oldest witnesses, and is recorded.

readings.title: Illness, or hatred?
readings.text: 疾 is "illness", the standing word (Shaughnessy too); 程頤 reads suspicion and jealousy, Wilhelm "Hass", Legge "dislike". We print "illness".

pinyinTones.name: Fēng
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng, wáng gé zhī. wù yōu, yí rì zhōng.
pinyinTones.image: léi diàn jiē zhì, fēng. jūn zǐ yǐ zhé yù zhì xíng.
lines: yù qí pèi zhǔ, suī xún wú jiù, wǎng yǒu shàng.
fēng qí bù, rì zhōng jiàn dǒu. wǎng dé yí jí, yǒu fú, fā ruò, jí.
fēng qí pèi, rì zhōng jiàn mèi, zhé qí yòu gōng, wú jiù.
fēng qí bù, rì zhōng jiàn dǒu, yù qí yí zhǔ, jí.
lái zhāng, yǒu qìng yù, jí.
fēng qí wū, bù qí jiā, kuī qí hù, qù qí wú rén, sān suì bù dí, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 假: gé (comes), as 陸德明 庚白反, "至也"; 馬融 古雅反 recorded
見: jiàn (seeing) in 見斗, 見沬: the book reads "to see"; 陸德明 gives no other sound
斗: dǒu (the Dipper)

hexagrams.image: 山上有火，旅。君子以明慎用刑而不留獄。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 旅瑣瑣，斯其所取災。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 旅即次，懷其資，得童僕，貞。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 旅焚其次，喪其童僕，貞厲。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 旅于處，得其資斧，我心不快。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 射雉一矢亡，終以譽命。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 鳥焚其巢，旅人先笑後號咷。喪牛于易，凶。

hexagrams.heading: 旅
hexagrams.name: 旅

wilhelm.name: Der Wanderer
wilhelm.judgment: Der Wanderer. Durch Kleinheit Gelingen. Dem Wanderer ist Beharrlichkeit von Heil.
wilhelm.image: Auf dem Berg ist Feuer: das Bild des Wanderers. So ist der Edle klar und vorsichtig in der Anwendung von Strafen und verschleppt keine Streitigkeiten.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Wenn der Wanderer sich mit kleinlichen Dingen abgibt, so zieht er sich dadurch Unglück zu.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Der Wanderer kommt zur Herberge. Er hat seinen Besitz bei sich. Er erlangt eines jungen Dieners Beharrlichkeit.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Dem Wanderer verbrennt seine Herberge. Er verliert die Beharrlichkeit seines jungen Dieners. Gefahr.
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Wanderer ruht an einem Unterkunftsort. Er erlangt seinen Besitz und eine Axt. Mein Herz ist nicht froh.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Er schießt einen Fasan, auf den ersten Pfeil fällt er. Schließlich kommt dadurch Lob und Amt.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Dem Vogel verbrennt sein Nest. Der Wanderer lacht erst, dann muss er klagen und weinen. Er verliert die Kuh im Leichtsinn. Unheil!
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Lü
legge.judgment: Lü intimates that (in the condition which it denotes) there may be some little attainment and progress. If the stranger or traveller be firm and correct as he ought to be, there will be good fortune.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a mountain and above it that for fire form Lü. The superior man, in accordance with this, exerts his wisdom and caution in the use of punishments and not allowing litigations to continue.
lines: The first line, divided, shows the stranger mean and meanly occupied. It is thus that he brings on himself (further) calamity.
The second line, divided, shows the stranger, occupying his lodging-house, carrying with him his means of livelihood, and provided with good and trusty servants.
The third line, undivided, shows the stranger, burning his lodging-house, and having lost his servants. However firm and correct he (try to) be, he will be in peril.
The fourth line, undivided, shows the traveller in a resting-place, having (also) the means of livelihood and the axe, (but still saying),‘I am not at ease in my mind.’
The fifth line, divided, shows its subject shooting a pheasant. He will lose his arrow, but in the end he will obtain praise and a (high) charge.

The sixth line, undivided, suggests the idea of a bird burning its nest. The stranger, (thus represented), first laughs and then cries out. He has lost his ox(-like docility) too readily and easily. There will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 187-188 (Image: Appendix II, p. 337)

en.name: The Wanderer
en.nameNote: 旅 is to lodge away from home, and the body of men on the march: "羇旅也 ... 王肅等以爲軍旅" (陸德明). The 雜卦: "親寡《旅》也", few kin. In the songs 旅 is most often the army. In the lines it is "travelling", and 旅人 "the traveller".
en.judgment: A small offering. The divination about travelling: auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: In the songs 旅 is mostly troops: "殷商之旅，其會如林" (大明, Mao 236). It is also those lodged away from home: "于時廬旅" (公劉, Mao 250); 陳完, fled to Qi, called himself "羇旅之臣" (左傳, 672 BC). 小亨 is an offering qualified as small, as 元 qualifies it in 元亨.
en.tradition: The mountain stays below, the fire flames above and does not stay; so the reading is a small success, and auspicious if the traveller keeps to what is right. Travel is no settled home, and seems a time when anything will do, but the Way is everywhere and has its right that may not be left for a moment.
en.image: On the mountain there is fire: The Wanderer. So the noble one is clear and careful in using punishments, and does not let trials linger.
en.imageNote: A later layer; the shelf gives nothing for its words in the text's own time. 侯果: fire on a mountain cannot last, the figure of the traveller. 朱熹: "慎刑如山，不留如火", careful with punishment like the mountain, not lingering like the fire.

lines.text: Travelling: petty, petty. This is where it takes its calamity from.
lines.note: 瑣瑣 is small, petty: "瑣瑣姻亞，則無膴仕" (節南山, Mao 191, 毛傳 "小貌"); 馬融 reads "worn out". The Chu slip has 此 for 斯 at the head of the second phrase. 王弼 reads 斯 with the service: at the very bottom, it does this lowly service, and takes calamity by it.

lines.text: Travelling, it comes to the camp, keeping its goods close, getting boy servants. A divination.
lines.note: 次 is an army's halt of more than two nights (左傳, 691 BC). 資 is "貨也" (說文). The Chu slip has 得僮僕之貞. 王弼 and every commentator read the servants' uprightness; 朱熹: settled in camp, goods at hand, servants true: the best of travel. A rhymed oracle (Shaughnessy).

lines.text: Travelling, burning its camp, losing its boy servants. The divination: danger.
lines.note: In the 左傳 a casting of 645 BC has "火焚其旗，不利行師", fire burns its banners: not favourable for marching the army; Shaughnessy sets it beside this line. 王弼: a lodger who gives to those below shares in power and is suspected by the host, so the camp is burnt and the servants lost. 朱熹 reads 貞 with 厲.

lines.text: Travelling, at a dwelling: getting its goods and axe. My heart is not pleased.
lines.note: A song has 處 and 旅 in one line (公劉). The king gave battle-axes for campaigns (虢季子白盤); the 子夏傳 and other teachers read 齊斧, an axe received in the temple after a fast (陸德明). 王弼: an axe for cutting thorns to make the lodging safe; not a camp, so the heart is not pleased.

lines.text: Shooting a pheasant: one arrow lost. In the end, with praise and a command.
lines.note: In the 左傳 an ugly officer shot a pheasant, and his wife, silent three years, first laughed (514 BC); nothing is built on it. A pheasant was a 士's gift on a first call (儀禮). 王弼: the arrow lost too, the pheasant cannot be had, yet in the end it is praised and given a command. 程頤: a sure shot.

lines.text: A bird burns its nest. The traveller first laughs, afterwards wails. Losing the ox at the border. Disaster.
lines.note: The reverse of 13 九五's "先號咷而後笑". 喪羊于易 is 34 六五's, with a sheep; 陸績 writes 埸, the border, which 朱熹 and the Qing scholars follow. 顧頡剛 and 李鏡池 read the Shang ancestor Wang Hai at Youyi. 程頤: "the traveller" is added, or it would be the bird that laughs and weeps.

essays.title: Fire on the mountain, and the camp burnt
essays.text: The lines follow one who is away from home: the camp reached and the goods kept close (六二), the camp burnt and the servants lost (九三), a dwelling and an axe (九四), a pheasant shot (六五), a nest burnt and an ox lost (上九). Fire comes twice, as the Image's "on the mountain there is fire". Shaughnessy counts four of the lines among the rhymed oracles, and notes a run of such oracles from 鼎 to 旅.

readings.title: The traveller or the troop?
readings.text: Lodging abroad (陸德明, 孔穎達, every later commentator; Wilhelm, Legge, Shaughnessy) or the army (王肅). The camp, the burning, the axe and the arrow fit a troop; the goods, the boy servants and the lodging fit a traveller. We print "travelling".

readings.title: 得童僕貞: one phrase or two?
readings.text: The commentators read "the uprightness of boy servants"; the Chu slip has 得僮僕之貞, "a divination for boy servants". We print "getting boy servants. A divination."; the Chu 之 argues for keeping the four words together, and is recorded.

readings.title: One arrow lost, or one arrow enough?
readings.text: One arrow lost (王弼, 虞翻, 干寶, 朱熹; Legge), or the pheasant falling at the one arrow (程頤; Wilhelm). We print "one arrow lost".

readings.title: At the border, or in ease?
readings.text: At the border (陸績, 朱熹, 王念孫); in ease (王弼, 程頤; Wilhelm, Legge); the place Youyi of Wang Hai (顧頡剛, 李鏡池; Shaughnessy "at Yi"). We print "at the border", as 34.

pinyinTones.name: Lǚ
pinyinTones.judgment: xiǎo hēng. lǚ zhēn jí.
pinyinTones.image: shān shàng yǒu huǒ, lǚ. jūn zǐ yǐ míng shèn yòng xíng ér bù liú yù.
lines: lǚ suǒ suǒ, sī qí suǒ qǔ zāi.
lǚ jí cì, huái qí zī, dé tóng pú, zhēn.
lǚ fén qí cì, sàng qí tóng pú, zhēn lì.
lǚ yú chǔ, dé qí zī fǔ, wǒ xīn bù kuài.
shè zhì yī shǐ wáng, zhōng yǐ yù mìng.
niǎo fén qí cháo, lǚ rén xiān xiào hòu háo táo. sàng niú yú yì, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 號: háo (wails), as 陸德明 戶羔反
易: yì, read 埸, the field border (GLOSSARY, 于易), as 陸德明 以豉反
處: chǔ (a dwelling)
喪: sàng (loses), as 陸德明 息浪反

hexagrams.judgment: 小亨。利有攸往。利見大人。
hexagrams.image: 隨風，巽。君子以申命行事。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 進退。利武人之貞。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 巽在床下，用史巫，紛若，吉，无咎。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 頻巽，吝。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 悔亡，田獲三品。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 貞吉，悔亡，无不利，无初有終。先庚三日，後庚三日，吉。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 巽在床下，喪其資斧，貞凶。

hexagrams.heading: 巽
hexagrams.name: 巽

wilhelm.name: Das Sanfte, (das Eindringliche, der Wind)
wilhelm.judgment: Das Sanfte. Durch Kleines Gelingen. Fördernd ist es, zu haben, wohin man geht. Fördernd ist es, den großen Mann zu sehen.
wilhelm.image: Einander folgende Winde: das Bild des sanft Eindringenden. So verbreitet der Edle seine Gebote und wirkt seine Geschäfte.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Beim Vorgehen und Rückweichen ist fördernd die Beharrlichkeit eines Kriegers.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Eindringen unter das Bett. Man benützt Priester und Magier in großer Zahl. Heil! Kein Makel.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Wiederholtes Eindringen. Beschämung.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Reue schwindet. Auf der Jagd fangt man drei Arten von Wild.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Beharrlichkeit bringt Heil. Reue schwindet. Nichts, das nicht fördernd ist. Kein Anfang, aber ein Ende. Vor der Änderung drei Tage, nach der Änderung drei Tage. Heil!
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Eindringen unter das Bett. Er verliert seinen Besitz und seine Axt. Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Sun
legge.judgment: Sun intimates that (under the conditions which it denotes) there will be some little attainment and progress. There will be advantage in movement onward in whatever direction. It will be advantageous (also) to see the great man.
legge.image: (Two trigrams representing) wind, following each other, form Sun. The superior man, in accordance with this, reiterates his orders, and secures the practice of his affairs.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject (now) advancing, (now) receding. It would be advantageous for him to have the firm correctness of a brave soldier.
The second line, undivided, shows the representative of Sun beneath a couch, and employing diviners and exorcists in a way bordering on confusion. There will be good fortune and no error.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject penetrating (only) by violent and repeated efforts. There will be occasion for regret.
The fourth line, divided, shows all occasion for repentance (in its subject) passed away. He takes game for its threefold use in his hunting.

The fifth line, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune (to its subject). All occasion for repentance will disappear, and all his movements will be advantageous. There may have been no (good) beginning, but there will be a (good) end. Three days before making any changes, (let him give notice of them); and three days after, (let him reconsider them). There will (thus) be good fortune.

The sixth line, undivided, shows the representative of penetration beneath a couch, and having lost the axe with which he executed his decisions. However firm and correct he may (try to) be, there will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 189-191 (Image: Appendix II, p. 338)

en.name: The Gentle (The Penetrating, Wind)
en.nameNote: 巽 is not the word for wind (風). It is to enter: "巽、入也" (說卦, 序卦, 陸德明); to yield, "順也" (廣雅); to lie hidden, "《巽》伏也" (雜卦); to set out, "具也" (說文). The 說卦: "巽為木，為風". In the lines we print "entering".
en.judgment: A small offering. Favourable to have somewhere to go. Favourable to see the great man.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment's words are the book's fixed phrases; the shelf gives nothing more for it. The 左傳 already reads the trigram as wind: "《巽》，風也" (672 BC). Mawangdui names the hexagram 筭, counting rods.
en.tradition: One yin line lies hidden under two yang; its nature is to yield and so get in; its image is the wind, also for entering. The yin line rules, so the reading is a small success; yin following yang, it is favourable to go on; but it must know whom to follow, so: favourable to see the great man.
en.image: Wind following wind: The Gentle. So the noble one renews his commands and carries out affairs.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 申命 is the Western Zhou act of renewing an appointment: "今余隹申京乃命" (集成 04296). 荀爽: two winds following each other, so commands are renewed; of all teachings, carrying out commands is first.

lines.text: Advancing and withdrawing. A favourable divination for a warrior.
lines.note: 武人 is a warrior on campaign (10 六三; "武人東征", 漸漸之石). 進退 is 20 六三's. 王弼: at the start of the command, not yet obeying, going forward and back; to set crookedness straight nothing is better than a warrior. Every commentator reads "the warrior's firmness".

lines.text: Entering beneath the bed. Using scribes and shamans: in a throng. Auspicious. No blame.
lines.note: A song has the cricket enter beneath the bed: "十月蟋蟀入我床下" (七月, Mao 154). The scribe cast the stalks at the household offering (儀禮, 少牢, with 鄭玄); the shaman brought down the spirits (國語, 楚語下). 孔穎達: both serve the ghosts and spirits; 紛若 is many and abundant.

lines.text: Entering again and again. Trouble.
lines.note: 頻 is 24 六三's "again and again". 王弼 and 鄭玄 read frowning, unhappy and forced; 虞翻 the bridge of the nose. 程頤: hard by nature in a time of yielding, it tries and fails again and again. The shelf gives nothing more.

lines.text: Regret gone. In the field, catching three kinds.
lines.note: 40 九二 has "田獲三狐". The 王制 (later) has the lords hunt three times a year: for the dried meat of the offering stands, for guests, for the lord's kitchen; the commentators read the three kinds so. 翟玄: fowl, sheep and pheasant. 朱熹: also an auspicious reading for divining a hunt.

lines.text: The divination: auspicious. Regret gone. Nothing is unfavourable. No beginning, but an end reached. Three days before geng, three days after geng: auspicious.
lines.note: 18's judgment has 先甲三日，後甲三日; 庚 is the seventh of the ten days. 朱熹 reckons ding before and gui after: ding a day of household offering, gui the day of the Shang ten-day divination. 王弼: three days of proclaiming a command before and after, then punishment brings no resentment.

lines.text: Entering beneath the bed, losing its goods and axe. The divination: disaster.
lines.note: 資斧 is 56 九四's, where the teachers have 齊斧, an axe received in the temple. 荀爽: when the army comes home it announces at the temple and returns the axe to the lord. 王弼: yielding too far, beneath the bed; the axe is what decides, and it is lost.

essays.title: Wind doubled
essays.text: Both trigrams are 巽; the Image: "wind following wind". The lines come back twice to the same place, "entering beneath the bed" (九二, 上九), with scribes and shamans the first time and the goods and axe lost the second. 九五's "three days before geng, three days after geng" answers 18's three days before and after jia.

readings.title: Entering, yielding, or presenting?
readings.text: Entering (說卦, 序卦, 陸德明, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge); yielding, humbling oneself (廣雅; 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤); lying hidden (雜卦); setting out, presenting (說文 "具也"; Shaughnessy). We print "entering", with the cricket that enters beneath the bed.

readings.title: In a throng
readings.text: Scribes and shamans many and abundant (孔穎達, 程頤; Wilhelm "in großer Zahl"); 荀爽 reads "change"; Legge "in a way bordering on confusion". We print "in a throng".

readings.title: Three kinds
readings.text: The three uses of the catch (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹, after the 王制; Wilhelm, Legge), or three beasts (虞翻, 翟玄). We print "three kinds".

readings.title: Geng: a day, or change?
readings.text: A day-name, as 18's jia; proclaiming before and after a command (王弼); 朱熹's ding and gui; Wilhelm and Legge read change, 庚 as 更. We print the days.

pinyinTones.name: Xùn
pinyinTones.judgment: xiǎo hēng. lì yǒu yōu wǎng. lì jiàn dà rén.
pinyinTones.image: suí fēng, xùn. jūn zǐ yǐ shēn mìng xíng shì.
lines: jìn tuì. lì wǔ rén zhī zhēn.
xùn zài chuáng xià, yòng shǐ wū, fēn ruò, jí, wú jiù.
pín xùn, lìn.
huǐ wáng, tián huò sān pǐn.
zhēn jí, huǐ wáng, wú bù lì, wú chū yǒu zhōng. xiàn gēng sān rì, hòu gēng sān rì, jí.
xùn zài chuáng xià, sàng qí zī fǔ, zhēn xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 先: xiàn in 先庚 (before), as 陸德明 西薦反
喪: sàng (loses), as 陸德明 息浪反 (旅, 下卦同)

hexagrams.image: 麗澤，兌。君子以朋友講習。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 和兌，吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 孚兌，吉，悔亡。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 來兌，凶。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 商兌未寧，介疾有喜。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 孚于剝，有厲。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 引兌。

hexagrams.heading: 兌
hexagrams.name: 兌

wilhelm.name: Das Heitere, der See
wilhelm.judgment: Das Heitere. Gelingen. Günstig ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Aufeinander beruhende Seen: das Bild des Heiteren. So tut sich der Edle mit seinen Freunden zusammen zur Besprechung und Einübung.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Zufriedene Heiterkeit. Heil!
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Wahrhaftige Heiterkeit. Heil! Die Reue schwindet.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Kommende Heiterkeit. Unheil!
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Überlegte Heiterkeit ist nicht beruhigt. Nach Abtun der Fehler hat man Freude.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Wahrhaftigkeit gegen das Zersetzende ist gefährlich.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Verführende Heiterkeit.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Tui
legge.judgment: Tui intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and attainment. (But) it will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
legge.image: (Two symbols representing) the waters of a marsh, one over the other, form Tui. The superior man, in accordance with this, (encourages) the conversation of friends and (the stimulus of) their (common) practice.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows the pleasure of (inward) harmony. There will be good fortune.
The second line, undivided, shows the pleasure arising from (inward) sincerity. There will be good fortune. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
The third line, divided, shows its subject bringing round himself whatever can give pleasure. There will be evil.
The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject deliberating about what to seek his pleasure in, and not at rest. He borders on what would be injurious, but there will be cause for joy.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject trusting in one who would injure him. The situation is perilous.
The topmost line, divided, shows the pleasure of its subject in leading and attracting others.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 192-193 (Image: Appendix II, p. 340)

en.name: The Joyous, Lake
en.nameNote: 兌 is not the word for the lake (澤). It is to delight: "《兌》者、說也" (彖, 序卦), every 說 read 悅 (陸德明). The 說卦 also makes it the mouth; in the songs 兌 opens a way (緜, Mao 237). We print "delight", keeping "joy" for 喜.
en.judgment: An offering. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: The judgment is the book's fixed words. The 左傳 never names the trigram 兌. The Qin 歸藏 has "兑兑", delighted, with yellow clothes, metal, and sun and moon coming out together. Mawangdui writes the name 奪.
en.tradition: One yin line rising above two yang, joy showing outwardly; its image is the lake, which delights the myriad things. Strong within, so delight gets through; soft without, so the right is favoured: delight has a way through, but false delight must be guarded against.
en.image: Lakes joined: The Joyous. So the noble one discusses and practises with friends and companions.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 麗 is "連也", joined (陸德明, 王弼), as 52's 兼山. 朋 and 友 are kept apart, as in the text. 孔穎達: fellow pupils of one gate are 朋, those of one purpose 友; living together, they discuss and practise the Way.

lines.text: Harmonious delight. Auspicious.
lines.note: The shelf gives nothing for 和兌 itself. 和 in the songs is the harmony of sounds and of the offering: "既和且平，依我磬聲" (那, Mao 301). 王弼: at the start, tied to no one: delight without flattery.

lines.text: Confirmed delight. Auspicious. Regret gone.
lines.note: 孚 is the standing "confirmation", modifying delight as 和 does in 初九; the commentators' good faith is theirs. 程頤: strong in the middle, good faith full within; near small men, it keeps itself: the noble one is in harmony without sameness.

lines.text: Coming delight. Disaster.
lines.note: 來 is "coming", as 55 六五's 來章. 王弼: in the wrong place, it comes seeking delight: a flatterer. 程頤: bending itself to the yang lines below to please them. The shelf gives nothing more.

lines.text: Deliberated delight, not yet at peace. A great illness: there is joy.
lines.note: The Chu charges about a client's person end "期中有喜", within the term there will be joy (包山 198); 41 六四 pairs illness and joy. 商 is "商量也", to weigh (陸德明); 虞翻 reads trade. 介 is "大也" (馬融); 王弼 reads "keeping apart", the flatterer kept from the ruler.

lines.text: Confirmation in stripping. There is danger.
lines.note: 剝 is "stripping", the flaying of the offerings (楚茨, "或剝或亨"); 孚于 + noun as 17 九五. 王弼: in the honoured place, it delights in and trusts yin, not yang. 程頤: the stripper is the top line; even the sage Shun feared clever words and a pleasing face.

lines.text: Drawn delight.
lines.note: 引 is 45 六二's "drawn". The line has no verdict. 王弼: quiet and withdrawn, it must be drawn in before it delights; 程頤: delight at its end, drawn out longer; 朱熹: it draws the two yang lines below, but cannot be sure they follow.

essays.title: The lake
essays.text: A Zhou 澤 is standing water gathered behind banks, with reeds at its edge. "澤，水之鍾也", where water gathers (國語, 周語下); "川壅為澤", a river dammed becomes a 澤 (左傳, 597 BC); its reeds and rushes were guarded by boat officers (左傳, 522 BC); on its bank "有蒲與荷" (澤陂, Mao 145). "Marsh" says the reeds, "lake" the gathered water, which is what the 國語 defines and the Images use. This edition prints "the lake" in every Image.

readings.title: Delight, or speech?
readings.text: Delight (the 彖, 序卦, 說卦, 陸德明, every commentator; Wilhelm, Legge); speech (the 說卦's mouth; the 歸藏's "其言語敦"; Shaughnessy "expressing"); opening a way (緜). We print "delight".

readings.title: A great illness?
readings.text: A great illness (馬融 介 "大也"; Shaughnessy); the sickness kept apart (王弼); firmly hating the bad (程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge). We print "a great illness", with the Chu records' joy in a divination about one's person.

readings.title: Deliberated, or traded?
readings.text: Deliberating (陸德明, 王弼, 程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge); trading (虞翻); the Shang (Shaughnessy). We print "deliberated".

readings.title: Confirmation in stripping
readings.text: The commentators read trusting the one who strips away the yang (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge); Shaughnessy "Trust in paring". We print the words.

pinyinTones.name: Duì
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: lì zé, duì. jūn zǐ yǐ péng yǒu jiǎng xí.
lines: hé duì, jí.
fú duì, jí, huǐ wáng.
lái duì, xiōng.
shāng duì wèi níng, jiè jí yǒu xǐ.
fú yú bō, yǒu lì.
yǐn duì.

pinyinNotes: 兌: duì (delight), as 陸德明 徒外反, "恱也"

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。王假有廟。利涉大川，利貞。
hexagrams.image: 風行水上，渙。先王以享于帝，立廟。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 用拯馬壯，吉。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 渙奔其机，悔亡。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 渙其躬，无悔。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 渙其群，元吉。渙有丘，匪夷所思。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 渙汗其大號，渙王居，无咎。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 渙其血，去逖出，无咎。

hexagrams.heading: 渙
hexagrams.name: 渙

wilhelm.name: Die Auflösung
wilhelm.judgment: Die Auflösung. Gelingen. Der König naht seinem Tempel. Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Der Wind fährt über das Wasser: das Bild der Auflösung. So opferten die alten Könige dem Herrn und bauten Tempel.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Er bringt Hilfe mit der Macht eines Pferdes. Heil!
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Bei der Auflösung läuft er seiner Stütze zu. Die Reue schwindet.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Er löst sein Ich auf. Keine Reue.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Er löst sich von seiner Schar. Erhabenes Heil! Durch Auflösung folgt Anhäufung. Das ist etwas, an das Gewöhnliche nicht denken.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Auflösend wie Schweiß sind seine lauten Rufe. Auflösung! Ein König weilt ohne Makel.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Er löst sein Blut auf. Weggehen, sich fernhalten, hinausgehen ist ohne Makel.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hwân
legge.judgment: Hwân intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and success. The king goes to his ancestral temple; and it will be advantageous to cross the great stream. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) water and that for wind moving above the water form Hwân. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, presented offerings to God and established the ancestral temple.
lines: The first line, divided, shows its subject engaged in rescuing (from the impending evil) and having (the assistance of) a strong horse. There will be good fortune.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject, amid the dispersion, hurrying to his contrivance (for security). All occasion for repentance will disappear.
The third line, divided, shows its subject discarding any regard to his own person. There will be no occasion for repentance.

The fourth line, divided, shows its subject scattering the (different) parties (in the state); which leads to great good fortune. From the dispersion (he collects again good men standing out, a crowd) like a mound, which is what ordinary men would not have thought of.

The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject amidst the dispersion issuing his great announcements as the perspiration (flows from his body). He scatters abroad (also) the accumulations in the royal granaries. There will be no error.
The topmost line, undivided, shows its subject disposing of (what may be called) its bloody wounds, and going and separating himself from its anxious fears. There will be no error.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 194-196 (Image: Appendix II, p. 341)

en.name: Dissolution
en.nameNote: 渙 is to disperse, to scatter, as water spreads: "散也。序卦云：離也" (陸德明). 孔穎達: "渙者，散釋之名". In the songs 渙渙 is the spring flood, the waters let loose. In the lines it is "dispersing".
en.judgment: An offering. The king comes to the temple. Favourable to ford the great river. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: The bronzes have the king come into the temple: "王各周廟宣榭" (虢季子白盤); Shaughnessy counts the phrase among formulas of about the ninth century BC. 渙渙 is the spring spate (溱洧, Mao 95); in a temple song the young king fears his fathers' way "判渙", scattered (訪落, Mao 288). The Chu slip has 王假于廟 and 利見大人 for 利貞.
en.tradition: Wind moving over water, the sign of things loosened and scattered, so the reading is success; and because the spirits of the ancestors have scattered, the king must go to the temple to gather them; wood on water is a boat, so it is favourable to ford the great river; "favourable to be correct" is a deep warning to the one who divines.
en.image: Wind moves over the water: Dissolution. So the former kings made offering to the High God and set up temples.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 42 六二 has "王用享于帝". 孔穎達: wind on water stirs up waves, the sign of scattering; when hardship has dispersed, the former kings offered to the High God to announce the peace, and built temples to the ancestors. 朱熹: all this is to gather what is scattered.

lines.text: Using it to rescue, the horse strong: auspicious.
lines.note: The same words as 36 六二; the 說文 quotes them under 抍, "上舉也". The Chu slip and Mawangdui add 悔亡. Some modern readers take the Chu graph as presenting a horse for the temple offering (陳斯鵬, through 謝向榮). 王弼: at the start of scattering, one can get away before things grow desperate.

lines.text: Dispersing, it runs to its armrest. Regret gone.
lines.note: 机 is read 几, the armrest (陸德明): "凭玉几", the dying king leans on the jade armrest (顧命); at the offering the invoker sets the armrest on the spirit's mat (儀禮, 少牢, 鄭玄). 虞翻: the dispersing is in the temple, so the armrest is set out. The Chu slip has 走 for 奔.

lines.text: Dispersing its person. No regret.
lines.note: 躬 is one's own person (4 六三; 39 六二). The Chu slip has 亡咎 for 无悔. 王弼: it disperses its person, its purpose turned outward, not clinging to what it holds. 程頤: "regret gone" means there was regret and it went; "no regret" that there was none.

lines.text: Dispersing its flock: greatly auspicious. Dispersing, there is a hill. Not level: what is thought of.
lines.note: 群 is a flock: "三百維群" (無羊, Mao 190). 夷 stands with 平, level (爾雅). The Chu slip has 渙其丘. 王弼 and 孔穎達: still the care of mounds not levelled. 程頤 and 朱熹: to gather a scattered realm, heaped like a hill, beyond common thought.

lines.text: Dispersing, sweating: its great crying out. Dispersing the king's dwelling. No blame.
lines.note: 汗 is sweat (說文 "人液也"); the Chu slip lacks it, and where we have 王居 it has the graph of 九二's 机. 九家易: commands go out like sweat that leaves the body and does not come back. 朱熹: dispersing its commands and its stores; 王弼: only a king may hold this place.

lines.text: Dispersing its anxiety. Going away, the alarm departs. No blame.
lines.note: 血 is read 恤, anxiety, as 9 六四, beside the same 去, 出 and 惕. The Chu slip writes 易, the sound element of 惕, and lacks 无咎. 程頤 and 朱熹 read 逖 as 惕; 王弼 reads it "far": furthest from harm, it disperses its grief and goes far out.

essays.title: Dispersing, and the temple
essays.text: The judgment brings the king to the temple, in the words of 45; the Image has the former kings make offering to the High God and set up temples. Every line but the first begins with 渙 and names what is dispersed or what disperses: a running to the armrest, the person, the flock, a hill, a great crying out, the king's dwelling, anxiety. 虞翻 reads 九二's armrest as the one set out in the temple.

readings.title: 初六: regret gone, or not?
readings.text: The Chu slip, Mawangdui, 虞翻's note and Wikisource end the line with 悔亡; 謝向榮 argues for it from the manuscripts, the book's 吉 ... 悔亡 habit and the rhyme. The base, the commentators and the 說文 lack it. We print the base; the case is recorded.

readings.title: Anxiety, or blood?
readings.text: We read 血 as 恤, anxiety, as in 9 六四. 王弼, 孔穎達, 程頤 and 朱熹 read blood, injury; Wilhelm "sein Blut", Legge "its bloody wounds". Read so: "Dispersing its blood".

readings.title: Alarm, or far?
readings.text: 逖 as 惕, alarm (程頤, 朱熹; the Chu 易; 9 六四 惕出), or far (王弼, 孔穎達, the 說文, the small image's 遠害; Wilhelm). We print "alarm".

readings.title: Not level, or not ordinary?
readings.text: 王弼 and 孔穎達 keep 夷 with the hill: not levelled. 程頤 and 朱熹 read the ordinary: beyond common thought (Wilhelm, Legge). We print "not level".

readings.title: Crying out, or commands?
readings.text: 號 as crying out, or as commands (九家易, 孔穎達, 程頤, 朱熹; Legge "great announcements"). We print "crying out".

pinyinTones.name: Huàn
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. wáng gé yǒu miào. lì shè dà chuān, lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: fēng xíng shuǐ shàng, huàn. xiān wáng yǐ xiǎng yú dì, lì miào.
lines: yòng zhěng mǎ zhuàng, jí.
huàn bēn qí jǐ, huǐ wáng.
huàn qí gōng, wú huǐ.
huàn qí qún, yuán jí. huàn yǒu qiū, fěi yí suǒ sī.
huàn hàn qí dà háo, huàn wáng jū, wú jiù.
huàn qí xuè, qù tì chū, wú jiù.

pinyinNotes: 假: gé (comes), as 陸德明 庚白反
机: jǐ, read as 几, the armrest, as 陸德明 音几
號: háo (crying out), as the book's English

hexagrams.image: 澤上有水，節。君子以制數度，議德行。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 不出戶庭，无咎。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 不出門庭，凶。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 不節若，則嗟若，无咎。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 安節。亨。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 甘節，吉，往有尚。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 苦節，貞凶。悔亡。

hexagrams.heading: 節
hexagrams.name: 節

wilhelm.name: Die Beschränkung
wilhelm.judgment: Beschränkung. Gelingen. Bittere Beschränkung darf man nicht beharrlich üben.
wilhelm.image: Oberhalb des Sees ist Wasser: das Bild der Beschränkung. So schafft der Edle Zahl und Maß und untersucht, was Tugend und rechter Wandel ist.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Nicht zu Tür und Hof hinausgehen ist kein Makel.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Nicht zu Tor und Hof hinausgehen bringt Unheil.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Wer keine Beschränkung kennt, wird zu klagen haben. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Zufriedene Beschränkung. Gelingen.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Süße Beschränkung bringt Heil. Hingehen bringt Achtung.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Bittere Beschränkung: Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil. Reue schwindet.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kieh
legge.judgment: Kieh intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and attainment. (But) if the regulations (which it prescribes) be severe and difficult, they cannot be permanent.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a lake, and above it that for water, form Kieh. The superior man, in accordance with this, constructs his (methods of) numbering and measurement, and discusses (points of) virtue and conduct.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject not quitting the courtyard outside his door. There will be no error.
The second line, undivided, shows its subject not quitting the courtyard inside his gate. There will be evil.
The third line, divided, shows its subject with no appearance of observing the (proper) regulations, in which case we shall see him lamenting. But there will be no one to blame (but himself).
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject quietly and naturally (attentive to all) regulations. There will be progress and success.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject sweetly and acceptably enacting his regulations. There will be good fortune. The onward progress with them will afford ground for admiration.

The topmost line, divided, shows its subject enacting regulations severe and difficult. Even with firmness and correctness there will be evil. But though there will be cause for repentance, it will (by and by) disappear.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 197-198 (Image: Appendix II, p. 342)

en.name: Limitation
en.nameNote: 節 is the joint of the bamboo: "竹約也" (說文); from it a division, a measure, a holding back. 陸德明: "止也。明禮有制度之名". The 雜卦: "《節》止也". In the lines it is "measure", as 27's Image 節飲食 "measured in drink and food".
en.judgment: An offering. Bitter measure: it may not be divined.
en.judgmentNote: In the 左傳 節 is to measure out and hold in: asked whether the sick lord of Jin may approach women, the physician He answers "節之", measure it; the former kings' music "所以節百事也" (541 BC). A song pairs bitter and sweet: "誰謂荼苦？其甘如薺" (谷風, Mao 35). In the Qin 歸藏 King Wu divines about attacking Yin, read auspicious.
en.tradition: Having a limit and stopping: water above a lake, whose room is limited; measure has its own way to success; the lines are half yin, half yang, with yang in the second and fifth places, so the reading is success; but carried too far it is bitter, so there is the warning that it may not be held to as right.
en.image: Above the lake there is water: Limitation. So the noble one fixes numbers and measures, and deliberates on virtue and conduct.
en.imageNote: A later layer; the 左傳's "節百事" is the nearest the shelf comes to its words. 侯果: water above the lake, the dykes are the measure. 孔穎達: numbers and measures are the counts of ranks and grants; virtue and conduct are men's fitness for office.

lines.text: Not going out of the door and courtyard. No blame.
lines.note: 戶 is "半門曰戶", the door of a room; 門 the compound's gate, two doors (說文). The 繫辭 quotes the line: a lord not discreet loses his servant, "是以君子慎密而不出也" (a later wing). 王弼: knowing when the way is open or blocked. 程頤 and 朱熹: the courtyard outside the door.

lines.text: Not going out of the gate and courtyard. Disaster.
lines.note: 門庭 is 36 六四's "gate and courtyard": the same words as 初九 with the gate for the door, and the opposite verdict. 王弼: the rules made, they should now be proclaimed; to keep them hidden misses the moment. 程頤: stingy measure in spending, timid measure in acting.

lines.text: Not measured, then sighing. No blame.
lines.note: 嗟若 is the sigh of grief (30 六五; 45 六三); a state and the state that follows it. 王弼: going against measure, it comes to lamenting; it brought this on itself and has no one to blame. 朱熹: this 无咎 means there is no one else to blame.

lines.text: Safe measure. An offering.
lines.note: 安 as in 2's 安貞 "the divination about safety"; the shelf gives nothing more for 安節. 亨 stands alone in a line here and in only three others (Shaughnessy). 程頤: not measure forced, but measure rested in, so it gets through; forced measure does not last.

lines.text: Sweet measure: auspicious. Going on, there is honour.
lines.note: 甘 is "sweet", as 19 六三's 甘臨. Shaughnessy pairs it with 上六: sweet measure auspicious, bitter not. 王弼: measure that is not bitter: what is that if not sweet? It wastes no wealth and harms no one.

lines.text: Bitter measure. The divination: disaster. Regret gone.
lines.note: 貞凶 and 悔亡 stand together, and the readers reconcile them. 王弼: imposed on others, more than they can bear; used to order oneself, without error. 程頤: here 悔亡 means something else. 朱熹: in the rites frugality is better than excess, so regret goes in the end.

essays.title: Bitter and sweet
essays.text: The judgment and the top line say "bitter measure", the fifth line "sweet measure": the bitter and the sweet in one hexagram, as the songs pair them. Shaughnessy reads 九五 and 上六 as a pair in which the verdicts follow the images: the sweet auspicious, the bitter not. The first two lines turn on going out of the house: by the door, no blame; by the gate, disaster.

readings.title: Measure, restraint, or rule?
readings.text: Measure (the bamboo joint; the 左傳's 節之; 27's Image); stopping (雜卦, 陸德明); rules and regulations (孔穎達; Legge); limitation (Wilhelm). We print "measure", keeping 27's word.

readings.title: May not be divined, or held to?
readings.text: 不可貞 is "it may not be divined" by the book's row; every commentator reads "may not be held to as right", Wilhelm "nicht beharrlich üben", Legge "cannot be permanent".

readings.title: No blame, or no one to blame?
readings.text: In 六三 we print the book's verdict "no blame". The small image ("又誰咎也"), 王弼, 朱熹 and Legge read "no one else to blame".

readings.title: One courtyard or two?
readings.text: 程頤 and 朱熹 read one courtyard named from the door and from the gate; Legge "one and the same". We print "the door and courtyard", "the gate and courtyard", as 36.

pinyinTones.name: Jié
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. kǔ jié, bù kě zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: zé shàng yǒu shuǐ, jié. jūn zǐ yǐ zhì shù dù, yì dé xìng.
lines: bù chū hù tíng, wú jiù.
bù chū mén tíng, xiōng.
bù jié ruò, zé jiē ruò, wú jiù.
ān jié. hēng.
gān jié, jí, wǎng yǒu shàng.
kǔ jié, zhēn xiōng. huǐ wáng.

pinyinNotes: 行: xìng (conduct) in 德行, as 陸德明 下孟反

hexagrams.image: 澤上有風，中孚。君子以議獄緩死。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 虞吉，有它不燕。

lines.label: 九二
lines.text: 鳴鶴在陰，其子和之。我有好爵，吾與爾靡之。

lines.label: 六三
lines.text: 得敵，或鼓或罷，或泣或歌。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 月幾望，馬匹亡，无咎。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 有孚攣如，无咎。

lines.label: 上九
lines.text: 翰音登于天，貞凶。

hexagrams.heading: 中孚
hexagrams.name: 中孚

wilhelm.name: Innere Wahrheit
wilhelm.judgment: Innere Wahrheit. Schweine und Fische. Heil! Fördernd ist es, das große Wasser zu durchqueren. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit.
wilhelm.image: Über dem See ist der Wind: das Bild der inneren Wahrheit. So bespricht der Edle die Strafsachen, um Hinrichtungen aufzuhalten.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Bereit sein bringt Heil. Sind Hintergedanken da, so ist das beunruhigend.
Neun auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Ein rufender Kranich im Schatten. Sein Junges antwortet ihm. Ich habe einen guten Becher. Ich will ihn mit dir teilen.
Sechs auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Er findet einen Genossen, bald trommelt er, bald hört er auf. Bald schluchzt er, bald singt er.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Der Mond, der beinahe voll ist. Das Gespannpferd geht verloren. Kein Makel.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Er besitzt Wahrheit, die verkettet. Kein Makel.
Oben eine Neun bedeutet: Hahnenruf, der zum Himmel dringt. Beharrlichkeit bringt Unheil.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kung Fû
legge.judgment: Kung Fû (moves even) pigs and fish, and leads to good fortune. There will be advantage in crossing the great stream. There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
legge.image: (The trigram representing the waters of) a marsh and that for wind above it form Kung Fû. The superior man, in accordance with this, deliberates about cases of litigation and delays (the infliction of) death.
lines: The first line, undivided, shows its subject resting (in himself). There will be good fortune. If he sought to any other, he would not find rest.

The second line, undivided, shows its subject (like) the crane crying out in her hidden retirement, and her young ones responding to her. (It is as if it were said), ‘I have a cup of good spirits,’ (and the response were), ‘I will partake of it with you.’
The third line, divided, shows its subject having met with his mate. Now he beats his drum, and now he leaves off. Now he weeps, and now he sings.
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject (like) the moon nearly full, and (like) a horse (in a chariot) whose fellow disappears. There will be no error.
The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject perfectly sincere, and linking (others) to him in closest union. There will be no error.
The topmost line, undivided, shows its subject in chanticleer (trying to) mount to heaven. Even with firm correctness there will be evil.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 199-200 (Image: Appendix II, p. 343)

en.name: Inner Truth
en.nameNote: 中孚 is 中, within, with 孚 in its default sense, "confirmation": confirmation within. The 雜卦: "《中孚》信也"; 陸德明: "信也". The name printed is Wilhelm's. Mawangdui writes 中復. The name stands in no line; 九五's 有孚 is 9 九五's phrase.
en.judgment: Piglets and fish: auspicious. Favourable to ford the great river. A favourable divination.
en.judgmentNote: Piglets and fish were the offerings of the lower ranks: "士有豚犬之奠，庶人有魚炙之薦" (國語, 楚語上). The wedding cauldrons held a pig and fish (儀禮, 士昏禮). The 曲禮 (later) names the temple's piglet "Fat and Plump" and its cock "Soaring Sound", 上九's 翰音.
en.tradition: 孚 is good faith: two yin within, four yang outside, the second and fifth central; empty in the middle as a whole, solid in the middle in each half: both are signs of good faith. Piglets and fish know nothing; the utmost good faith can move them; so one who can win their answer is auspicious and may ford the great river.
en.image: Above the lake there is wind: Inner Truth. So the noble one deliberates on trials and delays death.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 王弼: good faith springing from within, even a fault can be pardoned. 孔穎達: in an age of good faith, a fault is not done on purpose, so the noble one weighs the cases and puts off the death sentence. 朱熹: wind moves, water receives.

lines.text: Foreseeing: auspicious. There is something else: not at ease.
lines.note: 虞 is to foresee in Zhou prose: "不備不虞，不可以師" (左傳, 718 BC); 不虞 is the unforeseen of 45's Image. 燕 is at ease: "或燕燕居息" (北山, Mao 205). 王弼 reads single-mindedness, 荀爽 being at peace, 程頤 and 朱熹 weighing up what can be trusted.

lines.text: A crane calling in the shade; its young answer it. I have a good cup; I will share it with you.
lines.note: "鶴鳴于九皋，聲聞于野" (鶴鳴, Mao 184). 爵 is the cup at feast and offering: "洗爵奠斝 ... 或歌或咢" (行葦, Mao 246); the commentators' rank is later. A rhymed oracle. The 繫辭 quotes it first: the noble one's good words in his room are answered a thousand li away.

lines.text: Getting a match: some drum, some stop; some weep, some sing.
lines.note: 敵 is "匹也" (爾雅), a counterpart, a match, with 仇 and 匹. 或 ... 或 ... is "some ..., some ...", as at the feast of 行葦, "或歌或咢". 王弼: facing and not joining; blocked, it drums; unable to win, it stops; afraid, it weeps; unharmed, it sings. No verdict.

lines.text: The moon is almost full. The horse's mate lost. No blame.
lines.note: 月幾望 as 9 上九 and 54 六五; 荀爽 has 既望. 程頤: a chariot's four horses went in matched pairs, two to a 匹. 程頤 and 朱熹: almost full, not full, as a minister who does not rival his lord; it leaves its partner, the first line, to follow the fifth.

lines.text: There is confirmation, bound together. No blame.
lines.note: The same words as 9 九五. 陸德明 glosses 攣 by the 廣雅's 拲, bound hands, but no held source sets it there, so the context does not establish captives. 孔穎達: "相牽繫不絕之名也". 程頤: the lord's sincerity binds the realm's trust fast.

lines.text: The soaring sound climbs to the sky. The divination: disaster.
lines.note: 翰 is high flight: "翰飛戾天" (小宛, Mao 196, 毛傳 "高"). The 曲禮 calls the temple cock 翰音. 王弼: a sound that flies while the substance does not follow. 朱熹: a cock is no thing to climb the sky. We keep "the soaring sound" and leave the cock open.

essays.title: Piglets, fish, a cup and a cry
essays.text: The hexagram names things of the offering and the feast: piglets and fish in the judgment, a good cup shared in 九二, drumming and singing in 六三, and in 上九 翰音, which the 禮記 gives as the name of the cock at the temple offering. The 國語 makes piglets and fish the offerings of the lower ranks. It is the setting of an offering, in which a confirmation by the spirits is at home.

essays.title: What 孚 means
essays.text: 孚 stands 42 times in the book, 26 as 有孚. In the Shang bones the diviner's 孚 marks a result borne out: "茲孚。獲狐十又三", this is confirmed: thirteen foxes taken (合集 37473). The songs and every commentator read good faith, trust (文王, "萬邦作孚"). Most Western Zhou bronzes write 俘, the spoils of war, and modern readers since 郭沫若 have read captives. This edition renders 孚 by its context: confirmation by default, trust between parties, captives or booty where war and spoils are named.

readings.title: Piglets and fish: moved, or offered?
readings.text: The 彖 and every commentator read creatures reached even by good faith (Wilhelm, Legge too); the 國語 and the 曲禮 put piglets and fish among the offerings. We print the words, which hold both.

readings.title: 虞: foreseeing?
readings.text: Foreseeing (the 左傳's 不虞; near 程頤's and 朱熹's 度); single-mindedness (王弼, 孔穎達); being at peace (荀爽); the forester; the 虞 rite. We print "foreseeing"; Wilhelm "Bereit sein", Legge "resting".

readings.title: A cup or a rank; share or tie?
readings.text: 爵 is the cup of the songs, or rank (虞翻, 程頤). 靡 is to share (韓詩, 孟喜, 虞翻), share out (王弼), tie (朱熹 縻), drain (Shaughnessy). We print "a good cup" and "share".

readings.title: The soaring sound, or the cock?
readings.text: 翰 "高飛" (陸德明), or the cock (曲禮 "雞曰翰音"; 虞翻, 侯果, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge). We print "the soaring sound".

pinyinTones.name: Zhōng Fú
pinyinTones.judgment: tún yú, jí. lì shè dà chuān, lì zhēn.
pinyinTones.image: zé shàng yǒu fēng, zhōng fú. jūn zǐ yǐ yì yù huǎn sǐ.
lines: yú jí, yǒu tā bù yàn.
míng hè zài yīn, qí zǐ hè zhī. wǒ yǒu hǎo jué, wú yǔ ěr mí zhī.
dé dí, huò gǔ huò bà, huò qì huò gē.
yuè jī wàng, mǎ pǐ wáng, wú jiù.
yǒu fú luán rú, wú jiù.
hàn yīn dēng yú tiān, zhēn xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 和: hè (answers in song), as 陸德明 胡臥反
燕: yàn (at ease), as 陸德明 音鷰
好: hǎo (good), as 陸德明 如字; 王肅 hào recorded
靡: mí (share out), as 陸德明 亡池反
罷: bà (stop), as 陸德明 如字; 王肅 音皮 (pí) recorded
幾: jī (almost), as 陸德明 音禨

hexagrams.judgment: 亨。利貞。可小事，不可大事。飛鳥遺之音，不宜上，宜下，大吉。
hexagrams.image: 山上有雷，小過。君子以行過乎恭，喪過乎哀，用過乎儉。

lines.label: 初六
lines.text: 飛鳥以凶。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 過其祖，遇其妣。不及其君，遇其臣。无咎。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 弗過、防之，從或戕之，凶。

lines.label: 九四
lines.text: 无咎。弗過、遇之，往厲必戒。勿用永貞。

lines.label: 六五
lines.text: 密雲不雨，自我西郊。公弋取彼在穴。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 弗遇、過之，飛鳥離之，凶，是謂災眚。

hexagrams.heading: 小過
hexagrams.name: 小過

wilhelm.name: Des Kleinen Übergewicht
wilhelm.judgment: Des Kleinen Übergewicht. Gelingen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Man mag kleine Dinge tun, man soll nicht große Dinge tun. Der fliegende Vogel bringt die Botschaft: Es ist nicht gut, nach oben zu streben, es ist gut, unten zu bleiben. Großes Heil!
wilhelm.image: Auf dem Berg ist der Donner: das Bild von des Kleinen Übergewicht. So legt der Edle im Wandel das Übergewicht auf die Ehrerbietung, bei Trauerfällen legt er das Übergewicht auf die Trauer, bei seinen Ausgaben legt er das Übergewicht auf die Sparsamkeit.
lines: Anfangs eine Sechs bedeutet: Der Vogel kommt durch Fliegen ins Unheil.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Sie geht an ihrem Ahnherrn vorbei und trifft die Ahnfrau. Er erreicht nicht seinen Fürsten und trifft den Beamten. Kein Makel.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Wenn man sich nicht außerordentlich vorsieht, so kommt etwa einer von hinten und schlägt einen. Unheil!
Neun auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Kein Makel. Ohne vorbeizugehen, trifft er ihn. Hingehen bringt Gefahr. Man muss sich hüten. Handle nicht. Sei dauernd beharrlich.
Sechs auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Dichte Wolken, kein Regen von unserm westlichen Gebiet. Der Fürst schießt und trifft jenen in der Höhle.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Ohne ihn zu treffen, geht er an ihm vorbei. Der fliegende Vogel verlässt ihn. Unheil! Das bedeutet Unglück und Schaden.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Hsiâo Kwo
legge.judgment: Hsiâo Kwo indicates that (in the circumstances which it implies) there will be progress and attainment. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. (What the name denotes) may be done in small affairs, but not in great affairs. (It is like) the notes that come down from a bird on the wing;—to descend is better than to ascend. There will (in this way) be great good fortune.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) a hill and that for thunder above it form Hsiâo Kwo. The superior man, in accordance with this, in his conduct exceeds in humility, in mourning exceeds in sorrow, and in his expenditure exceeds in economy.
lines: The first line, divided, suggests (the idea of) a bird flying, (and ascending) till the issue is evil.

The second line, divided, shows its subject passing by his grandfather, and meeting with his grandmother; not attempting anything against his ruler, but meeting him as his minister. There will be no error.
The third line, undivided, shows its subject taking no extraordinary precautions against danger; and some in consequence finding opportunity to assail and injure him. There will be evil.

The fourth line, undivided, shows its subject falling into no error, but meeting (the exigency of his situation), without exceeding (in his natural course). If he go forward, there will be peril, and he must be cautious. There is no occasion to be using firmness perpetually.
The fifth line, divided, (suggests the idea) of dense clouds, but no rain, coming from our borders in the west. It also (shows) the prince shooting his arrow, and taking the bird in a cave.

The sixth line, divided, shows its subject not meeting the exigency of his situation), and exceeding (his proper course). (It suggests the idea of) a bird flying far aloft. There will be evil. The case is what is called one of calamity and self-produced injury.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 201-203 (Image: Appendix II, p. 344)

en.name: Preponderance of the Small
en.nameNote: 小過 is the small passing beyond, or a small passing; 陸德明: "義與大過同". The 彖: "小者過而亨也". In the lines 過 is "passing", going past: 過其祖, 弗過, 過之, as 28 上六's 過涉. Mawangdui writes 少過.
en.judgment: An offering. A favourable divination. Small matters may be done; great matters may not. A flying bird leaves its sound behind: not fitting upward, fitting downward. Very auspicious.
en.judgmentNote: "國之大事，在祀與戎", the great affairs of a state are offering and war (左傳, 578 BC). 38's judgment has "in small matters: auspicious". The songs have birds' cries low and high: "燕燕于飛，下上其音" (燕燕, Mao 28), of a girl going in marriage.
en.tradition: The small is yin; four yin outside, two yang within: the small passes beyond; so there is success, but one must keep to what is right. The second and fifth are soft and central, so small affairs may be done; the third and fourth are strong and out of place, so great affairs may not. The figure is a flying bird whose cry goes down and not up: one who meets this answer should go down, and it is very auspicious.
en.image: On the mountain there is thunder: Preponderance of the Small. So the noble one in his conduct goes beyond in reverence, in mourning goes beyond in grief, in spending goes beyond in frugality.
en.imageNote: A later layer; the shelf gives nothing for its words. Here 過 is excess, the wing's own sense. 侯果: the mountain is big and the thunder small, the small passing the great. 朱熹: all three are excesses of the small: one may go beyond in small things, not in great.

lines.text: A flying bird: with it, disaster.
lines.note: 朱熹 notes that in 郭璞's 洞林 (4th century AD, later) one who got this line sometimes brought on a plague of feathered creatures. 王弼: going up against the grain, it finds nowhere to set its foot: the disaster of the flying bird. The small image: nothing can be done.

lines.text: Passing his ancestor, meeting his ancestress. Not reaching his lord, meeting his servant. No blame.
lines.note: 祖 and 妣 receive the offering together: "烝畀祖妣，以洽百禮" (豐年, Mao 279); the Shang offered to ancestresses by name. 妣 is the dead mother (爾雅, 說文). 王弼: it passes but does not overstep, and goes only as far as the servant's place. 程頤 reads grandfather and grandmother.

lines.text: Not passing: guarding against it. Following: someone slays him. Disaster.
lines.note: 戕 is killing from outside: "凡自內虐其君曰弒，自外曰戕" (左傳, 591 BC), as 孔穎達 quotes. 或 is "someone". Shaughnessy pairs it with 上六. 王弼: strong and in place, it fails to guard in advance, then follows the small, and following is slain.

lines.text: No blame. Not passing: meeting it. Going on: danger; one must be on guard. Not to be used for a divination for the long run.
lines.note: 勿用 + noun is "not to be used for", as 11 上六's 勿用師; 永貞 is the divination for the long run. 王弼: out of place and unable to pass, it escapes blame; going on, it can only be on guard. 程頤: do not hold to it for ever. 朱熹 could not decide how 弗過遇之 reads.

lines.text: Dense clouds, no rain, from our western outskirts. The duke shoots a corded arrow and takes that one in the pit.
lines.note: The same words as 9's judgment: rain watched for and not come. 弋 is shooting with a corded arrow: "弋鳧與鴈" (女曰雞鳴, Mao 82). 穴 is 5's pit. 王弼: what is in the pit is hidden, small faults not yet grown, and the duke takes them. "That one" is left open.

lines.text: Not meeting: passing it. A flying bird is caught in it. Disaster. This is called calamity and blight.
lines.note: 離 is to be caught: "雉離于羅", the pheasant caught in the net (兔爰, Mao 70); the Chu slip writes 羅, the net. 是謂 is the formula of a reading (左傳, 545 BC). 王弼: passing with no limit, flying without stopping, the calamity is its own making. 程頤: 災 from heaven, 眚 from men.

essays.title: The flying bird
essays.text: The judgment's flying bird leaves its sound behind and is told down, not up; 初六 has the flying bird and disaster; 上六 the flying bird caught; 六五 the duke's corded arrow and something in a pit. The middle lines turn on passing and meeting and not reaching: passing the ancestor, meeting the ancestress; not passing, meeting it; not meeting, passing it. Shaughnessy sets 九三 and 上六 together as a pair of oracles.

readings.title: Passing, or exceeding?
readings.text: The lines' 過 is going past, against the wings' and the readers' excess (the Image; 孔穎達, 程頤; Wilhelm "Übergewicht", Legge "exceeding"). We print "passing" in the lines and "goes beyond" in the Image.

readings.title: Not passing: guarding against it
readings.text: Two acts side by side, with the base's pause, or one clause, "if one does not take precautions" (程頤, 朱熹, Wilhelm, Legge). We keep the pause.

readings.title: Not for the long run
readings.text: 勿用永貞 is "not to be used for a divination for the long run", against "do not hold firm for ever" (程頤; Wilhelm, Legge) and 荀爽's "do not stay long". 王弼's reading leans to ours.

readings.title: Caught, netted, or far off?
readings.text: Caught (兔爰; 孔穎達), netted (the Chu 羅; Shaughnessy), far off (程頤), leaving (Wilhelm). We print "caught in it".

pinyinTones.name: Xiǎo Guò
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng. lì zhēn. kě xiǎo shì, bù kě dà shì. fēi niǎo yí zhī yīn, bù yí shàng, yí xià, dà jí.

guò qí zǔ, yù qí bǐ. bù jí qí jūn, yù qí chén. wú jiù.
fú guò, fáng zhī, cóng huò qiāng zhī, xiōng.

pinyinNotes: 喪: sāng (mourning) in 喪過乎哀

hexagrams.image: 水在火上，既濟。君子以思患而豫防之。

lines.label: 初九
lines.text: 曳其輪，濡其尾，无咎。

lines.label: 六二
lines.text: 婦喪其茀，勿逐，七日得。

lines.label: 九三
lines.text: 高宗伐鬼方，三年克之，小人勿用。

lines.label: 六四
lines.text: 繻有衣袽，終日戒。

lines.label: 九五
lines.text: 東鄰殺牛，不如西鄰之禴祭，實受其福。

lines.label: 上六
lines.text: 濡其首，厲。

hexagrams.heading: 既濟
hexagrams.name: 既濟

wilhelm.name: Nach der Vollendung
wilhelm.judgment: Gelingen im Kleinen. Fördernd ist Beharrlichkeit. Im Anfang Heil, am Ende Wirren.
wilhelm.image: Das Wasser ist oberhalb des Feuers: das Bild des Zustands nach der Vollendung. So bedenkt der Edle das Unglück und rüstet sich im voraus dagegen.
lines: Anfangs eine Neun bedeutet: Er hemmt seine Räder. Er kommt mit dem Schwanz ins Wasser. Kein Makel.
Sechs auf zweitem Platz bedeutet: Die Frau verliert ihren Wagenvorhang. Lauf ihm nicht nach. Am siebenten Tag bekommst du ihn.
Neun auf drittem Platz bedeutet: Der hohe Ahn züchtigt das Teufelsland. Nach drei Jahren überwindet er es. Gemeine darf man nicht verwenden.
Sechs auf viertem Platz bedeutet: Die schönsten Kleider geben Lumpen. Den ganzen Tag sei vorsichtig.
Neun auf fünftem Platz bedeutet: Der Nachbar im Osten, der einen Ochsen schlachtet, bekommt nicht soviel wirkliches Glück wie der Nachbar im Westen mit seinem kleinen Opfer.
Oben eine Sechs bedeutet: Er kommt mit dem Haupt ins Wasser. Gefahr.
wilhelm.source: Richard Wilhelm, I Ging (Jena, 1924), as transcribed with modernised spelling at schuledesrades.org

legge.name: Kî Ȝî
legge.judgment: Kî Ȝî intimates progress and success in small matters. There will be advantage in being firm and correct. There has been good fortune in the beginning; there may be disorder in the end.
legge.image: (The trigram representing) fire and that for water above it form Kî Ȝî. The superior man, in accordance with this, thinks of evil (that may come), and beforehand guards against it.
lines: The first line, undivided, (shows its subject as a driver) who drags back his wheel, (or as a fox) which has wet his tail. There will be no error.
The second line, divided, (shows its subject as) a wife who has lost her (carriage-)screen. There is no occasion to go in pursuit of it. In seven days she will find it.
The third line, undivided, (suggests the case of) Kâo Ȝung who attacked the Demon region, but was three years in subduing it. Small men should not be employed (in such enterprises).
The fourth line, divided, shows its subject with rags provided against any leak (in his boat), and on his guard all day long.

The fifth line, undivided, shows its subject (as) the neighbour in the east who slaughters an ox (for his sacrifice); but this is not equal to the (small) spring sacrifice of the neighbour in the west, whose sincerity receives the blessing.
The topmost line, divided, shows its subject with (even) his head immersed. The position is perilous.
legge.source: James Legge, The Yi King (Sacred Books of the East 16, 1882), pp. 204-206 (Image: Appendix II, p. 345-346)

en.name: After Completion
en.nameNote: 既濟 is 既, already, done, and 濟, to cross a river: already across. 鄭玄: "既，已也，盡也。濟，度也". The 雜卦: "《既濟》、定也", settled. The name stands in no line; its pair 未濟 stands in 64 六三.
en.judgment: An offering, small. A favourable divination. At first, auspicious; in the end, disorder.
en.judgmentNote: A marriage song crosses water: "濟盈不濡軌", the crossing brimming, yet the axle-ends not wet; whoever crosses deep water must wet them (匏有苦葉, Mao 34, 鄭箋). In the Qin 歸藏 the king of Yin divines about his state under this figure, read "不吉". We cut 亨小 with 陸德明 and the 彖, against the base.
en.tradition: An affair already done; water and fire meet, each of use; every line in its right place: so, already across. 亨小 should be 小亨, a small success. This hexagram's reading and its six lines all carry a warning, as the time requires.
en.image: Water is above fire: After Completion. So the noble one thinks of misfortune and guards against it beforehand.
en.imageNote: A later layer. 孔穎達: water above fire is the pot on the stove, by which food is made. 王弼: already across, not forgetting not yet across. 程頤: realms that crossed and then fell into disorder did not think of misfortune and guard against it beforehand.

lines.text: Dragging its wheels, wetting its tail. No blame.
lines.note: A song has wheels cut and set down on the river's lip (伐檀, Mao 112), and a fox by the ford of the Qi (有狐, Mao 63). 程頤: a wheel dragged back does not go; a beast fording holds up its tail, and with it wet cannot cross: holding back at the start. Whose wheels and tail is left open.

lines.text: A wife loses her carriage screen. Do not chase it: in seven days, got.
lines.note: 茀 is the screen of a carriage, twice a lady's: "翟茀以朝" (碩人, Mao 57, 毛傳 "茀，蔽也"). 51 六二 has "勿逐，七日得" word for word. 王弼 reads a head ornament: a wife with a husband, wronged by another, and in seven days it comes back unchased. 程頤: seven is past the six places.

lines.text: Gaozong attacks the Gui lands; in three years he prevails over them. Small men: not to be used.
lines.note: Gaozong is Wu Ding of Shang (玄鳥, 毛傳); a song has him attack Jing-Chu (殷武, Mao 305). An early Western Zhou bronze records a war on the 鬼方: thousands of ears taken, captives, an offering in the Zhou temple, a divination, and gifts (集成 02839). 小人勿用 is 7 上六's.

lines.text: Wet: there are rags of clothing. The whole day, on guard.
lines.note: The Chu slip writes 需 here and for 上六's 濡; the 說文 quotes "需有衣䋈", worn wadding. 王弼, 程頤 and 朱熹 read 濡: rags to stop a leaking boat. 虞翻: soldiers' clothes worn to rags in the three years against the Gui lands. 戒 is on guard: "豈不日戒" (采薇, Mao 167).

lines.text: The eastern neighbour kills an ox: not as good as the western neighbour's yue offering. It is this that receives its blessing.
lines.note: The Zhou killed oxen at their great offerings (召誥, 洛誥). 禴 is a plain seasonal offering (天保, Mao 166); the Chu slip has 酌祭. In the 左傳, "黍稷非馨，明德惟馨" (655 BC). The 坊記 quotes the line with 寔, "this"; the Chu slip 是. The Zhou called themselves the west (牧誓).

lines.text: Wetting its head. Danger.
lines.note: 28 上六 has the crown of the head lost in wading across. In the marriage song 厲 is wading clothed in deep water (毛傳), recorded only; here it is the verdict "danger". 王弼: at the end of having crossed, it heads into not yet across, and the head goes in first.

essays.title: The crossing: wheel, tail and head
essays.text: The lines are a crossing of water: a wheel dragged and a tail wetted at the start, wet rags, the head wetted at the end. 64 has the same words, and the two share the campaign against the Gui lands. Between the crossing lines stand a lost carriage screen, a war and two offerings.

essays.title: The pair on a Western Zhou paddle
essays.text: A late Western Zhou pottery paddle found at Xiren has two columns of numbers, 一六一六一六 and 六一六一六一, which turned into lines give this hexagram and 64. A second paddle carries 師, 比, 小畜 and 履 in the received order. Shaughnessy takes them as "hard evidence that suggests that the received sequence of hexagrams was already available for quotation during the late Western Zhou dynasty".

readings.title: An offering, small, or a small offering?
readings.text: We cut 亨小 with 陸德明, the 彖, 王弼 and 程頤, against the base's 小利貞, and print "an offering, small": the small may qualify the offering (朱熹 小亨; Wilhelm, Legge) or name the small that receive it (the 彖, 王弼).

readings.title: Carriage screen, or head ornament?
readings.text: A carriage screen (the songs with 毛傳; 鄭玄, 程頤, 朱熹; Wilhelm, Legge); a head ornament (王弼, 馬融, 孔穎達); hair (虞翻); a knee-cover (荀爽). We print "her carriage screen".

readings.title: 繻: wet, or fine silk?
readings.text: Read 濡, wet (王弼, 程頤, 朱熹; the Chu slip's one graph with 上六); dyed silk (說文; Wilhelm's finest clothes turning to rags); a jacket (子夏傳 襦). We print the base's 繻, read "wet".

readings.title: This, or truly?
readings.text: 實 as 寔 or 是, "this" (the 坊記, the Chu slip, 爾雅, 毛傳), pointing to the western neighbour's offering; or "truly" (Wilhelm). We print "it is this that receives".

pinyinTones.name: Jì Jì
pinyinTones.judgment: hēng xiǎo, lì zhēn. chū jí, zhōng luàn.
pinyinTones.image: shuǐ zài huǒ shàng, jì jì. jūn zǐ yǐ sī huàn ér yù fáng zhī.
lines: yè qí lún, rú qí wěi, wú jiù.
fù sàng qí fú, wù zhú, qī rì dé.
Gāo Zōng fá Guǐ Fāng, sān nián kè zhī, xiǎo rén wù yòng.
rú yǒu yī rú, zhōng rì jiè.
dōng lín shā niú, bù rú xī lín zhī yuè jì, shí shòu qí fú.
